blocks.text: Optional and worth sending, because two of the activities work better when people arrive having already noticed something. Send it four days ahead and do not chase it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Take one implicit association test (15 minutes)
https://implicit.harvard.edu/implicit/selectatest.html
Your facilitator will tell you which one to take. Everyone in the session takes the same one, chosen for what is relevant where you work.

Two things worth knowing before you start. It is a timed keyboard task, so you need about fifteen quiet minutes and a computer rather than a phone. And the result is not a verdict on you as a person. It measures reaction time, it is noisy at the individual level, and the useful part is not the score but what you notice yourself thinking when you see it.
You will not be asked to share your result.
2. Answer three questions (10 minutes)
Write these down and bring them. The session uses them.

items: What personal experiences do I bring to this work? Not my qualifications. The things that actually shaped how I see this.
What was my reaction to the assessment result? Did I agree with it, argue with it, or explain it away?
Think of one recent decision at work. What did I bring to it that somebody else would not have?

blocks.text: If the result bothered you

That is common and it is not a sign that something is wrong. Most people who take one of these have a reaction, and the reaction itself is more informative than the number. Bring it. It is the most useful thing you could arrive with.
Facilitator note
Choose the test yourself and tell participants which one, rather than letting people take different ones. A room where everyone took a different assessment cannot compare anything.
Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. Every activity in the document supplies its own material for that reason.

[ALLISON AND LUBNA: the original pre-work also assigns a 7taps module, and points at an appendix for instructions on taking the test. Neither exists in the component files. Two comments on that bullet from May are still open asking for the 7taps link. If the module exists, please send the link and it will be added here and on the microlearning page. The appendix reference has been replaced with the short explanation above.]
Level: Level 1, low trust.
Group Size: Pairs or trios. Any total number.
Materials: None.
Purpose: Establish in the first ten minutes that this room talks about real things, using a question everybody can answer and nobody has to expose themselves to answer.
Set up (2 minutes)

Model it first, in about forty seconds, with something real and not too heavy. Then say this: “Think of a time when something you experienced changed how you saw a person, a group, or a situation. Not something you were told. Something that happened to you.”
Break into pairs or trios. Pairs go deeper, trios are safer for a group that does not know each other.
The activity (10 to 12 minutes)

items: Five to seven minutes for each person. Call the switch out loud rather than leaving groups to manage it, because one person will otherwise take the whole time.
The listener’s job is to ask one question and otherwise stay quiet. Say that explicitly.
Prompt at the halfway point of each turn: “What shifted for you in that moment?”

blocks.text: Share out and debrief (4 to 6 minutes)
Do not ask people to retell their partner’s story. Ask instead:

items: What did your stories have in common?
How many of these changes came from information, and how many from an experience?
How long ago was yours? Take a show of hands for more than ten years.

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Almost nobody names a change that came from being told something. They name experiences, and usually old ones. That is the finding: our views change slowly and through contact rather than through argument, which is worth remembering the next time we plan to persuade a community of something.
Facilitator notes

items: Your own example sets the depth. Go slightly deeper than you expect the room to and they will meet you. Go shallow and they will go shallower.
The show of hands at the end is the moment the point lands. Do not skip it.
Virtual: breakout rooms of two, twelve minutes, with a broadcast at the halfway mark.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Your own moment, in forty seconds: _____________________________________
Level: Level 1, low trust.
Group Size: Any, seated where people can see each other. Above about twenty, do it in table groups.
Materials: Card stock or folded paper, one per person, and a thick marker each. Thin pens do not work, the words have to be readable across a table.
Purpose: Get intention into the room in writing rather than in conversation, and let the group see its own themes before anyone has to speak.
Set up (2 minutes)

Say this: “Choose two to four words that capture how you want to show up in this work. Not how you want to be seen. How you want to show up. Write them large enough that somebody across the table can read them.”
The activity (5 minutes)

items: Two minutes of quiet writing. Protect the quiet; people will want to talk and the words get worse when they do.
Fold the card and stand it in front of them.
Everyone stands and walks the room for two minutes, reading, without discussing.

blocks.text: Debrief (3 minutes)

items: What themes did you notice?
Was there a word you saw that you wish you had written?
Was there anything you nearly wrote and did not?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The third question is the one that does the work, and it needs a pause after it. What people nearly wrote and edited out is usually the most honest thing in the room, and naming that out loud is a good early demonstration that this session can hold real answers.
Facilitator notes

items: Keep the cards up for the whole session. They are the cheapest callback you will get: at the close, ask people to look at their own card and say whether they did it.
Do not read anyone’s words out loud yourself. The walking is the share.
Virtual: a shared slide with a text box each, or everyone types four words into chat at the same moment on a count of three.

blocks.text: Level: Level 1, low trust.
Group Size: Any.
Materials: A spread of images, printed and laid on a table or projected in a grid. See the note below on how many.
Purpose: Let people say something about the skill before they have any vocabulary for it, using a picture as cover.
Set up (2 minutes)

Lay the images out or project them. Say this: “Look at these. Choose the one that best represents what self-discovery means to you. There is no right answer and I am not going to tell you what any of them mean.”
The activity (5 to 8 minutes)

items: Ninety seconds of quiet looking. People will want to choose fast; slow them down.
Survey which images were chosen. A show of hands per image is enough.
Take four or five people, not the whole room: what drew you to that one?

blocks.text: Debrief (3 to 4 minutes)

items: Did anyone choose the same image for opposite reasons?
What is missing from all of these?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Two people choosing the same image for opposite reasons is the point, and it happens most times you run this. It is a fast, harmless demonstration that people bring different meanings to the same thing, which is the entire skill in a form nobody has to be brave to participate in.
How many images

You need at least ten for a group of any size. Three or four does not produce differentiation and everybody ends up on the same one. Use abstract or ambiguous images rather than literal ones: doors, paths, mirrors, water, tools, roots, maps, windows, thresholds, hands. Avoid stock photos of people looking thoughtful, which produce identical answers.

[ALLISON AND LUBNA: the component file has three images embedded with no captions and no display instructions. Three is too few for this activity to work with a group over about eight. If you have a fuller image set, please send it. If not, this can be run from any ten ambiguous images and the facilitator can assemble their own.]
Facilitator notes

items: Print and lay out rather than project if you can. People choose differently when they can move around a table.
Virtual: a single slide with a numbered grid, and people type their number in chat.

blocks.text: Activity: The Identity Wheel
Level: Level 1, low trust.
Group Size: Individual work, then pairs or small groups.
Materials: The identity wheel worksheet on page 40, one per participant, and a pen.
Purpose: Separate the parts of identity a person thinks about constantly from the parts they have never had to, and notice that the split is not the same for everyone in the room.
Set up (3 minutes)

Hand out the worksheet. Say this: “This is not a test and nobody collects it. The interesting part is not which identities you have, it is which ones you spend attention on, because the ones you never think about are usually the ones that are working smoothly for you.”
Individual work (7 minutes)
Participants answer five questions on the worksheet:

items: Which identities do you think about most often?
Which do you think about least often?
Which of your own identities would you like to understand better?
Which have the strongest effect on how you see yourself?
Which have the greatest effect on how others see you?

blocks.text: Protect the quiet. Seven minutes feels long and people need about five of it before the useful answers arrive.
Pairs (6 minutes)
Three minutes each. The instruction is to talk about the gap between question 4 and question 5, not to read out all five answers.
Debrief (4 minutes)

items: Without naming which one: did anyone find that the identity they think about least is the one with the biggest effect on how others see them?
What is it like to hold an identity you never have to think about?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The two questions people find hardest are the least-often one and the gap between four and five. Name what the room found rather than explaining the concept: the things we do not have to think about are the things that are not costing us anything, and other people in this room are thinking about those same things daily.
Facilitator notes

items: This is Level 1 because nobody has to disclose. Keep it that way. If you ask people to name their answers out loud in the whole group, you have converted it into a Level 3 activity without telling anybody.
A participant who says none of this applies to me is giving you a real answer. Do not correct it. Ask what it is like to be able to say that.
Run this before Naming the Groups on page 27, never after. They cover the same ground at different depths.

blocks.text: Activity: Filibuster Topic
Level: Level 1, low trust.
Group Size: Pairs, then whole group.
Materials: None.
Purpose: Get at the difference between trained knowledge and lived knowledge using a question that is genuinely fun to answer, and then turn it toward whose expertise counts in a community meeting.
Set up (3 minutes)

Say this: “A filibuster topic is something you could talk about for an hour with no preparation. Not your job description. The thing your family teases you about knowing too much about. What is yours?”
Give your own first, and pick something genuinely unserious. The activity dies if the first example is professional.
Pairs (8 minutes)
Four minutes each. Alongside naming the topic, participants cover:

items: What are you really good at?
What do you enjoy learning about?
What could you teach someone else?
And the one that matters: where did that knowledge come from? Formal training, or living it?

blocks.text: Whole group (6 minutes)
Go round quickly, one topic each, no elaboration. It takes three minutes for a room of twenty and it is worth it, because the list is always more surprising than anyone expects.
Debrief (8 minutes)
This is where the activity earns its place. Do not cut it.

items: How many of the topics we just heard came from training, and how many from living something?
What does it actually mean to be an expert on something?
When is having a formal expert in the room useful? When is it an obstacle?
Think about the last community meeting you were in. Whose expertise counted, and who decided that?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Nearly every filibuster topic in the room will have come from lived experience rather than training, and the room notices that on its own. The move is to hold that next to how we run community meetings, where the person with the credential usually talks first and longest. Ask the last question and then stop talking.
Facilitator notes

items: The lightest activity in the document and one of the most effective, precisely because people relax into it. It is also the safest to run with a brand new group or a skeptical one.
Virtual: pairs in breakouts, then everyone types their topic in chat at once.

blocks.text: Activity: Gifts
Level: Level 2, some trust.
Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: The gifts capture sheet on page 41, one per participant, and a pen.

Purpose: Name what you actually bring, in four categories, before ever asking a community to do the same. The order matters: we use this on ourselves first because it is uncomfortable, and knowing that it is uncomfortable changes how you ask.
Framing (5 minutes)

This is the asset inventory from asset-based community development, from Kretzmann and McKnight, turned inward. In Asset Mapping you will use the same four categories on a community. Doing it on yourself first is not a warm-up, it is the point: you find out how hard it is to name your own gifts without either deflecting or performing.
Say this: “Four categories. At least two in each. Two is harder than it sounds and that difficulty is the exercise.”
The four categories
Gifts of the head, things you know. Local history or culture. Subjects you know something real about, from birds to housing policy to music.

Gifts of the heart, things you care about. Where your empathy actually goes. Children, older people, the environment, a particular neighborhood. Being good at keeping the peace or building a bridge between two people counts here.
Gifts of the hands, things you can do. Talents you are proficient enough at to teach. Cooking, gardening, fixing things, an instrument, a language.

Gifts of the conscience, what you stand for. Where you take a position. Usually connected to courage, integrity and commitment, and usually the hardest column to fill without sounding either grandiose or evasive.
Individual writing (10 minutes)
Quiet, on the capture sheet, at least two in each category. Say that nobody will collect it and that they choose what to share.
Pairs (16 minutes)
Eight minutes each. One person presents their four categories; the other listens, and has one job: notice which category the speaker moved through fastest and which they hesitated on.
At the end of each turn, the listener says only that: you moved quickly through hands and you hesitated on conscience. No interpretation.
Debrief (9 minutes)

items: Which category was hardest to fill? Take a show of hands for each.
What did your partner notice about where you hesitated?
What stopped you writing something down that you knew was true?
Now the turn outward: if this was hard for you, sitting with a colleague, what are we assuming when we ask a community to do it with a stranger holding a clipboard?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Conscience is the hardest category almost every time, and heart is the fastest. Name that. Then land the last question and let it sit, because it is the bridge from this skill into asset mapping and it is the only place in the set where somebody feels what we routinely ask of people.
Facilitator notes

items: People will try to fill hands with job skills. Push once: not what you are paid for, what you can do.
Ten minutes of writing feels long and is right. The second half is where the honest entries appear.
This is the activity most likely to run over. It is also the one most worth running over.

blocks.text: Activity: Style Under Stress
Level: Level 2, some trust.
Group Size: Individual, then pairs.
Materials: A device with internet for each participant. Check this before you plan the session.
Purpose: Find out what you actually do when a conversation gets hard, using an instrument rather than your own memory of yourself, which is unreliable in a predictable direction.
Before the session

The assessment is the Style Under Stress assessment from Crucial Learning, free at https://cruciallearning.com/assessments/free/style-under-stress-assessment/. Take it yourself first. It asks you to hold one specific relationship and situation in mind while you answer, which is worth telling people in advance so they choose deliberately rather than defaulting to whoever annoyed them most recently.
It asks for an email address. Say so up front rather than letting people discover it.
Set up (4 minutes)

Say this: “Pick one relationship where conversations get difficult. A colleague, a partner organization, someone on your board. Hold that person in mind for the whole thing. And you will not be asked to share your score.”
Taking it (12 minutes)
Individually. Thirty true or false items. Some people finish in eight minutes and some take fifteen; give the full twelve and let the fast ones read their results.
Pairs (8 minutes)
Four minutes each. The rule, said out loud: you do not have to say what your results were. Talk about these instead.

items: What was your first reaction to the score? Agreement, argument, or explaining it away?
What does it do to you to see this as a number?
Is there someone who would recognize this description of you?

blocks.text: Debrief (6 minutes)

items: How many of you argued with your result? Hands up.
For those who argued: what specifically did you object to?
What do you do in the first ten seconds when a conversation turns?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Most of a room argues with the result, and the arguing is the finding rather than a problem with the instrument. Under pressure people either move toward silence or toward force, and almost everybody believes they do neither. The useful question is not whether the score is accurate; it is whether anybody who works with you would be surprised by it.
Facilitator notes

items: The privacy provision is what makes this Level 2 rather than Level 3. Protect it. If you ask people to report their scores, you have changed the activity.
Have your own result ready and be willing to say it. You are asking for something you should be prepared to give.
If the room has no reliable internet, this activity does not run. There is no offline version, and substituting a made-up questionnaire is worse than skipping it.

blocks.text: Activity: Perceptions of Power
Level: Level 3, established trust.
Group Size: 10 to 25. Below ten the effect does not appear.
Materials: A deck of playing cards, masking tape or safety pins, and open floor space.
Purpose: Let people feel what it is like to be treated according to a status they cannot see and did not choose, in twenty minutes, without anyone having to disclose anything about their real life.
Set up (5 minutes)
Deal one card to each person, face down. They must not look at it. Tape it to their back with the face outward so everyone else can see it.

Say this: “In a moment you are going to move around the room as if at a work reception. Everyone can see everyone else’s card except their own. Treat people according to their rank: ace is highest, two is lowest. Do not tell anyone their card, and do not act it out so broadly that it becomes a pantomime. Small differences in how much attention you give somebody are enough.”

Offer the seated variant now rather than after: anyone who prefers not to move can stay seated with their card visible and people will come to them. Say it as a normal option, not as an accommodation.
The mingle (10 minutes)
Let it run. It is loud and slightly chaotic and that is correct. Circulate and watch faces rather than listening to content.
The line up (3 minutes)
Stop it. Say: “Without speaking, line up in what you believe your rank order is. Highest at that end.”
Let them sort themselves in silence. Then have everyone look at their own card.
Debrief (12 minutes)
This is the majority of the activity by value. Do not compress it.

items: How did you work out roughly where you were?
What specifically did people do that told you? Push for behavior rather than feeling: who turned toward you, who ended the conversation, who looked over your shoulder.
How did it feel to be treated as high status? As low?
Did anyone change how they behaved once they thought they knew their own rank?
Where in your real work does something like this operate?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

People place themselves accurately within a rank or two almost every time, within ten minutes, with no information other than how they were treated. That is the finding, and it is worth saying plainly: everybody in this room can read status that fast, which means the people we work with can read ours. The last question is where it lands for community work, and it deserves five of the twelve minutes.
Facilitator notes

items: Ace high, and say so. Face cards rank below the ace and above the ten in the usual way. Somebody will ask.

Use only part of the deck so the range is clear: for a group of fifteen, deal a spread from twos to aces rather than fifteen random cards, or you will get a cluster of middle ranks and a muddy result.
Watch the person holding the two. They will know quickly and it is not a pleasant ten minutes. Check in with them first at the break.
This does not work virtually. Appendix B has the alternative.

blocks.text: Activity: Counting the Advantages
Level: Level 3, established trust. Read the note below before you choose this.
Group Size: Any, seated. Nobody moves.
Materials: The tally sheet on page ?, one per participant, and a pen. Participants keep their sheets.
Purpose: Make the accumulation of unearned advantage countable, privately, so that the conversation afterward is about the pattern rather than about any individual in the room.
Read this before you choose this activity

This is the highest-risk activity in the document. In its original and better-known form, participants physically step forward and back, which makes each person’s position visible to the whole room. That form has been widely retired across the field over the last decade, because it asks people who are already marginalized to perform their disadvantage in front of colleagues, for the benefit of colleagues who are not.
The version here keeps the tally private throughout. Nobody moves, nobody’s number is visible, and sharing at the end is optional. That mitigation is real and it is not complete.

[ALLISON AND LUBNA: this activity was rated Level 2 in the component file, and by the file’s own definition of Level 3 it is a Level 3 activity. It has been re-rated here. More importantly, whether the Red Cross runs an exercise of this kind at all is a decision that should be made deliberately at leadership level rather than inherited, and a Perceptions of Power session on page 23 reaches much of the same ground at lower risk. Please confirm whether this stays in.]
Set up (5 minutes)
Set the ground rules from page 10 if you have not already, and add two more for this activity specifically:

items: Your number is yours. You will not be asked for it and you should not ask anybody else for theirs.
You can stop at any point, put the pen down, and stay in the room. That is a complete way to participate.

blocks.text: Then say this: “I am going to read a series of statements. If one applies to you, add or subtract a point on your own sheet. Start at zero. Nobody sees your sheet.”
The statements (12 minutes)
Read them steadily, with a beat between each. Do not add commentary. The full set is on the tally sheet, page ?, so participants can follow along.
Read all of the adding statements first, then all of the removing statements. Mixing them makes the tally hard to keep and the pattern harder to see.
Sitting with it (2 minutes)
Two minutes of silence before any discussion. Say: “Do not talk yet. Just look at your number.”
This pause is the most important instruction on the page. A room that goes straight from the last statement into conversation processes nothing.
Debrief (16 minutes)
Open with the safest question and work outward. Never start by asking for numbers.

items: What happened for you during that? Anything surprise you?
Was there a statement you had to think about? What made it hard to place?
Was there anything on the list you had never considered as an advantage or a disadvantage?
What is it like to know that everybody in this room now holds a number and none of us knows anybody else’s?
How does this show up in a community meeting where we are the organization with the resources?

blocks.text: Sharing numbers is optional and should be offered rather than requested: “If anyone wants to say their number out loud, you can. You do not have to, and it is fine if nobody does.”
Facilitator synthesis

The finding is not the spread of numbers. It is that most people found several items they had never counted in either direction, and that the list is made of ordinary things nobody chose. Say that, and then move to the last question, because the point of the activity is not what it reveals about the room, it is what it changes about how the room walks into a neighborhood.
Facilitator notes

items: Do not run this with a group who met this morning, and do not run it as the last thing before people leave. It needs an established room and it needs twenty minutes of session after it.
If somebody leaves during it, let them. Follow up privately at the break, not in the room.
Have a colleague in the room if you can. This is the one activity in the document worth co-facilitating.
Do not run it virtually.

blocks.text: Activity: Naming the Groups
Level: Level 3, established trust.
Group Size: Individual, then pairs or trios.
Materials: The social identity groups reference on page 43, one per participant.
Purpose: The Identity Wheel asks which identities you notice. This one asks which are claimed by you and which are assigned to you by other people, and what the gap between those two costs.
How this differs from the Identity Wheel

The two activities look similar and are not. The wheel is a private inventory at Level 1. This one names social identity groups explicitly, distinguishes self-claimed from ascribed identity, and uses the words marginalized and privileged out loud. That is what makes it Level 3, and it is why it should not be run with a group that has not already done Level 1 and Level 2 work together.
Run the wheel first, ideally in an earlier session. Never run both in the same hour.
Framing (5 minutes)

Say this, or something close to it in your own words: “Social identity groups are based on physical, social and mental characteristics. Some are obvious and some are not. Many are claimed by us and many are assigned to us by other people, and those two lists are not the same. Race is often both. Sexual orientation, religion and disability are often claimed and not announced.”

Then: “The terms on this sheet are examples, not a required vocabulary. Use your own words. Some of these terms are contested and you may disagree with them; disagreeing with a label is a legitimate thing to say out loud here.”
Individual work (7 minutes)
Working from the reference sheet, each person writes down two lists: the memberships they claim, and the ones they believe are ascribed to them by others.
Pairs or trios (8 minutes)
The conversation is about the gap, not the lists. Two questions:

items: Where do the two lists differ, and what does that difference cost you or spare you?
Which of these do you never have to think about at work?

blocks.text: Debrief (5 minutes)

items: Without naming the identity: did anyone find something ascribed to them that they do not claim?
What is it like to be described by a word you would not have chosen?
Where does that happen to the communities we work with?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The last question is the whole reason this activity is in a community mobilization curriculum rather than a diversity training. We assign identities to communities constantly, in our data, our program names and our funding applications, using words those communities did not choose. Ask it, and let the room make the connection rather than making it for them.
Facilitator notes

items: The reference sheet lists example terms and some of them are dated. Say so at the start rather than letting a participant discover it and lose confidence in the session. See the note on page 43.
Do not go round the room. Invitation only, every time.
This activity needs a closing. Use the five-minute close from page 10 without exception.

blocks.text: Field Activities

Three activities that use a live decision rather than a reflection. They are twenty minutes each, they work as a set or on their own, and they are the bridge from what a person notices about themselves to what they actually do on a Tuesday.
Use these when a group has done the reflective work and is asking, reasonably, what any of it changes.
Make the Call (20 minutes)
What it is. Rapid prioritization under pressure, run fast enough that people use their defaults rather than their principles.

items: Present a real chapter decision with a genuine tradeoff and a short clock: four minutes to decide, in groups of three.
Stop them at four minutes whether or not they are finished. The unfinished ones are more useful.
Then, individually, five minutes of writing: what did you argue for, and what does that tell you about what you weight?
Debrief eight minutes: who did your decision favor? Who was not represented in the room while you made it? What would have changed if they had been?

blocks.text: Why it works. Speed is the mechanism. Given fifteen minutes people produce their stated values; given four they produce their actual ones.
Step In, Step Back (20 minutes)
What it is. A structured conversation where participants track their own airtime and act on it in real time.

items: Give the group a real question worth ten minutes of discussion.
Each person privately tallies every time they speak.
At five minutes, call a pause. Anyone above three marks steps back for the rest. Anyone at zero or one is invited to step in.
Debrief eight minutes: what did you notice about your own count? What happened to the conversation after the pause? Who normally does the stepping back, and is it always the same people?

blocks.text: Why it works. The count is not a metaphor. People consistently estimate their own airtime wrongly and in a predictable direction, and a tally settles it without anyone having to be told.
The Missing Voice (20 minutes)
What it is. A planning conversation with a deliberate empty chair.

items: Take a real piece of work. Before discussing it, the group names one group of people affected by it who are not in the room, and places an empty chair for them.
Discuss the work for ten minutes. Anyone may pause the conversation at any point and speak from the chair.
Debrief eight minutes: how often was the chair used? What was said from it that nobody said otherwise? What would it take to have that person actually here next time?

blocks.text: Why it works. It gives permission. People often know whose perspective is missing and have no legitimate way to raise it mid-meeting; the chair is that way.
Facilitator notes

items: All three need a real decision or a real piece of work. Invented scenarios do not produce the defaults, which is the entire point.
The last question in each debrief is the one that changes anything. Protect the time for it.
The Missing Voice is the one to use if you only use one, and it is the easiest to keep using after the session ends.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
The real decision you will use for Make the Call: ______________________
The question you will use for Step In, Step Back: _______________________
Level: Levels 1 through 3 in sequence. The design is the ramp.
Group Size: 6 to 16. Above sixteen, every question goes to pairs first.
Materials: Chairs in a circle. No slides, no handout of the questions.
Purpose: An hour in which nobody is taught anything. The questions are the content and the facilitator’s discipline is not answering them.
The rule that makes this work

Better to explore one question deeply than to rush through several. Choose one or two per level and hold the rest in reserve. A session that gets through six questions well is far better than one that covers all nineteen.
Session flow

items: 0 to 8 minutes: Opening and agreements.
8 to 20 minutes: Entry. Low barrier, observational.
20 to 35 minutes: Understanding self in context.
35 to 50 minutes: Critical reflection.
50 to 58 minutes: Deep practice and systems awareness.
58 to 60 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: The last block is deliberately short. Reaching it at all is the achievement, and eight minutes of the fourth level lands better than twenty minutes of it reached too early.
Opening (8 minutes)
Set the ground rules from page 10. All five, read rather than paraphrased.

Then say this: “This will not be a normal session. I am not going to present anything and I am mostly not going to answer. I am going to ask questions and we are going to think together. Silence is fine. Some of this will not resolve today, and that is fine too.”
Then model: answer the first entry question yourself, in under a minute, honestly.
Level 1, entry (12 minutes)
Low barrier, observational, helps people ease in. Choose one or two.

items: What personal experiences do I bring to this work?
What stories about community have shaped how I see need, or resilience?
How does my upbringing or my training influence how I define success?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Notice how many of us answered with something from outside work. That is not a digression, it is the material.
Level 2, understanding self in context (15 minutes)
Builds awareness of identity, lens, and how others may experience you.

items: Who am I in this work?
How do my race, gender, age, class, ability and education shape how I move through the world?
In what ways might I be seen as an outsider, an authority figure, or an ally?
What parts of my identity do I struggle with, or want to understand better?

blocks.text: Synthesis. The third question is the one to spend time on. How we are seen and how we intend to be seen are different things, and only one of them is under our control.
Level 3, critical reflection (15 minutes)
Higher vulnerability. Examines reactions, bias, and daily practice.

items: When do I rely on training, and when do I let lived wisdom lead?
How do I make space for people with different kinds of knowledge?
How often do I reflect on my impact rather than my intent?
What spaces or people help me stay grounded and accountable?
How do I react when I am challenged or called in? Where does that come from?

blocks.text: Synthesis. The last question is the most useful in the whole guide and the most uncomfortable. Ask it late, and do not rescue the silence after it.
Level 4, deep practice and systems awareness (8 minutes)
Requires systems thinking, humility and ongoing commitment. Pick one. You will not get through more.

items: Where do I hold power and how do I use it? Where do I lack power, and how does that feel?
How might I unintentionally benefit from systems of inequity?
What does it look like to use power responsibly, to share it, or to step back?
What does helping mean in this context, and would the community agree?
Can I sit with tension and not rush to resolution?
Am I prepared to slow down and let a community set the agenda?
How will I keep growing through this?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Do not attempt to conclude this level. Name that it is unfinished and that being able to leave it unfinished is itself part of the skill.
The three follow-up probes
These are most of the facilitation. Use them constantly.

items: Can you say more about that?
What shaped that perspective?
How does that show up in your work?

blocks.text: Close (2 minutes)
One word each on how they are leaving, going round without comment. Then: “One thing you are taking with you. One sentence, no explanation.” Then stop.
Troubleshooting
If nobody responds. Thirty seconds of announced silence, then send it to pairs for ninety seconds before opening it back up. Do not fill it yourself.
If answers stay abstract. Ask for the specific moment. What was actually said, who was in the room, what week was this.
If one person dominates. Change the format rather than confronting the person. Move to pairs, then take answers from the far side of the circle first.

If somebody challenges the premise. Take it seriously and out loud. Ask what they would want the session to be about instead. A challenged premise that gets a real answer usually converts; a deflected one poisons the hour.
If somebody discloses something heavy. Thank them, reflect one sentence, do not probe, move on gently. Check in at the break, privately.
If the room wants tools. Say the tools are in the rest of the document and this hour is for something else. Then ask what they would do differently tomorrow with no new tool at all.
Facilitator notes

items: The hardest discipline is not answering. You will know what you think about every one of these questions.
Do not hand out the questions. A room that can read ahead prepares answers, and prepared answers are the thing this format exists to avoid.
If you have fifty minutes rather than sixty, cut Level 4 and close properly. Never cut the close.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
The six questions you will actually ask: __________________________________
Your own answer to the opening question: _________________________________
What you will do if the room challenges the premise: _____________________
Session Formats
Four written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document.
20 minutes. One Level 1 activity and a close. Enough to introduce the idea and not enough to open anything you cannot close.
1 hour. An opener, one activity, a real debrief.
2 hours. Two or three activities across two levels, with a break in the middle.
4 hours. Activities from all three levels, the Socratic hour, and a field activity to land it.
The selection rules

items: Always start at Level 1, whatever the length and however well the group knows each other.
Never end on a Level 3 activity. Leave twenty minutes of session after one.
Depth over coverage. Two activities done properly beat four rushed, and this is the one skill where a rushed activity is worse than no activity.
A session can be entirely Level 1 and be worth running.

blocks.text: A note on the arithmetic

The shortest activity here is twenty minutes, so a twenty-minute session runs one activity and nothing else, including no opener. The agendas below account for opening, transitions, break and close, which is why they hold fewer activities than a straight time division would suggest.
What every format shares

items: Ground rules at the start of anything over twenty minutes.
The facilitator models first, every time.
A close that names one concrete thing that happens next.

blocks.text: Purpose: Establish that the way you see this work is not the only way to see it. One idea, felt rather than explained.
Materials: None.
Agenda

items: 3 minutes: Framing.
15 minutes: The Moment It Shifted.
2 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: Framing (3 minutes)

Say this: “Before you say anything in a community meeting, the room has already read your title, your organization, and whether you look like the people who usually show up and then leave. You cannot put that down. What you can do is know what it is.”
Then one line about what this session is not: not therapy, not a personality test, and nobody has to disclose anything.
The Moment It Shifted (15 minutes)
Page 13. Full version including the show of hands at the end, which is where the point lands.
Close (2 minutes)
One question, answered by three or four people: “What is one thing you will notice about yourself this week?” Then stop.
Facilitator notes

items: Twenty minutes buys one felt experience. Do not add a second activity and do not introduce the five elements.
Do not open anything you cannot close in two minutes. This is the reason the format is Level 1 only.

blocks.text: Purpose: Two elements, one real conversation each, and a commitment. The workhorse session.
Materials: Identity wheel worksheets, pens.
Agenda

items: 5 minutes: Opening and ground rules.
10 minutes: Four Words.
20 minutes: The Identity Wheel.
20 minutes: Filibuster Topic.
5 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: Opening and ground rules (5 minutes)
Page 10, all five agreements. Then the framing from the twenty-minute session.
Four Words (10 minutes)
Page 14. Keep the cards up for the whole session.
The Identity Wheel (20 minutes)
Page 16. Individual work, pairs, debrief. Level 1 throughout, nobody discloses to the room.
Filibuster Topic (20 minutes)
Page 18, run slightly compressed: three minutes each in pairs, a quick whole-group round, and six minutes of debrief. Protect the last debrief question about whose expertise counts.
Close (5 minutes)
Ask everyone to look at their own card from Four Words and answer one question out loud: “Did you show up the way you wrote down?” Then one concrete thing that happens next.
Facilitator notes

items: Two Level 1 activities in an hour is deliberate. This session should leave people wanting the next one rather than needing recovery from this one.
If the room is senior and skeptical, swap the order: Filibuster first, because it is fun, then the wheel.

blocks.text: Purpose: Move a group from Level 1 to Level 2 and back down safely, covering three elements and landing on something they will do.
Materials: Identity wheel worksheets, gifts capture sheets, card stock and markers, pens.
Agenda

items: 8 minutes: Opening and ground rules.
10 minutes: Four Words.
20 minutes: The Identity Wheel.
10 minutes: Break.
40 minutes: Gifts.
20 minutes: The Missing Voice.
12 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: Opening and ground rules (8 minutes)
Page 10. Take the extra three minutes over the one-hour version, because this session goes to Level 2 and the agreements have to be real before it does.
Four Words and the Identity Wheel (30 minutes)
Pages 14 and 16, as written.
Break (10 minutes)
Take it before Gifts rather than after. The room needs to arrive at the Level 2 activity settled rather than tired.
Gifts (40 minutes)
Page 19. Full version including the closing question about what we ask of communities, which is the hinge of the whole session.
The Missing Voice (20 minutes)
Page 29. This is what brings the session back down and turns it into practice. Use a real piece of work the group holds.
Close (12 minutes)
One word each on how they are leaving. Then in pairs, five minutes: one thing you will do differently and when. Then take the dates out loud around the room.
Facilitator notes

items: The order matters more than the content here. Level 1, Level 1, break, Level 2, practice, close. Do not reorder it to fit an activity you like better.
Gifts will run over. Let it, and take the time from the close only if you can still do the pairs.

blocks.text: Purpose: The only format that reaches Level 3 safely, because it is the only one with enough time before and after to hold it.
Prerequisite: A group that has worked together before, or a group that has done the one-hour session at least a few weeks earlier. Do not run this as a first exposure.
Materials: Everything. Worksheets, capture sheets, card stock, markers, a deck of playing cards, tape.
Agenda

items: 10 minutes: Opening and ground rules.
15 minutes: The Moment It Shifted.
20 minutes: The Identity Wheel.
15 minutes: Break.
40 minutes: Gifts.
60 minutes: Socratic discussion.
15 minutes: Break.
30 minutes: Perceptions of Power.
20 minutes: Step In, Step Back.
15 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: The shape of the day

Up through Level 1, into Level 2, an hour of dialogue at the centre, then the single Level 3 activity, then back down into practice and a proper close. The two breaks are placed where the level changes, which is deliberate.
Hour 1: opening and Level 1
Pages 10, 13 and 16. Do not compress the ground rules. This is the day that needs them.
Hour 2: Gifts and the start of the Socratic
Page 19 at full length, then straight into the Socratic hour on page 31. The transition works because Gifts has already got people speaking in the first person about themselves.
Hour 3: the Socratic hour completes, then break
Reaching Level 4 of the Socratic guide at all is the achievement. Do not rush the earlier levels to get there.
Hour 4: Level 3, then land it
Perceptions of Power on page 23, then Step In, Step Back on page 29, then the fifteen-minute close.

The last two are in that order for a reason. The Level 3 activity opens something; the field activity converts it into a behavior; the close names what happens next. Ending on the Level 3 activity would send people home mid-experience.
If you only have three hours
Cut the Socratic hour, not the Level 3 activity or the close. A three-hour day of activities with a proper landing is better than a four-hour day that runs out of time at the end.
Facilitator notes

items: Co-facilitate this if you possibly can. One person runs the room and one person watches faces.
Two breaks, where they are marked.
Do not substitute Counting the Advantages for Perceptions of Power without reading page 25 in full first.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Who is co-facilitating, and which sections: ____________________________
Which Level 3 activity you are running, and why: _______________________
What happens after this session, and who owns it: ______________________
Handout: The Identity Wheel
One per participant. Nobody collects it.
The categories
These are prompts rather than a fixed list. Use your own words, and add anything missing.

Race · Ethnicity · Gender · Sex · Sexual orientation · Age · Ability · Religion or spiritual practice · Social class · Education · Nation of origin · Language · Family role · Where you grew up · Where you live now · Profession
1. Which of these do you think about most often?
2. Which do you think about least often?
3. Which would you like to understand better?
4. Which have the strongest effect on how you see yourself?
5. Which have the greatest effect on how others see you?
The gap
Look at your answers to 4 and 5. Where they differ is the interesting part. Write one sentence about it:

[ALLISON AND LUBNA: the component file embeds the Loden and Rosener diversity wheel as an image, with the attribution baked into the graphic and no citation in the text. The wheel is reproduced here as a written list so it can be filled in, since the image version has no space to write. If you would like the graphic reinstated alongside this, send a clean copy and the citation and both will go in.]
Handout: Gifts
At least two in each. Two is harder than it sounds, and the difficulty is the exercise. Nobody collects this.
Gifts of the head: things you know
Local history or culture. Subjects you know something real about.
Gifts of the heart: things you care about
Where your empathy actually goes. Keeping the peace and building bridges count here.
Gifts of the hands: things you can do
Talents you are proficient enough at to teach somebody else. Not what you are paid for.
Gifts of the conscience: what you stand for
Where you take a position. Usually connected to courage, integrity and commitment.
Afterward
What did you nearly write down and then leave out? ____________________
The four categories come from Kretzmann and McKnight’s asset-based community development work. You will use them again on a community in the Asset Mapping skill.
Handout: Counting the Advantages
Your sheet. Nobody sees it and you will not be asked for your number. Start at zero, and you can stop at any point and stay in the room.
Add a point

items: One or both of your parents graduated from college.
You attended a private school or a summer camp growing up.
You were told by your parents that you were beautiful, smart, or successful.
You knew as a child that you were expected to go to college.
You have immediate family members in professions that require a degree.
You studied the history and culture of your own ancestors at school.
Your family never had to move for financial reasons.
You almost always see people of your race, orientation, religion and class represented positively in the media.
If you walked into a business and asked for the person in charge, you would expect to see someone of your race.
School and work are not in session during the holidays you celebrate.
You almost always feel comfortable with people knowing your sexual orientation.
You feel certain you will not be followed or watched while shopping.
Your sex or race is widely represented in the US Congress.

blocks.text: Remove a point

items: You will be the first in your immediate family to graduate from college.
You started school speaking a language other than English.
You have been the only person of your race or ethnicity in a classroom or workplace.
You grew up in an economically disadvantaged or single-parent home.
You have had to sacrifice your own plans for the responsibility of others.
You or someone you know has been mistrusted or accused without evidence.
You have been embarrassed by your clothes, house or car and wished to change them to avoid being judged.
You have hesitated to speak to avoid being ridiculed for your accent or speech.
You have skipped a meal or left one hungry because there was not enough money for food.
Someone in your immediate family has served time in prison.
Someone in your immediate family has been addicted to drugs or alcohol.
You have been called names about your race, class, gender, orientation or disability and felt uncomfortable.
You have difficulty finding hair products, cosmetics for your skin tone, or a barber or stylist where you live.

blocks.text: Afterward, for you only
Total: ______ A statement you had to think about, or never counted either way:
Where does this show up when we walk into a neighborhood as the organization with the resources? _________________________________________________
Handout: Social Identity Groups
Reference for the Naming the Groups activity. These are examples, not a required vocabulary. Use your own words, and say so if a term here is one you would not choose.
Two definitions
Marginalized group. Social identity groups that are disenfranchised and exploited.
Privileged group. Social identity groups that hold unearned privilege in society.
Categories and example terms
Gender. Woman, man, non-binary, transgender, genderqueer, agender.
Sex. Female, male, intersex.
Race. Asian, Pacific Islander, Native American, Latino or Latina, Black, White, biracial or multiracial.
Ethnicity. Irish, Chinese, Puerto Rican, Italian, Mohawk, Jewish, Guatemalan, Lebanese, European American, and many more.
Sexual orientation. Lesbian, gay, bisexual, pansexual, asexual, heterosexual, queer, questioning.
Religion, spirituality or meaning. Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist, Jewish, Christian, Sikh, Pagan, agnostic, atheist, secular humanist.
Social class. Poor, working class, lower middle class, upper middle class, owning class.
Age. Child, young adult, middle-aged adult, older adult.
Ability and disability. People with disabilities, whether cognitive, physical, sensory or emotional. Temporarily able-bodied. Temporarily disabled.
Nation of origin or citizenship. Any.
Tribal or Indigenous affiliation. Mohawk, Navajo, Aboriginal, and many more.
Body size or type. Terms here are contested and people use very different words for themselves. Use your own.
Two lists
Memberships you believe are ascribed to you by others: ________________
The gap
Where do the two lists differ, and what does that difference cost you, or spare you?
Which of these do you never have to think about at work? ______________

[ALLISON AND LUBNA: the terminology table in the component file is uncredited, appears to come from a university handout from around the mid 2010s, and several of its terms have dated. The gender row listed post-gender and omitted non-binary; two orientation terms were nonstandard. The list above is a light revision. It is a live area and it will date again, so it is worth a review before this goes anywhere Red Cross branded. If there is a preferred national vocabulary, send it and this page will use it instead.]
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. Each entry says what it is for.
Start here

Project Implicit, Harvard University. The implicit association tests used in the pre-work. Free, well documented, and worth reading the caveats page as well as taking a test. https://implicit.harvard.edu/

Crucial Learning, Style Under Stress assessment. The instrument used in the comfort in discomfort activity. Free, takes about ten minutes. https://cruciallearning.com/assessments/free/style-under-stress-assessment/
On positionality and identity
Loden, M. and Rosener, J. (1991). Workforce America. Business One Irwin. The source of the diversity wheel, distinguishing primary and secondary dimensions of identity.

Tatum, B. D. (2017). Why Are All the Black Kids Sitting Together in the Cafeteria? Basic Books. On identity development and why some identities are constantly salient and others are invisible to the person holding them. The chapter on the complexity of identity is the one to read.
On reflective practice
Schon, D. (1983). The Reflective Practitioner. Basic Books. The distinction between reflection in action and reflection on action, which is what the two-minute debrief is built on.

Kegan, R. and Lahey, L. (2009). Immunity to Change. Harvard Business Review Press. Why people who genuinely want to change their behavior reliably do not, and what to do about it. The most practically useful book on this list.
On power and how it operates

McIntosh, P. (1989). White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack. The short essay that produced the whole genre of advantage-counting exercises, including the one in this document. Worth reading in the original rather than in summary.

Kretzmann, J. P. and McKnight, J. L. (1993). Building Communities from the Inside Out. ACTA Publications. The source of the gifts of head, heart, hands and conscience. Used here on ourselves and in Asset Mapping on a community.
Red Cross learning

[ALLISON AND LUBNA: the component file has a list of internal and external resources. Please confirm which of the internal ones are current, and send the 7taps link if the module exists, and both will be added here.]
If you read one thing
The McIntosh essay. Twenty minutes, written in 1989, and it is still the clearest account of why an advantage is hardest to see from inside it.
Optional but genuinely useful, because two activities in the session work best when the participant arrives with a real conversation in mind. Send it three days ahead and do not chase it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Read one thing (10 minutes)
The Leading Change Network guide to the one-to-one meeting. It is short.
https://leadingchangenetwork.org/

What to notice: a one-to-one is not networking and it is not data gathering. It is a specific tool for understanding what makes someone tick. Pay attention to the exploration phase, where the questions are about a person’s story and values rather than their role.
Why it matters: it moves a meeting from being a task to being a leadership act. That is a bigger shift than it sounds.
2. Watch one thing (5 minutes)
A short video on the difference between fixing a problem and connecting with a person.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Evwgu369Jw
What to notice: staying with the emotion instead of moving past it. That single behavior does more for trust than any amount of expertise.
3. Prepare one conversation (5 minutes)
Think of a community partner you struggle to connect with, or a conversation coming up in the next month that matters. Answer these and bring your answers. The session uses them.
What is my intention for this conversation? Am I trying to learn or to influence? Answer honestly, and notice that influence is not a shameful answer, it is just a different conversation.
Who is this person, and what do I actually want to learn about what matters to them?
Write one opening line. One sentence that states a relational purpose out loud.
Write one open-ended question, starting with how or why.
One question to sit with
If you were forbidden from mentioning Red Cross programs or data for the first twenty minutes of your next meeting, what would you ask instead?
Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. The Simple Flow Dry Run begins with five minutes of individual prep for exactly that reason, and participants who did the pre-work simply use those five minutes to sharpen what they brought.
The opening line and the open-ended question are the two artifacts that get used later. If you are short on time and can only ask for one thing, ask for those.

title: King or Queen for the Day

blocks.text: Group Size: Any. Works from six people to sixty.
Materials: None, or a paper crown if you have one and the room will take it.
Purpose: Break the expectation of a boring meeting in the first ninety seconds, and put level 1 of the question ramp in the room where everyone can feel it.
Set up (1 minute)
Say this: “We are going to start a little differently. No long introductions. This is fast, slightly competitive, and low pressure. Just jump in, do not overthink it. And yes, there may be a winner.”
The activity (4 to 7 minutes)
Ask a rapid-fire question from the level 1 bank. First person to shout out an answer wins that round.
Keep it fast. Energy matters more than depth. Do not let an answer turn into a story yet.
Pick four or five questions maximum. Stop while it is still fun.
Good ones to start with: worst meeting you have ever been in, what is your walk-out song, go-to comfort food, biggest pet peeve in meetings, what is a completely irrational fear you have.
Sharing out (1 to 2 minutes)

Crown the winner and give them a small role for the rest of the session: they pick the next question, or they choose who answers next. It keeps the energy attached to a person rather than to the facilitator.
Debrief
What. “What was the vibe in the room just now, compared to a minute ago?”
So what. Breaking the expected format is what made engagement possible. Nobody had to be persuaded to participate. Point out that this took ninety seconds and no preparation.
Now what. “What would it take to bring that same lack of performance into a real community meeting?” Sit with the answers rather than solving them.
Connects to
Level 1 of the question ramp. Connection over speed. Breaking the boring-meeting expectation.
Pairs well with
Bad and Good Conversations, run immediately after, which converts the energy into content.
Facilitator notes
The most common failure is running it too long. Five questions, then stop.
If the room is senior and reserved, model first: answer the first question yourself, badly and quickly, and the permission is granted.
Virtual: works well in chat. First answer posted wins. Read the winning answers out loud.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which five questions will you use? Write them here so you are not choosing in the moment.
Your own answer to question 1, ready to model: ____________________________
Group Size: Small to medium. Above about fifteen people, run it in pairs instead of as a whole group.
Materials: None.
Purpose: Show the entire skill in a single move. One follow-up question turns a fact into meaning, and everyone in the room can feel the moment it happens.
Set up (1 minute)
Say this: “Let us try something quick. Share one thing about you that people would not know just from your role.”
The activity (4 to 7 minutes)
Model it first. Share something small and real about yourself, then have someone ask you the follow-up so the room sees you answer it.
A participant shares a fact. Keep each share to thirty or forty seconds.
After they share, you or the group asks: “What is behind that?” or “Why does that matter to you?” Take four or five people, not the whole room.
Sharing out (1 minute)
Say this: “That right there, that second question, is the whole thing. That is where conversations start to matter.”
Debrief
What. “What happened to the conversation when we asked why does that matter to you?”
So what. The first answer is information. The second is lived experience. Most professional conversations stop after the first one, and the person on the other side notices.
Now what. “In your next partner meeting, where is the place you would normally accept the first answer and move on?”
Connects to
Level 2 of the question ramp. Step 3 of the Simple Flow, reflect what you hear. Lived experience.
Pairs well with
The Simple Flow concept presentation, delivered immediately after while the example is still in the room.
Facilitator notes
You must model first. If you do not, the first share will be safe and the activity will not go anywhere. Keep your own example light but real, the kind of thing you would tell a colleague at lunch.
If a share goes somewhere heavy, thank the person, reflect what you heard, and move on without probing further. The room is watching how you handle it.
FACILITATOR PREP
The thing you will model with, and what is behind it: ____________________
Group Size: Pairs. Any total number, odd numbers make a group of three with a rotating asker.
Materials: The level 3 questions from the question bank, projected or printed.
Purpose: Practice pure curiosity with the advice removed. This is the first time in the session that participants have to sit in the discomfort of not helping.
Set up (1 minute)
Say this: “This is where we actually try it. We are practicing pure curiosity. One rule, and it is the whole activity: no advice, no fixing. Only questions.”
The activity (5 minutes)
Pair participants. Person A asks only questions for two minutes. Person B answers.
A may not offer advice, share their own experience, or say anything that is not a question. A may say nothing at all if they cannot think of a question.
Call time at two minutes and switch roles. Two more minutes.
Prompts to offer: what motivates you to keep doing this work, what is something you wish people asked you more about, what has been meaningful in your work recently, what is on your mind lately.
Sharing out (1 minute)
Bring everyone back for a rapid whole-group check. Two or three voices, not a full round.
Debrief (3 minutes)
What. “What was harder than you expected? When did you want to jump in?”

So what. The urge to solve is not a character flaw, it is a trained reflex, and it is the single largest obstacle to this skill. Name that the discomfort people just felt is what a partner feels when we do jump in.
Now what. Have everyone complete out loud or on paper: “In my next conversation, I will practice ______ instead of ______.”
Connects to
Level 3 of the question ramp. Curiosity over expertise. The 70/30 listening discipline. Relational restraint.
Pairs well with
Curiosity Bingo, or the Socratic discussion, both of which assume the room has already felt this.
Facilitator notes
Two minutes is correct. It will feel long. That is the point and you should say so afterward rather than shortening it.
The activity is four minutes of practice and six minutes of set-up and debrief. Do not invert that ratio.
Watch for pairs who have turned it into a conversation. Interrupt gently: “Questions only.”
Virtual: breakout rooms of two, four minutes total, with a visible timer and a broadcast message at the halfway point.
Group Size: Any. Whole group.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard, two columns.

Purpose: Produce the room’s own list of what makes conversation work. Everything taught afterward is then something the room already said, which is a different thing from something the facilitator asserted.
The activity (5 to 8 minutes)
Ask: “What makes a bad conversation or a bad meeting?” Let people call things out. Capture every answer in the left column, in their words, without editing.
Let it run until the pace slows. Usually about ninety seconds. The list will be long and slightly cathartic.
Then ask: “So what makes a conversation good, or meaningful?” Capture in the right column.
The second list comes slower than the first. Wait through it. That gap is itself worth naming.
Sharing out and synthesis (2 minutes)

Read the right column back to the room and say this: “Everything on this side is a behavior, not a personality. That is good news, because behaviors are learnable. Every one of them shows up in the next hour.”
Then point at the items that map to the Simple Flow. There will usually be several: they actually listened, they did not have an agenda, I felt like they got it, something changed because of it.
Debrief
What. “Which side came faster, and why do you think that is?”
So what. We are all fluent in what does not work and much less fluent in what does. That asymmetry is why good conversations feel like luck rather than skill.
Now what. “Pick one item from the right-hand list that you are least reliable at. That is your focus for the rest of today.”
Connects to
The whole session. This is the activity the other icebreakers set up.
Facilitator notes
Keep the flip chart up for the rest of the session and point back at it. It is the room’s own authority and it is more persuasive than yours.
Run this immediately after King or Queen for the Day when you have the time. The energy converts directly.
If nobody speaks, start with your own worst meeting. It never fails.
FACILITATOR PREP
Two items you expect on the right-hand list, and the Simple Flow step each maps to:
The Question Bank
Thirty questions, grouped by the three levels of the question ramp. Use them for King or Queen for the Day, for Curiosity Roulette, or any time a room needs a way in.
How to use the ramp

Pick two or three from level 1, one or two from level 2, and one from level 3. Run them in that order. The whole sequence takes about six minutes and it does more for the rest of the session than any framing you could deliver.

The temptation is to skip to level 3 because those are the interesting questions. A room that has not been through levels 1 and 2 will answer them politely and generically, and you will have spent your best material on nothing.
Level 1: funny and energy (10 questions)
These wake up the room and lower the pressure. Speed matters more than depth.
What is a completely useless talent you have?
What is something you believed as a kid that was completely wrong?
What is your most awkward meeting moment?
Which animal is the rudest, and why?
What is a completely irrational fear you have?
What is your go-to excuse for being late?
Worst haircut you have ever had?
What is something you pretend to understand but do not?
What is the most overused phrase in meetings?
If you came with a warning label, what would it say?
Level 2: work relatable and relevance (11 questions)
These connect the room to daily working life. People recognize themselves and the energy stays high while the content gets closer to the point.
What is your biggest pet peeve in meetings?
What is the longest meeting you have ever survived?
What instantly makes a meeting better?
What instantly makes a meeting worse?
Camera on or camera off, and be honest about why?
What is your walk-out song?
What would your signature catchphrase be?
What is a hidden talent nobody here knows about?
If your job were a reality show, what would it be called?
What is your go-to comfort food after a hard week?
What is one small thing that reliably makes your day better?
Level 3: meaningful and depth (9 questions)
These surface values, motivations and lived experience. Use them in Curiosity Roulette and in real partner conversations. Ask one and then stop talking.
What has been on your mind lately?
What motivates you to keep doing this work?
What is most misunderstood about your role?
What has been meaningful in your work recently?
What is something you wish people asked you more about?
What is something people would not know about you from your job title?
What do you care about that does not usually come up at work?
What experience shaped how you see this work?
What experience changed how you approach people?
Three ways to run the bank
Rapid fire. Facilitator reads, first answer wins. Level 1 only. Ninety seconds.

Pass the deck. Print and cut the questions, hand the stack to one participant, they pick one and answer it, then pass the stack to whoever they choose. Self-running, and it moves the power around the room.
Ramp. Two from level 1, one from level 2, one from level 3, in that order, as the front end of any session over an hour.
Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: One printed bingo card per participant (page 43), pens, the personal reflection question bank (page 46).
Purpose: Turn seven abstract behaviors into twenty-five things a person can notice themselves doing or failing to do. The card is a mirror, not a scorecard.
Set up (2 minutes)

Say this: “This is not a game about winning and it is not role play. You are going to have a real conversation about real work. The card is there so you notice what you actually did. Mark a square only when the behavior genuinely happened. Learning matters more than finishing the card.”
Pairs decide who is the Conversation Lead, meaning the one practicing, and who is the Partner, meaning the one sharing honestly from real experience.
Round 1 (7 minutes)
The Lead runs a conversation using questions from the personal reflection bank or about real work.
The Lead marks squares as they go, only when the behavior actually happened.
The Partner answers honestly from real experience. No inventing, no scenarios.
Round 2 (7 minutes)
Switch roles. The new Lead practices the same behaviors on a fresh card while the new Partner shares a real story about their work or community.
Self-assessment (4 minutes)
Individually, look at your card and mark two things: which behaviors were natural, and which ones felt forced or did not happen at all. Write one sentence about the hardest square.
Debrief
What. Which square was easiest for you to mark? Which was hardest to perform while actually listening?
So what. What did you learn about your partner only because you were forced to slow down?
Now what. Which one behavior on the card will you use in your next community meeting?
Connects to
The Simple Flow. Curiosity over expertise. The 70/30 discipline. Asset-based thinking.
Facilitator notes
The most common problem is the Lead reading squares off the card and fishing for them. Say at the start: do not hunt for squares, have a conversation and mark what happened.
Nobody fills the card. Say so at the start or someone will feel they failed.
The free square in the middle reads “stay curious, not helpful.” Point at it when someone starts giving advice.
Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: Note paper. Nothing else.
Purpose: Interrupt the reflex that ruins most of these conversations, which is planning your response while the other person is still talking.
Framing (3 minutes)

Explain the ping-pong trap: in most professional conversations we are not listening, we are waiting. While the other person speaks we are assembling our reply, and the moment they stop we serve it back. The conversation looks like an exchange and it is actually two monologues taking turns.
Have participants write down the two intervention questions. These are asked silently, of yourself, mid-conversation.
What assumption am I making right now?
What would slowing down look like here?
Round 1 (5 minutes)
In pairs, one person shares a real challenge from their work.
The listener must wait three full seconds after the speaker finishes before responding, and must use those three seconds to silently answer the two intervention questions.
Three seconds is much longer than it sounds. Count it.
Round 2 (5 minutes)
Switch. The new listener practices letting the conversation breathe and resisting the urge to fix.
Individual reflection (2 minutes)

Write down one urgency trigger you noticed: the specific kind of thing that made you want to jump in with advice. Most people can name it immediately, and it is usually a topic they have expertise in.
Debrief
What. What happened in the three seconds of silence?
So what. What are we protecting by solving quickly? Answers usually include our own comfort, our sense of usefulness, and the schedule. All three are real.
Now what. How will you physically or mentally pause in your next high-stakes conversation? Name the actual mechanism, not the intention.
Facilitator notes

Three seconds is the number. Other versions of this material have said five seconds, ten percent, and thirty seconds. Three is short enough that people will actually do it and long enough that they feel it.
Speakers often report that the silence made them keep going and say something they had not planned to. That is the finding. Draw it out in the debrief.
Virtual: the lag makes three seconds feel like a technical failure. Warn both people first or it will not work.
Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: The conversation prep sheet (page 44), one per participant. The community discovery questions (page 45).
Purpose: Rehearse a real, specific, upcoming conversation rather than a general skill. This is the activity that survives contact with Monday morning.
Individual prep (5 minutes)
Each participant picks a real upcoming partner meeting and fills in the top of the prep sheet:
Who the person is and what you know about what matters to them.

A relational purpose, written as one sentence you would actually say out loud. Not “build the relationship.” Something like: I would like to understand what you have been carrying this year before we talk about anything we might do together.
One open-ended community discovery question, starting with how or what.
Participants who did the pre-work already have these. They use the five minutes to sharpen them.
Round 1 (5 minutes)

One person plays the partner, using what their pair member told them about the real person. The other practices Simple Flow steps 1 to 3: start with purpose, explore their story, reflect what you hear. Stop there. Do not go to next steps yet.
Round 2 (5 minutes)

Switch roles. This round pushes specifically on step 3. The listener must reflect at least twice, and each reflection must be about meaning or value rather than about facts. The partner says whether the reflection landed.
Feedback (5 minutes)
Partners use the seven observable behaviors on page 9 and answer two questions for each other, out loud:
Was the stated purpose relational or was it a task in relational clothing?
Were the questions genuinely open, or were they closed questions with a question mark on the end?
Debrief
What. Which step of the flow was the biggest departure from how you normally run a meeting?
So what. How does opening with learning rather than with the agenda change the energy of the whole thing?
Now what. Name the shared interest or the next step you are going to look for in your real meeting. Write it on the prep sheet and take it with you.
Facilitator notes

This practice deliberately rehearses steps 1 to 3 only. Steps 4 and 5 depend on what the partner actually says, and rehearsing them produces a script, which is the opposite of the skill. Say this out loud, because participants notice the gap.
The most common failure is a purpose that is a task: I want to explore how we might partner on preparedness. That is an agenda item. Push for one that could not appear in a work plan.
Collect nothing. The prep sheet goes with the participant to the real meeting. That is the entire point.
Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: Two bingo cards per participant, pens, the personal reflection question bank, the skill-to-practice map (page 47), the proficiency rubric (Appendix C).

Purpose: The same activity as the twenty-minute practice, with the two things the short version has to cut: a front end that makes participants choose their own hard behavior, and a back end that connects what they did to the rubric they will be assessed against.
Phase 1: mindset alignment (10 minutes)
Introduce the skill-to-practice map. Each bingo behavior corresponds to a named relational skill and a reason it matters in community work. Walk three rows of it, not all eleven.
Participants read the twenty-five squares and pick one behavior they personally find difficult under pressure. They write it down.
Take four or five out loud. The list will cluster, and the clustering is worth naming: almost everyone picks either reflecting meaning or resisting the fix.
Phase 2: round 1 (15 minutes)

Pair up. Person A is the Conversation Lead and practices the skill. Person B is the Partner and answers honestly from real experience. The Lead uses the personal reflection questions and marks squares only when the behavior genuinely happened.
At the ten-minute mark, call out: “One more question, and make it a why.”
Phase 3: round 2 (15 minutes)
Switch roles, fresh card. The new Lead practices curiosity and restraint while the new Partner shares a real story about their work or community. Same ten-minute prompt.
Phase 4: self-mapping (5 minutes)

Using the rubric in Appendix C, each participant privately scores themselves 1 to 4 on the seven dimensions, based only on what happened in the last thirty minutes. Nobody sees anybody else’s scores. Then they circle the one dimension where the gap between where they are and where they want to be is largest.
Debrief
What. Which square was easiest to mark? Which was hardest to perform while actually listening?
So what. What did you learn about your partner only because you were forced to slow down and listen?
Now what. Which single behavior will you use in your very next community meeting, and what will remind you to do it?
Where this is best used
The primary hands-on practice in the two-hour session, and the applied practice hour of the four-hour intensive. In a one-hour session use the twenty-minute version instead.
Facilitator notes
Phase 1 is what makes this the long version rather than a padded short one. Do not cut it to buy time; cut phase 4 instead and do the self-scoring in the coaching hour.
Self-scores run high in round one and drop in round two, once people know what the behaviors actually cost. Warn them, or the drop reads as failure.

title: Deep Dive on the Flow and the Ramp

blocks.text: Group Size: Small groups of three or four, with pair work inside.
Materials: Flip chart per group, markers, the question bank (page 17), the conversation prep sheet.

Purpose: Take the two frameworks from something participants can recite to something they can diagnose with. By the end they should be able to hear a conversation going wrong and name which step failed.

This hour is the one place in the skill where the frameworks get taken apart rather than presented. It belongs in the four-hour intensive and it works as a standalone for a team that already knows the vocabulary and is not getting results from it.
Segment 1: build the flow from the room (15 minutes)

Do not present the five steps. Ask instead: “Think of the best conversation you have had with a community partner. What happened first? Then what?” Capture the sequence on a flip chart in the room’s words.
