The room will produce something close to the five steps, usually with purpose missing and reflection buried. Then show the actual flow and put the two side by side.
Name the gap out loud: almost nobody lists starting with purpose, and almost everybody does it in the conversations that go well, without noticing.
Segment 2: the failure map (15 minutes)
In small groups, take one step of the flow each and answer three questions on a flip chart:
What does this step look like when it is done badly but looks fine?
What is the specific sentence someone says when they are skipping it?
What would you notice in the other person if it had been skipped?

Groups post and read out. The middle question is the one that produces the material. Facilitator captures the sentences on a separate sheet, because that list is the most useful thing the room will make all day.
Typical harvest: “So what we do is...” for a skipped purpose. “That makes total sense, so...” for a skipped reflection. “Why don’t we set up a follow-up” for a next step that is not mutual.
Segment 3: the ramp, run live (15 minutes)
Split the room in half. Half run a three-question sequence starting at level 3. Half run the full ramp: two level 1, one level 2, one level 3. Same final question for both halves.
Four minutes each in pairs, then compare across the room: what did the final answers sound like?
The level 3 cold group produces shorter, more general, more professional answers almost every time. Let the room notice this rather than telling them.
Segment 4: the hard case (15 minutes)

Each participant names a real conversation where the flow would break, and the group works one of them. Common ones: a partner who is openly hostile, a partner who wants a decision today, a partner with far more power than you, a partner you have already disappointed.
Working questions for the group: which step is actually blocked, and by what? What is the smallest version of that step that would still be honest? What would you have to accept about the timeline?
Debrief
What. Which step did your group find hardest to describe being done badly, and what does that tell you?
So what. The flow is not a script. It is a diagnostic. What can you now hear that you could not hear this morning?
Now what. Name the step you personally skip most, and the sentence you say when you skip it.
Facilitator notes
Segment 2 is the heart of this. If you are short on time, shorten segment 1 and keep segment 2 whole.
Keep the harvested sentences. They are excellent material for the coaching hour and for future deliveries.
This hour needs a facilitator who is comfortable not presenting. If that is not you today, run segment 1 as a short presentation and give the extra time to segment 4.
FACILITATOR PREP
Your own example of a conversation where the flow broke, and which step it was:
The step you personally skip: _________________ What you say when you skip it:
Group Size: Trios. Three roles, three rounds, everyone plays every role.
Materials: The community discovery question bank (page 45), the observation sheet below, the proficiency rubric (Appendix C), timer.
Purpose: The closest thing in this document to a real partner conversation. Longer than the drills, with an observer, and about a real community rather than a scenario.
The distinction that opens the hour (5 minutes)

Personal reflection questions are for internal practice. They are about the participant’s own work and they are how we build the muscle. Community discovery questions are for real partners. They are about the community, and they are what the muscle is for.
Say this: “For the last hour you have been practicing on each other. This hour you practice on a real community, and each of you brings one you actually work in.”
Setting up the trios (5 minutes)

Each participant names a real community, coalition or partner group they work with. Not a person, a community. In the rounds, the Partner role answers as someone from that community would, using what the participant actually knows.
Three roles, rotating each round:
Discoverer. Runs the conversation using the discovery questions. Their job is understanding, not information collection.
Partner. Answers about the community the Discoverer named, as honestly as their knowledge allows, including saying “I do not know” when they do not.
Observer. Says nothing. Tracks the seven behaviors on the observation sheet and counts questions against statements.
Three rounds (36 minutes total)
Each round is twelve minutes: eight minutes of conversation, then four minutes of feedback led by the Observer, then rotate.
The Observer speaks first and reports only what they saw and heard, with no evaluation: you asked six questions and made eleven statements, you reflected twice, you asked who the community trusts.
Then the Partner says one thing: the moment they felt most understood, and what caused it.
Then the Discoverer says one thing they will do differently next round.
The observation sheet
Observers tally as they go. Do not write sentences during the conversation, only marks.
Open questions asked (how, what, why): _______
Closed questions asked: _______
Statements made by the Discoverer: _______
Reflections offered, meaning rather than facts: _______
Longest silence, in seconds: _______
Was a relational purpose stated at the start? Yes / No
Was a shared interest named? Yes / No
Was a mutual next step agreed? Yes / No
Closing (14 minutes)
Individually, five minutes: write down one thing you now know about your own community that you had not put into words before, and one thing you realized you do not know and should.

Whole group, nine minutes: take the second answer from around the room. The list of things people do not know about communities they have worked in for years is the most honest moment in the whole skill.
Debrief
What. What was the ratio of questions to statements in your last round, and how different was that from your first?
So what. What does it mean that a room full of experienced people just found gaps in what they know about communities they have served for years?
Now what. Who are you going to ask, and when? Write the name and the date.
Facilitator notes
The Observer role is what makes this work. Protect it: observers who join the conversation stop being useful and the feedback collapses into general encouragement.
The tally is more persuasive than any coaching you could offer. People argue with judgments and they do not argue with counts.
If a participant does not have a community they work in, pair them as a permanent Observer across all three rounds. That is a genuinely good use of the hour for a new staff member.
Virtual: trios in breakout rooms, twelve minutes each, with the observation sheet in a shared document per trio.
Group Size: 6 to 20. Above twenty, use pairs at every prompt before opening it up.
Materials: Chairs in a circle if the room allows it. Nothing else. Do not use slides.
Purpose: Get a group to examine their own conversational habits without being told what those habits are. Nothing here is taught. Everything is surfaced.
What makes a conversation Socratic

A Socratic conversation uses thoughtful, open-ended questions to help another person examine their own thinking, assumptions and values, rather than giving advice or pushing a solution. The goal is not to persuade or to win. It is to deepen understanding and surface meaning.
Questions lead the way. The facilitator asks what do you mean by that, or what led you to that conclusion, rather than making statements.
Curiosity over certainty. The person asking takes a stance of not knowing, which creates space for the other person to think out loud.
Focus on assumptions and values. The dialogue explores what someone believes, why it matters to them, and how their experience shaped that belief.
No rush to action. It is fine if the session ends with more questions than answers. That productive uncertainty is part of it.

In community work this sounds less like an interview or a pitch and more like: what feels most important to you about what is happening in your community, or when you say trust is an issue, what experiences have shaped that. If you are unsure whether you are being Socratic, ask yourself whether you are guiding someone to your answer or helping them find their own.
Session flow
0 to 10 minutes: Opening. Deepen reflection early.
10 to 30 minutes: Guided dialogue. Examine assumptions and habits.
30 to 50 minutes: Application. Move from insight to practice.
50 to 60 minutes: Reflection and close. Anchor commitment.
Stage 1: Opening, 0 to 10 minutes
Goal. Move people from a nice story to meaning, values and conditions.
Open with this: “We are going to approach this differently. This is not a typical training. You will not hear me talk for long stretches. Instead, we are going to think together.”
Then: “Think about a conversation that changed something for you.”
Ask: What made it different?
Ask: Tell me more. What made it meaningful?
Opening, additional questions if needed
Use one or two, not all.
What was happening inside you during that conversation?
What did the other person do that helped you open up?
What made you feel safe enough to say what you really thought?
What was not happening that usually does?
If you had to name the value underneath that moment, what was it?
If engagement is low
Write one word that describes how that conversation felt.
Think of a conversation that should have been meaningful and was not. What got in the way?
Raise your hand if the conversation involved disagreement. Then ask: what helped it stay constructive?
Stage 2: Guided dialogue, 10 to 30 minutes
Goal. Help participants see their default patterns without shame.
Core question: why do some conversations feel meaningful while others do not?
Ask: Why do you think that happens? Who sees it differently?
Ask: What assumptions do we bring into conversations? Do we tend to listen or to solve?
Ask: How can you tell when someone feels heard?
Guided dialogue, additional questions if needed
What do we usually prioritize, being helpful or being curious?
When do we decide we have heard enough and move to action?
What makes listening feel risky?
Whose voice is easiest for you to listen to? Whose is harder?
What role does time pressure play in how we show up?
Prompts on power and positionality if needed
How does our role or title shape how people respond to us?
When have you realized later that someone was agreeing just to move on?
What does it cost people when they do not feel heard by us?
When responses stay abstract
This set is the most useful in the guide. Use it the moment the conversation turns into principles.
What did that look like in a real conversation?
Who was in the room when that happened?
What words were actually said?
Stage 3: Application, 30 to 50 minutes
Goal. Make the skill feel usable tomorrow rather than theoretical.
Ask: Where does this break down in your day-to-day work?
Ask: What makes this hard to do consistently?
Ask: Think about a real conversation coming up. What would you do differently?
Ask: What is one small shift that would change the outcome?
Application, additional questions if needed
What usually pulls your attention away in conversations?
What is the moment you are most likely to interrupt or redirect?
What signals tell you that you are about to start solving?
What is one question you already ask that works well?
What is one question you avoid asking, and why?
Try it prompts
Rewrite a question you usually ask into a more curious version.
Think of a partner you struggle with. What matters most to them?
What would it look like to slow the conversation by ten percent?
If people feel stuck
What makes this harder here than in your personal life?
What would doing this imperfectly look like?
What is one thing you could stop doing rather than start?
Stage 4: Reflection and close, 50 to 60 minutes
Goal. Create personal ownership without pressure.

Say this: “Everything we have discussed, the listening, the curiosity, understanding what matters, that is the skill. You do not need to do everything differently. Try one shift in your next conversation.”
Ask: What is one idea you are taking with you?
Ask: What is one thing you will try differently this week?
Reflection, additional questions if needed
What felt uncomfortable today, and why?
What surprised you about how you listen?
What will you pay attention to in your next conversation?
What is one sign you will notice if trust is growing?
Strong closing prompt, optional
Complete this sentence, out loud or on paper: In my next conversation, I will practice ______ instead of ______.
Closing script

“As we close, remember: the skill we practiced today is not about perfect conversations. It is about slowing down, staying curious, and listening for what matters. Take one small shift into your next conversation and notice what changes. That is the work. Not perfect conversations, just more intentional ones. Thank you for showing up thoughtfully today.”
Troubleshooting
If no one responds. Give thirty seconds of silence, out loud: “Take thirty seconds.” Then ask people to turn to a partner before opening it back up.
If silence continues. “Silence is okay, thinking is happening.” “This is a question without a right answer.” “I will wait. This matters.”
If one voice dominates. “Let us pause here. Who has not spoken yet?” “I am curious how others are experiencing this.” “Different perspectives help us learn. Who sees it another way?”
If responses stay surface-level. “Say more.” “Why do you think that is?” Then use the abstract-response set above: what words were actually said?
If defensiveness shows up. “This is not about doing it wrong, it is about noticing patterns.” “We are practicing awareness, not judgment.”

If the group wants tools too fast. “Before we jump to tools, what matters most here?” “What are we trying to protect by solving quickly?” This is the most common one and it usually arrives around minute twenty-five.
If energy drops. “What is a real example from your work?” Concrete beats abstract every time.
If the conversation goes off track. “How does this connect to trust?” Asked without irritation, this returns the room without anyone feeling corrected.
Facilitator notes
The hardest discipline is not answering. You will know the answer to most of what gets asked. Do not supply it.
Silence of ten to fifteen seconds is normal and productive. Silence of thirty seconds means the question was unclear, not that the room is unwilling. Rephrase rather than waiting longer.
Do not take notes on a flip chart during stages 1 and 2. Visible capture turns a dialogue into a brainstorm.
If you have fewer than fifty minutes, cut stage 3 rather than compressing all four. A shortened stage 2 produces nothing.
FACILITATOR PREP
Your own answer to the opening question, ready but held back:
The three questions you will definitely ask: ___________________________
What you will do with the last two minutes if the room runs long: ______
Group Size: Pairs, or trios with an observer.
Materials: The proficiency rubric (Appendix C), one printed copy per participant, pens.
Purpose: Use the rubric as a coaching instrument rather than a grading one. This is the fourth hour of the mastery intensive and it also works as a standalone for a team that has already practiced.
This hour only works after people have done something observable. Do not run it cold. It follows Curiosity Bingo, the Simple Flow Dry Run, or Community Discovery Practice.
Framing (5 minutes)

Say this out loud, because it determines whether the hour is useful: “Nobody is being rated. These scores go nowhere. The only thing that matters in the next hour is that you get specific about one dimension, and that specificity is impossible if you are managing an impression.”

Walk the four levels once. Emphasize the shape: level 1 is understanding, level 2 is doing it when you set out to, level 3 is doing it reliably including when the conversation is hard, level 4 is developing it in other people and building it into how the chapter works.
Self-assessment (10 minutes)
Each participant scores themselves 1 to 4 on the seven dimensions, based on real conversations in the last month rather than on today.
Then circle the dimension with the largest gap between the current score and where they want to be. Not the lowest score. The largest gap.
Write one sentence of evidence for the circled score. Evidence, not explanation: what actually happened.
Paired coaching, round 1 (15 minutes)
One person is coached, one coaches. The coach uses only these questions, in order, and adds nothing:
Tell me about the conversation behind that score.
What did you actually say?
What were you protecting in that moment?
What would level 3 have looked like there, in one specific behavior?
What would have to be true for you to do that next time?
The coach may not offer advice, share a similar experience, or reassure. If they do, the person being coached says “question only,” and both people learn something.
Paired coaching, round 2 (15 minutes)
Switch roles. Same five questions.
Observation practice, optional variant

In trios, add an observer who scores the coach against dimension 2, questions, and dimension 4, reflection, using the same rubric. Coaching is itself a trust-building conversation, and this is the sharpest demonstration of that in the whole document.
Commitment and close (15 minutes)
Individually, five minutes: write one behavior, one conversation it will happen in, and one date.
In pairs, five minutes: read them to each other and each person names one thing that would make their partner’s commitment more likely to survive the week.
Whole group, five minutes: take the dates out loud. Not the commitments, only the dates. It is faster and it is more binding.
Debrief
What. What did your coach ask that you would not have asked yourself?
So what. The coaching questions are the skill. Five questions and no advice is exactly what a good partner conversation looks like.
Now what. Who on your team could you run this with, and when?
Facilitator notes
Scores drift upward when people think anyone will see them. Say twice that scores go nowhere, and mean it.
The most valuable question is the third one, what were you protecting. It is also the one coaches skip. Watch for it and prompt.

Level 4 is about coaching others and building systems. Participants at level 3 often score themselves at 4 because they are good at the skill. The distinction to draw: level 4 is not doing it better, it is that other people are now doing it because of you.
FACILITATOR PREP
Your own current level on each of the seven dimensions, so you can answer honestly if asked:
Purpose ___ Questions ___ Listening ___ Reflection ___ Understanding ___ Shared interest ___ Next step ___
The dimension you are working on, and what you are doing about it:
Practices in Everyday Life

Seven things a participant can do on their own, between sessions or instead of them. These are not workshop activities. They are how the skill actually gets built, because two hours in a room does not change a twenty-year habit and four hundred small conversations do.
Give this page out at the end of any session. Suggest people pick one, not seven.
1. The learn or influence pre-check
Before your next meeting, whether it is with a neighbor, a volunteer or a board member, pause for sixty seconds and ask: am I trying to learn, or am I trying to influence?

If the answer is influence, that is not automatically wrong. But decide it deliberately, and consider whether five minutes of learning first would change what you are trying to influence. Opening move if you shift: “I would love to learn more about what matters to you in your work lately.”
2. The ten percent slower challenge

The biggest barrier to trust is the urgency habit. In your next conversation, slow the exchange by about ten percent. When the other person finishes speaking, count to three before you respond. That is all.
What usually happens: they keep talking, and the second thing they say is more useful than the first.
3. The 70/30 rule

During a lunch or a coffee with a colleague, aim to spend seventy percent of the time listening and thirty talking. Use your thirty mostly on how and why questions that invite the other person to lead.
Most people find this exhausting the first time. That is a useful piece of information about how much of a normal conversation we spend preparing to speak.
4. Everyday curiosity bingo
You do not need a workshop to use the bingo behaviors. Pick one square and focus on it for an entire day.
Option A, the reflection habit. Practice saying: “It sounds like ______ is really important to you.” Confirm the meaning behind the words, not the facts.

Option B, checking assumptions. Whenever you feel the urge to fix a problem someone mentions, stop and ask yourself what assumption you are making, then ask a follow-up question instead of offering a solution.
5. Value-based listening
Use a personal reflection question with a friend or family member and practice listening for the value underneath the answer rather than the content of it.
Try: “What is a conversation you still think about?” or “What makes it easier for you to open up?” Then name to yourself what they value. Reliability. Being taken seriously. Not being managed.
6. The Simple Flow dry run, on someone safe
Apply the five steps to a low-stakes interaction, deliberately, all the way through.
Start with purpose: tell a friend why you wanted to catch up.
Explore their story: ask about their week and let them pick the topic.
Reflect what you hear: say back the most meaningful thing they said.
Look for shared interest: name something you both care about, based on what they just said.
Agree on one next step: suggest one small way to stay connected.
7. The post-conversation debrief
After any meaningful interaction, take two minutes.
When did I feel the urge to jump in and fix something?
What did I learn only because I slowed down?
Did I leave with a clearer understanding of what matters to them?

Two minutes, and it is the single highest-return practice on this page. Nobody does it. Ask a participant a month later whether they did, and their answer will tell you more about their proficiency than any rubric.
Session Formats
Four written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document, so the pages are the plan and nothing else needs writing.
20 minutes. One mindset shift and one drill. For a staff meeting or the front end of something else.
1 hour. The core skills workshop. Concept, one practice, debrief.
2 hours. Applied practice. Adds the long Curiosity Bingo, the microlearning, and the proficiency standard.
4 hours. The mastery intensive. Socratic dialogue, the deep dive, community discovery, and coaching.
Choosing between them
If people have never heard of the Simple Flow, do not run the four-hour. Run the one-hour twice, a month apart.
The two-hour is the workhorse. If someone asks for a session and gives no constraint, run that one.
The four-hour needs a room that has already practiced. Its first hour assumes people have habits to examine.
Pre-work is genuinely optional for the twenty-minute and one-hour formats. For two and four hours, send it.
What every format shares
Real material, not role play. Participants talk about their actual work.
A named next step at the end. One behavior, one conversation, one date.
The facilitator models before asking. Every time, without exception.
A note on the session structure
Purpose: Shift the mindset from what can we deliver to how do we walk alongside each other. That is all. Do not try to teach the flow in twenty minutes.
Materials: None. Level 3 questions on a slide or read aloud.
Agenda
5 minutes: Introduction and the mindset shift.
10 minutes: Curiosity Roulette, run short.
5 minutes: Wrap and reflection.
Introduction and mindset shift (5 minutes)
Set the tone as a pause rather than another task. Presence matters more than perfection.

Say this: “A community leader once said, we do not need another program, we need someone who will listen long enough to understand why the last three did not stick. Trust grows when we honor history instead of bypassing it. Transactional engagement asks what can we deliver. Transformational engagement asks how do we walk alongside each other.”
Then one question to the room, answered by two or three people: “What is the difference you can feel between those two kinds of meeting?”
Curiosity Roulette (10 minutes)
Full instructions on page 15. In this format: one minute of setup, two minutes each way, and five minutes of debrief. The debrief is the content, not the drill.
Use level 3 prompts: what motivates you to keep doing this work, what is something you wish people asked you more about, what has been meaningful in your work recently.
Wrap and reflection (5 minutes)
“What was harder than you expected?”
“Identify one relational shift you will make in your next meeting.”
Close with the sentence stem: In my next conversation, I will practice ______ instead of ______. Take three of them out loud.
Facilitator notes
Twenty minutes is enough for one thing. The one thing is the felt experience of not being allowed to help.
Do not add the Simple Flow. Mentioning five steps in the last two minutes guarantees none of them is remembered.
Purpose: Hands-on practice of the behaviors that build trust. By the end participants have run two real conversations and know which behavior is hardest for them.
Materials: Bingo cards, pens, the personal reflection questions, level 3 prompts.
Agenda
10 minutes: Curiosity Roulette.
10 minutes: The Simple Flow, presented.
25 minutes: Curiosity Bingo, the twenty-minute version with five minutes of setup.
15 minutes: Debrief and commitment.
Curiosity Roulette (10 minutes)
Page 15. Two minutes each way, three minutes of debrief. This is the warm-up and the diagnostic: you will learn in these ten minutes which people in the room cannot stop helping.
The Simple Flow (10 minutes)
Present the five steps from page 9. Ten minutes is enough for the five steps and one example, and not enough for the ramp. Leave the ramp out.
Anchor it in what just happened: “In Curiosity Roulette you were doing step 2, exploring their story, with steps 1 and 3 removed. That is why it felt strange.”
Curiosity Bingo (25 minutes)
Page 19. Setup 3 minutes, two rounds of 9 minutes, self-assessment 4 minutes.
Prep: print bingo cards, two per participant.
Debrief and commitment (15 minutes)
Which square was easiest to mark? Which was hardest to perform while actually listening?
What did you learn about your partner only because you slowed down?
Which one behavior will you use in your next community meeting?
Close by taking the third answer around the whole room. One behavior each, no elaboration. It takes four minutes for a room of twenty and it is the most useful four minutes in the hour.
Facilitator notes
The fifteen-minute debrief is not padding. If you overrun, cut the Simple Flow presentation to five minutes, not the debrief.
Nobody fills the bingo card. Say so at the start.
Purpose: Practice long enough that the behaviors get uncomfortable, and establish the proficiency standard so participants know what they are working toward.
Materials: Bingo cards, prep sheets, question banks, the rubric, a screen for the microlearning.
Agenda
10 minutes: Opening. King or Queen for the Day, then Bad and Good Conversations.
15 minutes: The Simple Flow and the Question Ramp.
45 minutes: Curiosity Bingo at full length.
10 minutes: Break.
20 minutes: The Simple Flow Dry Run.
20 minutes: The proficiency standard and close.
Opening (10 minutes)
Pages 12 and 16. Four rapid-fire questions, then the two-column list. Keep the flip chart up all session.
The Simple Flow and the Question Ramp (15 minutes)

Page 9. Both frameworks, with the ramp explained by pointing at what you just did in the opening: “That was the ramp. Level 1 questions, then a level 2 conversation about meetings. You are now willing to talk about something real, and you were not fifteen minutes ago.”
Curiosity Bingo at full length (45 minutes)
Page 23. Four phases: mindset alignment 10, round 1 15, round 2 15, self-mapping 5.
The Simple Flow Dry Run (20 minutes)
Page 21. This is where the session stops being about the room and starts being about Monday. Participants leave with the prep sheet filled in for a real meeting.
The proficiency standard and close (20 minutes)
10 minutes: Walk the seven observable behaviors and show where they sit in the rubric. Explain that level 3, apply it consistently, is the target and that level 4 is a different job.
10 minutes: Commitment. One behavior, one conversation, one date, written down and said out loud in pairs.
Optional: the microlearning

If you have a screen and the room is flagging after the break, run the microlearning modules as a group and use the three quiz questions. Ten to fifteen minutes. Cut the dry run to fifteen minutes to make room, and be aware that is the wrong trade in most rooms.
Facilitator notes
The break is at ninety minutes for a reason. Curiosity Bingo is tiring in a way participants do not expect.
If the room is senior and skeptical, move Bad and Good Conversations to the very front. Letting people complain first buys a great deal of goodwill.

Purpose: For people preparing to hold real community partner relationships. Four hours that move from examining habits, to taking the frameworks apart, to practicing on a real community, to being coached.
Materials: Everything. Bingo cards, prep sheets, both question banks, observation sheets, rubrics, flip charts for four groups.
Prerequisite: This session assumes participants have habits to examine. Do not run it as a first exposure. Run the one-hour first, at least a few weeks earlier.
Agenda
60 minutes: Socratic presentation and dialogue.
15 minutes: Break.
60 minutes: Deep dive on the Simple Flow and the Ramp.
15 minutes: Break.
60 minutes: Community Discovery Practice.
60 minutes: Assessment and coaching.
Hour 1: Socratic presentation and dialogue
The full guide on page 29. Four stages, sixty minutes, no slides. This hour surfaces the habits that the rest of the day works on, so it goes first and it is not shortened.
If the room is small and already close, this hour is the best thing in the whole skill. If the room is large or brand new to each other, use the pair-first variant at every prompt.
Hour 2: Deep dive on the flow and the ramp
Page 25. Four segments: build the flow from the room, the failure map, the ramp run live, and the hard case.
Keep the failure-map flip charts. They are used in hour four when people are looking for evidence about their own patterns.
Hour 3: Community Discovery Practice
Page 27. Trios, three rounds of twelve minutes, with an observer counting behaviors.
This is the hour that distinguishes the intensive from the two-hour session, because it is the only activity in the document where participants practice on a real community rather than on each other.
Hour 4: Assessment and coaching
Page 33. Self-assessment, two rounds of paired coaching using five questions and no advice, then commitment.
Close the day by taking the dates out loud around the room.
If you only have three hours
Cut hour 2. The deep dive is the most sophisticated hour and the least essential, because a room that has done hours 1, 3 and 4 has still practiced, been observed, and been coached.
Facilitator notes
Two breaks, not one. This day asks for sustained attention of a kind most training does not.
Consider co-facilitating. Hour 1 and hour 2 want different facilitator temperaments, and hour 3 needs someone circulating while somebody else keeps time.
The day has no presentation longer than fifteen minutes. That is deliberate. If you find yourself building slides, you are rebuilding the wrong session.
FACILITATOR PREP

What happens after the session, and who owns it: _______________________
Handout: The Curiosity Bingo Card
Print one per participant per round, so two per person if you are running both rounds. Mark a square when the behavior genuinely happens during the conversation.
Row 1
Heard a real lived experience and clarified what matters most to them.
Noticed emotion and stayed with it.
Listened more than you talked.
Asked who the community trusts.
Learned something that shifted your understanding.
Row 2
Reflected back what you heard: true meaning, not just facts.
Heard how past experience shaped trust.
Stayed focused on the person, not the task.
Connected disaster work to lived experience.
Checked an assumption you were making.
Row 3
Someone shared difficulty or vulnerability.
Someone named strength or resilience.
FREE SQUARE. Stay curious, not helpful.
Asked what mattered most in that moment.
Stayed present during discomfort by using curiosity instead of expertise.
Row 4
Heard who or what the community relies on.
Asked about community impact, not programs.
Reflected a shared value or priority.
Asked a follow-up question that deepened trust.
Left with a clearer understanding.
Row 5
Noticed power or role differences.
Heard about a local asset or strength.
Let the conversation breathe, resisting the urge to fix, fill or control it.
Named a shared concern.
Identified one small, mutual next step.
How to print it

A five by five grid on one page, landscape, with the free square in the middle. The rows above are the grid rows in order. If you are producing it as a table, keep the squares large enough to write in, because participants annotate them.
One behavior I will use in my next real conversation: ___________________________
Handout: Conversation Prep Sheet
One page, filled in before a real conversation and reviewed after it. Used in the Simple Flow Dry Run and in the pre-work. Print one per participant, and expect them to take it with them.
Before the conversation
What I already know about what matters to them: ________________________
Am I trying to learn or to influence? _________________________________
My relational purpose, in one sentence I would actually say out loud:
One open-ended question I will ask (how or what):
What I will do when I feel the urge to solve something:
The five steps, as a check
Start with purpose. Stated out loud, relational, not an agenda item.
Explore their story. They lead. I follow what they choose.
Reflect what I hear. Meaning, not facts. At least twice.
Look for shared interest. Genuine overlap, not manufactured.
Agree on one next step. One. Mutual. Realistic.
After the conversation
What did I learn about what matters to them?
What values, motivations or lived experience did I hear?
When did I feel most present, and when did I want to jump in? _________
Did I reflect what I heard? What did I actually say? __________________
What shared interest did we identify? _________________________________
What was the next step, and was it mutual? ____________________________
Looking ahead
What would I do differently next time? ________________________________
One small shift I will try in my next conversation: ___________________
Handout: Community Discovery Questions

These are for real partners and real communities. Personal reflection questions, on the next page, are for practicing on each other. Do not mix them up: asking a community partner what motivates you to keep doing this work is fine, and asking them what is your walk-out song is not.
Opening, once purpose has been stated
What is something your community has dealt with recently that really stayed with you?
What is going well here that people outside would not know about?
How long have you been part of this community, and what brought you into this work?
When things go wrong
When something goes wrong here, what worries people most?
Who do people trust most in those moments?
What has happened before that shapes how people respond now?
What did people do for themselves the last time something happened?
Assets and strengths
Where have you seen neighbors step up for each other?
Who are the people here that everybody knows, whether or not they hold a title?
What organizations or places do people actually go to?
What is already working that should not be disturbed?
History with organizations like ours
What has your experience been with organizations that come in from outside?
What have people been promised before that did not happen?
What would make you skeptical of us, and be blunt about it?
Looking ahead
If things went well this season, what would look different for your community?
What would have to be true for this to be worth your time?
What is something you wish people asked you more about?
How to use them
Pick three. Not fifteen. A conversation with fifteen questions is an interview.
Ask one, then stop talking. The second half of most answers arrives after a silence.
The history questions are the most valuable and the most likely to be skipped. Ask them early, while there is still time for the answer to change the conversation.
Handout: Personal Reflection Questions

These are for practicing on each other, inside a session. They surface values and motivation between colleagues, which is what makes Curiosity Bingo and Curiosity Roulette work on real material rather than invented material.
About the work
What motivates you to keep doing this work?
What has been meaningful in your work recently?
What is most misunderstood about your role?
What part of the job would you keep if you could only keep one part?
What is something you have changed your mind about in this work?
About what is hard
What has been on your mind lately?
What is the part of the week you dread, and what is actually behind that?
When did you last feel out of your depth, and what did you do?
What do you carry from this work that you do not talk about?
About conversations
What is a conversation you still think about?
What makes it easier for you to open up in a conversation?
When have you felt genuinely heard at work, and what did the other person do?
What is something you wish people asked you more about?
About the person
What do you care about that does not usually come up at work?
What experience shaped how you see this work?
What experience changed how you approach people?
What is something people would not know about you from your job title?
How to use them
One question, then listen. The follow-up matters more than the question.
The best follow-up is almost always “what is behind that?” or “why does that matter to you?”
Answer one yourself first if the room is slow to start.
Handout: Skill-to-Practice Map

Each behavior on the bingo card corresponds to a named relational skill and to a reason it matters in community mobilization. Use this in the front end of the long Curiosity Bingo, and use it when a participant asks why a square is on the card.
Asked a how or why question. Curiosity over expertise. Invites story and lived experience instead of confirming assumptions.
Reflected back what you heard. Active listening. Reduces misinterpretation and is the single fastest way to build trust.
Paused before responding. Slowing down. Disrupts urgency-driven habits and creates space for the second half of the answer.
Asked about impact rather than programs. Discovery mindset. Keeps the focus on people rather than on what we happen to offer.
Listened more than you talked. The 70/30 discipline. Shifts power toward the community voice, measurably.
Noticed power or role differences. Power awareness. Supports more equitable engagement and explains a lot of polite agreement.
Noticed an assumption. Self-awareness. Interrupts bias and untested narratives before they become plans.
Asked who the community trusts. Asset-based thinking. Identifies informal leaders and trusted connectors who hold no title.
Heard about a local asset. Asset mapping. Reinforces resilience that is already present rather than importing it.
Stayed with emotion rather than moving past it. Comfort with discomfort. Most of what matters gets said right after the moment people usually change the subject.
Identified one small next step. Relational action. Translates trust into realistic, mutual movement, which is what keeps it from being just a nice conversation.
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. Each entry says what it is for, because a bibliography without that is a list of homework nobody does.
Start here

Leading Change Network, One-to-One Meeting Guide. The single most useful thing on this list, and it is short. A one-to-one is not networking and it is not data gathering. It is a specific tool for finding what makes someone tick and where your interests genuinely overlap. https://leadingchangenetwork.org/

Ganz, M. Public Narrative: Self, Us, Now. Harvard Kennedy School. Why people act out of values and why values travel in stories. Read the participant guide rather than the academic papers. https://ganzzz.scholars.harvard.edu/publications
On listening

Nichols, M. P. (2021). The Lost Art of Listening, 3rd edition. Guilford Press. The best single book on why listening fails between people who like each other. Chapters 3 and 6 are the ones to read if you read only two.

Stone, D., Patton, B. and Heen, S. (2010). Difficult Conversations. Penguin. The three-conversations structure, what happened, feelings, identity, explains most of what goes wrong when a partner brings up history.
Kline, N. (1999). Time to Think. Cassell. On attention as the thing that makes other people able to think. The chapter on the incisive question is worth the book.
On organizing and relationships

Industrial Areas Foundation, relational meetings. The origin of the one-to-one as a discipline. Search for IAF relational meeting rather than a specific URL, since chapter sites move. The core idea: you are looking for self-interest, which is not selfishness, it is what someone is actually trying to protect or build.

Kretzmann, J. P. and McKnight, J. L. (1993). Building Communities from the Inside Out. ACTA Publications. The founding text of asset-based community development. The introduction is enough for this skill. Relevant here because the question who do people already trust is an asset question.
On the Socratic method
Copeland, M. (2005). Socratic Circles. Stenhouse. Written for classrooms and transfers directly. Useful for the mechanics of running a dialogue where you do not answer.
Schein, E. (2013). Humble Inquiry. Berrett-Koehler. The shortest and most practical book on asking rather than telling, from someone who spent a career watching experts fail to.
Red Cross learning
If you read one thing
The Leading Change Network guide. Fifteen minutes, and it changes what a meeting is for.

Pre-work strengthens the session but the session works without it. Send it at least three days ahead. Participants bring their results, not their scores; nobody is asked to disclose a result they would rather keep.
Leadership Self-Assessment (15 minutes)

The Purdue Leadership Self-Assessment is a reflective diagnostic that helps individuals identify leadership strengths, gaps, and growth areas across personal, interpersonal, organizational, and community domains. Use it to inform intentional development planning, not to rank anyone.

items: Bring one sentence: which domain surprised you, and why?

blocks.text: Communication Style Assessment (15 minutes)

A style assessment identifies your dominant communication pattern and how it lands on others. The build currently names the Maxwell DISC assessment, which is a paid commercial product. Confirm your region has access before assigning it. If it does not, any free DISC-style instrument serves the same purpose here.

items: Bring one sentence: when your style is under pressure, who in a meeting is most likely to go quiet?

blocks.text: Facilitator note
Neither assessment is the point. The point is that participants arrive already thinking about their own effect on a room, which is what the first icebreaker then makes visible.
The purpose of this icebreaker is to help leaders recognize how influence shapes whose voices are heard. Our mission is strongest when every perspective can inform our decisions.
Prep: print and cut the role cards (page 8). One role per participant.
Instructions:

items: Distribute one role per participant (Mayor, Executive Director, Major Donor, Long-time Volunteer, New Community Member, Disaster Survivor)
Say: “Who has the most power in a meeting? Line up in a single-file line. Most power in the front. Least power in the back. You’ll have one minute to line up. One rule: no talking.
After 1 minute, ask, “are you comfortable with this positioning?” If needed, give them 1 more minute.
While standing in this order, start debriefing.

blocks.text: Debrief Questions:

items: Who had the most power?
Who had the least?
Who SHOULD have more voice?
What surprised you?
How does power (lack of) influence decisions?
How does this affect service delivery?

blocks.text: Icebreakers: Two Still To Be Built

The component spec calls for three icebreakers. This skill currently has one, Who Holds the Power? (page 6). Design the Meeting and Facilitator in the Hot Seat are logged as core experiences rather than icebreakers, and both run 20 minutes, which is too long to open with.
Two more are owed. They should do work the existing one does not:

items: One that surfaces communication style rather than positional power, so the pre-work has somewhere to land.
One that can be run seated and virtually, since Who Holds the Power? requires participants to physically line up.

blocks.text: This page is a placeholder so the gap stays visible. Remove it once the two icebreakers exist.
The purpose of this activity is to build meetings that welcome participation intentionally. Strong meetings do not happen by accident. They are designed with care.
Instructions:

items: Ask the participants to break into small groups (3-5 people)
Say: “In groups, design a meeting that ensures equitable participation. Include:
Opening strategy
Participation structure
Inclusion strategy
Dominance management plan”
After 10 minutes, walk to each group and introduce one of the following disruptions:
Donor dominance, silence, or time pressure.
Say: "You now have another 5 minutes to adapt your design while protecting broad participation.”

blocks.text: Debrief Questions:

items: What worked?
What failed?
What will you use in real life?

title: Activity: Facilitator in the Hot Seat

blocks.text: The purpose of this activity is to practice real-time leadership under pressure. Leadership is often tested live, in moments that cannot be rehearsed.
Prep: print and cut the role cards (page 11).
Instructions:

items: Assign one participant to be the facilitator for this activity.
Assign the following roles to the rest of the participants:
Dominant voice
Resistant partner
Silent participant
Say: “The role of the assigned facilitator is simply to lead an effective and inclusive meeting. Your meeting topic is [choose one from the list below]. You have 10 minutes.”

blocks.text: Debrief Questions:

items: What did facilitator notice?
What did observers see?

blocks.text: Sample Meeting Topics:

items: Disaster Cycle Services: How can we increase attendance at community preparedness events in our county?
Biomedical Services: How can local organizations work together to increase blood donor participation among younger adults?
Service to the Armed Forces: What community partners should be involved in supporting military members, veterans, and military families?

blocks.text: Goal: To shift internal leadership perspective from tracking transactional community outputs to fostering authentic, equity-based relationship structures where external community voice directly influences strategic decisions.
Prep: print the Growth Gauge (page 16) and the 4-Column Matrix (page 17); one copy of each per participant.
Learning Objectives:

items: Analyze standard operational metrics (events, installations, partner volume) to identify where they mask structural exclusion or silence community representation.
Diagnose internal and external power dynamics using the 4-Layer Power-Aware Engagement Matrix.
Formulate immediate, concrete adjustments to meeting formats, tracking criteria, and agenda-setting to share convening authority.

blocks.text: Measurable Outcomes:

items: 100% of participating leaders will complete a 'Power Map Quick Scan' diagnostic on an active regional project.
Participants will map out at least one specific organizational or procedural metric to pause, audit, or restructure within 24 hours.
Leaders will self-assess their current operational capacity and map out future professional development paths using the specialized Growth Gauge framework.

blocks.text: Phase 1: The Disruption, Shattering the Metric Illusion (5 Minutes)
Objective: Disrupt the comfort of positive operational data and highlight the deep gap between output and community voice.
Script:

"When we review our regional strategies and quarterly dashboards, we love to point to our success metrics. We track how many community events we attended, how many smoke alarm installations we completed, and the total number of partner MOUs we have. The information looks great, the volume is high, and the deliverables are checked off. But let me ask you a transactional question: Does hitting a high number of smoke alarm installations or attending a community event actually represent true community voice, authentic representation, and deep engagement? Or are those metrics simply measuring our internal ability to execute tasks, while masking the fact that the community had zero say in how the program was designed or prioritized? Today, our skill focus is 'Inclusive Facilitation.' We are going to conduct an internal diagnostic on what our output numbers are hiding from us, because counting presence and tracking transactions is not the same as sharing power. Internal insight must precede external impact."
Phase 2: The Framing, Explaining the 4 Layers of Power (15 Minutes)
Objective: Provide a sharp, shared lexicon to view standard meeting and performance data through an equity and belonging framework.
Guide the room through each layer briefly using the following operational scripts and prompts:
Layer 1: Decision-Making Power (The Visible Layer)

items: What it is: The formal, easily identifiable authority to sign off, fund, or veto. It sits at the top because it is the most obvious form of control.

Socratic Prompt for the Room: "Think about the numbers that trigger an initiative. Who holds the “authority” to declare that a metric or partner count is 'sufficient' to move forward? Why is that sign-off power bound to that specific role?"

blocks.text: Layer 2: Procedural Power (The Operational Layer)

items: What it is: Power over the 'how,' the 'when,' and the 'where.' It dictates the rules of engagement, logistics, and timelines. This is where we see how high-volume metrics can mask structural exclusion.

Socratic Prompt for the Room: "Look at our smoke alarm installations or our community events. When we boast about hosting a high number of community events a month, whose administrative convenience is that frequency built for? Does a high volume of installations or community meetings measure community access, or does it just measure our internal operational speed?"

blocks.text: Layer 3: Cultural & Linguistic Power (The Relational Layer)

items: What it is: This layer dictates which communication styles, behaviors, and languages are treated as the 'professional baseline standard.' It determines who carries the uncompensated cognitive burden of translation.

Socratic Prompt for the Room: "When we track 'active participation' or 'verbal input' in our meetings, what communication style are our metrics rewarding? If our criteria favor the loudest, most corporate or institutional articulation, who gets penalized by our data simply for communicating differently?"

blocks.text: Layer 4: Narrative Power (The Root Layer)

items: What it is: The ultimate power to frame reality. It determines who gets to write the definitions of core concepts like 'need' and 'success.' If a group lacks narrative power, it doesn't matter how many times they 'speak' in a meeting; their voice has already been pre-filtered through someone else's scorecard.

Socratic Prompt for the Room: "We consistently track 'community needs' and 'program success' alongside our smoke alarm data. But let's look at the transactions: Who defined the benchmarks for that success? Did the community build the scorecard, or did we engineer the numbers to match our existing internal goals?"

blocks.text: Phase 3: The Diagnostic, Power Map Quick Scan (20 Minutes)
Objective: Ground the framework by having leaders run a rapid, gut-level audit on an active project's meeting and delivery data.

5 Mins | Individual Audit: Distribute the 4-Column Handout matrix. Instruct participants to select an active regional initiative where they track events, installations, or partner numbers, and complete the chart based on the past 30 days of raw operational reality.

10 Mins | Strategic Peer Calibration: Move leaders into pairs, intentionally cross-cutting operational lines. Have them exchange maps to seek out discrepancies, focusing exclusively on where their power perceptions do not align.

5 Mins | Collective Census: Have participants place physical or digital sticky notes onto a giant room-sized master matrix to visually surface clusters and systematic blind spots across the executive team.
Phase 4: The Socratic Harvest, The Deep Dive (15 Minutes)
Objective: Link internal metric systems to external community trust, using purposeful Socratic progressions to block common mission-driven defensive evasions.

The Pattern Scan: "Look at the 'Who Is Missing' column compared to our packed calendar schedules. If our event attendance numbers look great on paper, but this visual map shows key internal and external voices are consistently locked out of the planning room, what are our metrics actually measuring?"

Deconstructing Partner Value: "We’ve listed 'number of community partners' in our data rows. Look at your 'Who Decides' column for that same project: If we have 20 signed-up partners, but none of them hold the transactional authority to alter our meeting formats, shift event locations, or redefine what a successful deployment looks like... what are we actually partnering with them to do? Are they partners, or are they just a demographic metric for our reports?"

Linking Internal to External: "If our internal colleagues who work closest with external stakeholders are hitting 100% of their event and installation targets, but they feel completely trapped in the 'Who Speaks' column internally without any say in how the strategy is evaluated, how does that internal power imbalance limit their ability to build authentic, trust-based relationships externally?"

Confronting the Friction: "If we alter our performance metrics to prioritize the depth of community voice over the volume of outputs, what institutional friction will we face with our funders or oversight boards tomorrow? Who is willing to stand up and defend slower, deeper numbers?"
THE PARTICIPANT GROWTH GAUGE: FACILITATION/WHO SPEAKS MATTERS

This self-reflection framework serves as an alternative to traditional, static evaluation matrices. It acts as an immediate self-reflection checkpoint and a future strategic map for ongoing executive development:
🟩 Layer 1: Surface Awareness

Current Marker: I evaluate engagement success based on raw output data, like the volume of community events hosted, smoke alarm installations completed, or the number of partners signed up.The Growth Path to Layer 2: To move forward, I must stop treating numbers as a proxy for engagement. I need to actively audit who is setting the agenda for these events and begin tracking who remains silent during our partner calls.
🟨 Layer 2: Structural Sight

Current Marker: I routinely notice when high partner numbers hide the fact that the same three dominant voices control the meetings. I track how institutional formats, formal jargon, and rushed 45-minute meetings exclude specific internal and external voices, and I am starting to point these out in regional planning sessions.The Growth Path to Layer 3: To move forward, I must go beyond pointing out gaps. I need to start redesigning the evaluation criteria itself, ensuring that external partners hold a pen when we define project benchmarks.
🟥 Layer 3: Systemic Disruption

Current Marker: I actively disrupt how 'success' and 'need' are measured in our regional strategies. I refuse to use empty volume metrics to prove community alignment. I consistently restructure internal processes to decentralize convening authority, share scorecard design, and distribute actual decision-making power to grassroots partners and front-line staff.The Growth Path Forward: I hold peer executives accountable to these same transactional standards, systematically shifting funding metrics away from extractive numbers toward relational milestones.
PARTICIPANT HANDOUT: THE 4-COLUMN MATRIX
Instruct leaders to select an active project (e.g., Regional Smoke Alarm Blitz or Partner Coalition Campaign) and cross-audit it against these rows:
Who Decides?
Who Speaks?
Who Benefits?
Who is Missing?
Layer 1: Data & Control• Who determines if event or installation data is 'enough'?• Who sets output targets?• Who controls the calendar?
[Field Notes Workspace]
Layer 3: Participation Style• Who dominates meeting airtime?• Whose style fits standard criteria?• Who speaks effortlessly?
[Field Notes Workspace]
Layer 4: Metric Outcomes• Who looks good on regional charts when targets are hit?• Whose strategic goals are satisfied by outputs?
[Field Notes Workspace]
Layer 2:The Silent Gaps• Who is present but silent during partner calls?• Whose constraints make event times unviable?• Who is left out of scorecard design?

Workshops: Two Still To Be Built

The component spec asks for enough workshop material to cover four hours. This skill currently has a 30-minute workshop, a one-hour workshop, and the one-hour Socratic session, which is two and a half hours at most.
Two more are owed:

items: A two-hour session. The most natural build combines the Socratic 4-Layer framework with Design the Meeting, so participants diagnose power and then redesign a real meeting against what they found.
A four-hour session. Facilitator in the Hot Seat is the obvious spine, run in rounds with the Growth Gauge as the through-line and the observation checklist in Appendix D used live.

title: Workshop: Disrupting Power Dynamics: Internal Culture Shift

blocks.text: Goal: Shift internal Red Cross leadership culture from a top-down command structure to an equitable, power-aware space where frontline expertise drives strategic decision-making.
Objectives:

items: Identify hidden power dynamics and conversational "anchoring" within internal regional meetings.
Apply the "Warm Handoff" protocol to actively redistribute airtime to staff closest to local communities.

blocks.text: Outcomes: Participants will leave with an immediately actionable behavioral framework to increase psychological safety and regional staff participation by 20% in their very next team assembly. The purpose of this activity is to practice real-time leadership under pressure. Leadership is often tested live, in moments that cannot be rehearsed.
Prep: create a slide deck with 3 slides:

items: Your chapter’s org chart side-by-side with a sliding scale icon labeled “Power Meter: Who Commands the room?”
Three clean, minimalist icons: an Agenda Book, a Shield (Safety), and a Megaphone (Voice)
Internal Growth Gauge (page 20).

blocks.text: The Hook: The Power Meter (5 Mins)

items: Visual Setup: Slide showing a standard Red Cross hierarchical org chart side-by-side with a sliding scale icon labeled "Power Meter: Who commands the room?"

Facilitator Script: "Good evening, team. When a disaster strikes, our operational response is naturally command-and-control. It has to be, it saves lives. But when we bring that same rigid, top-down hierarchy into our routine planning and strategy meetings, we accidentally silence the very people who hold our deepest community insights. Power-aware engagement starts behind closed doors. If our Regional Directors and Community Disaster Program Managers (CDPMs) don't feel safe challenging a directive internally, we cannot expect them to facilitate authentic, equitable conversations externally. Today, we look at how to balance that scale."

blocks.text: Core Concept: The 3 "P"s of Internal Equity (8 Mins)

items: Visual Setup: Slide displaying three clean, minimalist icons: an Agenda Book, a Shield (Safety), and a Megaphone (Voice).

Facilitator Script: "To build true internal equity, we must audit our meetings against the Three Ps: First: Privilege of Agenda. Who writes it? If headquarters or executive leadership always dictates the bullet points, we inherently bypass ground-level realities. Second: Psychological Safety. Are we settling for a passive, 'polite consensus'? When a CDPM tells you a timeline won't work for their neighborhood, do you view it as a logistical roadblock to be managed, or do you welcome that friction as vital field data? Third: Proportional Voice. As executives, when we speak first, we 'anchor' the room. Everyone else subconsciously aligns. Equitable participation means the people closest to the ground speak first; leadership speaks last."

blocks.text: Practical Tool: The "Warm Handoff" Protocol (5 Mins)

items: Directions: Facilitator introduces a rapid 2-minute practice. If virtual, use the chat panel. If in person, have participants turn to an adjacent colleague.

Facilitator Script: "Here is your micro-practice for this week: The Warm Handoff. In your next briefing, instead of dropping a top-down directive, intentionally yield your power using active language. Try this phrasing: 'From a bird's-eye view, this is our operational timeline. But [Name], you have the ground-truth context for this area. What blind spots are we missing, and how does this look from your perspective?' Turn to your neighbor or use the chat right now: Practice reframing a standard directive into an active Warm Handoff."

blocks.text: Wrap-Up & The Growth Gauge Mirror (2 Mins)

items: Directions: Distribute the physical or digital one-pager. Point directly to the printed rubric below.

Facilitator Script: "We do not expect proficiency overnight. Equity work is fluid. Instead, use this Growth Gauge as a mirror. Before your next team meeting, look at the Power Distribution column. Commit to shifting from Stage 1 to Stage 3 just once this week by speaking last and handing off the floor."

blocks.text: Core Goal: To shift institutional leadership from defensive/passive postures into power-aware, equitable engagement that actively operationalizes belonging across regional and community structures.

items: Objective 1: Differentiate structural belonging from basic inclusion using targeted, real-world community disaster scenarios.
Objective 2: Map regional power dynamics to identify where communication defaults to purely transactional exchange rather than co-created partnership.
Objective 3: Formulate at least three context-specific Socratic questions to audit equity in immediate operational planning.

blocks.text: By the conclusion of this high-impact session, participants will understand:

items: Structural Analysis: Disrupt conventional "top-down" presentation models, replacing them with equitable participation management tools.
Operational Pivot: Transition ambiguous regional goals into distinct, localized equity benchmarks.
Socratic Competency: Deploy precise, power-aware inquiry during community planning conflicts rather than defaulting to authority assertions.

blocks.text: Prep: Print a copy of the Growth Gauge (page 23) for each participant in your group.
Note for facilitator:

The Prompting Strategy: Do not lecture. To provoke a sharper, more rigorous dialogue among seasoned executives, explicitly frame leadership interactions as transactional. Forcing participants to navigate this stark contrast prevents comfortable platitudes and drives real accountability regarding structural power. Ensure quiet contributors have dedicated airtime via structured round-robins, balancing dominant executive voices.
Instructions on the next page.

Parker, P. (2018). The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why It Matters. Riverhead Books.
