blocks.text: How to use this list
Books build the mindset. Talks are the fastest way to give a skeptical group a shared reference. Toolkits are what you reach for when you have to design a real engagement next month.

Optional. The session does not depend on it, because Fill the Four Corners (page 11) builds a working inventory in the room. Pre-work makes the session sharper because participants arrive already thinking in assets rather than needs. Send it three days ahead and do not chase it.
1. One question, answered honestly (5 minutes)
Think about a community you serve. Write down the first five things that come to mind about it.
Now count: how many are problems, and how many are strengths? Do not change your answers. The ratio is the point, and it is the thing the session works on.
2. Name nine things (10 minutes)
For that same community, name:

items: Three groups or associations. Not organizations with staff, groups: a block club, a walking group, a church committee.
Three institutions. Schools, clinics, businesses, libraries.
Three individuals. Actual people, by name, who others go to.

blocks.text: If the third list is the hardest, that is the most useful thing you will learn from this pre-work.
3. One risk (5 minutes)
In one sentence, what is the major disaster risk this community faces? Bring it; the activation plan uses it.
Optional deeper reading

items: The Serving Leader, available as an eBook and audiobook through Percipio.
Cross Sector Partnerships and Asset Based Community Development, workshop series, part 1 of 3.

blocks.text: Facilitator note
Do not collect or review the pre-work. Its whole function is that participants notice their own ratio of problems to strengths before anyone tells them there is a ratio to notice.
Setup (say this to participants):
Give participants 2–3 minutes to independently write down their answers to the question below.
The Activity (what participants do):
“Write down the first and last names of five people who live geographically closest to them (neighbors, not friends or coworkers unless they also live nearby).”
Encourage specificity: people on the same street, same apartment building, or within a block or two.
Group Reflection (2–4 minutes).
Bring the room back together and ask:

items: How many neighbors were you able to name?
Was that easy or difficult?

blocks.text: Optional Deeper Prompt (if time allows)

items: Why do you think this was challenging?
What does this say about our level of connection to the people physically closest to us?
How might stronger neighbor relationships benefit the community in times of need?
Can neighbors be considered community assets? Why or why not?
What are small ways we could begin to build those connections?

blocks.text: Setup (say this to participants):
Ask participants to form a circle or remain seated.
If the group is large, have people pair up or form small groups. They will ask the questions below and then report out key themes.
The Activity (what participants do):
Go around the room and have each person briefly share:

items: Where they volunteer or give their time in the community.
Why they choose to be involved there.
Encourage concise responses (about 30–60 seconds per person).

blocks.text: Group Reflection (2–4 minutes). Bring the room back together and ask:

items: What motivates you to give your time?
What need does this place or role fill for you or for the community?

blocks.text: Optional Deeper Prompt (if time allows)

items: What patterns did you notice in where people volunteer?
Were there organizations or causes that came up multiple times?
What does this tell us about the values and priorities of this group?
How might these existing connections and organizations serve as community assets?

blocks.text: Setup (say this to participants):
Give participants paper and drawing materials. They will have 5-7 minutes to complete the task below.
The Activity (what participants do):
“Think of a familiar route you travel frequently (e.g., home to work, grocery store, school). Draw that route from memory. Include as many details as possible:

items: Streets and turns
Landmarks (churches, parks, stores, etc.)
Traffic lights or stop signs
Notable buildings or features”

blocks.text: After 5-7 minutes of drawing:
"Pull up the same route on Google Maps (or similar tool on phone). Compare your drawing to the actual map.”
Group Reflection (2–4 minutes). Bring the room back together and ask:

items: What differences do you notice between your mental map and the actual map?

blocks.text: Optional Deeper Prompt (if time allows)

items: What did you remember well? What did you miss?
Did you include places that are meaningful to you but might not appear on a standard map?
How aware are you of your surroundings during your daily routines?
What does this tell us about how people experience and define their community?
Are informal landmarks (like ‘the big tree’ or ‘that corner store’) also assets?

blocks.text: Materials: Four sheets of easel paper posted around the room, one per ABCD category, or four areas on a shared digital board. Sticky notes and markers.

Purpose: Produce the asset inventory the rest of the session works from, in the room, without depending on anyone having done pre-work. Also teaches the four categories by using them rather than by explaining them.
Why this comes first

Every activity after this needs an inventory to act on. Relying on pre-work to supply it splits the room into people who are ready and people who are catching up. Building it together removes that problem and produces a richer inventory than any one person would write alone, because the four categories force people past the organizations they already partner with.
Setup
Post four sheets before participants arrive, headed Individuals, Associations, Institutions, and Physical and Cultural. Do not explain the categories yet.
Choose the community first
Pick one of these before the session. All three work; the choice depends on the room.

Option A, one shared community. You name a single neighborhood or corridor and everyone maps it together. Best for mixed groups and for people from different chapters. Also the safest with a new group.

Option B, one participant’s community. A participant offers a real community they serve and the room maps it for them. Best for a single chapter team, and it produces the most usable wall. Ask privately beforehand.

Option C, everyone contributes from their own. Each participant adds from their own community and the group looks at patterns across them. Best for a large or geographically spread group. Produces breadth rather than depth.
The Activity
Step 1 (2 min): Name the place

items: State the community in one sentence: where it is, roughly how many people, and one thing it is known for. Write it where everyone can see it.

blocks.text: Step 2 (7 min): Fill the corners

items: Participants write one asset per sticky note and post it under whichever heading they think fits. No discussion, no permission needed, no evaluating.
If a corner is thin after three minutes, read the heading out and give one example, then stop talking. Do not give three examples; the room will just echo them.

blocks.text: Step 3 (3 min): Look at the distribution

items: Which corner is fullest? Which is emptiest?
Almost every group fills Institutions first and Individuals last. Ask why that is, before offering a reason.

blocks.text: Step 4 (3 min): The names test

items: Go to the Individuals corner. How many notes name an actual person rather than a role or a category?
Star every note that names a real, specific human being. Those are the ones the rest of the session can actually act on.

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: what is on this wall is what we could see from in here. It is weighted toward the institutions we already work with, and toward roles rather than people, and that is normal on a first pass. The rest of the session is about what is missing and what to do with what is here.
Facilitator note

The distribution across the four corners is the teaching moment, not the content of any one note. A wall heavy on Institutions and light on Individuals is a picture of how the chapter currently sees that community, and saying that out loud lands harder than any slide about ABCD.
Photograph the wall before teardown and send it to participants.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which option will you run, and why does it fit this group?
If Option A, which community will you name? Be specific: a corridor, a neighborhood, a set of blocks, not a county.
One example you will offer if a corner stalls (one only):
Materials: The wall from Fill the Four Corners, Asset Inventory handout (page 26) for each participant, sticky notes, markers

Purpose: Practice running the session itself. Participants do not just build a map, they take turns facilitating the building of one, because the skill this document is teaching is not making a map. It is convening a community that makes its own.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Everything we have done so far, you did as the expert in the room. That is the opposite of how this works in a community. In the next fifty minutes you are going to take turns being the facilitator of a mapping session, and the rest of us will be residents. The point is not to produce a beautiful map. The point is to feel the difference between asking a community what it has and telling a community what you found.”
The Activity
Step 1 (5 min): Assign roles

items: Groups of five or six. One facilitator per round, rotating. Everyone else plays a resident.

Give each resident a short card: how long they have lived there, what they do, and one thing they are quietly proud of in their neighborhood. Residents do not volunteer that last thing unless they are asked well.

blocks.text: Step 2 (10 min per round, three rounds): Facilitate
Each facilitator gets ten minutes to surface assets from the group, using the four categories. They may not present, lecture, or use the word asset in the first two minutes.

items: Round 1 facilitator: focus on Individuals. The hardest corner, and the one that matters most.
Round 2 facilitator: focus on Associations. Look for the groups with no letterhead.
Round 3 facilitator: focus on Physical and Cultural. Ask where people actually gather, not where meetings are held.

blocks.text: Step 3 (5 min): Residents report
Residents, not facilitators, answer these:

items: When did you feel like you were being consulted, and when did you feel like you were being surveyed?
What did you know that never got asked for?
Which question opened you up?

blocks.text: Debriefing Questions

items: What did the best facilitator in your group do that the others did not?
How long did it take before someone named a person rather than an organization?
What would have happened if you had walked in with a list already prepared?
What is the first question you will ask in a real session?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Participants will drift into interviewing rather than convening. The tell is that every exchange goes through the facilitator instead of between residents. When you see it, stop the round and ask the residents to talk to each other about the same question. The difference is immediately obvious to everyone watching.
Resist letting anyone skip their turn as facilitator. The discomfort of the first two minutes is the content.
FACILITATOR PREP
Write the resident cards for your group before the session. Six short cards, each with a length of residence, an occupation, and one quiet source of pride. Base them on people you have actually met.
Materials: The four-corner wall, Connector Map handout (page 28), markers in two colors, string or tape if working physically
Purpose: Move from an inventory to a network. An inventory tells you what exists. A network tells you what can move, and who it moves through.
Setup (say this to participants)

“A list of assets is not a map. Right now we have four walls of things that exist near each other. What we do not know is which of them talk to each other, which of them would show up for each other, and which single person is holding three of them together without anyone noticing. That last person is the most valuable name on the wall, and we are about to find them.”
The Activity
Step 1 (8 min): Pull the top twenty

items: From the whole wall, move the twenty most significant assets onto a fresh sheet, spread out with space between them.
At least six must come from the Individuals corner. If the group resists that, note the resistance and hold the line.

blocks.text: Step 2 (10 min): Draw the ties

items: Draw a line between any two assets that have a real working relationship. Not could have, do have.
Solid line for strong, dashed for occasional or strained.
Where nobody in the room knows, draw nothing and put a question mark by the asset. Do not guess.

blocks.text: Step 3 (7 min): Find the connectors

items: Circle anything with three or more lines. These are your connectors.
Note how many are individuals versus institutions. In most communities the real connectors are people, and in most institutional maps they are organizations.
Star any connector who bridges two categories, for example a person who links an association to an institution. Those are the rarest and most useful.

blocks.text: Step 4 (7 min): Find the isolates and the gaps

items: Which assets have no lines at all? Are they genuinely isolated, or does nobody in this room know them?
Where are there two clusters with nothing between them? That gap is a job.
Who would you have to know to close it?

blocks.text: Step 5 (8 min): The question marks

items: Look at every question mark. Each one is a relationship the chapter does not have.
Pick the three that matter most and write, next to each, who could introduce you.

blocks.text: Debriefing Questions

items: Who is your most connected asset, and is that person on the Red Cross radar today?
How many question marks were there, and what does that number say?
What surprised you about the shape of the map?
Which single introduction would change this map the most?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The question marks are the finding. Groups treat them as a failure to complete the exercise, and they are actually the most honest output of the session: a precise list of the relationships the chapter does not have. Say that explicitly, or the group will paper over them by guessing.
Materials: The connector map, Activation Plan handout (page 29), pens
Purpose: Put specific assets to work on a specific task, so the map changes what the chapter does rather than what it knows.
Setup (say this to participants)

“A map that does not change anything is a poster. In the next forty-five minutes you are going to take one real task, something you actually have to deliver this year, and staff it from the map. Not from your volunteer roster. From the wall.”
The Activity
Step 1 (5 min): Name the task

items: Pick one real preparedness, response or recovery task with a deadline. A smoke alarm campaign in a specific area, a shelter agreement, a recovery outreach push.
Write what success looks like in numbers, not adjectives.

blocks.text: Step 2 (10 min): Staff it from the map
For this task, and using only assets on your map, name:

items: Who reaches the people we cannot reach?
Whose voice makes this credible in a way ours is not?
Whose building or space do we need?
Who already does something adjacent that we could join rather than duplicate?

blocks.text: Step 3 (10 min): Name the exchange
For each asset you just named, write two lines. Both are required.

items: What are we asking of them?
What do they get? Not gratitude. Something they would recognize as worth their time.
If you cannot fill the second line, you are not ready to make the ask, and the asset should come off the plan.

blocks.text: Step 4 (10 min): Sequence and date

items: Number your approaches in order. The usual mistake is starting with the biggest institution.
Ask instead: whose yes makes the next conversation easier?
Put a real date next to each, inside ninety days.

blocks.text: Step 5 (10 min): Pressure test in trios
Each person presents in two minutes. The other two ask one question each:

items: What happens if your first approach says no?
Which of these assets is doing you a favor rather than getting something?

blocks.text: Debriefing Questions

items: How much of your plan could you have written without the map?
Which asset did you almost use in a way that would have burned it?
What did the second line, what they get, change about your plan?
What is the first conversation, and when?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The “what do they get” line is where this activity earns its time. Groups write gratitude, visibility, or being part of something bigger, all of which mean nothing. Push until the answer is something the asset would say out loud: a room full of people they have been trying to reach, a problem of theirs that gets solved, a relationship they wanted anyway.
FACILITATOR PREP
Decide before the session what happens after it. A commitment with no follow-up is one people learn to make lightly.
Format: Facilitated dialogue. Participants build shared understanding through guided questioning rather than lecture.
Purpose: Frame asset mapping as a leadership posture rather than a technical tool, and surface the deficit-thinking participants are already carrying.
Agenda at a glance

items: 0 to 5 minutes: Opening frame, setting the inquiry
5 to 15 minutes: Examining assumptions, deficits versus assets
15 to 25 minutes: Defining the skill through dialogue
25 to 35 minutes: From knowledge to leadership behavior
35 to 45 minutes: Application through scenario
45 to 55 minutes: Leadership identity and power
55 to 60 minutes: Reflection and commitment

blocks.text: 0 to 5 minutes: Opening frame, setting the inquiry
Purpose: Establish psychological safety and frame asset mapping as a leadership posture rather than a technical tool.

items: When you hear the word community, what do you instinctively look for first?
Where did that instinct come from?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Deficit-thinking is often automatic in disaster work. This session invites leaders to notice and question that instinct.
5 to 15 minutes: Examining assumptions, deficits versus assets
Purpose: Surface mental models and assumptions.

items: If we only start with needs, what invisible costs might that create?
Who gains power when we define the problem?
What capacities get missed when we focus on gaps?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Leaders begin to distinguish between doing for communities and building with them.
15 to 25 minutes: Defining the skill through dialogue
Purpose: Co-create a shared understanding rather than being handed a definition.

items: If asset mapping were done well, what would we actually see happening?
Who would be talking more? Who would be talking less?

blocks.text: Capture the elements as they emerge. Do not supply them.
Facilitator synthesis: Participants articulate the core elements of asset mapping without being given a definition.
25 to 35 minutes: From knowledge to leadership behavior
Purpose: Translate understanding into observable leadership behaviors.

items: What would a leader who practices asset mapping stop doing?
What would they start doing immediately?
What would they do consistently, even when it feels inefficient?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Asset mapping is expressed through leadership behavior, not tools alone.
35 to 45 minutes: Application through scenario
Purpose: Practice applied reasoning against a real situation.

items: How would decisions differ with a living asset map versus only a needs assessment?
Who becomes a messenger, a convener, or a hub?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Pre-existing relationships reduce time to mobilization.
FACILITATOR PREP
Bring a real scenario from your own region for this segment. Name the community and the event. A generic scenario works; a real one stops people reasoning in the abstract.
45 to 55 minutes: Leadership identity and power
Purpose: Connect the skill to leadership identity and power. Do not cut this segment for time.

items: What kind of leader does asset mapping require you to become?
Where must control be shared or released?
Whose legitimacy matters most in a crisis?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Asset mapping develops leaders who elevate community capacity rather than replace it.
55 to 60 minutes: Reflection and commitment
Purpose: Solidify learning and move it toward action.

items: What assumption are you now questioning?
What relationship do you need to see differently?
What is one action you will take in the next 30 days?

blocks.text: Field Assignments

These are not room activities. They are things participants do out in the community between sessions, and they are where the skill actually develops. Assign one at the close of a session and open the next session with what people found.
Field Assignment 1: Your own leadership team
Start inside the building. You cannot map a community if you cannot map your own team.

items: Who is on your chapter leadership team? Not their titles. Who are they?
Can you say and spell every name correctly?
What is each person’s official title? Could you introduce them without checking?
What is each person genuinely good at, beyond their job description?

blocks.text: Bring back: One thing you learned about a colleague you have worked with for over a year.
Field Assignment 2: One influential person
Choose one influential individual in a community you serve, and work out what kind of influence they hold.

items: Trusted official authority. Their standing comes with the role.
Trusted unofficial authority. People listen regardless of position.
Trusted community connector. Their value is who they can reach, not what they decide.
What is their actual reach? Who would follow them, and who would not?

blocks.text: Bring back: Which of the three they are, and how you know.
Field Assignment 3: Go and listen
Attend three multi-partner community events. Do not present. Do not table. Do not bring materials.

items: Who convened it, and who actually ran it?
Who did people go to during the breaks?
What came up more than once that the Red Cross was not part of?
Who was not there who should have been?

blocks.text: Bring back: Three names you did not know before, and what each one is connected to.
Using these with data

Before or after Field Assignment 2, look the community up in the public datasets: the CDC Social Vulnerability Index, the FEMA National Risk Index, the FEMA Resilience Analysis and Planning Tool, and the US Census. Then ask two questions: who is most at risk here, and which organizations are already working with them? The data tells you where to look. It does not tell you who to talk to, which is what the map is for.
Session Formats
Four written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document; nothing new has to be written to deliver any of them.
20 minutes. Count the Corners. One idea, delivered inside a meeting you were already having.
1 hour. Seeing What Is Already There. Introduces the four categories and produces an inventory.
2 hours. From Inventory to Network. Adds the connector map.
4 hours. The Full Arc. Ends with an activation plan carrying real dates.
How to choose

Choose by what participants walk out holding, not by how much time you have. A group that leaves with an inventory and no plan will not act on it. If you only have an hour, say so at the close and book the next session rather than rushing the activation.
20-minute version: Count the Corners
Purpose: Show a team how it currently sees a community, in one number.

items: Name a community. Individually, list ten assets in it (5 min)
Sort your ten into individuals, associations, institutions, physical and cultural (5 min)
Round the room: read out how many landed in each category (5 min)
One question: why is Individuals almost always the shortest column, and what does that cost us? (5 min)

blocks.text: What they leave with: Their own distribution, and the question it raises.

title: One-Hour Workshop: Seeing What Is Already There

blocks.text: Purpose: Introduce the four categories and produce a first asset inventory for a real community.
Pre-work: Optional (page 7).
Materials: Four sheets of easel paper posted as corners, sticky notes, markers, Asset Inventory handout (page 26) for each participant.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: we usually start with what a place lacks, today we start with what it has (5 min)
Icebreaker: Do You Know Your Neighbors, page 8 (8 min)
Icebreaker: Fill the Four Corners, page 11 (15 min)
Name the four categories out loud now that the room has used them, and give one example each (7 min)
Individually, transfer the wall onto the Asset Inventory handout and add anyone specific to your own community (15 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Which corner was hardest to fill, and why that one?
How many entries name a specific human being?
Who is on this wall that the chapter has never contacted?
What is one name you will follow up on this month?

blocks.text: What they leave with: An asset inventory for one real community, sorted into the four categories, and the number that says how they currently see it.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which community will you name, and which Fill the Four Corners option will you run?

title: Two-Hour Workshop: From Inventory to Network

blocks.text: Purpose: Take a group from no shared starting point to a connector map showing who bridges to whom, and a named list of the relationships the chapter does not have.
Materials: As for the one-hour, plus the Connector Map handout (page 28) and markers in two colors.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (5 min)
Icebreaker: Mapping From Memory, page 10 (15 min)
Icebreaker: Fill the Four Corners, page 11 (15 min)
The four categories, named and worked through with the wall in front of the room (10 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: Connect the Map, page 15 (40 min)
Closing debrief and commitments (15 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: Mapping From Memory before Fill the Four Corners is deliberate. It establishes that people see the same place differently before anyone is asked to be authoritative about what is in it.
Do not start the activation plan in the last fifteen minutes. A half-built plan is worse than an honest stop.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Who is your most connected asset, and are they on the chapter’s radar today?
How many question marks are on your map?
Which single introduction would change the map most?
What will you do with the map before the planning session?

blocks.text: What they leave with: A connector map, a named set of connectors and isolates, and a precise list of the relationships the chapter is missing. Say clearly that they have a map and not yet a plan.
FACILITATOR PREP
When is the follow-on session where they build the activation plan? Book it before you deliver this one.

title: Four-Hour Workshop: The Full Arc
duration: 4 hours, including two breaks totalling 25 minutes

blocks.text: Purpose: Take a group from no shared starting point to an activation plan with real dates, and put them through the experience of facilitating a mapping session rather than only attending one.
Materials: Four corner sheets, sticky notes, markers in two colors, string or tape, all three handouts for every participant, resident cards for the Participatory Mapping Session.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (10 min)
Icebreaker: Where Do You Show Up, page 9 (10 min)
Icebreaker: Fill the Four Corners, page 11 (15 min)
The four categories, named and worked through (10 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: The Participatory Mapping Session, page 13 (50 min)
Core Experience: Connect the Map, page 15 (40 min)
Break (15 min)
Leadership identity and power segment from the Socratic guide, page 19 (20 min)
Core Experience: From Assets to Activation, page 17 (45 min)
Closing round: first conversation and date, said out loud (15 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: The Participatory Mapping Session is the spine of this format. It is the only place in the whole skill where participants practice convening rather than analyzing, and it is what separates this from a planning exercise.

The power segment sits between the map and the plan on purpose. Participants have just built a picture of a community and are about to decide how to use it. That is the moment to ask what kind of leader this requires them to become.
Keep the four-corner wall up all day. In the final round, point at it: this is what we could see this morning.
If the group is over sixteen, run Fill the Four Corners on two walls and compare them before Connect the Map.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Look at the wall from this morning. What was missing from it?
Who is on your activation plan that you would not have approached before today?
What did being the facilitator, rather than the expert, change?
What is your first conversation, and what date is it?

blocks.text: What they leave with: An asset inventory in four categories, a connector map with named connectors and gaps, an activation plan with the exchange named for every asset and real dates, and the experience of having facilitated a mapping conversation.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which community, and which Fill the Four Corners option? _______________
Your six resident cards written, and the regional power scenario: ______
Who follows up on the commitments, and when? __________________________
Handout: Asset Inventory
Use during Fill the Four Corners and the Participatory Mapping Session. One per participant. Add rows as needed.
Individuals
People with everyday skills. Name real people wherever you can, not roles.
Associations
Block clubs, tenant groups, mutual aid, sports teams, faith groups, informal networks.
Institutions
Libraries, clinics, businesses, community centers, schools, local government.
Physical and cultural
Parks, gathering spaces, routes, landmarks, and the informal places people already feel safe.
The names test
How many entries above name a specific human being rather than a role or a category? ______
Which corner is thinnest, and what does that say about how we currently see this community?
Handout: Connector Map
Use during Connect the Map. Work on a large sheet or a digital board; this page is the guide and the record.
How to build it

items: Move your top twenty assets onto a fresh sheet, well spaced. At least six from Individuals.
Draw a solid line between any two with a strong working relationship, a dashed line where it is occasional or strained.
Where nobody knows, draw nothing and mark the asset with a question mark. Do not guess.
Circle anything with three or more lines. Star anyone who bridges two categories.

blocks.text: Record what you found
Connectors, three or more ties:
Isolates, no ties at all. Genuinely isolated, or unknown to this room?
The gap. Two clusters with nothing between them:
The question marks
Each one is a relationship the chapter does not have. Pick the three that matter most.
Handout: Activation Plan
Use during From Assets to Activation. One per participant.
The task
What success looks like, in numbers: __________________________________
Staffing it from the map
Who reaches the people we cannot reach? _______________________________
Whose voice makes this credible in a way ours is not? _________________
Who already does something adjacent we could join? ____________________
The exchange
Both lines are required for every asset. No second line means no ask.
Pressure test
If my first approach says no, my alternative is: ______________________
The asset doing us a favor rather than getting something: ______________
Ninety-day check, which conversations happened and what changed: _______
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. The first three are what you hand someone who asks for more; the rest are for a facilitator going deeper.
Start here

items: Participatory Asset Mapping: A Community Research Lab Toolkit (2012). The most practical guide to running a mapping session with residents rather than about them. Community Science.
Introduction to Community Asset Mapping. Center for Court Innovation, training developed for the New York City Department of Probation. Short, applied, and unusually clear on the participatory piece.
Kretzmann, J. P. and McKnight, J. L. (1996). Mapping Community Capacity. Institute for Policy Research, Northwestern University. The founding text of asset-based community development.

blocks.text: Toolkits and workbooks

items: ABCD Institute: workbooks and guides library.
ABCD Institute: book list.
Dorfman, D. (1998). Mapping Community Assets Workbook. Northwest Regional Educational Laboratory.

blocks.text: Background reading

items: Asset Mapping (1999). University Outreach and Extension, University of Missouri System and Lincoln University.
Best Practice Briefs (1999). The Several Forms of Community Mapping. Michigan State University.
Social Design Notes (2004). What Is Asset Mapping?

blocks.text: Data sources for community context

items: CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index
FEMA National Risk Index
FEMA Resilience Analysis and Planning Tool
United States Census data

blocks.text: How to use this list

The toolkits are what you reach for when you have to design a real mapping session next month. The founding texts are worth reading once so you can tell when someone is doing asset mapping and when they are doing a stakeholder list with better branding. The data sources tell you where to look; they never tell you who to talk to.

Optional. The session does not depend on it, because Name the Decision (page 14) builds a working inventory in the room. Pre-work makes the session sharper because participants arrive with a real decision of their own rather than borrowing the group’s. Send it three days ahead and do not chase it.
1. Name one decision (5 minutes)

Pick one real decision you have to make in the next twelve months about where to put people, money, or attention. Not a hypothetical. Write it in one sentence, including what has to be decided and by when.
Then write down how you would decide it today, honestly, if nobody asked you to justify it.
2. List what you would need to know (5 minutes)
List up to six things you would want to know in order to decide it well. Do not filter for what is available. Write what would actually change your mind.
3. Mark what you have (10 minutes)
Go back through your list and mark each item:

items: H if you have it and could put your hands on it this week.
G if it exists somewhere and you would have to go get it.
N if nobody has it, or you do not know.

blocks.text: Bring the marked list to the session. That is the whole assignment, and it is the only thing you need to have written down.
If you have time, look at one of these

items: CDC Social Vulnerability Index, interactive map: https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/place-health/php/svi/svi-interactive-map.html
FEMA National Risk Index, by county: https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/map
US Census Bureau data explorer: https://data.census.gov
CDC PLACES local health data: https://www.cdc.gov/places/

blocks.text: Find your own county in one of them. Two questions: what does it say about the people you serve, and what would it not tell you?
Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. That is what Name the Decision is for. The pre-work is deliberately short; an earlier version of this module ran close to an hour across three parts and that version does not survive contact with a chapter calendar. If your group wants the longer version, the external data review is the part worth extending.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard divided into two columns, markers
Purpose: Establish that everyone in the room already uses both kinds of evidence fluently, before anyone is told what quantitative and qualitative mean.
Setup (say this to participants)
“Imagine you are visiting a new city and need to choose a restaurant for dinner tonight. Take thirty seconds. How do you decide?”
The Activity

items: Take answers fast and write every one on the board, unsorted. Do not evaluate.
Once you have fifteen or so, draw a line down the middle and ask the room to sort them into two columns. Do not name the columns.
When the sorting is mostly done, ask what the two columns are. Someone will say numbers and feelings. Rename them out loud: quantitative and qualitative.

blocks.text: Typical left column: star rating, number of reviews, distance, price range, how busy it is. Typical right column: a friend said so, the photos looked right, it smelled good, the menu was in the language of the food.
Debrief

items: Which column did you fill first, and which one actually decided it?
Has a four-star average ever been wrong for you? What did it miss?
Would you go somewhere with two hundred reviews and no recommendation, or one recommendation and no reviews?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: nobody in this room needs to be taught to combine these. You do it every week. What is hard at work is that the numbers arrive on a dashboard and the reasons arrive in a conversation you have to go and have.
Facilitator note

Do not label the columns before the room sorts. The moment where a participant names the distinction themselves is worth more than the definition, and it makes the Teaching Note later feel like a summary rather than a lecture.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard divided into two columns, markers
Purpose: The same two-column exercise, raised to a decision with real consequences, where people notice that the qualitative column starts to outrank the quantitative one.
Setup (say this to participants)
“Now imagine you are choosing a day care for a one-year-old. Same question. How do you decide?”
The Activity

items: Run it exactly as before: collect, sort into two columns, name them.

Left column will include licensing status, accreditation, staff-to-child ratio, inspection history, cost, curriculum. Right column will include how the room felt, how staff spoke to the children, whether a parent you trust sends their child there, whether anyone made eye contact with you.

blocks.text: Debrief

items: What changed between the restaurant and the day care?
The stakes went up. Which column got more weight, and why that one?
Would you enroll on a perfect inspection record and a bad visit? On a great visit and a poor record?
Who would you actually call before deciding, and what does that tell you about where trusted information lives?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: when it matters most, people go and look, and they ask someone they trust. That instinct is correct, and it is exactly what gets dropped when the decision is about a community rather than about your own child.
Facilitator note

Run this one or the restaurant, not usually both, unless you want the escalation. If you run both, run them back to back and make the comparison the whole point; the second one takes half as long because the room already knows the move.
Materials: None. Small groups of three or four.
Purpose: Move from personal decisions to organizational ones, and get the words familiarity and convenience said out loud by participants rather than by the facilitator.
Setup (say this to participants)
“In small groups, take five minutes on these three questions. We will come back together after.”
The Activity

items: What information most influences your operational decisions?
Have you ever seen a decision made based on familiarity or convenience rather than need?
What risks emerge when an organization relies on gut instinct alone?

blocks.text: Sharing out
Bring the room back and collect themes rather than stories. Four will come up almost every time, and it is worth naming them on the board as they surface:

items: Familiarity bias. We go where we already know people.
Low-hanging fruit. We go where it is easy to hit the number.
Evidence versus anecdote. One vivid story outweighs a table.
The tension between relationships and equitable allocation. Both are real, and they do not always point the same way.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The second question is the one that does the work, and it needs a beat of silence. Someone will eventually name a decision their own chapter made. Do not rescue the room from that pause, and do not let the group turn it into a complaint about leadership; the useful version is the one where a participant describes a decision they made themselves.
Materials: None. Small groups of three or four.
Purpose: Open the improvement half of the skill by starting from a broken process everyone in the room has personally suffered, rather than from a definition of Lean.
Setup (say this to participants)
“In small groups, think of one operational process you have been through that was genuinely frustrating. Ours or anyone’s. You have ten minutes on these four questions.”
The Activity

items: What caused the breakdown?
Where was there waste? Waiting, duplicated effort, rework, information that had to be entered twice.
Whose perspective was missing from the design of that process?
How could a feedback loop or a conversation across teams have caught it earlier?

blocks.text: Sharing out
Collect and name the pattern rather than the incidents:

items: Waste shows up as delay, duplication, unclear ownership, and communication that goes one direction.
Almost every example involves two functions that never talked to each other.
The person who could have named the problem on day one is usually the person doing the work, and usually was not asked.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Keep this from becoming a venting session by holding people to the fourth question. The test of a good share-out here is whether the group names a fix rather than a villain. If a story lands on a named individual, redirect once: “What in the process let that happen?”
Materials: A whiteboard or three sheets of easel paper, sticky notes in two colors, markers. A shared digital board works if the columns are pre-drawn.

Purpose: Produce the two things the rest of the session works from, in the room, without depending on anyone having done pre-work: one real decision, and an honest inventory of the evidence available to make it.
Why this comes first

Every core experience in this skill acts on a decision and the evidence behind it. If you rely on pre-work to supply those, the session splits into people who are ready and people who are catching up. Building them together removes that problem, and the inventory a group produces jointly is always more honest than the one an individual writes alone, because somebody will say out loud that a report everyone cites has not been updated in two years.
Choose the decision first
Pick one of these before the session. All three work; the choice depends on the room.

Option A, one shared decision. You supply a single decision and everyone works it together. Best for mixed groups, for people from different chapters, and whenever you cannot count on participants having a live one. Also the safest with a new group, because nobody is exposing their own work.

Option B, one volunteered decision. A participant offers a real decision they are responsible for and the room works it for them. Best for a single chapter team, and it produces the most usable wall. Ask privately beforehand rather than on the spot.

Option C, everyone contributes their own. Each participant adds from their own decision and the group looks at the pattern across them. Best when most people did the pre-work, and for large groups. Produces breadth rather than depth.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Before we can talk about evidence, we need something to decide. In the next fifteen minutes we are going to put one real decision on this board, and then be honest about what we actually know. This stays up all session. Everything after this is a revision of it.”
The Activity
Step 1 (2 min): Name the decision

items: Write it at the top of the board in one sentence: what has to be decided, for whom, and by when.
Underneath it, write how it would be decided today if nobody asked for a justification. Say that this is not a confession, it is the baseline.

blocks.text: Step 2 (5 min): What would change our mind?
On the first color of sticky note, one per note: what would you need to know to decide this well? Push past the obvious. Prompt with the categories rather than with examples:

items: Who is most at risk here, and how do we know?
Who is already being reached, and who is not?
What has been tried here before, and what happened?
Who would have to say yes for this to work?
What would tell us afterward whether it worked?

blocks.text: Step 3 (5 min): Mark what we have
Go through the notes as a group and mark each one:

items: H, we have it and could produce it this week.
G, it exists and we would have to go get it. Write where from.
N, nobody has it, or nobody in this room knows.

blocks.text: Put the second color of sticky note next to any item where the group disagreed about which letter it gets. Those are the interesting ones.
Step 4 (3 min): Read it back

items: How many of the things that would change our mind are marked N?
Of the things marked H, how many are numbers and how many are things people told us?
Is there anything on this board we have never actually looked at, but cite anyway?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: this board is the honest version. Most groups find they hold plenty of operational data about themselves and very little about the people they are not currently reaching, which is exactly the shape that keeps a chapter working where it already works. The rest of the session is about what to do with that.
Facilitator note

Resist letting the group solve the decision during this activity. They will want to. The point is to expose the evidence base, not to close it out, and there are three core experiences after this that need somewhere to go.

A good board has twelve to twenty notes with at least four marked N. Fewer than eight notes means the decision was too vague; restate it with a real place and a real deadline and take another two minutes. Photograph the board before teardown and send it to participants.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which option will you run, and why does it fit this group?
If Option A, what decision will you supply? Write it as one sentence, with a real place and a real deadline.
If Option B, who have you asked in advance, and have they agreed?

title: Teaching Note: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Asset Data

blocks.text: Purpose: Give the room the three lenses the prioritization exercises assume, after they have already used two of them in the icebreakers.
This is the one place in the skill where the facilitator talks for more than a few minutes at a time. Keep it to the three lists and the five questions; the questions are where the learning is.
Quantitative: what exists at scale

items: Fire incident rates and historical disaster impact data
Census demographics: age, income, language, disability, housing tenure and age
CDC Social Vulnerability Index
FEMA National Risk Index
Poverty and housing indicators
Our own service delivery data: response times, client demographics, training completions, volunteer participation

blocks.text: Qualitative: what explains it

items: Resident interviews and community concerns
Volunteer observations, which are the most underused data source most chapters have
Partner feedback
Lived experience
After-action reviews

blocks.text: Asset data: what is already there
Borrowed from Asset Mapping, and the reason this skill draws on it. Risk data tells you where to go. Asset data tells you how to get in.

items: Community strengths and networks
Trusted local organizations and the people who convene them
Volunteer and neighborhood capacity
Existing community leadership, formal and informal
Local partnerships that make outreach land

blocks.text: Key discussion questions

items: What can numbers tell us that relationships alone cannot?
What can lived experience reveal that statistics alone may miss?
Why can gut instinct unintentionally reinforce inequities?
How can an organization avoid prioritizing communities simply because they are easier to engage?
What responsibility do we have to make sure resources reach those at greatest risk?

blocks.text: Facilitator talking point

Say this one plainly, because it is the thesis of the whole skill: the correct operational outcome is not distributing resources where it is easiest, fastest, or most familiar. It is making sure resources reach the populations with the greatest demonstrated need, using the best available evidence.
FACILITATOR PREP
Name one dataset your own region actually uses, and one it should use and does not. Have both ready; a live example beats the generic list.

title: Teaching Note: Lean Thinking, Feedback Loops, and PDSA

blocks.text: Purpose: Give the room the improvement cycle and the disposition that makes it work, before the simulation asks them to run one.
What a feedback loop is

A structured, repeatable process: collect information, analyze it, learn from it, change something, then check whether the change improved the outcome. The word repeatable is doing the work. A one-time after-action review is not a loop.
Most organizations ask whether services were delivered. A loop asks four harder questions: did it actually help, who benefited most, who did we fail to reach, and what should change next time.
PDSA
Plan. Name the change you will test, what you expect to happen, and how you will know. Small enough to run in weeks, not quarters.
Do. Run it, at small scale, and record what actually happened rather than what was supposed to.
Study. Compare what happened to what you predicted. This is the step organizations skip, because it is the step where you find out you were wrong.
Act. Adopt it, adapt it, or abandon it. Then start the next cycle. Abandon is a legitimate outcome and saying so out loud is what makes the next test honest.
Lean ideas worth carrying

items: Respect for people. The person doing the work knows where it breaks. Ask them first.
Waste is anything the person you serve would not pay for: waiting, duplication, rework, unnecessary handoffs, information entered twice.
Improvement over blame. Ask what in the process allowed this, not who did it.
Disagreement is data. When two functions describe the same process differently, one of them is seeing something the other cannot.
Root cause over symptom. The wait time is the symptom. The staging distance is the cause.

blocks.text: Discussion prompts

items: How can disagreement reveal process weaknesses or blind spots?
What happens when an organization avoids the difficult conversation?
Where in our work do we collect information that nobody ever looks at again?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The temptation is to teach PDSA as a diagram. Do not. Ask the room for one process they would test a change on this month and walk that one example around the cycle out loud. Fifteen minutes on a real example beats thirty on the model.

Materials: Water pitchers, sugar, citric acid or lemons and lemon juice, flavorings or syrups or fruit, measuring cups and spoons, mixing cups, disposable tasting cups, napkins, pens, and the PDSA Cycle Worksheet (page 41) for each group. Yes, you are really making lemonade.
Purpose: Run a full PDSA cycle twice, with a real product and real disagreement, in a setting where being wrong costs nothing.
Setup (say this to participants)

“You are going to make the best lemonade in this room. You will get two attempts. Between them you are going to do the thing organizations almost never do, which is look honestly at what happened and change something specific because of it.”
Break into groups of four to six. Every group gets the same ingredients and one worksheet.
The Activity
Round 1: Plan (5 min)

items: What should this taste like? Agree on it before you pour anything.
What proportions are you starting with, and why those?
What are you assuming? Write the assumptions down; you will check them later.
Write version one on the worksheet, with measurements. If it is not written down you cannot study it.

blocks.text: Round 2: Do (5 min)

items: Make it and taste it. Everyone tastes.
Rate it on the worksheet: taste balance, sweetness, sourness, flavor strength, overall.

blocks.text: Round 3: Study (5 min)

items: What worked and what did not?
What feedback came from people in the group, and did anyone disagree?
Which of your written assumptions turned out to be wrong?
Where did you waste something: ingredients, time, an argument you had twice?

blocks.text: Facilitator highlights while groups work: different perspectives improve outcomes, testing beats asserting, and observation and taste are data even though they are not numbers.
Round 4: Act (5 min)

items: Change one thing, deliberately, because of something in Study. Not three things.
Make version two, taste, and rate it on the same five measures.

blocks.text: Debrief (5 min)

items: What changed between version one and version two, and what evidence drove it?
Did disagreement help or slow you down?
Which assumption turned out to be wrong, and how long would you have held it without the taste test?
How is this like improving an onboarding process or a distribution site?
What would a third cycle have changed?

blocks.text: Connecting it back
The cycle. Plan a change, test it, study what happened, adjust. Groups that changed one variable can say what worked. Groups that changed four cannot.
Respect for people. The person who tasted it and made a face gave you better data than the person who measured the sugar.
The point. Organizations do not improve by getting it right the first time. They improve by building something that learns.
Variations

items: Start every group with a deliberately bad batch, far too sour or with no flavor at all, and have them improve from there. Faster, and it removes the temptation to defend version one.
Give groups a target to replicate, a named commercial lemonade, so there is an external standard rather than a group preference.
Give one group a member who was not in the room for Plan. Watch what happens in Study.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The timing is tight and the debrief is what matters, so hold the rounds to five minutes each even if a group is not finished. A group that runs out of time in Round 1 has learned something real about planning.

Ingredients cost about fifteen dollars for a group of twenty and the exercise fails without them. Do not run this as a thought experiment; the entire point is that the feedback is physical and immediate.
Materials: Prioritization Scoring Worksheet (page 39) for each group, this scenario printed, pens
Purpose: Work a real prioritization problem end to end with a method that can be defended out loud, and discover that health risk alone does not answer it.
Setup (say this to participants)

“You are a preparedness and community resilience team in Alabama. Your job this year is to reduce deaths from cardiac arrest outside a hospital, by putting citizen CPR training, first aid training, and AED access where they will save the most lives. You have six census tracts, one budget, and sixty minutes.”
Why this matters, in four numbers

items: More than 356,000 cardiac arrests happen outside a hospital in the United States each year.
About 70 percent happen at home, so the first person available is a family member or a neighbor.
Bystander CPR can double or triple the chance of survival.
Survival falls roughly 7 to 10 percent for every minute without CPR or defibrillation, and brain injury can begin within 4 to 6 minutes.

blocks.text: In rural Alabama, emergency response plus transport can exceed the window in which irreversible injury begins. That is the whole argument for training the neighbors.
The practice dataset
Modeled figures patterned on CDC PLACES indicators for six Alabama census tracts. Real tract identifiers, teaching numbers. Read the row, not the identifier.

[MADELINE AND CAROL: these are modeled values, not the published CDC PLACES figures. Modeled is defensible for teaching and it keeps the contrasts sharp. Tell us if you would rather this ran on the real published values for these tracts and we will pull them.]
