blocks.text: Part 1: Read the data (10 min)

items: Which tract carries the highest cardiovascular burden?
Which tract is most vulnerable to a bad outcome once an arrest happens? Notice that this is a different question.
Which tracts combine high disease burden, long response times, and poor access?
Which are least served by existing CPR programming?

blocks.text: Part 2: Score them (20 min)

Use the Prioritization Scoring Worksheet. The method is on the handout and it takes ranks rather than raw values, because a percentage and a distance in miles cannot be added together. Weights for this decision:

items: Coronary heart disease, 25 percent
High blood pressure, 15 percent
Diabetes, 15 percent
Adults 65 and over, 15 percent
Distance to hospital, 15 percent
Emergency response time, 10 percent
Poverty rate, 5 percent

blocks.text: Rank the six tracts on each indicator, 6 for the highest need down to 1 for the lowest, multiply each rank by the weight, and total. Then name your top two for immediate CPR and AED investment, and one for preventive outreach, and be ready to say why in one sentence each.
Part 3: The equity conversation (15 min)

items: Why might a rural community need more investment in citizen CPR than an urban one with the same disease rates?
How does poverty affect a household’s preparedness capacity?
Why is geographic access an equity issue rather than a logistics issue?
Which populations are least likely to receive bystander CPR, and what would change that?

blocks.text: Part 4: Two things only (15 min)

You have resources for two interventions in your chosen tracts this year. Choose from: community CPR classes, high school based CPR education, partnerships with churches and community centers, volunteer responder networks, multilingual outreach.

items: Which two, and in which tracts?
What would tell you a year from now whether it worked? Name the measure, not the activity.
What would make implementation fail, and who would you need on your side to prevent that?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide: where the scoring lands

Wilcox County, tract 01131000400, ZIP 36793, comes out first on almost any reasonable weighting. It is highest on every disease measure, highest on age and poverty, farthest from a hospital, longest response time, and has no existing programming. Greene County is a clear second.
The point is not that the group finds Wilcox. It is what they notice on the way. Three teaching points, in order of how often they land:

Disease burden alone is not the answer. Mobile County has meaningfully higher disease rates than Madison County, but a nine minute response and a hospital seven miles away. Access changes what the same disease rate means.
CPR training is a resilience strategy, not a class. It extends the chain of survival across the gap between the call and the ambulance. The longer that gap, the more a trained neighbor is worth.

Geography creates health inequity. Nobody chose to put Wilcox County 33 miles from a hospital, and no amount of individual preparedness closes that distance. That is what makes it a targeting question rather than an education question.
Extension for groups with GIS access

Optional and only if someone in the room already works in a mapping tool; do not schedule it into a session. Pull real Alabama tract data from the CDC PLACES portal, map coronary heart disease, hypertension and diabetes prevalence, then overlay hospital locations, emergency service stations, the Social Vulnerability Index, population 65 and over, and poverty. Look for high-risk clusters, training deserts, and candidate AED sites. Hospital and station locations are not in the practice dataset and would have to be sourced separately.
Sources for the framing numbers

items: CDC PLACES data portal: https://www.cdc.gov/places/tools/data-portal.html
CDC, cardiac arrest: https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/about/cardiac-arrest.html
American Heart Association, CPR facts and statistics: https://cpr.heart.org/en/resources/cpr-facts-and-stats

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP

This scenario is Alabama. If your region is not, decide before you deliver whether to run it as is, which works because the distances are stark, or to rebuild it with tracts from your own state, which lands harder but takes an evening in CDC PLACES.
Which will you do, and if rebuilding, which county? ______________________
One local fact you can add about response times where you work: ________
Materials: This scenario printed for every group, Prioritization Scoring Worksheet (page 39), markers
Purpose: Make a real allocation decision where the numbers point one way, the relationships point another, and the group has to say out loud which one wins.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Everyone wants smoke alarms. The disaster team wants them. Two board members have asked. Three communities have requested support. You have 300 alarms and twelve volunteer install days, and that is the whole year. In the next fifty-five minutes you are going to decide where they go, and then defend it.”
The scenario: Cedar County
Fictional, built so that the obvious answer is defensible and probably wrong. Four neighborhoods. Give every group the same pack.
Riverbend

items: 4,100 households. Home fires: 3.1 per 1,000 households per year, five-year average. Four fire injuries or deaths in five years.
Poverty 18 percent. Renter-occupied 46 percent. Housing built before 1975: 38 percent. Adults 65 and over living alone: 9 percent. Primary language other than English: 11 percent.
Estimated smoke alarm coverage 74 percent. Red Cross installs in the last three years: 610.

blocks.text: What people say. The community center director: “You all were just here last year. We love you, but I think the folks who need it already have them.”
What is already there. Riverbend Community Center, an established partner. Easy to schedule, reliable turnout, they will do the outreach for you.
Old Mill

items: 1,250 households. Home fires: 7.8 per 1,000 households per year. Nine fire injuries or deaths in five years.
Poverty 34 percent. Renter-occupied 71 percent. Housing built before 1975: 86 percent. Adults 65 and over living alone: 17 percent. Primary language other than English: 38 percent.
Estimated smoke alarm coverage 41 percent. Red Cross installs in the last three years: 20.

blocks.text: What people say. A resident, through an interpreter: “The last time somebody from an agency knocked, my neighbor did not open the door. She thought it was about her lease.”

What is already there. Rosa Villalobos runs a Saturday market in the church parking lot and the tenants association meets there monthly. One management company owns roughly 400 of the units and has never been asked for anything.
Fairview Terrace

items: 2,900 households. Home fires: 2.2 per 1,000 households per year. One fire injury or death in five years.
Poverty 12 percent. Renter-occupied 22 percent. Housing built before 1975: 15 percent. Adults 65 and over living alone: 6 percent. Primary language other than English: 5 percent.
Estimated smoke alarm coverage 88 percent. Red Cross installs in the last three years: 340.

blocks.text: What people say. Your own volunteer coordinator: “Fairview is where most of our volunteers live, so it is the easiest install day to staff. We fill it every time.”
What is already there. A very active neighborhood association that asks for a preparedness event every spring, and two board members who live here.
Kettle Flats

items: 860 households. Home fires: 6.9 per 1,000 households per year. Five fire injuries or deaths in five years.
Poverty 41 percent. Renter-occupied 63 percent. Housing built before 1975: 79 percent. Adults 65 and over living alone: 22 percent. Primary language other than English: 9 percent.
Estimated smoke alarm coverage 38 percent. Red Cross installs in the last three years: 0.

blocks.text: What people say. A volunteer firefighter: “We have had three calls out there this year where the alarm was sitting on the counter with the battery out because it kept chirping.”

What is already there. Dale Whitcomb at the volunteer fire department knows every road and every household. There is no community organization of any kind. Housing is dispersed and drive times between installs are long.
Part 1: What do the numbers say? (10 min)

items: Which neighborhood has the most home fires per year in absolute terms? Do the arithmetic; it matters.
Which has the highest rate?
Which has the lowest alarm coverage, and where have we already been?

blocks.text: Part 2: Score it (15 min)
Use the Prioritization Scoring Worksheet. Suggested weights for a smoke alarm decision, and groups may argue with them, which is a good use of five minutes:

items: Home fires per 1,000 households, 30 percent
Estimated alarm coverage, lower is higher need, 25 percent
Housing built before 1975, 15 percent
Households below poverty, 15 percent
Adults 65 and over living alone, 10 percent
Prior Red Cross installs, fewer is higher need, 5 percent

blocks.text: Part 3: Now add what people said (15 min)
Go back through with the quotes and the asset information in front of you.

items: Does anything you were told change the ranking, or does it change how you would implement it?
Kettle Flats has alarms that were installed and then disabled. What does that do to the value of installing 300 more?
Old Mill has the second highest rate and a door that does not open. Who opens it, and what do you have to do first?
You have twelve install days. Kettle Flats is dispersed and slow. Does operational cost belong in an equity decision, and if you say no, say what you would cut to pay for it.

blocks.text: Part 4: Decide and defend (10 min)
Each group states, in three sentences: where the 300 alarms go, how the twelve days are split, and what they are telling the community that does not get them.
Debrief (5 min)

items: Which evidence moved you most, and was it a number or a sentence?
Did anyone start with Riverbend because it had the most fires? What is wrong with that, and what is right about it?
Who found the Fairview quote, and what did the room do when it was read out?
What would you have to say to the Fairview neighborhood association, and who says it?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide: what is in the scenario

Riverbend is the trap of scale. It has the most fires per year in raw count, roughly 13, because it is the biggest neighborhood. It also has decent coverage and 610 recent installs. Groups that rank on absolute counts land here, and the community center director tells them not to.

Fairview is the trap of convenience, and it is named. The quote is from the chapter’s own staff. Every group notices it eventually and the room usually goes quiet. That is the moment the session exists for. Do not fill the silence.

Old Mill is the highest scoring on most weightings, and it is the hardest to enter. The answer is not to skip it; it is that the first install day is not an install day. It is Rosa Villalobos, the tenants association, and one conversation with a management company nobody has ever called.

Kettle Flats is the one that tests whether the group is listening. The firefighter quote says alarms were installed and disabled. More alarms without addressing the chirping, the ten-year sealed battery option, and someone residents trust is money spent on a number rather than on safety.
What the facilitator should say at the close

items: The mission-driven responsibility is to serve the populations most at risk.
Combining the two kinds of evidence produces a better decision than either alone, and this scenario cannot be solved with only one of them.
Existing relationships and operational ease are real constraints. They are not the criteria.
Equity usually costs more operationally. If your allocation did not cost you anything, check whether you actually changed it.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Do not hand out the quotes with the numbers. Give the numbers first, let groups start scoring, and distribute the quotes at the ten minute mark. Watching a group revise a ranking it already committed to is worth more than watching it weigh everything at once, and it is a fair simulation of how this information actually arrives.
FACILITATOR PREP
Cedar County works anywhere, but a real one works better. Decide whether to swap in four neighborhoods from your own region with real fire data.
Where you would get the fire incident data: ___________________________
One place your own chapter has gone because it was easy: _______________

Materials: Role cards below, printed and cut. The process map below, printed for every group. PDSA Cycle Worksheet (page 41). A tracking sheet for each observer, described below. A stack of blank forms to act as volunteer applications.
Purpose: Run a broken process, feel where it breaks from inside a role that is not your own, then improve it with a real PDSA cycle and measure whether it worked.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Volunteer satisfaction is falling and onboarding takes about two months. Every team has an explanation and every explanation blames a different team. You are going to run the process, twice, and find out where it actually breaks.”
The process, as it exists today
Print this and post it. Seven steps, four handoffs.

items: 1. Prospective volunteer submits an application online.
2. Volunteer Services reviews it for completeness and requests anything missing.
3. Background check is initiated and returns, on paper, to a different inbox.
4. Volunteer Services confirms the check and forwards the file to the program lead.
5. Program lead approves the placement, or asks for a phone conversation first.
6. Training coordinator assigns a course and a date from a monthly schedule.
7. Volunteer completes training and is activated.

blocks.text: Roles
Print one card per participant. Groups of six to eight. Every group needs one Observer.

Volunteer Services Lead. You process every application. You are measured on the number of volunteers activated per month. You cannot start a background check until the application is complete, and roughly a third arrive incomplete. You are convinced the delay is the program leads, who sit on files.

Background Check Coordinator. Checks come back to you in batches, twice a week. You process them in the order received. You have no visibility into which applicants are urgent, and nobody has ever told you that anyone is waiting.

Program Lead. You approve placements. You want a phone conversation with anyone going into a client-facing role and you are only free on Tuesdays and Thursdays. You believe the real problem is that Volunteer Services sends you people who are a poor fit.

Training Coordinator. You run courses monthly. If someone misses the cutoff by two days they wait four weeks. You are measured on course completion rates, so you would rather hold a person than have them start and drop out.
New Volunteer, applicant A. You applied six weeks ago and you have heard nothing since the automatic confirmation email. You have called twice. You are starting to assume they do not need you.

New Volunteer, applicant B. You applied last week. Your application was incomplete because the form asked for a supervisor reference and you have not worked in nine years. You do not know it was incomplete.

Longtime Volunteer. You have been here eleven years. You brought applicant A in personally and you are embarrassed. You know four workarounds nobody has ever written down, and you will not offer them unless asked.
Observer. You do not speak during the rounds. You hold the tracking sheet and you record what actually happens, not what people say happens.
The Observer tracking sheet
Four columns, and the Observer fills them during both rounds. This is the only quantitative data the group will have, so it matters.

items: Volunteers activated, count.
Elapsed steps for each applicant, and where each one is sitting when the round ends.
Every handoff, and how long the file waited before the next person touched it.
Every rework: anything asked for twice, entered twice, or sent back.

blocks.text: Round 1: Run it as written (10 min)

items: Play it in real time, compressed. One minute of play equals one week of calendar.
Everyone stays in role. The Volunteer Services Lead may not simply fix things by fiat.
Observers say nothing and write everything.

blocks.text: Debrief 1 (10 min)

items: Observers report the numbers first, before anyone explains. Numbers before narrative.
Where did the file wait longest, and did the person who was waiting know?
Which two roles never spoke to each other?
What did each of you think the problem was, and were you right?
Ask the Longtime Volunteer what workarounds they know. Ask why nobody had asked.

blocks.text: PDSA cycle (10 min)
Using the PDSA Cycle Worksheet, each group plans exactly one change. One. Groups that change four things cannot tell you which one worked.

items: Plan: what will you change, what do you expect to happen, and what number will tell you?
Predict it out loud before you run it. Write the prediction down.

blocks.text: Round 2: Run it again (10 min)

items: Same roles, same applicants, one change.
Observers track the same four columns.

blocks.text: Debrief 2 and Act (15 min)

items: Study: what actually happened, compared to what you predicted? Where were you wrong?
Act: adopt, adapt, or abandon. Say which, and say it as a group.
What did the change cost, and who absorbed that cost? Improvements usually move work rather than remove it.
Which measure would you watch for the next three months to know it held?
What is the second change you would test, and why not that one first?

blocks.text: Debrief questions worth keeping

items: What perspective was hardest to hear?
Where did operational silos appear, and were they anyone’s fault?
What assumptions surfaced that nobody had ever said out loud?
How did respectful disagreement change the conversation?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The most common change groups pick is a shared tracker so everyone can see where a file is. It usually works, and it is worth pointing out that it did not remove a single step; it removed the waiting that nobody could see. That is a real Lean result and a good place to land.

The role cards are written so that every person is behaving reasonably and being measured on something that conflicts with somebody else’s measure. If a group starts blaming an individual, ask what that person is measured on. That question ends the blame every time.
If you have fewer than six participants, cut applicant B and the Longtime Volunteer first. Never cut the Observer.
FACILITATOR PREP

Substitute your own process if you have one that is genuinely broken and people can speak about without it becoming personal. Onboarding is the safe default because everyone has suffered it and nobody owns it alone.
If you use your own, who has to be comfortable with it being the example? ____
Format: Facilitated dialogue. Participants build shared understanding through guided questioning rather than lecture.
Purpose: Frame data-informed learning as a leadership posture rather than a technical capability, and surface the reasons people in this room already distrust or avoid data.
Agenda at a glance

items: 0 to 5 minutes: Opening frame
5 to 15 minutes: What we mean by the words
15 to 27 minutes: What we actually do now
27 to 42 minutes: Where it breaks
42 to 53 minutes: What a better version looks like
53 to 60 minutes: Commitment and close

blocks.text: Before you start

Two rules, said out loud. First, there are no wrong answers about how decisions are currently made, and nothing said here is a performance conversation. Second, when someone describes a decision made on instinct, nobody rescues them.
Opening frame (0 to 5 min)

Say: “This hour is not about dashboards. It is about what happens in the ten seconds before a decision, when you already know what you are going to do and you are looking for a reason. We are going to be honest about that.”
Segment 1: What we mean by the words (5 to 15 min)

items: When you hear data-informed learning, what does it mean to you?
What kinds of decisions in your role rely most on data?
Can you share an example of when data changed, or confirmed, a decision?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Most rooms define it as measurement. Name the difference: measurement is counting what happened, and this skill is about changing what you do next. Also note whether the examples offered are all confirmations rather than changes, because that is usually true and it is worth saying.
Segment 2: What we actually do now (15 to 27 min)

items: In your role, how do you currently use and interpret data?
What tools or sources do you use most often? Internal systems, or external ones?
What types of data do you trust most, and why that one?
Why is data important for decision making in a chapter?
How can data help us reach people we are currently missing?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. The trust question is the useful one. People trust what they collected themselves and distrust what arrives from above, which is rational and also means most external risk data goes unread. Say that, and ask whether it is serving them.
Segment 3: Where it breaks (27 to 42 min)

items: What are the biggest challenges you face in collecting data?
In interpreting it?
In turning findings into action?
What barriers prevent data from informing an operational decision?
Where do feedback loops break down in your work?
What are the risks of deciding without data?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Three answers recur: we collect things nobody looks at, the data arrives after the decision, and the person who could interpret it was not in the room. All three are process problems rather than analysis problems. Name that, because it moves the conversation from “we need better data” to “we need a different loop,” which is the thing they can actually change.
If the room goes quiet. Ask which report their chapter produces that nobody reads. Somebody always knows.
Segment 4: What a better version looks like (42 to 53 min)

items: How can feedback loops support continuous improvement?
In an ideal world, how would you use data to set priorities?
What skills, tools, or support would help you use data more effectively?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Push past “a better system.” Ask what they would do differently on Monday with the data they already have. The honest answer is usually that they would look at something they have been avoiding.
Segment 5: Commitment and close (53 to 60 min)

items: What is one insight you are taking away from this discussion?
What is one small change that would improve data-informed decision making in your work?

blocks.text: Take the second answer from every person, out loud, and hold them to one sentence. Write them down and send them back to the group afterward.
The ethics segment, if you have the time
Worth ten extra minutes whenever the group is senior enough to act on it. Incomplete data, biased collection, and missing voices can reinforce inequity rather than reveal it. Three questions:

items: Whose experience is missing from the data we hold, and why is it missing?
What would we conclude about a community if we only ever counted the people who came to us?
What are we obligated to tell a community about data we collected from them?

blocks.text: Train-the-Trainer
Read this before your first delivery.
What this session is for

It is not an introduction to analytics. It is the session where a group admits how decisions actually get made, which is what makes the prioritization exercises land later. If you teach content here, the exercises become an academic problem instead of a mirror.
Four guardrails
Do not defend data. Someone will say the numbers are always wrong or always late. They are often right. Agree, and ask what they use instead, and then ask how they know that is better.

Do not let it become a technology conversation. The room will drift toward systems, licenses, and who owns which dashboard. Redirect once: “Suppose the system were perfect. What would you do differently?”

Hold the silence after the honest answers. The most valuable moment is when a participant describes a decision they made on familiarity. Do not thank them, do not soften it, and do not follow it with a better example. Wait.

Synthesize, do not conclude. End each segment by naming the pattern in the room’s answers rather than by giving the right one. The synthesis lines above are prompts, not scripts; use the room’s own words.
Common failure modes

items: The facilitator answers their own question within four seconds. Count to ten.
One participant with a technical background becomes the room’s expert and everyone else stops talking. Ask a non-technical participant a question directly by name.
The group agrees enthusiastically that data is important and nothing is at risk. If nobody has been uncomfortable by minute thirty, ask segment three’s barrier question again, harder.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP

Bring one decision from your own work that you made on instinct and later found the evidence against. You will need it in segment three, and a borrowed example does not buy the same honesty from the room.
What the evidence turned out to say: __________________________________
Decide what you will do with the commitments from segment five, and say so at the close.
Field Assignments

These are not room activities. Two of them happen in your own kitchen, which is deliberate: the cycle is easier to feel on something you care about and cannot blame anyone else for. Assign one at the close of a session and open the next session with what people found.
Field Assignment 1: Recreate a recipe you never wrote down
Pick something a family member made that you have never made correctly. Chili, a sauce, a bread. You have no written recipe.

items: Plan: write down what you think is in it and in what proportion. Write the assumption you are least sure about.
Do: make it. Once.
Study: taste it against your memory, and ask one other person. Where is it wrong, specifically?
Act: change one thing. Make it again.

blocks.text: Bring back. The assumption you were most confident about that turned out to be wrong, and how many cycles it would take to get there.
Field Assignment 2: Run one week of groceries on evidence
Instead of shopping on habit, decide with data for one week.

items: Gather: your last two months of receipts, and what actually got thrown away.
Find the pattern: what do you buy and not eat? What do you buy repeatedly? Where does the money go that you would not have guessed?
Prioritize: buy the things that get eaten, drop or substitute the things that get wasted.
Check: at the end of the week, what did you spend and what did you throw away?

blocks.text: Bring back. One thing the receipts told you that you would have denied beforehand. That gap is the whole skill in miniature.
Field Assignment 3: Find the report nobody reads
Inside your own chapter or region.

items: Find one recurring report, dashboard, or data collection that somebody produces on a schedule.
Ask three people what decision it informs. Write down the answers.
Ask the person who produces it how long it takes them.
Then find one decision your team makes regularly with no data at all.

blocks.text: Bring back. The hours per month going into something nobody uses, and the decision that has nothing behind it. In most chapters these are the same number of hours.
Using these with public data

Before or after any of the three, look your own county up in the CDC Social Vulnerability Index, the FEMA National Risk Index, and the Census data explorer. Two questions: who is most at risk here, and which organizations are already working with them? The data tells you where to look. It does not tell you who to talk to, which is what Asset Mapping and Stakeholder Mapping are for.
Session Formats
Four written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document; nothing new has to be written to deliver any of them.
20 minutes. Two Kinds of Evidence. One idea, delivered inside a meeting you were already having.
1 hour. From Instinct to Evidence. Introduces both kinds of data and produces an honest inventory.
2 hours. Deciding Where the Need Is Greatest. The targeting half, ending in a defended allocation.
4 hours. The Full Cycle. Both halves, ending with a tested change and a measure.
How to choose

This skill has two halves and they do not fit in the same hour. If you have two hours, teach targeting. If you have two hours and the group already targets well, teach the loop. Do not attempt both in under four hours; the version that tries produces a room that can define PDSA and has not used it.
20-minute version: Two Kinds of Evidence

items: Run How Do You Choose, page 10 (10 min)
Name the two columns and give three work examples of each (5 min)
One question: what is a decision we are about to make where we have one column and not the other? (5 min)

blocks.text: What they leave with: the distinction, and one decision it applies to.

title: One-Hour Workshop: From Instinct to Evidence

blocks.text: Purpose: Establish the two kinds of evidence, and produce an honest inventory of what this group actually has for one real decision.
Pre-work: Optional (page 9).
Materials: Whiteboard or easel paper, sticky notes in two colors, markers, Data Inventory handout (page 38) for each participant.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: we usually decide by proximity, today we decide by evidence (5 min)
Icebreaker: How Do You Choose, page 10 (10 min)
Icebreaker: What Data Shapes Your Decisions, page 12 (10 min)
Icebreaker: Name the Decision, page 14 (15 min)
Individually, transfer the board onto the Data Inventory handout and add anything specific to your own work (10 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: How many of the things that would change our mind are marked N?
What do we hold a lot of, and what do we hold almost none of?
What is one thing marked G that you could actually go and get this month?
What will you do differently on Monday?

blocks.text: What they leave with: one real decision written down, an inventory of the evidence behind it, and a named gap.
Notes on running it

items: This hour deliberately does not reach a decision. Say so at the close, or the room will feel it stopped early.
If the group is senior and impatient, swap How Do You Choose for Choosing the Right Day Care, page 11. Higher stakes, same move, and it takes the eye-roll out of the restaurant question.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Which Name the Decision option will you run, and what decision will you supply?

title: Two-Hour Workshop: Deciding Where the Need Is Greatest

blocks.text: Purpose: Take a group from no shared starting point to an allocation decision they have argued for out loud, and confront the gap between where the need is and where it is convenient to work.
Materials: As for the one-hour, plus the Cedar County scenario printed for each group and the Prioritization Scoring Worksheet (page 39).
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (10 min)
Icebreaker: What Data Shapes Your Decisions, page 12 (10 min)
Teaching Note: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Asset Data, page 16 (25 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: Allocating Scarce Resources, page 24 (55 min)
Reflection and closing (10 min)

blocks.text: Framing message, said in the first ten minutes

items: The goal is not equal distribution. It is equitable distribution.
Scarce resources should go to the populations with the greatest demonstrated need and risk.
Evidence-informed decisions will challenge assumptions, habits, and existing relationships, and that is what they are for.
Operational convenience is not the same thing as impact.
Neither kind of evidence is sufficient alone.

blocks.text: Reflection and closing

items: One assumption that was challenged during the exercise.
One insight about balancing the two kinds of evidence.
One way asset information would strengthen equitable outreach where you work.
One operational change you could make to reduce low-hanging-fruit decision making.

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: Do not shorten Allocating Scarce Resources to fit a break. If you are running behind, cut the reflection to five minutes and keep the exercise whole.
Distribute the Cedar County quotes at the ten minute mark, not with the numbers. The revision is the lesson.

blocks.text: What they leave with: a defended allocation, a scoring method they can reuse, and the sentence they would have to say to the community that did not get chosen.
FACILITATOR PREP
Will you run Cedar County as written, or rebuild it with your own neighborhoods?

title: Four-Hour Workshop: The Full Cycle
duration: 4 hours, including two breaks totalling 25 minutes

blocks.text: Purpose: Both halves of the skill: decide where to work using evidence, then build and test a loop that tells you whether it worked.

Materials: All three handouts for every participant, the Cedar County pack, role cards cut and ready, the process map posted, sticky notes in two colors, and lemonade ingredients if you are running the Lemonade Challenge.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (10 min)
Icebreaker: Name the Decision, page 14 (15 min)
Teaching Note: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Asset Data, page 16 (25 min)
Core Experience: Allocating Scarce Resources, page 24 (55 min)
Break (15 min)
Icebreaker: The Cost of Friction, page 13 (15 min)
Teaching Note: Lean Thinking, Feedback Loops, and PDSA, page 18 (30 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: The Volunteer Onboarding Simulation, page 27 (60 min)
Closing round: one change, one measure, one date, said out loud (15 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: The seam is the first break. Say explicitly what changes after it: the morning was about choosing where to work, the afternoon is about whether what you do there works. Groups that are not told this experience the afternoon as a different training.

If you prefer a lighter afternoon, substitute the Lemonade Challenge, page 19, for the simulation and add the remaining time to the closing round. It teaches the same cycle with a fraction of the setup, and it is the better choice for a group that does not share a process.
Keep the Name the Decision board up all day. In the closing round, point at it: this is what we knew this morning.
If the group is over sixteen, run two simulation tables and compare which change each one picked. The comparison is worth more than either table alone.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Look at the board from this morning. What was marked N that you now think you could get?
Which decision would you make differently after today, and what evidence changed it?
What is the one change you are going to test, and what number will tell you whether it worked?
When will you look at that number, and who will you have told by then?

blocks.text: What they leave with: a defended allocation decision, a completed PDSA cycle on a real process, a scoring method and a worksheet they can reuse, and one change with a measure and a date attached.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which decision, which allocation scenario, and simulation or lemonade?
If the simulation, whose process are you using and have you cleared it? ____
Handout: Data Inventory
Use during Name the Decision and the one-hour workshop. One per participant. This is the artifact everything else works from, so fill it in even if the room built one on the wall.
The decision
What has to be decided, for whom, and by when:
How it would be decided today if nobody asked for a justification:
What would change my mind
Up to eight things. For each one mark H if you have it this week, G if it exists and you would have to go get it, or N if nobody has it. Write the source in the last column.
The two columns
Of the items above, which are numbers and which are things people told you?
If one column is empty, that is the finding. Write what you would do about it:
Who is not in this data
Whose experience would be missing if I decided on this alone?
One thing I will go and get
Handout: Prioritization Scoring Worksheet
Use during Targeting What Matters Most and Allocating Scarce Resources. One per group.
Why ranks and not raw numbers

The indicators you are weighing are on incompatible scales. A hypertension rate of 47 percent and a distance of 33 miles cannot be added together, and multiplying either by a weight produces a number that means nothing. Ranking fixes this: it converts every indicator to the same scale, it can be done on paper in a room with no spreadsheet, and it is transparent enough that someone who disagrees with your answer can point at exactly where.

The cost is that ranking loses the size of the gaps. If two communities are nearly identical on an indicator and a third is far worse, ranking treats those as evenly spaced. Note where that happens and say so when you present.
The method

items: Step 1. List your communities across the top. Four to six works; more than eight is unmanageable on paper.
Step 2. List your indicators down the side, with the weight for each. Weights must total 100.
Step 3. For each indicator, rank the communities by need. Highest need gets the highest number. With six communities the range is 6 down to 1; with four it is 4 down to 1.

Step 4. Watch the direction. For most indicators a higher value means higher need. For some, such as existing coverage or prior service, a LOWER value means higher need. Mark those rows before you start.
Step 5. Multiply each rank by its weight. Weight 25 means multiply by 0.25.
Step 6. Total each column. Highest total is the highest priority.
Step 7. Ties are real information, not a failure. If two communities tie, say what would break the tie and whether you have it.

blocks.text: The grid
Indicator ____________________ Weight ____ Direction: high / low = more need
Indicator ____________________ Weight ____ Direction: high / low = more need
Indicator ____________________ Weight ____ Direction: high / low = more need
Indicator ____________________ Weight ____ Direction: high / low = more need
Indicator ____________________ Weight ____ Direction: high / low = more need
Indicator ____________________ Weight ____ Direction: high / low = more need
Before you present it
Three questions the scoring cannot answer. Write the answers down; they are what make the ranking a decision rather than a calculation.
What did people tell us that the numbers do not show?
Who is already trusted in our top-ranked community, and have we spoken to them?
What would we have to stop doing to serve the top-ranked community properly?
A caution
A weighted score is an argument, not an answer. Whoever chose the weights chose the winner. Show the weights whenever you show the ranking, and be ready to run it again with somebody else’s weights.

This is the step that gets skipped. If you find yourself writing “it worked” without a number and without a quote, you have not done Study, you have done Hope. Go back and find out what actually changed.

blocks.text: Optional. The session does not depend on it, because Build the Board (page 9) creates a working list in the room. Pre-work makes the session sharper, because participants arrive with a real situation of their own rather than borrowing the group’s. Send it at least three days ahead and do not chase it.
1. Pick your initiative (5 minutes)
Choose one real, current initiative or community challenge you are responsible for. It should be specific enough to name and live enough that you will still be working on it in three months.

items: Good: a smoke alarm campaign in one corridor, a shelter agreement with a school district, a coalition you are trying to convene.
Too broad: preparedness, volunteer engagement, community resilience.
Write it as one sentence: what are you trying to make happen, and by when?

blocks.text: 2. List who comes to mind (5 minutes)

Without looking anything up, list every person, organization, institution and informal leader connected to that initiative. Do not organize the list. Do not filter it. Ten to twenty names is a good target.
Then, next to each, write one word: what is their connection? Decides, funds, implements, blocks, is affected, is trusted.
3. Answer two questions (5 minutes)

items: Who on your list have you personally spoken with in the last ninety days?
Who is on your list because they hold a title, rather than because you know they matter?

blocks.text: Bring to the session

items: Your one-sentence initiative
Your unfiltered list
Your answers to the two questions

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The unfiltered list is the point. Participants revise it three times during the session, and the value is in watching what they missed the first time. Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. That is what Build the Board is for; run it as your opener and the people who did the pre-work simply have more to contribute.
Materials: A whiteboard, three sheets of easel paper taped together, or a shared digital board. Sticky notes and markers, or the digital equivalent.
Purpose: Produce the stakeholder list that the rest of the session works from, in the room, in ten minutes, without depending on anyone having done pre-work.
Why this comes first

Every activity after this one needs a list of stakeholders to act on. If you rely on pre-work to supply it, the session splits into people who are ready and people who are catching up, and the catching up is visible. Building the board together removes that problem and gets you a richer list than any one person would have written alone.
Choose how the group builds it
Pick one of these before the session. All three take about the same time and produce a usable board. The choice depends on who is in the room.

Option A, one shared situation. You supply a single initiative and everyone maps it together. Best for mixed groups, for people from different chapters, and whenever you cannot count on participants having a live project. Also the safest option with a new group, because nobody is exposing their own work.

Option B, one volunteered situation. A participant offers a real initiative they are responsible for, and the room maps it for them. Best for a single chapter team. Produces the most useful board in the room and asks the most of the volunteer, so ask privately beforehand rather than on the spot.

Option C, everyone adds their own. Each participant contributes stakeholders from their own initiative and the group clusters them by type. Best when most people did the pre-work, and when the group is large. Produces breadth rather than depth, and works well as a lead-in to Shift the Lens.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Before we can look at power, trust or engagement, we need something to look at. In the next ten minutes we are going to build a stakeholder list together, on this board, and it is going to stay up for the rest of the session. Everything we do after this is a revision of what we put up now. So do not try to get it right. Get it down.”
The Activity
Step 1 (2 min): Name the situation

items: State the initiative in one sentence, including what needs to happen and by when. Write it at the top of the board where it will stay visible.
If you are running Option C, ask each person to write their own one-sentence version on a card first, so the clustering later has something to hang on.

blocks.text: Step 2 (5 min): Fill the board

Call for names. Take them as fast as they come and write them all down. Do not evaluate, do not group yet, do not ask anyone to justify a name. If the room slows, prompt with the categories rather than with examples:

items: Who decides?
Who funds it?
Who does the actual work?
Who could stop it?
Who is affected by it?
Who do residents already trust?

blocks.text: Step 3 (3 min): Mark the board

items: Go back through and put a star next to anyone who holds no formal position. Those are usually the most valuable names on the board and the easiest to lose.
Put a question mark next to any name where the room disagreed or hesitated.

blocks.text: Step 4 (3 to 5 min): Read it back

items: How many names are organizations, and how many are people?
How many did we get to before the first starred name?
Who is on this board only because someone in this room happens to know them?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: this board is the raw material. It is almost certainly incomplete and probably weighted toward the people we already work with, and that is normal. The rest of the session is about finding what is missing and working out what to do about it.
Facilitator note

Resist organizing the board while it is being built. Groups will want to sort as they go and it slows the generation down; there is a structured revision coming in Shift the Lens and a full reorganization in Mapping Power and Trust. Fifteen to twenty-five names is a good board. Fewer than ten means the situation was too abstract, so restate it more specifically and take another two minutes.
Photograph the board before teardown and send it to participants. It is the thing they will actually use afterward.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which option will you run, and why does it fit this group?
If Option A, what is the shared initiative you will supply? Write it as one sentence, with a real place and a real deadline.
If Option B, who have you asked in advance, and have they agreed?
Setup:
"I am going to ask some open-ended questions. Feel free to call out your answers."
The Activity:

items: "Name one place where the community naturally gathers."
Allow 2 minutes to call out answers.
“What makes this place trusted?”
Allow 2 minutes to call out answers.

blocks.text: Closing:
Tie back to the skill: Helps identify trusted spaces and community access points.
Setup:
"Think about a community you know well." Let them call out their answers to each of the questions below. Allow 2 minutes per question.
The Activity:

items: What place is important to residents but may not appear important on an official map?
Why does that place matter?
Who gathers there?
What does that place reveal about the community?

blocks.text: Closing:
Connection to the Skill: This helps participants identify community assets, gathering places, and trusted spaces that may be overlooked.
Setup:
Give participants paper and drawing materials. They will have 5-7 minutes to complete the task below.
The Activity:
“Think of a familiar route you travel frequently (e.g., home to work, grocery store, school). Draw that route from memory. Include as many details as possible:

items: Streets and turns
Landmarks (churches, parks, stores, etc.)
Traffic lights or stop signs
Notable buildings or features”

blocks.text: After 5-7 minutes of drawing:
"Pull up the same route on Google Maps (or similar tool on phone). Compare your drawing to the actual map.”
Group Reflection (2–4 minutes)
Bring the room back together and ask: What differences do you notice between your mental map and the actual map?
Optional Deeper Prompt (if time allows)

items: What did you remember well? What did you miss?
Did you include places that are meaningful to you but might not appear on a standard map?
How aware are you of your surroundings during your daily routines?
What does this tell us about how people experience and define their community?
Are informal landmarks (like ‘the big tree’ or ‘that corner store’) also assets?

blocks.text: Materials: printed stakeholder list
Setup:
Participants place their initial stakeholder list in front of them.
The facilitator introduces several “lenses,” one at a time. The table of lenses and associated questions is on the next page.
The Activity:

items: For each lens, participants reconsider their project or community challenge and write down new people, groups, organizations, informal leaders, barriers, or community strengths that become visible.
After each lens, participants answer: “Who is missing from our map now that we looked through this lens?”
They then add those stakeholders to their original list.

blocks.text: For example, imagine the challenge is hurricane preparedness. The original stakeholder list might include emergency management, the Red Cross, police, fire departments, hospitals, and nonprofit organizations.

After shifting the lens, participants might identify additional stakeholders such as pastors, neighborhood organizers, promotors/community health workers, school bus drivers, apartment managers, food pantry volunteers, disability advocates, home-health workers, bilingual radio personalities, colonia residents, local store owners, senior caregivers, transportation providers, and residents who have experienced previous disasters.
Debriefing Questions:

items: Who appeared on your map that was not there before?
What assumption caused us to overlook them?
How might including them change the way we approach this community?

blocks.text: Lens
Questions to Ask
Trust
Who do residents already listen to or trust? Who might people approach before they approach an organization or government agency?
Access
Who has difficulty accessing services, information, meetings, or resources? Who helps people gain access?
Language
Who may not receive information in their preferred language? Who are the trusted translators, bilingual leaders, or culturally familiar messengers?
Transportation
Who cannot easily travel to meetings, shelters, clinics, food distributions, or services? Who provides transportation or helps people get around?
Culture
What cultural traditions, beliefs, relationships, or institutions influence how people respond to this issue?
Geography
Which neighborhoods, rural areas, colonias, apartment complexes, or isolated communities may experience the issue differently?
Lived
Experience
Who has personally experienced the problem we are trying to address?
Whose experience should inform decisions?
Community
Strengths
What already works in this community?
Who is already helping, organizing, sharing resources, or solving problems informally?
Materials: Influence and Interest Matrix handout (page 31), the participant’s stakeholder list, sticky notes in two colors, pens

Purpose: Move a list of names into a picture. Participants position their stakeholders by influence and interest, then add the dimension most maps leave out, which is trust, and see what the combination reveals.
Setup (say this to participants)

“You have a list. A list tells you who exists. It does not tell you who matters, who is going to move, or who you need to talk to first. We are going to turn the list into something you can act on. Two things to know before we start. First, you will be guessing about some of these people, and that is fine, because a guess you can see is more useful than an assumption you cannot. Second, when we add trust to the picture, some people are going to end up in a place you do not like. That is the part worth paying attention to.”
The Activity
Step 1 (8 min): Place by influence and interest

items: Write one stakeholder per sticky note, using the first color.
Place each note on the matrix. Horizontal is interest, meaning how much they care about this specific initiative. Vertical is influence, meaning how much they can affect whether it happens.
Do not overthink placement. Where you hesitate, put the note down and move on; the hesitation is information for later.

blocks.text: Step 2 (7 min): Add trust

items: For each stakeholder, mark the note: does the community trust this person or organization? Not whether you trust them, and not whether they are competent. Whether residents would open the door.
Use a plus, a minus, or a question mark. Question marks are honest and useful.

blocks.text: Step 3 (7 min): Add the second color

items: Using the second color, add anyone the community trusts who is not already on your map. Informal leaders, people who hold no position, the person everyone calls first.
Place them by influence and interest like the rest. Notice where they land.

blocks.text: Step 4 (8 min): Read the map
Working in pairs, look at each other’s maps and answer in this order:

items: Who is high influence, low trust? That is your risk. Anything you do through them will be read through that.
Who is high trust, low influence? That is your carrier. They cannot decide anything and they can change whether anyone shows up.
Who is high influence, low interest? That is your swing. They are not opposed, they are elsewhere.
Which quadrant is emptiest, and what does that say about who you have been working with?

blocks.text: Step 5 (10 min): Draw the relationships

items: Draw a line between any two stakeholders who have a real working relationship. Solid for strong, dashed for strained.
Circle anyone with three or more lines. Those are your connectors, and they are usually not the people with the titles.
Mark with an X any pair you would not want in the same room yet.

blocks.text: Debriefing Questions

items: What surprised you about where someone landed?
Who did you have to guess about, and what would it take to stop guessing?
Where on your map does trust and influence not line up, and what has that cost you already?
Who is your most important connector, and when did you last talk to them?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The high-influence, low-trust quadrant is where the useful discomfort lives, and groups will move past it quickly if you let them. Slow down there. Ask directly: what happens to your initiative if that person is the face of it? Expect at least one participant to realize their own chapter belongs in that quadrant for a particular community. That realization is the most valuable thing this activity produces, and it needs to be received without defensiveness.
FACILITATOR PREP

Bring one example from your own region of a stakeholder who held high influence and low community trust, and what the chapter did about it. Use it in Step 4 when the room reaches that quadrant. A specific story is worth more than the whole activity, and a borrowed one does not land the same way.
The stakeholder or organization: ______________________________________
What the chapter did, and whether it worked: __________________________
Materials: The completed map from Mapping Power and Trust, Engagement Plan handout (page 32), pens
Purpose: Convert a stakeholder map into a sequenced engagement plan, so that the analysis produces action rather than a nice diagram nobody looks at again.
Setup (say this to participants)

“A map that does not change your calendar is decoration. In the next forty-five minutes you are going to decide who you engage, in what order, at what level, and what you actually want from each conversation. You will not be able to do this for everyone on your map, and that is the exercise. Choosing is the skill.”
The Activity
Step 1 (5 min): Pick five

items: From your whole map, circle the five stakeholders who most determine whether this initiative moves in the next ninety days.
At least one must be someone the community trusts who holds no formal position.

blocks.text: Step 2 (10 min): Choose a level for each

For each of the five, decide what the relationship needs to be. These are borrowed from the IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation and they are not a ladder to climb; they are a choice to make honestly.
Inform. We tell them what is happening. Appropriate when they are affected but not deciding.
Consult. We ask for their input and we decide. Only choose this if you will actually report back on what you did with it.
Involve. They work with us throughout and we make sure their concerns are reflected.
Collaborate. We decide together, including on what the problem is.
Empower. They decide and we support. Rare, and the direction this work is meant to travel.

items: Write the level next to each name. If you find yourself writing Consult for everyone, you are avoiding the choice.

blocks.text: Step 3 (10 min): Name the ask and the offer
For each of the five, write two sentences:

items: What do I need from them? Be specific enough that you would know whether you got it.
What is in this for them? If you cannot answer this, you are not ready to make the ask.

blocks.text: Step 4 (8 min): Sequence

items: Number your five in the order you will approach them.
The usual mistake is starting with the most powerful person. Ask instead: who do I need on board before that conversation will go well?
Write a date next to each. A real date, in the next ninety days.

blocks.text: Step 5 (12 min): Pressure test in trios
In groups of three, each person presents their plan in two minutes. The other two have one job each:

items: One asks: what happens if the first person says no?
One asks: whose voice is missing from these five?

blocks.text: Debriefing Questions

items: Who did you almost put in your five and cut? Why?
Where did the level you chose differ from the level you have actually been operating at?
What did the sequencing question change about your plan?
What is the first conversation, and when is it?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Hold the line on real dates. A plan with no dates is the same as no plan and participants will resist this step politely. It is also the step that makes follow-up possible, because you can ask them in ninety days whether the conversation happened.
FACILITATOR PREP
Decide before the session what happens after it, and say so at the close. A commitment with no follow-up is a commitment participants learn to make lightly.
Format: Facilitated dialogue. Participants build shared understanding through guided questioning rather than lecture.
Purpose: Examine how leaders identify, analyze and engage stakeholders in complex community systems, and surface the assumptions they are already carrying.
Agenda at a glance

items: 0 to 5 minutes: Opening frame, why stakeholders matter
5 to 15 minutes: Surfacing assumptions about power and influence
15 to 25 minutes: Defining the stakeholder landscape through dialogue
25 to 35 minutes: From analysis to leadership behavior
35 to 45 minutes: Applied scenario, navigating competing stakeholders
45 to 55 minutes: Leadership judgment, power and ethics
55 to 60 minutes: Reflection and commitment

blocks.text: 0 to 5 minutes: Opening frame, why stakeholders matter
Purpose: Frame stakeholder analysis as a leadership discipline rather than a checklist.

items: When you hear the word stakeholder, who comes to mind first?
Who tends to be named last, or not at all?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Stakeholder visibility is shaped by power, proximity, and habit.
5 to 15 minutes: Surfacing assumptions about power and influence
Purpose: Examine assumptions about influence, legitimacy and voice.

items: Who actually influences outcomes, versus who appears influential on paper?
How do urgency and crisis distort stakeholder prioritization?
Whose interests are easiest to overlook?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Leaders often confuse authority with influence.
15 to 25 minutes: Defining the stakeholder landscape through dialogue
Purpose: Co-create a working definition of the skill rather than being handed one.

items: If this skill were done well, what would leaders clearly understand?
What dimensions matter besides support or opposition?

blocks.text: Capture dimensions on the board as they emerge. Expect influence, interest, alignment, trust and risk. Do not supply them.
Facilitator synthesis: Stakeholder analysis is dynamic, relational, and contextual.
25 to 35 minutes: From analysis to leadership behavior
Purpose: Translate analysis into observable leadership behaviors.

items: What decisions improve when stakeholder landscapes are clear?
What mistakes become less likely?
What does proactive engagement look like in blue-sky conditions?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: The skill shows up in how leaders plan, communicate, and sequence action.
35 to 45 minutes: Applied scenario, navigating competing stakeholders
Purpose: Apply the reasoning to a realistic leadership challenge.
Scenario: Multiple partners, local officials and community groups are competing for influence during a disaster response.

items: How would you map stakeholders before taking action?
What tradeoffs become visible?
Where might engagement now prevent conflict later?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Early analysis enables strategic sequencing and reduces downstream friction.
FACILITATOR PREP

Replace the generic scenario above with a real one from your own region before you deliver. Name the actual organizations. The generic version works; a real one produces a different quality of argument, because people stop reasoning in the abstract.
The parties competing for influence: __________________________________
How it turned out (do not reveal this until the debrief): ______________
45 to 55 minutes: Leadership judgment, power and ethics
Purpose: Examine the ethical use of the skill. Do not skip this segment for time.

items: How can this skill be misused?
Where does influence cross into manipulation?
What guardrails should leaders hold themselves to?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis: Ethical stakeholder analysis centers transparency and long-term trust.
55 to 60 minutes: Reflection and commitment
Purpose: Consolidate learning and move it toward action.

items: What stakeholder do you need to better understand?
What assumption about influence are you questioning?
What is one action you will take in the next 30 days?

blocks.text: Session Formats

This skill ships four one-hour workshops, which follow this page. They can be run standalone, or assembled into the longer formats below. Everything in the longer formats is already in this document; nothing new has to be written to deliver them.
What you can run
20 minutes. Who Is Missing. One idea, delivered in a staff meeting. See below.
1 hour. Any of the four workshops on the following pages, standalone.
2 hours. From List to Map. Takes a group from nothing to a completed stakeholder map. Full agenda below.
4 hours. Map the People, Understand the Power, Mobilize the Community. Takes a group from nothing to an engagement plan with dates. Full agenda below.
How to choose

Choose by what you want participants to walk out holding, not by how much time you have. A group that leaves with a map but no plan will not act on it. If you only have two hours, say so at the close and book the second half rather than rushing the planning.
20-minute version: Who Is Missing
Purpose: Make one gap visible. Not a session; a lever you can pull in a meeting you were already having.

items: Icebreaker: The Missing Landmark, page 12 (10 min)
Individually, list every stakeholder for one real initiative, then name three people the community trusts who are not on the list (7 min)
Round the room: one name each, and why they were missed (3 min)

blocks.text: What they leave with: Three names they had not thought of, and the question that produced them.
One-Hour Workshops
Four one-hour sessions. Each stands alone, and run in order they form the four-hour session. Each has a stated purpose, a timed agenda, and one artifact the participant walks out with.

Every one of them needs a stakeholder list to work on. Workshop 1 creates it. If you are running Workshop 2, 3 or 4 standalone with a group that has not done Workshop 1, run Build the Board (page 9) first and take the extra fifteen minutes from the discussion time.
Purpose: Introduce the skill and produce a first stakeholder list for a real situation.
Materials: Whiteboard or easel paper, sticky notes, markers, Stakeholder List handout (page 30)
Agenda

items: Welcome and the slogan: map the people, understand the power, mobilize the community (5 min)
Partner list versus stakeholder landscape. A partner list is who we already work with. A landscape is everyone connected to the outcome, including people who will never sign an agreement (10 min)
Icebreaker: Build the Board, page 9 (15 min)
Formal and informal: go back through the board and mark who holds a position and who holds standing without one (10 min)
Small groups: each participant transfers the board to their own Stakeholder List handout and adds anyone specific to their own initiative (12 min)
Closing debrief (8 min)

blocks.text: Guiding questions

items: Who is connected to this issue or initiative?
Who has decision-making authority?
Who has community trust?
Who may be affected by the outcome?

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: What is the ratio of formal to informal names on our board?
Who did we name first, and what does that say about how we see this work?
Who would a resident have named first?

blocks.text: What they leave with: An initial stakeholder list for one real project, initiative or community challenge.

title: Workshop 2: Looking Through a Different Lens

blocks.text: Purpose: Move past titles and formal authority, and find the people the first pass missed.
Materials: The stakeholder list from Workshop 1, or a board built at the start of this session. Pens.
Agenda

items: Welcome and recap of the list so far (5 min)
Formal power versus informal influence. Short input, not a lecture: authority is granted, influence is earned, and they are frequently held by different people (10 min)
Core Experience: Shift the Lens, page 14 (30 min)
Add the new names to the list and mark which lens surfaced each one (5 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Guiding questions

items: Who has trust but no formal title?
Who understands the lived experience of this issue?
What barriers may keep people from participating?
What community strengths are we overlooking?

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Which lens surfaced the most new names, and why that one?
What assumption caused us to overlook them the first time?
Which new name is the one we are least likely to actually contact, and what would change that?

blocks.text: What they leave with: A revised list that includes overlooked voices, informal leaders and community assets.

title: Workshop 3: Mapping Power, Trust, and Relationships

blocks.text: Purpose: Turn the list into a map, and add the dimension most stakeholder tools leave out.
Materials: The revised list, Influence and Interest Matrix handout (page 31), sticky notes in two colors, markers
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: a list tells you who exists, a map tells you what to do (5 min)
Core Experience: Mapping Power and Trust, page 16, Steps 1 to 4 (30 min)
Step 5, relationship lines and connectors, page 16 (10 min)
Gallery walk: look at two other maps without commenting (5 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Guiding questions

items: Who has formal authority?
Who has informal influence?
Where does trust already exist?
Where are relationships weak, strained, or missing?
Who can help connect others?

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Who is high influence and low trust, and what does that mean for how you approach them?
Who is your most important connector, and when did you last talk to them?
What did you see on someone else’s map that is missing from yours?

blocks.text: What they leave with: A stakeholder map showing influence, interest, trust and key relationships.
Purpose: Convert the map into a sequenced plan with real dates, so the analysis changes someone’s calendar.
Materials: The completed map, Engagement Plan handout (page 32), pens
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: a map that does not change your calendar is decoration (5 min)
Core Experience: From Map to Plan, page 18 (45 min)
Closing round: first conversation and date, said out loud by each participant (10 min)

blocks.text: Guiding questions

items: Who should be engaged first?
What outcome do we need from each stakeholder?
What message or approach will work best?
What barriers should we consider?
Who is responsible for follow-up?

blocks.text: Closing debrief
The closing round is the debrief. Each participant says one name and one date out loud. Do not let anyone pass, and do not let anyone give a date more than ninety days out.
What they leave with: An engagement plan naming priority stakeholders, the level of engagement for each, the ask, the offer, the order, and the dates.
FACILITATOR PREP
Who follows up on these commitments, and when?

title: Two-Hour Workshop: From List to Map

blocks.text: Format: Instructor-led, small groups at tables, one shared board
Purpose: Take a group from no shared starting point to a completed stakeholder map showing influence, trust and relationships.
Pre-work: Optional (page 8). The session works without it.

Materials: Whiteboard or easel paper for the shared board, sticky notes in two colors, markers, tape. Stakeholder List handout (page 30) and Influence and Interest Matrix handout (page 31) for each participant.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (5 min)
Icebreaker: Mapping From Memory, page 13 (15 min)
Icebreaker: Build the Board, page 9 (15 min)
Core Experience: Shift the Lens, page 14 (30 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: Mapping Power and Trust, page 16, Steps 1 to 4 only (30 min)
Closing debrief and commitments (15 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: Mapping From Memory before Build the Board is deliberate. It establishes that people see the same place differently before anyone is asked to be authoritative about who matters.
Drop Step 5 of Mapping Power and Trust, the relationship lines. It is the first thing to cut and the least damaging, because relationships can be added later to a map that exists.
Do not start From Map to Plan in the last fifteen minutes. A half-finished plan is worse than an honest stop.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: What is on this map that would not have been on your list this morning?
Which quadrant is emptiest, and what does that tell you?
What is the one conversation this map says you should have first?
What will you do with the map between now and the planning session?

blocks.text: What they leave with: A stakeholder map for a real situation, showing influence, interest and trust, plus a named first conversation. Say clearly that they have a map and not yet a plan.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which Build the Board option will you run, and if Option A, what shared initiative will you supply?
When is the follow-on session where they build the plan? Book it before you deliver this one.

title: Four-Hour Workshop: Map the People, Understand the Power, Mobilize the Community
duration: 4 hours, including two breaks totalling 25 minutes

blocks.text: Format: Instructor-led applied lab, small groups at tables, one shared board that stays up throughout
Purpose: Take a group from no shared starting point to a sequenced engagement plan with real dates, and expose the ethics of the skill along the way.
Pre-work: Optional but genuinely useful at this length (page 8).

Materials: Whiteboard or easel paper, sticky notes in two colors, markers, tape. All three handouts for each participant: Stakeholder List (page 30), Influence and Interest Matrix (page 31), Engagement Plan (page 32).
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (10 min)
Icebreaker: Map the Heartbeat, page 11 (5 min)
Icebreaker: Build the Board, page 9 (15 min)
Workshop 1 content: partner list versus stakeholder landscape, formal versus informal, page 23 (25 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: Shift the Lens, page 14 (30 min)
Workshop 2 discussion: who did we miss, and why them, page 23 (20 min)
Core Experience: Mapping Power and Trust, page 16, all five steps (40 min)
Break (15 min)
Ethics segment from the Socratic guide, page 20 (20 min)
Core Experience: From Map to Plan, page 18 (45 min)
Closing round: first conversation and date, said out loud (15 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: The ethics segment sits between the mapping and the planning on purpose. Participants have just finished analyzing people who are not in the room, and they are about to decide how to approach them. That is the moment the question of manipulation actually bites. Moved to the end it becomes a coda nobody engages with.
Keep the board from the opener visible all day. In the final round, point at it: this is where we started, and look what we know now.
The closing round is out loud and by name. A commitment said in front of eleven colleagues behaves differently from one written on a worksheet.
If the group is more than sixteen, run Build the Board in two halves on two boards and compare them at the end of Shift the Lens. The comparison is worth the extra ten minutes.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Look at the board we built this morning. What was missing from it?
Who on your final plan would you not have approached before today?
Where did you change the level you were going to engage someone at?
What is your first conversation, and what date is it?

blocks.text: What they leave with: A defined initiative, an initial and revised stakeholder list, a map showing influence, trust and relationships, a named list of missing voices, and an engagement plan with five stakeholders, levels, asks and dates.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which Build the Board option, and what shared initiative if Option A?
Your regional example of high influence and low community trust, for Mapping Power and Trust:
Your regional scenario for the ethics segment:
Who follows up on the commitments, and when?
A Note on Building Longer Sessions
This is written for whoever extends this skill later, and can be removed once the question is settled.
What the skill currently holds

Four icebreakers (5 to 15 minutes each), three core experiences (30, 40 and 45 minutes), a one-hour Socratic session, and four one-hour workshops. Distinct, non-repeating material comes to roughly three hours and forty minutes, plus the workshop content.
What that supports

items: The 20-minute, one-hour and two-hour formats have slack. You can swap activities and still fill the time.
The four-hour format uses nearly everything once. That is the correct design for a single four-hour session, and it means there is no spare material inside it.
A second, different four-hour session would need new content. Roughly one more core experience and one more icebreaker would do it.

blocks.text: If a second four-hour session is wanted

The gap worth filling is practice under pressure. Everything here is analysis performed calmly. Nothing asks a participant to map stakeholders while a situation is changing, which is the condition in a disaster response, and it is where the skill is hardest and most valuable.

items: A timed simulation where the stakeholder landscape shifts mid-activity, so participants have to revise a map they have just committed to.
A shorter, seated icebreaker for virtual delivery, since three of the four current openers assume a physical room.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Does your region need a second four-hour session, or is one enough?
Handout: Stakeholder List
Use during pre-work and Workshop 1. Add rows as needed. Do not filter while you are listing; filtering comes later.
My initiative, in one sentence:
Stakeholders
For each: name, what kind (person, organization, institution, informal leader), and their connection in one word (decides, funds, implements, blocks, affected, trusted).
Two questions
Who on this list have I spoken with personally in the last ninety days?
Who is on this list because of a title, rather than because I know they matter?
After Shift the Lens, add anyone you missed
Handout: Influence and Interest Matrix
Use during Mapping Power and Trust (page 16) and Workshop 3. One per participant. Place one stakeholder per sticky note.
Draw the grid below across a full sheet of easel paper, or use this page for individual work.
The four quadrants
High influence, high interest. Engage closely. These people will shape the work whether or not you plan for it.
High influence, low interest. Your swing. Not opposed, just elsewhere. The question is what would make this matter to them.
Low influence, high interest. Often where the community is. Frequently the most affected and the least consulted.
Low influence, low interest. Keep informed. Revisit, because interest changes when something visible happens.
Mark every note for trust
Plus if the community trusts them. Minus if it does not. Question mark if you are guessing. Trust is about whether residents would open the door, not about whether you find them reliable.
What to look for once the notes are placed

items: High influence, low trust: your risk. Anything routed through them carries that.
High trust, low influence: your carrier. Cannot decide anything, can change whether anyone shows up.
The emptiest quadrant: what it says about who you have been working with.
Question marks: each one is a conversation you have not had.

blocks.text: Relationships

Draw a solid line between stakeholders with a strong working relationship, a dashed line where it is strained. Circle anyone with three or more lines; those are your connectors. Mark an X on any pair you would not put in a room together yet.
Notes
Handout: Engagement Plan
Use during From Map to Plan (page 18) and Workshop 4. One per participant.
My five priority stakeholders
At least one must be someone the community trusts who holds no formal position.
Level (inform / consult / involve / collaborate / empower): ______________
Order: ______ Date I will make contact: ______________
Order: ______ Date I will make contact: ______________
Order: ______ Date I will make contact: ______________
Order: ______ Date I will make contact: ______________
Level: ______ What I need from them, and what is in it for them:
Order: ______ Date I will make contact: ______________
Pressure test and ninety-day check
If my first conversation goes badly, my alternative is: ________________
The voice still missing from these five is: ____________________________
At ninety days, what changed on the map: _______________________________
Further Learning
Short reads and tools

items: Community Tool Box: Identifying and Analyzing Stakeholders and Their Interests. Best for learning how to identify stakeholders, understand their interests, and bring them into the work.
Community Tool Box: Stakeholder Analysis Checklist. Best as pre-work or a workshop handout.
IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation. The inform, consult, involve, collaborate, empower ladder used in From Map to Plan. One page, and the most portable idea in this skill.

blocks.text: Longer reads

items: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2011). Principles of Community Engagement, second edition. A strong foundation on trust-building, community participation, and working collaboratively with partners.
Kretzmann, J. and McKnight, J. (1993). Building Communities from the Inside Out. The asset-based counterweight to deficit mapping.
Freeman, R. E. (1984). Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. The origin of the framework, worth knowing even if you never read it cover to cover.
Ganz, M. (2010). Leading Change: Leadership, Organization, and Social Movements. Where the relational organizing tradition in this skill comes from.

blocks.text: Tools and toolkits

items: Aspen Institute: Community Change and Power Mapping resources.
Stanford d.school: systems mapping tools. Useful when the stakeholder picture is genuinely a system rather than a list.

blocks.text: Podcasts

items: Stanford Social Innovation Review podcast. Big-picture conversations on nonprofit leadership, systems change, and social impact.

blocks.text: How to use this list

The Community Tool Box pages are what you hand a participant who asks for more. The CDC principles are what you read before designing an engagement for a community that has been badly engaged before. The IAP2 spectrum is the one thing worth memorizing.
