Optional. The session does not depend on it, because Put a Meeting on the Table (page 16) produces a working meeting in the room. Pre-work makes the session sharper because participants arrive with their own meeting rather than borrowing the group’s. Send it three days ahead and do not chase it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Pick a meeting you have to run (5 minutes)
Choose one real meeting you will lead in the next thirty days. A board meeting, a leadership team meeting, a volunteer meeting, a partner meeting, a planning session. Bring three things with you:

items: The current agenda, if there is one. If there is not, that is useful information and you should bring that fact.
The invitation, including who is on it.
One sentence on what the meeting is for.

blocks.text: 2. Look back at the last one (10 minutes)
Think about the last meeting you led and answer these honestly. Nobody will collect them.

items: What was the purpose of the meeting?
What outcome were you hoping for?
Was that outcome communicated to anyone before the meeting started?
Did the right people attend? Was anyone there who did not need to be?
Did it end with clear next steps, and did people know who owned what?
If you ran it again tomorrow, what would you change?

blocks.text: 3. Rate yourself (5 minutes)
One to five, where one is rarely and five is consistently. Keep this; you will be asked to look at it again at the end of the session.
Before the meeting

items: I identify the purpose before I schedule it. ____
I communicate the expected outcome in advance. ____
I invite only the people necessary for that outcome. ____

blocks.text: During the meeting

items: I keep discussion focused on the intended outcome. ____
I manage participation so the quiet people are heard. ____
I move the group toward decisions and action. ____

blocks.text: After the meeting

items: I send follow-up notes promptly. ____
I assign ownership and deadlines clearly. ____
I evaluate whether the meeting worked and ask for feedback. ____

blocks.text: Two questions: which of the three sections scored highest, and which is your biggest opportunity? Write both down.
If you have time: watch this

Priya Parker, Three steps to turn everyday get-togethers into transformative gatherings, TED, about 12 minutes. https://www.ted.com/talks/priya_parker_3_steps_to_turn_everyday_get_togethers_into_transformative_gatherings
One question afterward: what is one thing you currently do, or fail to do, that shapes the quality of your meetings?
Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. That is what Put a Meeting on the Table is for. If you use the self-assessment, plan to return to it at the close; an earlier version of this pre-work collected the ratings and then never mentioned them again, which teaches participants that the reflection was decorative.
Materials: Two sheets of easel paper posted on opposite walls, one labelled MEETING and one labelled EMAIL. The scenarios below, printed or on your phone.
Purpose: Establish in the first ten minutes that a meeting is a choice, not a default, and that reasonable people disagree about which choice is right.
Setup (say this to participants)

“I am going to read out some situations. If you think it should be a meeting, go stand under MEETING. If you think it should be an email, go stand under EMAIL. If you are torn, stand in the middle, but you will have to say why.”
The scenarios

Read them in this order. The first three are easy on purpose; the room needs to feel confident before it gets uncomfortable. Do not tell anyone which answer is right, because for most of these there is not one.

items: 1. The parking lot will be resurfaced next Tuesday and everyone needs to park on the street.
2. Three departments each think a different one of them owns volunteer onboarding.
3. The quarterly numbers are in and they are roughly what everyone expected.
4. A long-standing community partner has told you privately that they felt sidelined at the last coalition meeting.
5. You need everyone to review a forty-page plan and give comments.
6. You need to decide which of two shelter sites to use, and the two people who know the sites disagree.
7. A volunteer has done something remarkable and you want people to know about it.
8. Someone has to tell the team that the grant was not renewed.
9. The board wants a monthly update on chapter activity.
10. Two staff members have been copying each other on increasingly sharp emails for a week.
11. You want ideas about how to reach a neighborhood you have never worked in.
12. The date of the annual event needs to move and it affects four teams.

blocks.text: Debrief

items: Which one split the room most, and what was the disagreement actually about?
What did the meeting answers have in common? What did the email answers have in common?
Number 8 is bad news. Number 10 is conflict. Number 4 is a repaired relationship. Why did most of us put those in the same column?
How many meetings on your calendar this week would have survived this exercise?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: the useful test is not importance. Plenty of important things belong in an email. The test is whether you need people to react to each other. If the value is in the exchange, meet. If the value is in the information, send it.
Facilitator note

Scenario 5 is the trap and it is worth spending an extra minute on. Almost every room says meeting, and almost every room is wrong: reviewing a document is asynchronous work, and the meeting people actually want is the one after the comments are in. If nobody catches it, ask what they would do in the first twenty minutes of that meeting.
If someone stands in the middle, take it seriously rather than pushing them to choose. “Email first, then a short meeting” is the most sophisticated answer available and it is worth surfacing.
FACILITATOR PREP
Add two scenarios from your own chapter, one obvious and one genuinely contested. Local ones get the strongest reaction.
Materials: The statements below, one per index card if you want groups working on different ones. Groups of four to six.
Purpose: Teach the goal-versus-outcome distinction by having participants perform the rewrite, before anyone defines the terms.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Here are some sentences that get said in real meeting invitations. In your group, take each one and answer a single question: what is the actual result this meeting should produce? Then rewrite the sentence so it says that.”
The statements

items: We need to talk about volunteer engagement.
We are meeting about disaster preparedness.
We need to discuss partnerships.
Touching base on the shelter plan.
Let us circle back on the budget.

blocks.text: If a group is stuck, offer the menu
Every meeting is doing one of these. Naming which one usually unlocks the rewrite:

items: Make a decision
Gather input
Assign actions
Coordinate effort across people who are already doing the work
Share information

blocks.text: The worked example
Show this one only after groups have attempted at least two on their own.
Before. Discuss volunteer engagement.
After. By the end of this meeting we will have identified three strategies to improve volunteer retention and named an owner for each.
Sharing out

items: Take one rewrite from each group, read out loud.
Ask the room after each one: could you tell, an hour later, whether that meeting worked?
Notice how many rewrites contain a number, a name, or a decision. Those three are what make an outcome checkable.

blocks.text: Closing
Tie back to the skill: the first version of every one of these is a topic. A topic fills an hour. An outcome ends one.
Facilitator note

The most common failure is a rewrite that is longer but still a topic: “Discuss volunteer engagement and identify challenges.” Ask what would be different at the end. That question does the work every time and is worth using rather than correcting the group yourself.
Materials: A board or easel paper where everyone can see it, markers.
Purpose: Surface the room’s actual relationship with meetings in ninety seconds, and give the session something honest to work against.
Setup (say this to participants)
“One word. How do meetings make you feel? Not the good ones or the bad ones, just meetings. Call it out and I will write it down.”
The Activity

items: Take every word and write it up without comment or reaction. Do not group them yet.
When the calling out slows, read the whole list back out loud. Reading it back is the activity; the list on its own does not land.
Ask whether anyone wants to add one now that they have heard the others. Somebody usually does, and it is usually more honest than the first round.

blocks.text: Debrief

items: How many of these are positive? Count them out loud.
How would you like meetings to feel, and what would have to shift to get there?
Everyone here also runs meetings. Whose list are we on?

blocks.text: Closing
Tie back to the skill: keep the board up. At the close of the session, come back to it and ask which words would change if the next month of meetings were designed rather than scheduled.
Facilitator note

The third debrief question is the one that turns this from a complaint into a leadership conversation, and it needs to be asked lightly. It lands badly if it sounds like an accusation and lands very well if it sounds like an observation you are including yourself in.
If the room gives you only positive words, they are managing you. Say so, cheerfully, and ask again.

title: Put a Meeting on the Table

blocks.text: Materials: Meeting Design Worksheet (page 39) for each participant, a board or easel paper, markers.
Purpose: Produce the real meeting that the rest of the session works on, in the room, without depending on anyone having done pre-work.
Why this comes first

Nearly every activity in this skill acts on a meeting the participant actually has to run. Workshop 1 alone asks participants four separate times to work on “their meeting.” If you rely on pre-work to supply it, a third of the room sits through four activities they cannot do. Fifteen minutes here removes that entirely, and the meetings the room produces out loud are usually better examples than the ones people bring on paper.
Choose how the room does it
Pick one before the session. All three take the same time.

Option A, everyone brings their own. Each participant names a meeting they have to run in the next thirty days and works it individually all session. Best when most people did the pre-work, and for groups from different chapters. Produces the most personally useful output and the least shared discussion.

Option B, one volunteered meeting. One participant offers a real meeting they are responsible for and the whole room designs it. Best for a single chapter team. Produces the sharpest conversation and asks the most of the volunteer, so ask privately beforehand.

Option C, one supplied meeting. You provide a meeting everyone works on together. Safest with a new group and the only option that guarantees nobody is exposed. Use the leadership meeting from The Meeting Makeover (page 20) if you want the session to build toward that activity.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Before we talk about how to run a meeting well, we need a meeting. In the next fifteen minutes you are going to put one on paper, and it is going to stay in front of you all session. Everything we do after this is a revision of it. Do not try to get it right. Get it down.”
The Activity
Step 1 (3 min): Name it

items: On the worksheet: what is this meeting called, when is it, how long is it, and how many people are on the invitation?
If it is recurring, write down when it was last redesigned. Most people cannot answer that and the silence is instructive.

blocks.text: Step 2 (4 min): Say why it exists

items: In one sentence, what is this meeting for? Write the honest version, not the one on the invitation.
Then, in one sentence, what would be different when it is over?
If those two sentences are the same sentence, you have a goal and not an outcome. Leave it; that is the material.

blocks.text: Step 3 (4 min): List who is on it

items: Write every name. Not roles, names.
Next to each one, write one word for why they are there: decide, inform, do, or represent.
Put a question mark next to anyone you could not assign a word to.

blocks.text: Step 4 (4 min): Read it back to the room
Take three or four, not everyone.

items: How many people are on your invitation, and how many got a question mark?
Whose meeting is this? Who would notice if it stopped happening?
Was your why sentence and your what-would-be-different sentence the same sentence?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: most rooms find that a third of the invitation list has a question mark next to it, and that the purpose and the outcome came out identical. Both are normal, and both are exactly what the rest of the session is for.
Facilitator note

The question-mark step is where the value is and people will want to skip it, because writing a question mark next to a colleague’s name feels disloyal. Say out loud that a question mark means you have not articulated it yet, not that the person should be removed. That reframing is what makes people honest.
Recurring meetings produce the best material. If someone offers a one-off, that is fine, but if you are choosing under Option B, take the standing meeting.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which option will you run, and why does it fit this group?
If Option B, who have you asked in advance, and have they agreed?
Reference: The Four Meeting Types

Five activities in this document ask participants to name a meeting type. These are the four, defined. Read this before delivering any of them, because the definitions are asked for every time and an improvised answer is worse than no answer.
The type is not about the topic or the seniority of the room. It is about what the group is empowered to produce.
1. Input
What it produces. Perspectives the decision-maker did not have. The decision is made later and elsewhere.
Who should be there. People with information or experience the decision needs. They do not need authority.
How it fails. The convener has already decided and is collecting cover. People can tell, and they stop giving real input to that person permanently.
Say this at the start. “I am going to make this call next week. I want to hear what I am missing before I do.”
2. Consultation
What it produces. A recommendation, or a shared reading of a situation. Stronger than input, short of a decision.
Who should be there. People whose judgment carries weight, and people who will have to live with the result.
How it fails. The group believes it is deciding. Then the decision comes back different and the room concludes the meeting was theatre.
Say this at the start. “We are shaping a recommendation today. The board decides in March.”
3. Coordination
What it produces. Alignment between people who are already doing the work. Sequencing, handoffs, and the discovery that two teams were about to do the same thing.
Who should be there. The people actually doing the work. Not their supervisors, unless the supervisor is doing some of it.
How it fails. It becomes serial status reporting, where each person speaks to the convener rather than to each other. That version is a written update wearing an hour.
Say this at the start. “Nobody is deciding anything new today. We are making sure the four things already in motion do not collide.”
4. Decision-making
What it produces. A decision, in the room, that people leave treating as settled.
Who should be there. Whoever has the authority, plus anyone whose objection afterward would reopen it. That second group is the one people forget.
How it fails. Two ways. The decision is not named out loud at the end, so everyone leaves with a different version. Or the person who could have blocked it was not in the room, and does, later.
Say this at the start. “We are picking one of these three today and we are not leaving without it.”
Using this in the room

items: Most bad meetings are two types stapled together, usually coordination and decision-making. The fix is rarely a better agenda; it is two shorter meetings, or one meeting with a stated seam in the middle.
The type determines the guest list, not the other way around. If you find yourself choosing a type to justify who is already invited, the invitation is driving the meeting.
Saying the type out loud in the first minute costs nothing and prevents the most common failure in each of the four.

blocks.text: How this relates to the IAP2 spectrum

The spectrum, inform through consult, involve, collaborate and empower, describes how much influence participants have over the result. The four types describe what the meeting is for. They are different axes, and both are worth stating. A decision-making meeting where the decision belongs to one person sits at inform; a decision-making meeting where the group decides together sits at empower. Same type, very different room.

Materials: The scenario packet below, printed for every group. Meeting Design Worksheet (page 39) and Agenda Template (page 40) for each participant. The four meeting types (page 18) posted or printed.
Purpose: Redesign a deliberately broken meeting from the invitation up, and discover that the agenda is the last thing you fix rather than the first.
Setup (say this to participants)

“You have been handed somebody else’s meeting. It is happening on Thursday. In the next forty-five minutes your group is going to rebuild it, and you are going to have to decide what this meeting is actually for before you can touch the agenda.”
Groups of four to six. Every group works the same scenario; the comparison at the end is the point.
THE SCENARIO PACKET, page 1: The invitation
Print this as written. The flaws are deliberate.
Subject: Chapter Leadership Meeting
When: Thursday, 9:00 to 10:00 a.m.
Where: Main conference room, dial-in for anyone remote

Invited (14): Executive Director; Development Director; Disaster Program Manager; two Disaster Program Specialists; Volunteer Services Manager; Communications Lead (shared with two other chapters); Finance Business Partner; three board members; the Regional Executive; an AmeriCorps member who joined last week; the office administrator.

Body of the invitation, in full: “Hi all, putting time on the calendar to touch base on a few things that have come up. We will cover volunteer numbers, readiness for the season, the partnership situation, and the budget. Agenda to follow.”
THE SCENARIO PACKET, page 2: The agenda that followed, sent at 8:41 a.m. on Thursday

items: Welcome and introductions
Volunteer engagement update
Disaster readiness for the season
Partnership concerns
Budget challenges
Round robin, anything else

blocks.text: THE SCENARIO PACKET, page 3: What is actually going on
Give this to groups at the same time as the other two pages. Without it they redesign in the dark.

items: Volunteers: active volunteers are down 22 percent year over year. Nobody disputes the number. Two people have theories and they contradict each other.
Readiness: the chapter needs 40 trained shelter workers by 1 September and currently has 17. This is the only item with a deadline.
Partnership: a long-standing faith-based partner has stopped returning calls since a coalition meeting in April. One board member is close to them personally.

Budget: a grant that funded 0.4 of the Volunteer Services Manager role was not renewed. A decision about that position has to be made this month and only three people in the room have any authority over it.
The AmeriCorps member has been in the building for six days.
The Communications Lead covers three chapters and has a conflicting meeting at 9:30.

blocks.text: Part 1: Diagnose (10 min)
Before redesigning anything, name what is wrong. Groups should find at least six things.

items: What is this meeting for? Can you tell from the invitation?
Which of the four types is it? Trick question, and the group should say so.
Who on that list has no reason to be there, and who is missing?
How many of the four topics can be resolved in an hour with fourteen people?

blocks.text: Part 2: Rebuild (25 min)
Using the Meeting Design Worksheet and the Agenda Template, the group produces a redesign. It does not have to stay one meeting.

items: Name the type or types. If it splits, say what splits and when each piece happens.
Write the outcome as a sentence that could be checked afterward.
Rebuild the invitation list from the outcome. For every name, one word: decide, inform, do, or represent.
Build the agenda with time allocations and a decision point marked on every item that has one.
Say what is sent in advance, to whom, and how many days before.
Write the first two sentences the facilitator says when the meeting opens.

blocks.text: Part 3: Compare (10 min)
Each group presents in ninety seconds: how many meetings did you end up with, who did you cut, and what is the outcome sentence?

items: Where did groups differ most? It is almost always the guest list.
Did anyone keep all fourteen people? Did anyone cut a board member, and how did that feel?
How many groups put the shelter worker deadline first? It is the only item with a date and it is fourth on the original agenda.
What did you do with the round robin?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide: what is planted in the scenario

It is four meetings. Volunteer numbers is input or analysis. Readiness is coordination with a hard deadline. The partnership is a relationship repair that should be a phone call from the right person, probably the board member who knows them. The budget is a decision that only three of the fourteen can make. Groups that produce one redesigned meeting have not finished; groups that produce two or three have.
The agenda arrived nineteen minutes before the meeting. No preparation was possible. Groups often fix the agenda’s content and never mention when it was sent.

The guest list is the real exercise. Fourteen people, and the budget decision needs three of them. The AmeriCorps member and the office administrator are there by habit. The Regional Executive is there because someone thought it looked good. Watch whether anyone will actually say a board member should not attend.
The one item with a deadline is buried fourth. Seventeen of forty trained by September is the only thing on the agenda that fails on a date. If a group leads with it, say so out loud.
Round robin is where the hour dies. It is on every real agenda and it converts a designed meeting into an undesigned one in the last ten minutes.
The conflicting 9:30. The Communications Lead leaves halfway through. Almost no group notices, and it is the reason to ask who actually needs to be present for which item.
Facilitator note

The instinct is to fix the agenda first, because an agenda is a visible artifact and rewriting it feels productive. Do not intervene when you see it. Let a group spend eight minutes reordering six bullets, and then ask them what the meeting is for. That sequence teaches the lesson better than the instruction does.
If a group finishes early, hand them the second question: which of your redesigned meetings would you cancel entirely if you had to give one hour back?
FACILITATOR PREP

This scenario is generic on purpose so it can be printed as is. If your group is a single chapter and you can build a local version, it lands harder, but only build one you can circulate without anyone recognizing themselves in it.
Using the scenario as written, or building your own? _____________________
One flaw from a real meeting you would add: ___________________________
Materials: The two stimulus sets below, printed. Groups of three or four.
Purpose: Practice the two sentences that decide whether a meeting works: the one that opens it and the one that closes each item. Both are said out loud, so both get rehearsed out loud here.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Two sentences do most of the work in a meeting. The first one tells people what we are here to produce. The last one tells them what just got decided and who owns it. Almost everybody skips both. You are going to write and say fourteen of them in the next half hour.”
Part 1: Openings (15 min)

Each of these is a real way meetings get opened. Rewrite each so that it names what will be different when the meeting ends. Then say it out loud, because a written outcome and a spoken one are not the same thing.

items: 1. “We are discussing staffing.”
2. “Thanks everyone for making time. I know we are all busy. Let us get started.”
3. “This is our monthly check-in on the community partnership work.”
4. “I wanted to get everybody in a room on the shelter question.”
5. “We are here to talk through the volunteer situation.”
6. “Quick one today, just want to align on the event.”
7. “Before we get into the agenda, does anyone have anything?”

blocks.text: Model rewrites, for the facilitator only
Do not distribute these. Use one or two if a group stalls, and use the room’s versions in the share-out even when yours are tighter.

items: 1. “By the end of this hour we will have decided staffing assignments for the September shelter activation.”
2. Has no content at all to rewrite, which is the finding. Ask the group what they had to invent, and note that participants invent it too, differently, every time.
3. “In forty-five minutes we will have agreed which two of our seven partnerships get active investment this quarter.”
4. “We are choosing between the high school and the community center today, and we are not leaving without a choice.”
5. “By the end we will have named the top three reasons volunteers are leaving and assigned someone to test each one.”
6. “Fifteen minutes. We need a final date and a confirmed venue, nothing else.”
7. Is an invitation to lose the first twelve minutes. Ask the group where that question belongs instead.

blocks.text: Part 2: Next steps (15 min)

These are real closing lines from real meetings. Each one is missing at least two of the three things an action needs: who, what exactly, and by when. Rewrite each as an action statement that could be pasted into a tracker.

items: 1. “We will look into that.”
2. “Someone should probably reach out to them.”
3. “Let us keep an eye on the numbers.”
4. “We will circle back on this next month.”
5. “I think we all agree that is the direction.”
6. “Can we get something on paper for the board?”
7. “We need to be more proactive about recruitment.”

blocks.text: The test
A rewritten action passes if a person who was not in the meeting could read it and know whether it had been done. Read a few out and apply that test to each.
Debrief (5 min)

items: Which was harder, the openings or the next steps, and why that one?
How many of your rewritten actions named a person who was not in the room? What has to happen before that is a real commitment?
Number 5 in Part 2 is agreement without a decision. How often does that end a meeting you run?
What is the shortest opening sentence you produced, and is it worse than the long one?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Insist on saying them out loud. Participants write good outcome sentences and then cannot say them, because spoken openings feel abrupt in a way written ones do not. That discomfort is the actual barrier to using this in a real meeting, and it only surfaces if they hear themselves.
Number 2 in Part 1 and number 5 in Part 2 are both traps with nothing to rewrite. Do not rescue them. A group that says “there is nothing here” has understood the exercise.
Materials: The sample email below, printed. Meeting Notes and Action Tracker handout (page 41) for each participant.
Purpose: Fix the third failure point. Most meeting training stops when the meeting ends, which is exactly where most meetings fail.
Setup (say this to participants)
“Everyone has been in a good meeting where nothing happened afterward. In the next forty minutes we are going to work out why, starting with a follow-up email that is worse than it looks.”
Part 1: What is missing from this email? (15 min)
Print and hand out. Groups of three or four. Ask a single question: what is missing?
Subject: Notes from today
Hi all,
Thanks for a great discussion this morning. Really appreciate everyone making the time, I know calendars are tight right now.

We talked through the volunteer numbers and there was a lot of good input. Marcus raised a good point about the onboarding process and we agreed that is something we should look at. Dana is going to think about the training piece. There was some discussion about whether the September date still works, we did not land on anything firm but the general feeling was that it is tight.
We also touched on the partnership question. We will pick that up next time.
Let me know if I missed anything.
Thanks again,
Britt
What groups should find
For the facilitator. There are eight. Most groups get four or five, and the last three are the interesting ones.

items: 1. No decision is recorded anywhere. Three things were discussed and nothing is stated as settled.
2. No dates. “September” appears as a worry, not a deadline.
3. “We agreed that is something we should look at” has no owner. Who is we?
4. “Dana is going to think about the training piece” is not an action. Thinking is not checkable.
5. The unresolved item, the September date, is described but not assigned to anyone or to a next step.
6. The partnership item is deferred with no owner and no date, which is how items disappear.
7. “Let me know if I missed anything” puts the burden of accuracy on people who were not taking notes. It reads as humility and functions as an escape hatch.
8. Nothing tells a person who was absent what happened. The email is written to the people who were already there.

blocks.text: Part 2: Rewrite it (15 min)
Same meeting, same content. Rewrite the email so that:

items: Every decision is stated as a decision, in its own line.
Every action has a name, a specific verb, and a date.
Every open item is named as open, with who owns getting it closed and by when.
Somebody who missed the meeting could read it and know where things stand.

blocks.text: Where information is genuinely missing, write the question you would have had to ask before the meeting ended. Those questions are the real output of this activity.
Part 3: The three questions (10 min)
Individually, using the Meeting Notes and Action Tracker handout, each participant writes three short feedback questions they would send after their own meeting. Three, not five. Nobody answers five.
Starting points, if people need them:

items: Was the purpose of this meeting clear to you?
Do you know what you are responsible for and by when?
What would make the next one better?

blocks.text: Debrief

items: How many of the eight did your group find, and which one did you miss?
Number 7, “let me know if I missed anything,” appears in almost every follow-up email ever sent. What is it actually doing?
When should this email go out? The room will say twenty-four hours. Ask what happens to an action assigned on Thursday and sent on Friday afternoon.
Who else should get it besides the people who attended?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The email is written to be likeable. It is warm, it credits people by name, and it is completely useless as a record. That combination is deliberate, because the problem in real chapters is not rudeness, it is that pleasant notes feel like they did the job. If a group defends it as “a nice email,” agree, and then ask what Dana is supposed to do on Monday.
Finding number 8 usually takes a prompt. Ask who on the invitation list did not attend, and what they now know.
FACILITATOR PREP
Decide whether to use this email or one of your own with the names removed. A real one from your region is more powerful and more delicate; only use it if it cannot be traced.
Format: Facilitated dialogue, running alongside the Meetings as a Leadership Tool slide deck. Participants build shared understanding through guided questioning rather than lecture.
Purpose: Frame meetings as a leadership instrument rather than an administrative task, and get the room to articulate the standard before anyone is taught it.
Agenda at a glance

items: 0 to 10 minutes: The worst meeting ever, and what it cost
10 to 25 minutes: Before the meeting
25 to 42 minutes: During the meeting
42 to 53 minutes: After the meeting
53 to 60 minutes: Reflection and close

blocks.text: Before you start
Two rules, said out loud. Nobody names a colleague, and everyone in this room also runs meetings, so this is not a complaint session about other people.
Segment 1: The worst meeting ever (0 to 10 min)

items: Think about the worst meeting you have ever attended. What made it ineffective?
What was the actual cost of that meeting? Count it in hours if you can.
Who was affected beyond the people in the room?
How did it affect trust, productivity, or morale?
Why do you think this happens so often?
If ineffective meetings create confusion and frustration, what do effective ones create?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Capture the themes on a board as they come: no purpose, too many people, no decision, no follow-up, drift. You will point at this list four times in the next hour. On the last question, steer toward clarity, decisions, alignment, accountability and action, and write those up too.
Segment 2: Before the meeting (10 to 25 min)

items: What should happen before a meeting appears on someone’s calendar?
Why are we meeting? What should exist when it ends?
What is the difference between discussing a topic and achieving an outcome?
When should something be a meeting, and when should it be an email?
What changes when a meeting is for input rather than for a decision?
Who absolutely needs to be in the room? How do you know?
What happens when a key stakeholder is missing? What happens when unnecessary people are included?
What are the risks of over-inviting, and of under-inviting?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. This is the longest segment because it is where most meetings are lost. Close it on the deck’s line: effective meetings are designed before they begin. If the room has not raised the guest list on its own by minute twenty, ask directly who the hardest person to uninvite would be.
Segment 3: During the meeting (25 to 42 min)

items: What causes a meeting to lose momentum once it starts?
How do conversations drift off track, and what is the facilitator’s role in that?
What is the difference between equal participation and equitable participation?
How do power dynamics affect what gets said in a meeting?
How do you create a space where people are willing to disagree?
How do you know when a discussion is ready for a decision?
What happens when a meeting ends without one?
How do you keep conflict productive rather than personal?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Equal participation gives everyone the same two minutes. Equitable participation accounts for the fact that people process differently, that the newest person and the Regional Executive are not equally free to speak, and that some contributions arrive better in writing. Close the segment on the deck’s line: effective leaders do not just facilitate discussion, they move a group toward clarity and action.
If the room goes quiet. Ask who in their meetings speaks least, and whether that person has the least to contribute. Nobody says yes.
Segment 4: After the meeting (42 to 53 min)

items: Have you ever been in a productive meeting where nothing happened afterward?
Why does momentum disappear once people leave the room?
What causes action items to be forgotten?
How do participants know what happens next? What creates clarity, and what creates confusion?
What role does follow-up play in trust and accountability?
If no action occurs after a meeting, was the meeting successful?
How would you know whether a meeting worked?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. The last two questions are the segment. The room will want to say a meeting can succeed on alignment alone, which is sometimes true and usually an excuse. Close on the deck’s line: the meeting is one part of the leadership process, and follow-through is what produces the result.
Segment 5: Reflection and close (53 to 60 min)

items: What do the most effective meetings you have been in have in common?
What insight challenged your thinking today?
Which part of the lifecycle, before, during or after, is your greatest opportunity?
What is one thing you will do differently in your next meeting?

blocks.text: Take the last answer from every person, out loud, one sentence each. Write them down and send them back to the group afterward.

Facilitator synthesis. Close by walking the three phases: before is purpose, outcomes and stakeholders; during is facilitation, participation and decisions; after is accountability, follow-up and reflection. Then point back at the worst-meeting list from the first ten minutes and ask which phase each of those failures actually happened in. Nearly all of them are before.
The five questions to ask repeatedly
These are worth putting on a card. They work in this session and in any real meeting.

items: What outcome are we trying to achieve?
Who needs to be involved for that outcome to happen?
What is preventing clarity right now?
How will people know this meeting was successful?
What needs to happen next, and who owns it?

blocks.text: Train-the-Trainer
Read this before your first delivery.
What this session is for

It is not a lesson about meetings. It is the session where a room articulates a standard it already holds and then notices it is not meeting it. If you teach content here, the workshops afterward become compliance rather than recognition.
Running it with the deck

items: The deck is Meetings as a Leadership Tool, eighteen slides. It maps onto the five segments above in order.
Five slides carry their questions inside diagrams rather than text, so the questions in this guide are the reliable version. Use the guide, and let the deck be what the room looks at.
Notes exist on only seven of the eighteen slides. The synthesis lines in this guide cover the other eleven; that is the reason this guide exists.
Advance the deck to match the segment rather than the question. Sitting on one slide through four questions is fine and better than clicking through.

blocks.text: Four guardrails
Do not answer your own question. Count to ten. This material is familiar enough that facilitators fill silences fast, and every filled silence is a participant who was about to speak.

Do not let it become a complaint session. The turn happens in segment one. When somebody describes a terrible meeting, ask who ran it, then ask whether anyone here runs one like it. That question converts the room from audience to practitioner.

Protect the quiet ones during the participation segment. Talking about equitable participation in a session where three people do all the talking undermines itself. Use a written round or a small-group turn at least once during segment three.
Synthesize, do not conclude. End each segment by naming the pattern in the room’s answers, in the room’s words. The synthesis lines above are prompts for you, not scripts to read.
Common failure modes

items: Segment 2 runs long and segments 4 and 5 get compressed. Before is the richest material and after is where the behavior change is. Watch the clock at minute twenty-five.
The room agrees enthusiastically and nothing is at stake. If nobody has been uncomfortable by minute thirty, ask the guest list question harder.
Somebody senior describes a meeting everybody recognizes. Do not follow it up; move to the pattern. Naming the person is what makes the rest of the hour cautious.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Bring one meeting of your own that failed, and be ready to say what you would do differently. You will need it in segment one, and the room gives back roughly what you put in.
What went wrong, and which phase it failed in: ________________________
Who follows up on the segment five commitments, and when? _____________
Field Assignments

These are not room activities. They happen in the participant’s own calendar, which is where this skill is either practiced or not. Assign one at the close of a session and open the next session with what people found.
Field Assignment 1: The calendar audit
Look at every recurring meeting on your calendar for the next two weeks.

items: For each one, write the outcome in one sentence. Not the topic, the outcome.
Mark the ones where you could not do that in under thirty seconds.
For each of those, ask: when was this meeting last redesigned, and who would notice if it stopped?
Pick one and either give it an outcome or cancel it.

blocks.text: Bring back. How many hours a month are in the meetings you could not write an outcome for. Most people are surprised by the number and it is the most persuasive fact in this whole skill.
Field Assignment 2: Run one meeting properly
Pick one real meeting in the next two weeks and do all four things, not two of them.

items: Write the outcome and send it with the agenda at least two days ahead.
Cut the invitation list to the people the outcome needs, and tell the people you cut why.
Say the outcome out loud in the first sixty seconds.
Send notes within twenty-four hours with every decision, owner and date named.

blocks.text: Bring back. The reaction of the people you uninvited. It is almost never what people expect, and it is the thing that stops most participants from ever trying this.
Field Assignment 3: The fifteen-minute check-in
Run a short, deliberately designed check-in with a team, a group of volunteers, or a project group. Fifteen minutes, standing up if you can.

items: State the outcome in the first sentence.
Hold it to fifteen minutes even if it is going well.
End with actions, owners and dates, said out loud.
Do it three times in three weeks with the same group.

blocks.text: Bring back. What changed between the first one and the third. Short meetings are where design is most visible, because there is no room to recover from a bad opening.
A note on all three

The hardest part of this skill is not knowing what to do, it is doing it when the meeting is already on the calendar and the invitation already went out. All three assignments are built to be done inside the constraints people actually have rather than after a reorganization that will not happen.
Session Formats
Seven written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document; nothing new has to be written to deliver any of them.
20 minutes. Meeting or Email. One idea, delivered inside a meeting you were already having.
4 x 1 hour. Four standalone hours, one per phase, that can be run separately or in sequence: pre-meeting design, facilitation, driving outcomes, and post-meeting accountability.
2 hours. Meeting Design Snapshot. The whole lifecycle at altitude, built around the Meeting Makeover.
4 hours. Leading Meetings That Drive Results. The full arc with all three core experiences.
How to choose

The four one-hour workshops are the distinctive thing about this skill and they are worth using as designed. Chapters rarely give up a half day, and one hour a month for four months produces more behavior change than one four-hour session, because participants run real meetings in between. If you only get one session, run the two-hour, not one of the hours; a single hour on facilitation with no design work in front of it teaches technique without judgment.
20-minute version: Meeting or Email

items: Run Meeting or Email, page 11, with six of the twelve scenarios (10 min)
Name the test out loud: if the value is in the exchange, meet. If the value is in the information, send it. (3 min)
Everyone opens their calendar and finds one meeting this month that fails the test (5 min)
One round: say what you are going to do about it (2 min)

blocks.text: What they leave with: one meeting they are going to cancel or convert.
Purpose: Creating clarity and alignment before the conversation. Participants leave with a redesigned outcome, guest list and agenda for a real meeting.
Pre-work: Optional (page 9). Not required, because the workshop opens by producing the meeting.
Materials: Meeting Design Worksheet (page 39) and Agenda Template (page 40) for each participant, the four meeting types (page 18) posted, board and markers.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: most meeting failure is designed in before anyone sits down (5 min)
Icebreaker: Put a Meeting on the Table, page 16 (15 min)
The four meeting types, named and worked against the meetings now in the room, page 18 (8 min)
Icebreaker: What Is the Real Outcome, page 13 (10 min)
Individually, rewrite your own meeting’s outcome and rebuild its guest list from that outcome (12 min)
Build the agenda on the template, with times and decision points marked (5 min)
Closing debrief (5 min)

blocks.text: The two things to say in the framing

items: A goal is what we are generally trying to accomplish. An outcome is what is different when the meeting is over. Almost every invitation in this room contains a goal.
The type determines the guest list. If you are choosing a type to justify who is already invited, the invitation is running the meeting.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Who did you cut from your invitation list, and what will you tell them?
Did your outcome sentence change your agenda, or did you keep the agenda you had?
How far in advance will the agenda go out, and what has to change for that to be possible?
What is the one thing you will do before your next meeting?

blocks.text: What they leave with: a written outcome, a rebuilt guest list with a reason next to every name, and an agenda with times and decision points on it.
Notes on running it

items: The guest list is the hard part and it will take longer than twelve minutes if you let it. Let it, and cut the agenda build to three minutes; the template can be finished afterward, the guest list conversation cannot.

Somebody will say they cannot uninvite a board member. Ask what would happen if the board member received the notes instead, and watch the room work out that the objection is social rather than practical.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Which Put a Meeting on the Table option will you run?

title: One-Hour Workshop 2: Facilitation and Meeting Dynamics

blocks.text: Purpose: Leading productive conversations where people are willing to disagree, and where the quiet person with the relevant information actually says it.
Materials: Board and markers. Sticky notes for the written round.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (5 min)
Icebreaker: One Word Check-In, page 15 (10 min)
Equal versus equitable participation, taught against the board from the icebreaker (12 min)
The four kinds of conflict, and which one you actually have (10 min)
Small groups: what makes a meeting feel safe enough to disagree in? Then rank your list (13 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Equal versus equitable participation
Equal. Everyone gets the same thing. Two minutes each, round the table.
Equitable. Everyone gets what they need in order to contribute meaningfully.
Why equal is not enough, and it is worth naming all five out loud:

items: Some people process before they speak and some while they speak. A round-robin rewards the second kind.
Some people need the question in advance and never get it.
Power is in the room whether or not anyone acknowledges it. A senior leader, a new employee, a volunteer, a community partner, and someone speaking their second language are not equally free.
A quiet person may not be uncertain. They may be unwilling.
Equal time can still be dominated, because the loudest contribution sets what the rest of the room responds to.

blocks.text: What equitable looks like in practice: more than one way to contribute, questions sent ahead, a written round before an open one, small groups before large discussion, and a facilitator who notices who has not spoken and creates a doorway rather than putting them on the spot.
This is a compressed version. Inclusive Facilitation is the skill that treats it properly, and participants who want more should be pointed there.
The four kinds of conflict
Task. We disagree about what to do. Productive, and the kind you want more of.
Process. We disagree about how to decide. Usually mistaken for task conflict, and resolvable by naming the process out loud.
Relationship. We disagree because of history between us. Not resolvable in the meeting and should not be attempted there.
Power. We disagree about who gets to decide. The one people most often pretend is task conflict.
The facilitator move is the same in all four: name which one you think it is, out loud, and ask whether you have it right. Being wrong is fine; being silent is not.
Small group task
In groups of four: what makes a meeting feel safe enough to disagree in? List as many as you can in six minutes, then rank your top three and be ready to say why the top one is top.
Closing debrief

items: What was on every group’s list?
How much of what you listed is set before the meeting starts rather than during it?
Whose job is it to create that, and is it only the facilitator’s?
Look back at the one-word board. Which of those words would change first?

blocks.text: What they leave with: language for what is happening in a difficult meeting, and one practice they are going to use in the next one.
Notes on running it

items: Run the small group task with a written round first: two minutes of silent writing, then talking. Modelling the practice inside the workshop about the practice is the strongest thing this hour does.
This is the hour most likely to become a lecture, because it has the most content. If you are talking for more than twelve consecutive minutes, stop and ask the room for an example.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Bring one meeting you facilitated where the conflict was not the kind you thought it was.

title: One-Hour Workshop 3: Driving Outcomes During Meetings

blocks.text: Purpose: Keeping a meeting focused and converting discussion into decisions, with the two sentences that do most of that work rehearsed out loud.
Materials: The From Vague to Verbatim stimulus sets (page 23) printed, board and markers.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: the two sentences (5 min)
Core Experience: From Vague to Verbatim, page 23 (35 min)
Keeping alignment: drift, the parking lot, and the difference between flexibility and losing control (10 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Framing: the two sentences

Say this at the start. “Two sentences decide whether a meeting works. The first tells the room what we are here to produce. The last, on every item, says what we just decided and who owns it. Most meetings have neither and nobody notices until afterward.”
Keeping alignment

items: Drift is not the enemy. Undeclared drift is. The move is to name it: “This is a different question and it might be a better one. Do we want to be on it?”
The parking lot only works if somebody owns it and it is read out before the meeting ends. An unread parking lot teaches people that raising things is pointless.
Discussing, brainstorming and deciding are three different modes and a group can only be in one. Saying which one you are in is the single highest-value facilitator sentence after the opening.
Before you close an item: restate the decision, name the owner, name the date, and pause. The pause is what catches the person who thought it meant something else.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Which was harder to write, the openings or the next steps?
What would it cost you to say your outcome sentence out loud in your next meeting?
When did you last read a parking lot back before a meeting ended?
What is the one sentence you are going to use this week?

blocks.text: What they leave with: fourteen rehearsed sentences and a specific one they have committed to using.
FACILITATOR PREP
Add two vague openings and two vague next steps from meetings in your own region. Anonymize them.
Purpose: Strengthening follow-through, documentation and reflection, which is where good meetings most often stop producing anything.
Materials: The sample follow-up email (page 25) printed, Meeting Notes and Action Tracker handout (page 41) for each participant.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: everyone has been in a good meeting where nothing happened (5 min)
Core Experience: What Happens After, page 25 (40 min)
Reflection: the four questions to ask yourself after every meeting (8 min)
Closing round (7 min)

blocks.text: The four reflection questions
Give these out as a card. They take four minutes after a meeting and they are the whole of the improvement half of this skill.

items: What helped this meeting succeed?
Where did momentum slow?
Was the outcome achieved, and were the right people there to achieve it?
What feedback would participants give me if I asked, and am I going to ask?

blocks.text: Closing round
One sentence each: what is going into your notes template that was not there before?
What they leave with: a rewritten follow-up email, a notes and action tracker they will reuse, and three feedback questions they have written themselves.
Notes on running it

items: This hour has the least content and the most behavior change in it, because the practices are small and nobody teaches them. Resist adding material.

If the group is senior, the interesting question is not how to write notes but who writes them. Ask whether the person who facilitates should also be the person recording, and let the room work out that the answer is usually no.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Decide whether you are using the sample email as written or one of your own with the names removed.
Purpose: The whole meeting lifecycle at altitude, ending with a fully redesigned meeting. The right choice when you get one session rather than four.
Materials: All three handouts for every participant, the Meeting Makeover scenario packet printed per group, the four meeting types posted, board and markers, sticky notes for the parking lot.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (5 min)
Icebreaker: One Word Check-In, page 15 (10 min)
The three phases and the four meeting types, page 18 (15 min)
Goals versus outcomes, using What Is the Real Outcome, page 13 (10 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: The Meeting Makeover, page 20 (45 min)
Debrief (15 min)
Reflection and close (10 min)

blocks.text: Debrief

items: What was hardest about the redesign?
Which change would improve that meeting most, if you could only make one?
How many meetings did your group end up with, and what does that tell you about the original?
What did you do with the round robin?

blocks.text: Reflection and close
Every person completes and says out loud: “One thing I will do differently is...” Hold them to one sentence and write them down.
What they leave with: a redesigned meeting they can compare against the original, and one committed change.
Notes on running it

items: Put the parking lot up at the start and use it visibly. This workshop is about meeting design and participants notice whether you are running it well.
Do not shorten the Makeover to protect the debrief. If you are behind, cut the goals-versus-outcomes segment to five minutes; the distinction lands inside the Makeover anyway.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Which community or chapter context will you frame the Makeover in, and what will you say if a group recognizes their own meeting in it?

title: Four-Hour Workshop: Leading Meetings That Drive Results
duration: 4 hours, including two breaks totalling 25 minutes

blocks.text: Purpose: The complete lifecycle with all three core experiences, ending with a real meeting redesigned, rehearsed, and its follow-up already drafted.

Materials: All three handouts for every participant, the Meeting Makeover packet per group, the vague openings and next steps sets, the sample email, two labelled flip charts for Meeting or Email, board, markers, sticky notes.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: the three phases (10 min)
Icebreaker: Meeting or Email, page 11 (10 min)
Icebreaker: Put a Meeting on the Table, page 16 (15 min)
The four meeting types, worked against the meetings in the room, page 18 (15 min)
Core Experience: The Meeting Makeover, page 20 (45 min)
Break (15 min)
Equal versus equitable participation, and the four kinds of conflict, from Workshop 2 (25 min)
Core Experience: From Vague to Verbatim, page 23 (35 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: What Happens After, page 25 (40 min)
Apply it: return to your own meeting and revise the outcome, guest list, agenda and follow-up plan (20 min)
Closing round: one change, one meeting, one date, said out loud (10 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: The arc is before, during, after, in that order, and it should be visible on the wall all day. Write the three words up in the first ten minutes and point at them as you move.
The twenty-minute apply-it segment is what makes this a four-hour workshop rather than three activities in a row. Do not cut it; cut the meeting-types segment to ten minutes if you need the time.
Keep the Put a Meeting on the Table worksheets in front of participants all day. Every core experience is a rehearsal for the thing on that sheet.
If the group is over sixteen, run two Makeover tables and compare how many meetings each ended up with. The comparison is worth more than either table alone.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Look at your worksheet from this morning. What has changed on it?
Which of the three phases is your weakest, and what did you learn today that addresses it?
What is the meeting you are going to run differently, and when is it?
Who is going to notice, and what will they notice first?

blocks.text: What they leave with: a redesigned real meeting with an outcome, a guest list, a timed agenda, an opening sentence, a notes template and three feedback questions. Everything needed to run it differently on Monday.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which Put a Meeting on the Table option, and whose Makeover scenario? Who follows up on the commitments, and when? ____________________________
Handout: Meeting Design Worksheet
Use during Put a Meeting on the Table and The Meeting Makeover. One per participant, per meeting.
The meeting
Recurring? Y / N. If yes, when was it last redesigned? ________________
Why it exists
What is this meeting for, in one honest sentence?
What will be different when it is over?
If those are the same sentence, you have a goal and not an outcome yet.
The type
Circle one: INPUT / CONSULTATION / COORDINATION / DECISION-MAKING
If you circled two, this is more than one meeting. What splits, and when does each part happen?
Who is on it
Names, not roles. Next to each, one word: decide, inform, do, or represent. Question mark if you cannot assign one.
How many question marks? ______ Who is missing? _______________________
What goes out in advance
How many days ahead: __________
The first sixty seconds
Write the two sentences you will open with. You will say these out loud.
Afterward: who sends the notes, by when, and how will you know it worked?
Handout: Agenda Template
Use during The Meeting Makeover and Workshop 1. This is a template and a standard: an agenda without times and without decision points marked is a list of topics.
The elements of a working agenda
These are the six things missing from most agendas, in the order they matter.

items: 1. The outcome, at the top, before any item. Not the topic of the meeting, what will be different when it ends.
2. A time allocation on every item, adding up to less than the meeting length. Leave ten percent unallocated or you will run over.
3. A mode on every item: discuss, decide, or inform. The room behaves differently for each and cannot tell which one you want without being told.
4. An owner on every item, which is often not the person who called the meeting.
5. What people need to read or do beforehand, and by when.
6. The hardest thing first, or at least second. Energy is highest in the first twenty minutes and most agendas spend it on updates.

blocks.text: The template
OUTCOME: by the end of this meeting we will have
Type: INPUT / CONSULTATION / COORDINATION / DECISION-MAKING
Mode key: D = discuss, X = decide, I = inform.
Close and next steps: ______ minutes. Parking lot read back: Y / N
Total allocated: ______ of ______ minutes.
A test before you send it
Read the agenda as if you were the most junior person invited. Can you tell why you are there, what you are expected to contribute, and what you need to have done first? If not, it is not ready.
Handout: Meeting Notes and Action Tracker

Use during What Happens After, and reuse for every real meeting. The point of this format is that decisions and actions are separated from discussion, because discussion is what gets recorded and decisions are what get forgotten.
The rule
Somebody who was not in the meeting should be able to read this and know where things stand. If they cannot, the notes are a diary rather than a record.
Header
Did we achieve it? YES / PARTLY / NO
DECISIONS made today
One line each. State it as settled or do not put it here.
ACTIONS
Every line needs a name, a specific verb, and a date. Thinking about something is not an action.
STILL OPEN
Things we did not settle. Each one needs an owner for closing it and a date, or it disappears.
PARKING LOT
Read this back before the meeting ends. An unread parking lot teaches people not to raise things.
My three feedback questions
My four reflection questions, answered before I forget
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. The first three are what you hand someone who asks for more; the rest are for a facilitator going deeper. Resource type is marked on each.
Start here

items: Lencioni, P. (2004). Death by Meeting: A Leadership Fable About Solving the Most Painful Problem in Business. Jossey-Bass. The argument that meetings are boring because they lack conflict, not because they lack structure. Short, and the fable format makes it easy to hand to a skeptic. Book.

Parker, P. (2018). The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why It Matters. Riverhead Books. The best book on purpose in any kind of gathering, and the source of the idea that a gathering with no specific purpose is a gathering that serves the convener. Book.

Parker, P. Three steps to turn everyday get-togethers into transformative gatherings. TED, about 12 minutes. The short version of the book, and the right thing to send as pre-work. Video. https://www.ted.com/talks/priya_parker_3_steps_to_turn_everyday_get_togethers_into_transformative_gatherings

blocks.text: Facilitation

items: Kaner, S., with Lind, L., Toldi, C., Fisk, S., and Berger, D. (2014). Facilitator’s Guide to Participatory Decision-Making, 3rd edition. Jossey-Bass. The standard reference. The chapter on the groan zone, the uncomfortable middle of any real decision, is the single most useful thing in it for meeting facilitators. Book.

Edmondson, A. C. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 350 to 383. The original research behind a term that now gets used loosely. Worth reading once so you use it precisely. Journal article. https://doi.org/10.2307/2666999

Edmondson, A. C. (2018). The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth. Wiley. The applied version, with what a leader actually does differently. Book.

blocks.text: Decisions and participation

items: International Association for Public Participation. IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation. One page: inform, consult, involve, collaborate, empower. The clearest tool for being honest about how much influence people in the room actually have. Reference. https://iap2.org/resources/

Friedman, M. Results-Based Accountability, and the Results-Based Accountability Guide. Start from the result and work backwards. The population-versus-program accountability distinction is the part that transfers to meetings. Guide. https://www.dhs.state.il.us/onenetlibrary/27896/documents/by_division/dchp/rfp/rbaguide.pdf

Center for the Study of Social Policy. Using Results-Based Accountability for Performance Accountability with Community Partnerships. The applied version for coalitions. Brief. https://cssp.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/First-5-LA-Best-Practice-Brief-RBA-PerformAcct-FINAL-1.pdf

blocks.text: Listening and watching

items: Lencioni, P. At the Table: Make Your Meetings Matter. The Table Group. The author on his own framework, and a good thing to send someone who will not read the book. Podcast episode, on video. https://youtu.be/zJhOmVqLRIQ
How to Organize Effective Meetings. A short practical overview, useful as a refresher rather than as a first source. Video. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qrd_8IrErIM

blocks.text: Within the Red Cross

items: Inclusive Facilitation, the Community Mobilization skill build. Workshop 2 of this skill compresses equitable participation into twelve minutes. That skill treats it properly and is where to send anyone who wants more. Skill build.
Leading Through Influence, the Community Mobilization skill build. For the meetings where you are convening people who do not report to you, which is most of the ones that matter. Skill build.

blocks.text: Optional. The session does not depend on it, because Name the Partner (page 17) produces a working partnership in the room. Pre-work makes the session sharper because participants arrive with a real relationship rather than a remembered one. Send it three days ahead and do not chase it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Pick a partner (5 minutes)

Choose one real organization you are working with, or trying to work with, right now. Not the easiest one. Pick one where you want more than you are currently getting, or where you suspect the relationship is running on goodwill rather than on anything specific.
Write down: who they are, who your main contact is, how long the relationship has existed, and what the last concrete thing was that either party did because of it.
2. Answer these about them (10 minutes)
Answer as best you can, and mark anything you are guessing with a question mark. The question marks are the useful part.

items: What is this organization trying to achieve this year?
What is their leadership measured on? Who do they report to?
What is their biggest constraint right now: money, people, time, credibility, or something else?
What would make this year a success for them, in their words rather than ours?
What do they get from working with us today? Be specific and be honest.

blocks.text: 3. Answer the same thing about us (5 minutes)

items: What are we trying to achieve with this partnership, stated as an outcome rather than an activity?
What are our real constraints, including the ones we do not usually say out loud?
What are we asking them for?
What are we offering, other than the Red Cross name?

blocks.text: Bring both sets of answers. That is the whole assignment.
If you have time: on trust
Alignment requires both parties to say true things about their constraints, which requires trust. Two short pieces worth the time:

items: Brene Brown, The Anatomy of Trust, about 23 minutes. The seven elements, one of which is the willingness to say you do not know. https://brenebrown.com/videos/anatomy-trust-video/
Amy Edmondson, What is psychological safety, about 8 minutes. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GZgmoxOgfig

blocks.text: One question afterward: in your partner relationship, which side is currently doing more of the pretending?
Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. That is what Name the Partner is for. The question marks in part 2 are the most valuable thing the pre-work produces, so if you send it, say explicitly that guessing and marking the guess is the assignment rather than a failure to prepare.
Materials: A large drawn version of the poster on a flipchart or whiteboard, showing the four prompts.
Purpose: Get every voice into the room in the first ten minutes, and introduce people by what they bring rather than by their job title.
Set-up

items: Display or pre-draw the poster so participants can see the four prompts clearly.
Position it as both a guide and a visual anchor for the room.

blocks.text: The Activity
Invite each participant to introduce themselves using the four prompts:
1. Your name. Start with your name, and what you would like to be called in this space.
2. The kind of work you do with groups. Share a bit about your work, especially anything that involves working with groups, communities, or teams.
3. One thing you must learn. Name one thing you are actively trying to learn or get better at right now, especially something connected to this work.

4. A superpower you have. Finish by naming a strength, skill, or quality you bring that others might benefit from in this space. We know you have many. Finish by sharing one that this group might benefit from.
Facilitation guidance

items: Model the tone by going first. Keep it concise and authentic.
Encourage brevity, 30 to 45 seconds per person, to keep the energy high.
Listen for themes: learning edges, strengths, shared challenges. You will reference these later.
Affirm contributions, especially when someone names a learning edge rather than only a strength.

blocks.text: Why this works
It quietly establishes four things this skill depends on:
Voice. Everyone speaks early, which lowers the barrier to speaking later.
Transparency. People name both strengths and learning edges, which models the honesty alignment requires.
Belonging. Participants begin to see themselves as contributors rather than attendees.
Asset-framing. People are introduced through what they bring, not just their role. That is the same move this skill asks you to make with a partner organization.
Facilitator note

The fourth prompt is the one people resist, and the resistance is worth naming lightly. Someone will deflect with a joke about not having one. Wait, and let the room supply it if they know each other. The discomfort of naming your own asset is exactly the discomfort a partner feels when we ask what they bring, and saying so afterward makes the connection land.
Materials: A large jar drawn on a flipchart or whiteboard, round sticky notes as marbles, one or two per person, markers.
Purpose: Co-create what matters in how this group works together, shifting the focus from tasks to the conditions that make honest conversation possible.
Set-up

items: Display or pre-draw the large marble jar.
Give each participant one or two round sticky notes and a marker.
Explain that each note represents something that contributes to a full, healthy, high-functioning jar.

blocks.text: Step 1: Individual reflection (2 min)

Say: “Think back to when you were in school. Did your class ever have a marble jar? When the class did something well you earned a marble, and when the jar was full there was a reward. Let us bring that into this room. What would need to happen here for you to feel like this group deserves a marble? What actions, behaviors or ways of showing up would make this a group you want to contribute to?”
The prompt on the poster: what will fill our marble jar?

Offer examples only if the room stalls: a behavior such as listening or curiosity, a value such as trust or transparency, a condition such as psychological safety or shared purpose. Participants write one word or short phrase per note.
Step 2: Add to the jar (2 to 3 min)

items: Invite participants to place their marbles inside or around the jar.
As they place them, encourage them to say the word out loud.

blocks.text: Step 3: Group noticing (2 min)

items: What are you noticing in what is filling our jar?
What themes or patterns are emerging?
What feels essential to how we want to show up together?

blocks.text: Facilitation guidance

items: Keep the pace quick. This is collective creation, not careful drafting.
Circle repeated words to reinforce the shared ones.
Do not evaluate responses. Every marble contributes.
This is not about perfection, it is about shared ownership from the start.

blocks.text: Close (30 seconds)

Say: “What fills a marble jar are the small, consistent actions that shape how we show up together. That is the foundation of this work: creating the conditions where trust, alignment and shared ownership can grow.”
Why this works

items: It centers shared meaning: what matters in how we work, not what we produce.
It creates a visible artifact the group can point at later.
It reinforces with, not for, through collective contribution.
It frames the room as a community of practice rather than an audience.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Keep the jar up and use it. This icebreaker claims to create an artifact the group can reference, and in most deliveries nobody ever references it again, which teaches the room that the exercise was decorative. Point at it at least once during a difficult moment later in the session.
Materials: A large drawn version of the belonging visual, optional. One sheet of 8.5 by 11 cardstock per person, markers.
Purpose: Connect participants to the experience of belonging and turn it into a visible personal commitment they carry through the session.
Set-up

items: Display or pre-draw the belonging visual if you are using it.
Each participant receives a cardstock sheet and markers.
The sheet becomes a placard displayed in front of them for the whole meeting.
Encourage large lettering, color, simple sketches.

blocks.text: Step 1: Individual reflection (2 min)
Say: “Think of a moment when you felt genuine belonging. Anywhere. What three words describe that experience?” Participants write their three words on the placard, large and visible.
Step 2: Table share (5 min)

items: At tables, each participant shares their three words.
Listen for common threads and for differences.
This is about recognition, not reduction. Do not let tables start merging words.

blocks.text: Step 3: Whole group activation (3 min)

items: Invite participants to place their placard in front of them, visible to the room.
Say: “Look around. This is what belonging looks like in this room.”
Pause briefly. Do not fill the pause.

blocks.text: Key framing statement, do not skip
Say: “These words are the DNA of our purpose.”
Facilitation guidance

items: Do not over-process the table share. Keep the energy moving.
Let the visual field of all the placards do the work.

blocks.text: Close (30 seconds)
Say: “You are not just naming words, you are carrying them. These are the conditions people need to experience if we are going to mobilize with communities. This is where the work begins.”
Why this works

items: It makes belonging visible and present for the whole session rather than for one exercise.
It puts individual accountability for how we show up in front of each person.
It creates a distributed visual field of shared meaning rather than one wall.
It models that shared agendas are built from many voices held in view at once.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Do not run this and then run the Shared Agenda Session (page 29) in the same day. That session opens with the identical belonging prompt and collects three words again, so participants would do the same exercise twice within a few hours. If you are running the Shared Agenda Session, open with the Marble Jar or with Name the Partner instead.
Materials: Partner Profile handout (page 38) for each participant, board and markers.
Purpose: Produce the real partner relationship that the rest of the session works on, in the room, without depending on anyone having done pre-work.
Why this comes first

Every core experience in this skill acts on a specific partner organization. If you rely on pre-work to supply one, part of the room spends three activities working on a hypothetical while everyone else works on something real, and the difference in what they get out of it is enormous. Fifteen minutes here removes that.
Choose how the room does it
Pick one before the session.

Option A, everyone brings their own. Each participant names a real partner and works it individually all session. Best when most people did the pre-work and for groups from different chapters. Most personally useful, least shared discussion.

Option B, one volunteered partnership. One participant offers a real relationship and the room works it together. Best for a single chapter team, produces the sharpest conversation, and asks a lot of the volunteer. Ask privately beforehand, and agree what they are comfortable having said out loud.

Option C, one supplied partnership. You provide one and everyone works it together. Safest with a new group. Use the scenario in Where It Breaks (page 21) if you want the session to build toward that activity.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Before we can talk about alignment we need something to align. In the next fifteen minutes you are going to put one real partner organization on paper, including the parts you are not sure about. This stays in front of you all session.”
The Activity
Step 1 (3 min): Name them

items: Who are they, who is your contact, and how long has the relationship existed?
What is the last concrete thing either organization did because of this relationship? If you cannot name one, write that down; it is the most useful answer on the sheet.

blocks.text: Step 2 (5 min): What are they trying to achieve?
On the Partner Profile, answer in their words rather than ours. Put a question mark next to anything you are guessing.

items: What are they trying to achieve this year?
What is their leadership measured on, and who do they answer to?
What is their biggest constraint right now?
What do they currently get from us? Be specific. The Red Cross name is not an answer.

blocks.text: Step 3 (4 min): What are we trying to achieve?

items: What do we want from this partnership, as an outcome rather than an activity?
What are our real constraints, including one we do not usually say out loud?
What are we asking for, and what are we offering?

blocks.text: Step 4 (3 min): Read it back to the room
Take three or four, not everyone.

items: How many question marks are on your partner side, and how many on ours?
Could you answer what they get from us without using the words visibility or credibility?
Whose sheet has more written on our side than theirs? Almost everyone’s does.

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: most rooms find that they can describe their own goals in detail and their partner’s in generalities, and that they cannot name what the partner actually gets. That asymmetry is not a research problem, it is the reason the partnership feels like a request. The rest of the session is about closing it.
Facilitator note

The question marks are the point and participants will be embarrassed by them. Say early and clearly that a sheet full of question marks about a partner you have worked with for three years is completely normal and is exactly what this session is for. Without that, people fill the boxes with plausible guesses and the whole session runs on invented information.
If someone chooses a partnership that is already working well, ask them to choose a harder one. A partnership with nothing wrong with it teaches nothing.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which option will you run, and why does it fit this group?
If Option B, who have you asked in advance, and what did you agree is off limits?
