Materials: Partner Profile from Name the Partner, Overlap Map handout (page 39) for each participant, easel paper for each pair, markers.
Purpose: Find where two organizations’ priorities genuinely overlap, and discover that the overlap is smaller, more specific, and more useful than the one everyone assumed.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Two columns. Everything they are trying to achieve on one side, everything we are trying to achieve on the other. Then we go looking for the place where those are the same piece of work. Not the same values. The same work.”
Part 1: Fill both columns (12 min)
On easel paper, working from the Partner Profile.

items: Left column: their goals for this year. Five to eight, as specific as you can make them. What are they measured on, what is their board asking for, what did they say in the last meeting they were worried about?
Right column: our goals for this year for the community or program this partnership touches. The same number, the same specificity.
Mark anything you are guessing on either side.

blocks.text: Rule: no entry may be a value. Trust, equity, resilience and collaboration are not goals, they are the reason goals matter. If you cannot say what someone would do differently on Monday, it does not go on the wall.
Part 2: Find the overlap (15 min)
On the Overlap Map, work through four categories. Most pairs find items in all four, and the distribution is the finding.
Genuine overlap. The same piece of work serves both goals. Both organizations would want this done even if the other one disappeared.
One-way. It serves our goal and not theirs, or theirs and not ours. Not a problem, but it is a favor rather than a partnership, and it should be named as one and paid for somehow.
Adjacent. Close but not touching. Usually the most interesting column, because a small change to either side would move it into genuine overlap. Note what that change would be.
Competing. The same resource, the same funder, the same community’s attention, or the same credit. Real partnerships have these and pretending otherwise is what makes them fail later.
Part 3: Pressure test (10 min)
Pairs swap sheets with another pair and interrogate the genuine overlap column. Three questions, asked hard.

items: Would the partner actually describe this as one of their priorities, in these words? How do you know?
Is this a goal or an activity? If the partner stopped doing this specific thing tomorrow, would they have failed at something they care about?
What does the Red Cross have to change for this to be genuine rather than convenient?

blocks.text: Anything that survives all three stays in the column. Anything that does not moves to adjacent or one-way. Most groups lose half.
Part 4: Name the one (8 min)
Each participant picks the single strongest item of genuine overlap and writes one sentence: the work, why it serves them, why it serves us. Read a few out loud.
Debrief

items: How many items survived the pressure test, and how many did you start with?
Which column was fullest? Most rooms find one-way is the biggest, and that it points our way.
What is in your competing column, and has anyone ever said it out loud to the partner?
What would the Red Cross have to change for your best overlap to be real?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide: what usually happens

The first pass is too abstract. Groups write “improve community resilience” on both sides and declare alignment. The no-values rule catches most of this; enforce it visibly in the first three minutes and the rest of the activity works.

The overlap shrinks and people find that discouraging. Say the opposite out loud: a partnership with one genuine overlap and a plan is worth more than one with six imagined ones and a memorandum. Shrinking is the activity working.

The competing column is the one people skip. Almost nobody fills it unprompted. Ask directly: are you and this partner ever going to the same funder, or asking the same community for the same hour of its time?

Adjacent is where the value is. The best partnerships in most chapters started as adjacent and moved, because somebody changed a timeline or a location. Ask each pair to name the specific change their best adjacent item would need.
Facilitator note

The pressure test is the whole activity and it needs to be done by another pair rather than by you. Participants will not interrogate their own sheet honestly, and they interrogate somebody else’s with enthusiasm. If you are short on time, cut Part 4 and keep Part 3.
FACILITATOR PREP
Bring one partnership from your own region where the overlap turned out to be different from what everyone assumed. You will need it in the Part 2 framing.
What everyone assumed the overlap was: _______________________________
What it actually turned out to be: ___________________________________
Materials: The four scenarios below, printed, one per group. Board and markers.
Purpose: Recognize misalignment early. Every scenario here is a partnership that looks healthy and is not, and each one fails in a different way.
Setup (say this to participants)

“These four partnerships all have a signed agreement and a friendly relationship. All four are going to fail. Your job is to work out what is actually wrong, and what you would have to say to fix it, this week.”
Groups of three or four, one scenario each. If you have more than four groups, double up and compare readings at the end.
Scenario 1: The willing partner with nothing to give

A community health organization has agreed enthusiastically to co-host preparedness events. Their director is genuinely committed and says so in every meeting. Nine months in, three events have been scheduled and two were cancelled by them at short notice. Their staff turnover last year was 40 percent. They have one program manager covering what used to be three roles, and she has never been in any of the planning meetings.
Scenario 2: The partnership that is really a favor

A large employer lets the chapter run blood drives in their lobby four times a year and has done for six years. The relationship is warm. Their community relations lead attends the annual chapter breakfast. When the chapter asked them to help recruit volunteers for disaster response, the answer was a polite deferral. When the chapter asked for a meeting about their emergency plan, the answer was that their facilities team handles that.
Scenario 3: The alignment that was real and is not any more

A regional food bank and the chapter built a joint distribution model two years ago that worked well. It was built around the food bank’s goal of expanding rural reach. Six months ago their major rural funding ended and their board redirected them toward a downtown hub strategy. Nobody at the chapter noticed. Joint distributions have quietly dropped from monthly to twice this year, and both sides describe the partnership as strong.
Scenario 4: The competing priority nobody will name

The chapter and a well-established local disaster relief nonprofit both serve the same county. They coordinate well operationally and the two directors like each other. They have applied to the same three foundations in the past eighteen months and neither has ever mentioned it to the other. Last month a county emergency management official asked the chapter, privately, which of the two organizations should be the lead for shelter coordination.
Part 1: Diagnose (12 min)

items: What is actually misaligned here? Name it in one sentence.
Is this a will problem, a capacity problem, an authority problem, or a competing-priority problem? These need different responses and are constantly confused for each other.
Who in each organization knows there is a problem? Somebody usually does.
What did the Red Cross assume that was not checked?

blocks.text: Part 2: The conversation (15 min)
Draft the opening of the conversation that would surface this. Not the whole conversation, the first ninety seconds, written out and then said out loud to your group.

items: What are you naming, and how do you name it without it being an accusation?
What are you offering to change on our side? A conversation that only asks them to change is not a repair, it is a complaint.
What question are you asking that you genuinely do not know the answer to?

blocks.text: Part 3: Share and compare (13 min)
Each group reads its scenario in one sentence, its diagnosis, and its opening ninety seconds. Then the room responds.

items: Would you have opened it that way?
What would the partner hear in that opening that we did not intend?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide: what each scenario is

Scenario 1 is capacity, not will. The director means every word and cannot deliver, and the person who would have to do the work has never been in the room. The fix is not more commitment, it is a smaller commitment plus getting the program manager into the planning. Groups almost always diagnose this as a commitment problem first.

Scenario 2 is a one-way relationship that everyone has agreed to call a partnership. Six years of blood drives is a real contribution and it is the whole of the overlap. The mistake is treating warmth as evidence of alignment. The honest move is to stop asking for things outside the overlap, and to ask what would make the blood drives better for them.

Scenario 3 is alignment decay, and it is the most common failure in real chapters. Nothing went wrong. Their priorities moved and nobody had a mechanism for noticing. This is why the third core experience puts a review date on every commitment.

Scenario 4 is a competing priority that both sides are managing by not mentioning. It is survivable and it is not survivable silently, because the emergency management question forces it into the open on somebody else’s timeline. Watch whether any group proposes actually raising the funding overlap. Most will not.
Facilitator note

The four categories in Part 1 are the teaching content and they are worth putting on the board: will, capacity, authority, competing priority. Most partnership problems get diagnosed as will problems, which leads to more meetings about commitment, which fixes nothing. If the room takes only one thing from this activity, it should be the habit of asking which of the four it is before deciding what to do.
Scenario 4 makes people uncomfortable and they will try to solve it by improving communication. Press them: what specifically do you say, to whom, and when?
FACILITATOR PREP
Add a fifth scenario from your own region if you can, with the organization anonymized. A local one is worth more than all four of these.
Which of the four categories it is: ___________________________________
Materials: Overlap Map from The Two Columns, Joint Commitment Sheet (page 41) for each participant, pens.
Purpose: Turn one piece of genuine overlap into something both organizations could actually commit to, with named people, dates, and a mechanism for noticing when it stops working.
Setup (say this to participants)

“You have found where your priorities overlap. That is worth nothing until somebody does something differently. In the next fifty minutes you are going to build the thing you would put in front of your partner, and it has to be good enough that they would say yes for their own reasons rather than as a favor.”
Part 1: The ask and the offer (12 min)
On the Joint Commitment Sheet, working from your strongest overlap.

items: What are we asking them to do? One sentence, specific enough to schedule.
What are we offering? Not the Red Cross name, not visibility, not the opportunity to serve. Something they would put in their own board report.
What does this cost them, honestly, in hours and money and attention?
What does it cost us, in the same terms?

blocks.text: The test: read only the offer to your neighbour, without the ask. If it does not sound like something worth having on its own, it is not an offer.
Part 2: The mutual-benefit line (10 min)
Write one sentence, in the partner’s language, that says why this is worth their time. Then write the same sentence in ours. Both go on the sheet.
Two rules that make this hard and are the point:

items: Neither sentence may contain the words partnership, collaboration, synergy, or leverage.
Their sentence must be true if the Red Cross were not involved. If the only reason it is good for them is that we are in it, we have written a pitch rather than found an overlap.

blocks.text: Part 3: Make it real (12 min)

items: Who does what, by when? Names, not organizations. A commitment owned by an organization is owned by nobody.
Who on their side has to say yes for this to happen, and have they ever been in a room with us?
What is the first thing that happens, and what is its date?
What would tell us in six months that this worked? One measure, not four.

blocks.text: Part 4: Keeping it alive (8 min)
This is the part every partnership skips and it is why scenario 3 in Where It Breaks happens.

items: When do we deliberately check whether this is still serving both sides? Put an actual date on the sheet.
What would tell us their priorities had moved? Name two specific signals: a funding change, a leadership change, a strategy document, a partner who stops attending.
Who is responsible for noticing, and what do they do when they notice?
What is the honest exit? A partnership nobody can leave is not a partnership. Say how either side would end this well.

blocks.text: Part 5: The pressure test (8 min)
Swap sheets. Read somebody else’s as if you were the partner organization’s director, and answer three questions out loud:

items: Would I say yes to this? If not, what is missing?
Is the offer real, or is it the ask wearing a jacket?
What is this asking me to trust that I have no evidence for yet?

blocks.text: Debrief

items: Whose offer survived being read alone?
How many of you named a specific person on their side who has to say yes, and how many of you have met them?
What review date did you put down, and what will actually happen on that date?
What did you have to change on our side to make this genuine?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide

The offer is where this activity lives. Most participants write an ask and then write a second ask dressed as an offer. The read-it-alone test catches it every time and is worth doing out loud rather than in pairs.

The word “visibility” is a warning sign. It is what we offer when we have not worked out what they need. When it appears, ask what they would do with the visibility, and keep asking until there is an answer or the offer changes.

The review date gets treated as bureaucracy. It is the single highest-value line on the sheet, because alignment decays silently and a date is the only thing that interrupts that. Point back at scenario 3.

The exit question surprises people. Naming how a partnership would end well is what makes it safe to be honest during it. Some participants find it disloyal; say plainly that the alternative is a relationship that limps for four years because nobody could say it was over.
Facilitator note

If the group has done The Two Columns immediately before this, they will be tired and this is the harder activity. Consider a break, and consider cutting Part 5 to five minutes rather than cutting Part 4, which is the part nobody else will teach them.
FACILITATOR PREP
Decide what happens to these commitment sheets after the session. A sheet nobody follows up on teaches participants that the planning was an exercise.
Format: Facilitated dialogue. Participants build shared understanding through guided questioning rather than lecture.
Purpose: Frame partnership as a discipline rather than a disposition, and surface how much of what a chapter calls partnership is actually goodwill with no overlap underneath it.
Agenda at a glance

items: 0 to 8 minutes: The partnership that faded
8 to 22 minutes: What do they actually want
22 to 35 minutes: What do we actually want
35 to 48 minutes: Where it gets hard
48 to 60 minutes: What we would do differently, and close

blocks.text: Before you start

Two rules, said out loud. No partner organization gets named in a way that identifies it, and nobody in this room has a partnership portfolio that would survive this hour untouched, including the facilitator.
Segment 1: The partnership that faded (0 to 8 min)

items: Think of a partnership that started with real energy and quietly stopped. What happened?
When did you first suspect it was over? How much later did anyone say so?
Whose fault was it? Sit with that question for a second before answering.

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Almost nobody can name a moment it failed, because nothing failed. Name that: partnerships rarely break, they decay, and the absence of a failure point is why nobody intervenes. Capture the reasons on a board; you will point at this list three times in the next hour.
Segment 2: What do they actually want (8 to 22 min)

items: Take one partner you work with. What are they trying to achieve this year?
How do you know that? Did they tell you, or did you infer it?
What is their leadership measured on? Who do they have to satisfy?
What do they get from us, specifically? Not the Red Cross name. What do they get?
When did we last ask them any of this directly?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. The fourth question is the one that goes quiet, and it should. Most rooms cannot answer it without reaching for visibility or credibility, which are what we say when we have not found out. Say so gently, and note that we usually know our own ask in detail and their benefit in generalities.
Segment 3: What do we actually want (22 to 35 min)

items: What are we trying to achieve through this partnership? Say it as an outcome, not an activity.
Have we ever told them our real constraints, or only our aspirations?
What would we have to change about our own plan for this to work for both sides?
What is the difference between a partner and a volunteer organization that we have not paid?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. The third question is the pivot of the whole hour. Alignment that costs the Red Cross nothing is not alignment, and rooms resist this. Do not argue it; ask for one example of a partnership where we changed something, and let the difficulty of producing one make the point.
Segment 4: Where it gets hard (35 to 48 min)

items: When have you been in a partnership where you both wanted the same funder, the same community’s attention, or the same credit? What did you do?
What is the difference between a partner who will not and a partner who cannot?
Who in your partner organizations has authority you have never spoken to?
How would you know if their priorities had moved? What would you notice?
What does it cost to keep a partnership going that is not producing anything?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Will, capacity, authority, competing priority. Put those four on the board; almost every partnership problem is one of them and almost all of them get treated as the first. The last question is the one people avoid: keeping a dead partnership alive costs staff time, credibility with the community, and the chapter’s capacity to build a live one.
Segment 5: What we would do differently, and close (48 to 60 min)

items: What is one question you would ask a partner this month that you have never asked?
Which of your partnerships would not survive being honest, and is that the partnership’s fault or ours?
What is one thing you will do differently in your next partner conversation?

blocks.text: Take the third answer from every person out loud, one sentence each. Write them down and send them back afterward.

Facilitator synthesis. Close by pointing back at the faded-partnership list from the first eight minutes and asking which of those failures would have been caught by the question they just committed to asking. Usually most of them.
Train-the-Trainer
Read this before your first delivery.
What this session is for

It is not an introduction to partnership. Everyone in the room has partners. It is the hour where a group notices that its partnership portfolio is largely built on goodwill and inference, and that this is normal and fixable. If you teach content here, the core experiences afterward become paperwork rather than repair.
Four guardrails

Do not let it become a partner-blaming session. The room will describe unreliable partners. Redirect once, early: what did we assume that we never checked? That question holds for the rest of the hour.
Protect segment 3. It is the shortest and the most important, and it is the one facilitators cut when segment 2 runs long. Watch the clock at minute twenty-two.

Hold the silence after the benefit question. When you ask what a partner actually gets from us and the room cannot answer, wait. That silence is the most valuable ten seconds in the session and facilitators consistently rescue it.
Bring your own. Have a partnership of your own that faded, and be able to say what you did not ask. A room gives back roughly what the facilitator puts in.
Common failure modes

items: The hour becomes a list of partner names and stories. Ask for the pattern rather than the next example.
Somebody senior describes a partnership everyone recognizes. Move to the pattern quickly; naming the organization makes the rest of the hour cautious.
Everyone agrees partnerships matter and nothing is at risk. If nobody has been uncomfortable by minute thirty-five, ask the what-would-we-change question again, harder.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Bring one partnership of your own that faded, and the question you now wish you had asked.
Decide what happens to the commitments from segment five, and say so at the close.
Materials: A sticky wall or a long stretch of wall and painter’s tape. Note paper for each person, private to them. Cardstock sheets and several fat markers per table. Dot stickers, three per person.
Purpose: Shape a shared agenda for a group of people who work together, by naming the work they do when they are in community with one another rather than by listing what they deliver.
Read this before you schedule it

This session is different from the rest of this document, and running it in place of the core experiences is the most common mistake with this material. The core experiences teach a chapter how to align with a partner organization. This session helps a group articulate its own collective purpose. Both are useful and they are not substitutes.

Use it when a group does not have a clear shared vision of how to move forward together, or when a group wants to produce a purpose statement it will actually use. It is excellent for a leadership team, a community of practice, or a coalition that has been meeting without ever saying what it is for. It is not a partner-alignment session.

On the timing. The written segments total about 62 minutes. The remaining time is real and is needed: transitions, the sticky wall, people finishing, and the harvest running long. Plan the 90 minutes and expect the gallery walk and the weaving to expand.
On overlap. The warm-up here is the same exercise as the Belonging Words icebreaker (page 15). Run one or the other, never both.
Prepare four posters in advance

items: “A shared agenda is not a brand statement. It is a declaration of belonging, partnership, and shared purpose.”
“Today we are gathering to name the work we do, and the work we are becoming, as a community of practice committed to mobilizing with communities, not for them.”
“What does it look like when we mobilize with communities rather than for them?”
“We are... (identity) who... (practice) so that... (shared purpose)”

blocks.text: Opening frame (2 min)

Say: “The purpose of this session is to shape a shared agenda for community mobilizers. Not by listing tasks or describing what we deliver, but by naming the work we do when we are in community with one another and with the communities we mobilize alongside.”

Say: “A shared agenda is not a brand statement. It is a declaration of belonging, partnership, and shared purpose. Today we are here to articulate that shared work, the commitments and practices that make mobilization possible, so we can equip our Executive Directors, Community Disaster Program Managers, staff and volunteers to step into this work with clarity and confidence.”
Peter Block on community (5 min)

Say: “Today is deeply influenced by the work of Peter Block, author of Community: The Structure of Belonging. Block reminds us that community is not defined by systems or services, but by the experience of belonging, and that belonging is created through the invitations we extend and the commitments we make to one another.”

Say: “That matters here because a shared agenda is not a plan or a list of actions. It is a relational act. It only holds when the people involved see themselves as part of a community, rather than as separate actors delivering services to one. Mobilization begins long before execution. It begins with how we show up, how we gather, and how we choose to be in relationship.”

Say: “If we are going to facilitate a shared agenda, we have to recognize our place inside the community rather than outside it. As Block writes, we create a future by paying attention to the ways we gather.”
Creative warm-up: belonging words (12 min)

Individual (2 min). “Think of a moment when you felt genuine belonging, in any context. What three words describe that experience? You have two minutes before I ask you to share them with your table.”
Table share (5 min). Tables share their words. At the four-minute mark, ask each table to choose the three words that feel most resonant. Each word goes on its own sheet and onto the sticky wall.

Whole group harvest (5 min). Gather the words where everyone can see them. This becomes the creative palette for the rest of the session. Themes usually emerge already: trust, invitation, shared power, listening, courage, co-creation, presence.
Say: “These words are the DNA of our purpose.”
Identity and partnership reflection (10 min)
Say: “Now we shift from belonging to practice.”
Individual (2 min). Two prompts, not one. Who are we, as a group, when we are at our best? And what does it look like when we mobilize with communities rather than for them?
Small group clustering (6 min). Groups cluster their responses and name each cluster with a short phrase. These clusters become the backbone of the purpose statement.
Transition (2 min). Read three or four cluster names out loud before moving on. This is what the next segment builds from and groups work faster if they have heard the others.
Purpose statement sprint (10 min)
Each small group drafts one sentence using the structure: We are (identity) who (practice) so that (shared purpose).
The structure is generative rather than restrictive. It produces statements with movement in them. You will end up with three to six drafts.
Gallery walk and dot voting (5 min)

items: Post every statement. Everyone gets three dots and votes for the ones that feel most true.
This surfaces the shared center of gravity quickly and without discussion, which is the point.

blocks.text: Creative weaving (10 min)

Refine the statement (5 min). Using the top-voted statement, guide the group to one strong sentence. Prompts: what word or phrase must stay? Is there anywhere we need to shift from for to with? Does this sound like us at our best?
Motto or tagline (5 min). “If this purpose statement had a heartbeat, a short phrase that captures its spirit, what would it be?” Take five to seven rapid suggestions, vote, pick one. Fast and fun.
Guiding paragraph (8 min)

Say: “We have named words of belonging, clustered our practices, and shaped a purpose statement. Now we turn that into a short guiding paragraph. Not to explain everything we do, but to anchor how we work together. This is not a marketing paragraph. It is a practice-level narrative that guides decisions, facilitation, and teaching.”
Read it aloud (30 sec). Read the chosen purpose statement slowly, once. Pause. Let it land. Listen not for what sounds polished but for what feels true.
Harvest the non-negotiables (3 min). Ask: what two or three ideas from our clusters must be included to explain this purpose more fully?
Facilitation moves for the harvest:

items: Call for short phrases, not speeches.
Capture words verbatim on a board or shared document.
If the room is large, invite three to five voices at most. You are surfacing signal, not building consensus.

blocks.text: Probe gently if needed: what way of being together does this purpose require? What would be missing if this paragraph did not name how we partner with communities? Which idea protects us from slipping into for instead of with?
You are listening for shared power, trust-building, transparency, learning alongside communities, and accountability to relationships rather than only to outcomes.

Live weaving (3 min). Say: “I am going to weave these ideas into a short paragraph using your language. This will not be perfect, and that is fine. It is a working narrative we can refine.” Then draft live, speaking as you write. Aim for two or three sentences, plain grounded language, relational stance over technical detail.

Model your transparency as you work: “I am choosing this word because it showed up several times.” “I am combining these two to keep it readable.” “I am avoiding jargon here so this stays usable.” This models shared agenda development in action, which is the real lesson of the segment.

Resonance check (1 min). Read it aloud and ask: what word feels essential to keep? Is there anything here that pulls us back toward for instead of with? Does this sound like us at our best in practice, not just in theory? Make one or two light edits only. Do not reopen the paragraph.

Name what it does (30 sec). This paragraph is now three things: the narrative of how we understand ourselves, the bridge to shared agendas, and the articulation of with rather than for. Invite participants to notice that this process is exactly what they will ask others to do.
Closing (2 min)

Say: “What we just did is shared agenda development in practice. We created shared meaning, surfaced what matters most, integrated multiple perspectives, and produced something we can act from together. And we did it in a way that built trust, shared power, and made different voices visible.”

Say: “This is the work we are asking Executive Directors and Community Disaster Program Managers to facilitate, again and again. Not once. Not perfectly. But consistently. They step into rooms with urgency, complexity and competing priorities, and they are asked to lead without full authority, to align people who do not report to them, and to move action forward without erasing lived experience or local expertise. A shared agenda is what makes that possible.”

Say: “When this is done well, meetings stop producing polite agreement and start producing real alignment. Confusion turns into clarity. Tension becomes useful information. And leaders do not carry the burden alone, because the work becomes owned by the group. Notice that what made this work was not the paragraph. It was how we gathered, how meaning was created together, and how decisions were made visible. That is the standard we are setting.”
Facilitator note
If the group gets conceptual, bring it back with: “Where would this show up in a real meeting you facilitate?” That question anchors the paragraph in practice every time.

Whatever the group produces has to go somewhere. Photograph the sticky wall, type the paragraph up the same day, and send it back within 48 hours while people still recognize their own words in it. A purpose statement that reaches people three weeks later reads as someone else’s writing.
FACILITATOR PREP
What is this group, and what will they use the guiding paragraph for? If you cannot answer the second part, do not run this session yet.
Who types it up and sends it back, and by when? ______________________
Field Assignments

These are not room activities. They happen with real partners, which is the only place this skill is actually practiced. Assign one at the close of a session and open the next session with what people found.
Field Assignment 1: Ask them
Take the question marks from your Partner Profile and go and get the answers. One conversation, thirty minutes, with one partner.

items: Ask what they are trying to achieve this year and what their leadership is measured on.
Ask what they get out of working with us. Ask it plainly and then be quiet.
Ask what would make this partnership more useful to them.
Do not bring an ask to this conversation. If you arrive with a request, you will get a polite answer instead of a true one.

blocks.text: Bring back. The one answer that surprised you. There is almost always one, and it is usually about what they get from us.
Field Assignment 2: The partnership audit
List every organization your chapter describes as a partner. Then, for each one, answer two questions.

items: What did either organization actually do differently in the last twelve months because of this relationship?
Which of the four is it: genuine overlap, one-way, adjacent, or competing?
Mark the ones where you cannot answer the first question.

blocks.text: Bring back. How many partners are on the list, and how many produced something. The gap between those two numbers is the most useful fact a chapter can have about its own partnership work.
Field Assignment 3: Meet the person who has to say yes
In every partner organization there is somebody with authority over the thing you want who you have never met. Usually a program director, a chief of staff, or a board chair.

items: Identify who that is for one partner.
Ask your existing contact to introduce you, and say plainly why.
Meet them. Do not ask for anything in the first meeting.

blocks.text: Bring back. What that person cared about that your existing contact had never mentioned. Partnerships stall at the level of the person you have been talking to, and this is the single highest-return thing on this page.
A note on all three

All three assignments involve going and asking rather than analyzing. That is deliberate. Every orphaned assumption in this skill exists because somebody inferred instead of asking, and no amount of mapping in a room substitutes for one honest thirty-minute conversation.
Session Formats
Five written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document; nothing new has to be written to deliver any of them.
20 minutes. What Do They Get. One question, delivered inside a meeting you were already having.
1 hour. Understanding the Partner. Produces a filled partner profile and a list of what you do not know.
2 hours. Finding the Overlap. Adds the two columns and a pressure-tested overlap.
4 hours. From Overlap to Commitment. The full arc, ending in a joint commitment with a review date.
90 minutes, separate. The Shared Agenda Session (page 29). A different session for a different purpose; read its opening note.
How to choose

Choose by what participants walk out holding. A group that leaves with an overlap map and no commitment will not act on it, and a group that leaves with a commitment they built without ever asking the partner anything has written a wish. If you only have an hour, spend it on understanding the partner and book the next session, rather than rushing to a plan.
20-minute version: What Do They Get

items: Everyone names one partner organization, silently (2 min)
Write down what that partner gets from working with us. Specific. Not the Red Cross name, not visibility (5 min)
Round the room: read yours out (8 min)
One question: how many of us were guessing, and what would it take to find out? (5 min)

blocks.text: What they leave with: one honest sentence, or the discovery that they cannot write one.
Purpose: Produce a real partner profile and an honest list of what the chapter does not know about an organization it already calls a partner.
Pre-work: Optional (page 9).
Materials: Partner Profile handout (page 38) for each participant, board and markers.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing: partnerships fail politely, and the reason is usually that nobody asked (5 min)
Icebreaker: What Is Your Superpower, page 11 (8 min)
Icebreaker: Name the Partner, page 17 (15 min)
Individually, complete the Partner Profile and mark every guess (12 min)
Pairs: interrogate each other’s profile. Only one question, asked repeatedly: how do you know that? (10 min)
Closing debrief (10 min)

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: How many question marks ended up on your sheet?
Could you write what the partner gets from us without using visibility or credibility?
Which side of your sheet has more on it, theirs or ours?
What is the one question you are going to ask them this month, and when?

blocks.text: What they leave with: a partner profile, a marked list of assumptions, and one question with a date on it.
Notes on running it

items: This hour deliberately does not reach a plan. Say so at the close or the room will feel it stopped early.
The how-do-you-know pairs exercise is the hour. Protect the full ten minutes; it is where the guesses get exposed.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Which Name the Partner option will you run?
Purpose: Take a group from a partner they think they understand to a pressure-tested overlap they can defend, and to an honest reckoning with what is one-way.
Materials: As for the one-hour, plus the Overlap Map (page 39) and easel paper for each pair.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (5 min)
Icebreaker: Name the Partner, page 17 (15 min)
What alignment is not: agreement, paperwork, or them adopting our priorities (10 min)
Core Experience: The Two Columns, page 19 (45 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: Where It Breaks, page 21, scenarios 1 and 3 only (25 min)
Closing debrief and commitments (10 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: Running only two of the four scenarios is deliberate. One and three are the two that most chapters are living inside right now.
Do not shorten The Two Columns. If you are behind, cut the framing segment to five minutes; the content lands inside the activity anyway.
The no-values rule in The Two Columns needs enforcing in the first three minutes or the whole activity stays abstract.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: How much overlap survived the pressure test?
What is in your one-way column, and what are you going to do about it?
Which of your partnerships is scenario 3, and how long has it been that way?
What is the one conversation you are going to have, and with whom?

blocks.text: What they leave with: a pressure-tested overlap map, an honest read on which partnerships are one-way, and the four categories of misalignment. Say clearly that they have analysis and not yet a plan.
FACILITATOR PREP
When is the follow-on session where they build the commitment? Book it before you deliver this one.

title: Four-Hour Workshop: From Overlap to Commitment
duration: 4 hours, including two breaks totalling 25 minutes

blocks.text: Purpose: The complete arc: understand one partner, find the real overlap, recognize the ways it breaks, and leave with a joint commitment carrying names, dates and a review point.
Materials: All three handouts for every participant, the four Where It Breaks scenarios printed, easel paper for each pair, board, markers.
