items: Welcome and framing (10 min)
Icebreaker: The Marble Jar, page 13 (7 min)
Icebreaker: Name the Partner, page 17 (15 min)
What alignment is not, and the three questions underneath the skill (13 min)
Core Experience: The Two Columns, page 19 (45 min)
Break (15 min)
Core Experience: Where It Breaks, all four scenarios, page 21 (40 min)
Break (10 min)
Core Experience: The Ask and the Offer, page 24 (50 min)
Closing round: one conversation, one person, one date, said out loud (15 min)

blocks.text: Notes on running it

items: The arc is understand, find, protect, commit. Write those four words up in the first ten minutes and point at them as you move.

Where It Breaks sits between the overlap and the commitment on purpose. Participants have just found an overlap and are about to build on it, which is exactly the moment to show them four ways it decays.
Keep the Partner Profiles in front of participants all day. Every activity is a revision of them.
If the group is over sixteen, run The Two Columns in pairs rather than individually and have pairs swap for the pressure test across tables.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Look at the profile from this morning. What has changed on it?
What did the Red Cross have to change for your commitment to be genuine?
Who is the person on their side you have never met, and when are you meeting them?
What is the review date on your commitment, and what happens on that date?

blocks.text: What they leave with: a partner profile, an overlap map, a joint commitment sheet with names and dates, a review date, and the four categories for diagnosing what is going wrong when it does.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which Name the Partner option, and are you adding a local scenario to Where It Breaks?
Who follows up on the commitment sheets, and when? __________________
Handout: Partner Profile
Use during Name the Partner and the one-hour workshop. One per participant, per partner. Mark every answer you are guessing with a question mark. The question marks are the point.
The relationship
How long we have worked together: ______________
Last concrete thing either organization did because of this relationship:
Them
What are they trying to achieve this year?
What is their leadership measured on, and who do they answer to?
Biggest constraint now (money, people, time, credibility, other): ______
What would make this year a success for them, in their words?
What do they get from working with us? Not the Red Cross name. Not visibility.
Us
What are we trying to achieve here, as an outcome rather than an activity?
Our real constraints, including one we do not usually say out loud: _____
The people
Who on their side has authority over the thing we want? ________________
Have we met them? YES / NO. Who on our side owns this relationship?
The count
Question marks on their side: ______ On ours: ______. One question I will ask them, and when: ______________________________________________
Handout: Overlap Map
Use during The Two Columns. One per participant or pair.
The rule

No entry may be a value. Trust, equity, resilience and collaboration are not goals; they are why goals matter. If you cannot say what someone would do differently on Monday, it does not go on this sheet.
GENUINE OVERLAP
The same piece of work serves both goals. Both organizations would want this done even if the other disappeared.
ONE-WAY
Serves one of us and not the other. Not a problem, but it is a favor rather than a partnership. Mark which way it runs.
ADJACENT
Close but not touching. Note the specific change that would move it into genuine overlap; this column is where most good partnerships actually start.
COMPETING
The same funder, the same resource, the same community’s attention, or the same credit. Real partnerships have these. Write them down.
The pressure test
For each item in GENUINE OVERLAP, answer all three. Anything that fails moves to another column.
Would the partner describe this as a priority, in these words? How do I know?
Is it a goal or an activity? If they stopped, would they have failed at something they care about?
What does the Red Cross have to change for this to be genuine rather than convenient?
The one
The strongest overlap, in one sentence: the work, why it serves them, why it serves us.
Handout: Joint Commitment Sheet
Use during The Ask and the Offer. One per participant. This is the sheet you would put in front of a partner, so write it as if they will read it.
The work
What we are proposing, in one sentence: ______________________________
The ask and the offer
Read the offer aloud on its own. Does it sound like something worth having? YES / NO
What it costs them (hours, money, attention): ________________________
Why it is worth it
In their language. May not contain partnership, collaboration, synergy or leverage. Must be true even if the Red Cross were not involved.
In ours:
Who does what
Names, not organizations.
Who on their side has to say yes? ____________________________________
Have we met them? YES / NO. If no, by when? ________________
First thing that happens, and its date: ______________________________
How we will know it worked
Keeping it alive
The date we deliberately check whether this still serves both sides: __________
Two signals that their priorities have moved (funding, leadership, strategy):
Who notices: ______________ How either side would end this well: ______
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. The first three are what you hand someone who asks for more; the rest are for a facilitator or a chapter going deeper. Resource type is marked on each.
Start here

items: Kania, J. and Kramer, M. (2011). Collective Impact. Stanford Social Innovation Review, Winter 2011. The foundational article on cross-sector alignment: a common agenda, shared measurement, mutually reinforcing activities, continuous communication, and a backbone organization. The common agenda is the piece this skill builds. Article. https://ssir.org/articles/entry/collective_impact

Block, P. (2018). Community: The Structure of Belonging, 3rd edition. Berrett-Koehler. Community is created through the invitations we extend and the commitments we make, not through programs. The third edition is the one worth reading; it reflects Block’s thinking about gathering in a more fractured and institutionally distrustful world, and it moves past theory into questions and invitations a leader can use on Monday. Book.

Arnstein, S. R. (1969). A Ladder of Citizen Participation. Journal of the American Institute of Planners 35(4), 216 to 224. The classic account of participation from manipulation through tokenism to citizen power. The most useful single page for asking whether an engagement is genuinely with or still for. Journal article. https://doi.org/10.1080/01944366908977225

blocks.text: On trust, which alignment depends on

items: Covey, S. M. R. (2006). The Speed of Trust: The One Thing That Changes Everything. Free Press. Turns trust from a value into a set of observable behaviors. Note this is Stephen M. R. Covey, not Stephen R. Covey of The 7 Habits; they are father and son and the books are often confused. Book.

Brown, B. (2018). Dare to Lead: Brave Work. Tough Conversations. Whole Hearts. Random House. Courage and vulnerability as leadership practice. Where this skill provides the structure for collaboration, this provides the human capacity that makes it work. Book.

Brown, B. The Anatomy of Trust. About 23 minutes. The seven elements of trust as BRAVING: boundaries, reliability, accountability, vault, integrity, non-judgment, generosity. A useful checklist when a partnership is strained and nobody can say why. Video. https://brenebrown.com/videos/anatomy-trust-video/
Edmondson, A. What is psychological safety? About 8 minutes. Why people stay quiet, and what it costs. Video. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GZgmoxOgfig

blocks.text: On community and belonging

items: Born, P. (2014). Deepening Community: Finding Joy Together in Chaotic Times. Berrett-Koehler. On moving from isolated effort to community-owned change, and on the role of small groups and local leadership in making it last. Book.

Wise, S. (2022). Design for Belonging: How to Build Inclusion and Collaboration in Your Communities. Ten Speed Press. The most practical book here, and beautifully illustrated. It translates belonging, power and participation into concrete design choices about how a space, an agenda and a conversation are structured. Book.

Zander, R. S. and Zander, B. (2000). The Art of Possibility: Transforming Professional and Personal Life. Harvard Business Review Press. On shifting a group from constraint to possibility. Worth hearing rather than reading if you can: Benjamin Zander is a conductor and the audio carries the musical illustrations that make the argument land. Book, and audiobook.

blocks.text: Frameworks and toolkits

items: International Association for Public Participation. IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation. One page: inform, consult, involve, collaborate, empower. Use it to be honest about how much influence a partner actually has over a plan we are calling joint. Reference. https://iap2.org/resources/

Kretzmann, J. P. and McKnight, J. L. Asset-Based Community Development. Start from what each party already has rather than from what the collaboration lacks. ABCD Institute, DePaul University. Reference. https://resources.depaul.edu/abcd-institute/

Federal Emergency Management Agency (2011). A Whole Community Approach to Emergency Management. Guidance on engaging the full capacity of community stakeholders. Aligns closely with Red Cross work on shared responsibility and coordinated action. Guide. https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/whole_community_dec2011__2.pdf
Community Tool Box, University of Kansas. A large free toolkit covering facilitation, coalition building and community engagement, with step-by-step methods. Toolkit. https://ctb.ku.edu/en
Everyday Democracy. Dialogue guides and facilitation resources for inclusive, equity-centered conversation. Toolkit. https://everyday-democracy.org/resources/

blocks.text: Where to start

Books give depth of mindset. Articles give the shared frameworks and language. Toolkits give the method. Videos are fast reinforcement and good discussion starters for a team. Together they support moving from understanding, to practising, to facilitating, to embedding.

Three questions worth holding as you read: how do these ideas change how I show up in a room? What would move me from directing outcomes to facilitating shared meaning? Where could I apply this in a real partner conversation this month?
Element: 1. Reading power and influence.
Group Size: Any. Above about thirty, use the hands version rather than the movement version.
Materials: None. Two signs if you want the sides labeled.
Purpose: Get the distinction between influence and authority into the room physically, before anybody has to define it, and find the statements where the room splits.
Set up (2 minutes)

Designate opposite sides of the room: one side is Leading with Influence, the other is Formal Authority. If the room will not allow movement, or anyone in it would be excluded by moving, use hands instead: left hand for influence, right hand for authority.

Say this: “I am going to read a series of statements. For each one, decide: is this primarily leading with influence, or formal authority? Move to the side of the room that best represents your answer. There is no trick, just go with your instinct.”
The activity (6 to 9 minutes)

items: Use 6 to 12 statements from the bank on page 12. Start with the clear ones and increase the nuance as you go.
After a statement where the room splits, ask one person from each side: “What made you choose that side?” Do not do this after every statement or you will run out of time.
Keep the pace quick. This activity dies if each statement becomes a discussion.
If energy drops, ask someone to argue the opposite side of where they are standing, or to give a real example.

blocks.text: Debrief (3 to 4 minutes)

items: What patterns did you notice?
Which ones were harder to decide?
What does this tell us about how we lead when we do not have authority?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis
Close on this: “Most of our work does not live entirely on one side of the room. We move between them constantly. Today is about strengthening how we lead when authority is not the driver.”
Facilitator notes

items: Do not over-correct. The answer key in the bank exists so you can hold a position when asked, not so you can grade people. The ambiguous statements have no answer and that is the point.
Watch who moves last. People who wait to see where the room goes are telling you something useful about the group, and it is worth a private note rather than a public one.
Virtual: see page 47. Use a poll or two reaction icons and count down from three so everyone answers at once.

blocks.text: Statement Bank: This or That
Use 6 to 12 depending on time. Start simple, then increase nuance. The answers in the last two tiers are discussion openers rather than answers.
Clear distinctions, for warming up
Assigning someone a task and setting a deadline. Formal authority.
Building relationships before asking for action. Leading with influence.
Telling a team what must be done to meet requirements. Formal authority.
Inviting partners to co-create a plan. Leading with influence.
Moderate
Framing a shared goal so people want to take action. Leading with influence.
Escalating an issue up the chain to get a decision made. Formal authority.
Using data and stories to persuade others to shift direction. Leading with influence.
Setting priorities and reallocating resources unilaterally. Formal authority.
Ambiguous, and the best part of the activity
Following up persistently until something gets done. Could be either. Ask what makes the difference.
Convening a group to decide next steps. Often influence, but it depends entirely on how it is facilitated.
Speaking last in a meeting so others contribute first. Leading with influence.
Using your title to gain access to a conversation. A bridge between both, and a good gray area.
Clarifying roles and expectations across partners. Can be either.
Saying, “Here is what I recommend, and why it matters.” Leading with influence.
Stretch
Success is measured by whether others chose to act. Leading with influence.
Success is measured by whether directives were followed. Formal authority.
Element: 5. Adapting leadership posture.
Group Size: Best with 10 or fewer. Above that the line gets crowded and the follow-up questions stop reaching everybody.
Materials: Three sheets of paper for the spectrum labels, a marker, tape.
Purpose: Move from a binary to a spectrum, and get people to notice where on it they habitually operate.
Set up (2 minutes)
Tape three labels along one wall to make a line across the room: Pure Authority at one end, A mix of both in the middle, Pure Influence at the other.

Seated version, and use it whenever movement would exclude anyone: number the spectrum 1 to 10, with 1 as pure authority and 10 as pure influence. Participants hold up fingers or write their number on a card and reveal at the same moment.
The activity (6 to 9 minutes)

items: Read a statement from the bank on page 14. Participants stand where they think it falls.
Ask two people, from different points on the line: “Why did you stand there?”
Then ask the room: “What would move this closer to influence? What would move it closer to authority?”
Use 5 to 8 statements for a short version, 8 to 15 for a deeper one. Mix at least two easy, two moderate and two ambiguous.

blocks.text: Debrief (3 to 4 minutes)

items: Where do you naturally operate, and why?
What do your choices say about your leadership approach?
Was there a statement where you moved after hearing someone else?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Close on this: “Most leadership moments are not clearly one or the other. We move along this spectrum constantly. This exercise helps us notice how we lead when authority is not guaranteed.” The useful finding is usually that people cluster in one third of the line and had not noticed.
Facilitator notes

items: Ask the two people standing furthest apart, rather than the two who volunteer. The gap is where the content is.
This one works better with experienced or reflective groups than with a brand new room. If the group does not know each other, run This or That instead.
Virtual: see page 47. A 1 to 10 poll works well, and showing the distribution before calling on anyone is worth doing.

blocks.text: Statement Bank: Influence Continuum
Seven themed banks. Pick across them rather than working down one. The prompt under each bank is the follow-up question that fits those statements best.
Foundational, good warm-ups

items: Setting expectations for how a team operates.
Communicating a clear goal and desired outcome.
Assigning roles for a project.
Following up on agreed next steps.
Providing guidance on priorities.

blocks.text: Prompt: What makes this lean more toward authority or influence?
Collaboration and coordination

items: Bringing partners together to align on a common goal.
Clarifying roles across multiple groups.
Facilitating agreement in a cross-functional meeting.
Encouraging collaboration between teams with different priorities.
Navigating competing perspectives to move forward.

blocks.text: Prompt: Where does influence become necessary here?
Decision making and momentum

items: Moving a group toward a decision without full consensus.
Determining when it is time to act rather than continue discussing.
Recommending a path forward in a group setting.
Breaking a stalemate in a meeting.
Helping a group focus on what matters most.

blocks.text: Prompt: What shifts this from influence to authority?
Accountability and follow-through

items: Addressing when someone does not follow through.
Holding partners accountable to commitments.
Reinforcing shared expectations.
Ensuring work gets completed on time.
Managing performance concerns on a team.

blocks.text: Prompt: How do you maintain accountability without relying on authority?
Challenging and high ambiguity

items: Redirecting a group that is heading in the wrong direction.
Speaking up when you disagree with a decision.
Influencing someone with more positional authority than you.
Getting buy-in for a new idea.
Balancing speed with inclusion in decision making.

blocks.text: Prompt: How does context change where you stand on this one?
Leadership behavior and style

items: Choosing when to step in and when to step back.
Leading a meeting where you are not the decision maker.
Using your role or title to open doors.
Building trust before taking action.
Letting others take ownership of decisions.

blocks.text: Prompt: Where do you naturally operate, and why?
Values and outcomes, for reflection

items: Success is defined by shared ownership of outcomes.
Success is defined by efficiency and speed.
Decisions are made by those closest to the work.
Leaders are responsible for ensuring alignment.
Relationships matter more than control in getting results.

blocks.text: Prompt: What do your choices say about your leadership approach?
Element: 3. Building legitimacy.
Group Size: Groups of 2 or 3. Pairs if time is tight.
Materials: None.
Purpose: Ground the skill in things participants have already done, across chapter work, community engagement, and response, before anybody is taught anything.
Set up (1 minute)

Groups of two or three. Say this: “As Executive Directors, you are constantly leading without formal authority. Across your chapter, in your community, and often in response operations. Let us take a moment to reflect on what that actually looks like in practice.”
The activity (5 to 7 minutes)

Say this: “In your group, each of you share one example of when you relied on influence instead of authority in each of these areas: your chapter, your community, and a disaster response or other high-pressure situation.”
Keep each example to about 60 seconds, enough to describe the situation, who you needed to influence, and what you did.
If you are short on time: assign one category per person instead of all three. Person 1 takes chapter, person 2 takes community, person 3 takes response.
Debrief (3 to 5 minutes)

items: What did you notice across your examples?
What did you rely on most when you did not have authority?
What made those efforts successful, or challenging?
If time allows: what did you do in those moments that helped others choose to act?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Ask these two in order and then stop talking: “How many of those situations could you have solved faster with authority?” and “Why was authority not actually the better tool anyway?” The point of the activity is that influence is not a limitation people work around. It is frequently the better approach, and the room usually gets there without being told.
Facilitator notes

items: Rotate quickly. One person will otherwise take all three categories and the other two will get one story between them.
This is the safest opener in the document for a skeptical or brand new group, because nobody has to learn anything to participate.
Virtual: see page 47. Breakouts of three with a visible timer, and broadcast the category change.

blocks.text: Element: 3. Building legitimacy.
Group Size: Any, seated in pods.
Materials: Easel pad or whiteboard, markers, one sticky note per participant.
Purpose: Establish that the expertise this session needs is already in the room, and build a bank of real examples you can call back to for the rest of the day.
Set up (1 minute)
Post a sheet of easel paper at the front titled: What we already know about getting people to act.

Say this: “Everyone in this room has already gotten someone to do something they had no power to require. A partner, a volunteer, a board member, a family member. You have done this. Today is not about learning it from scratch. It is about naming what you already do, so you can start doing it on purpose.”
The activity (7 minutes)
Write (2 minutes). On a sticky note, each person finishes this sentence: “The thing I do that most often gets people to say yes is ______.”
Pair (3 minutes). Turn to one person, read each other your sentence, and ask one follow-up question: “When did that last work?”
Harvest (4 minutes). Go around the room. Each person reads their sentence in under 15 seconds. Capture short phrases on the easel pad. Do not discuss yet, just collect.
Debrief (2 minutes)

items: What showed up more than once?
What is on this list that has nothing to do with anyone’s title?
What is missing that you wish you were better at?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis
Almost nothing on the sheet will depend on a title, and the room notices that itself once the list is visible. Name it plainly and move on rather than explaining it.
Facilitator notes

items: Leave the sheet posted for the whole session. Return to it in the closing debrief and ask what the group would now add, sharpen, or take off. This is the cheapest callback you will get and it costs nothing to keep.
Photograph the sheet before teardown and send it out. People use it afterward.
Virtual: see page 47. Everyone types their sentence into chat without sending, then sends on a count of three.

blocks.text: Activity: Map Influence Before Acting
Group Size: Individual work, then pairs.
Materials: Paper or a worksheet and a pen each.
Purpose: Identify who actually holds influence, formal, informal and moral, before engaging, rather than working from titles and the org chart.
Set up (1 minute)
Say this: “Before you try to move a decision, you need to know who is really in it. Not who is on the invitation list. This is ten minutes on a real situation of your own, and nobody collects it.”
The activity (10 minutes)
Step 1 (2 minutes). Identify a real decision or situation you are working on right now where you do not have formal authority.
Step 2 (3 minutes). List every stakeholder involved: individuals, groups, partner organizations. Quantity over precision.
Step 3 (3 minutes). For each one, write their level of influence, formal, informal or moral, and their likely interests or concerns.
Step 4 (2 minutes). Circle the two or three people who will most strongly determine whether this moves forward.
Debrief (3 to 4 minutes)

items: What did you notice about who actually holds influence versus who holds formal roles?
How does this change how you would approach moving this decision forward?
What is one relationship you need to engage or strengthen next?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The finding is almost always the same and it is worth letting the room say it rather than saying it yourself: the circled names in step 4 are frequently not the people with the biggest titles, and in many cases they are people who were not going to be invited to the meeting.
Facilitator notes

items: Moral influence is the category people skip. It is the person others look at before they answer. Prompt for it directly in step 3 if nobody uses it.
If somebody says they cannot think of a situation where they lack authority, ask them about their board, or their region, or a partner. It arrives quickly.
Run this before the Stakeholder Mapping Wall on page 19 rather than after. This one is individual, that one is collective, and they work in that order.

blocks.text: Activity: Stakeholder Mapping Wall
Group Size: Whole group, working at one wall. Above about twenty, build two walls.
Materials: Large wall space or three sheets of easel pad taped together, sticky notes in three colors, markers, tape.
Purpose: Build one shared, physical picture of an influence landscape, so the group can see that formal position and real influence do not line up.
Set up (3 minutes)
Draw a large target on the wall with three rings, labeled from the outside in: Aware, Engaged, Committed. Along the bottom write an axis reading: Formal authority, low on the left, high on the right.

Assign the sticky note colors before you start. Color 1 is internal Red Cross people and functions. Color 2 is partner organizations, agencies and institutions. Color 3 is individual community members and informal leaders.
The activity (20 minutes)

Step 1 (4 minutes). Name the shared situation: either the workshop scenario on page 41 or a live situation the group agrees on. Working individually and silently, each participant writes one stakeholder per note, using the color code.

Step 2 (5 minutes). Participants place their notes. Horizontal position shows how much formal authority that stakeholder holds. The ring shows how engaged they are today, not how engaged you wish they were. No talking during placement.
Step 3 (4 minutes). Silent gallery walk. Everyone looks at the whole wall without commenting.
Step 4 (7 to 12 minutes). Read the wall together, in this order.

items: Who is in the Committed ring with little or no formal authority? Those are your carriers.
Who has high formal authority and sits out in the Aware ring? Those are your risks.
Who is missing from the wall entirely?
Which color is thinnest, and what does that tell us about who we are actually working with?

blocks.text: Debrief (3 to 5 minutes)

items: What surprised you about where people ended up?
Whose name appeared on the most notes, and why that person?
If you could move exactly one note one ring inward, which would it be, and what would it take?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The thinnest color is usually color 3. Say that out loud when it happens, because it is the most useful thing the wall produces: a group that maps mostly institutions is a group that is working with institutions and calling it community.
Facilitator notes

items: Protect the silence in steps 2 and 3. The moment people start explaining their notes, the wall becomes a discussion and stops being a picture.
Leave the wall up for the rest of the session. Later activities refer back to it.
Photograph it before teardown and send the photo to participants. It is the artifact people actually use afterward.
Virtual: see page 47. Build the target and the axis on a digital whiteboard before the session.

blocks.text: Activity: Design the Decision Process
Group Size: Individual work, then pairs.
Materials: Paper or a worksheet and a pen each.
Purpose: Stop trying to solve the decision and start designing how it will get made. This is the move that shifts a person from reacting in meetings to shaping what happens before them.
Set up (1 minute)

Say this: “Most stalled decisions are not stalled because nobody knows the right answer. They are stalled because nobody designed how the answer would get chosen. That is the thing you can control without any authority at all.”
The activity (12 minutes)
Step 1 (2 minutes). Write down a decision you need to move forward but do not own.
Step 2 (3 minutes). Clarify two things: what specifically needs to be decided, and what happens if no decision is made. Be concrete about the second one.
Step 3 (4 minutes). Map the decision pathway. Who needs to be aligned first? What conversations must happen? Where could momentum begin? Sequence it: one to one, then small group, then full group.
Step 4 (3 minutes). Identify your next one or two influence moves. A conversation, a connection, a reframing of the goal. Something you could do this week.
Debrief (3 to 4 minutes)

items: What did you notice when you shifted from solving the decision to designing it?
How might this approach prevent decisions from stalling?
What is the next intentional step you will take?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Ask how many people’s step 3 has the full group meeting first. It usually does. Name the pattern: alignment gets built before the meeting, and a meeting is where you confirm alignment rather than where you manufacture it.
Facilitator notes

items: Step 2’s second question does the work. If nothing bad happens when no decision is made, the participant has picked a decision nobody needs and should pick another.
Push back on a step 4 that is a meeting. A meeting is not an influence move, it is a container for one.
Virtual: this transfers directly. Send a fillable worksheet in advance and keep people off camera during writing time.

blocks.text: Activity: Create Alignment Through Shared Understanding
Group Size: Individual work, then pairs.
Materials: Paper and a pen each.
Purpose: Surface a stakeholder’s interests and constraints before pushing toward action, and practice the questions that surface them.
Set up (1 minute)
Say this: “You cannot connect your goal to somebody else’s priorities until you know what their priorities actually are. Most of us are guessing, and most of us are guessing confidently.”
The activity (12 minutes)
Step 1 (2 minutes). Think of a stakeholder or group where alignment is currently low.
Step 2 (3 minutes). Write down what you believe they care about most, and what their constraints or concerns might be. Mark each line with how you know: told, observed, or assumed.
Step 3 (4 minutes). Draft two or three questions you could ask to understand their perspective better. Start from: “What matters most to you in this?” and “What concerns do you have?”
Step 4 (3 minutes). Identify how you could connect their priorities to a shared goal. Not your goal restated warmly. A goal that contains something they want.
Debrief (3 to 4 minutes)

items: What new perspectives or assumptions surfaced?
How much of your step 2 was marked assumed?
How does understanding their priorities change your approach?
What conversation will you initiate to build alignment?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The marking in step 2 is where this activity earns its time. Most people find that the majority of what they know about an important stakeholder is assumed, and that they have never asked. That is a solvable problem and it is solvable this week.
Facilitator notes

items: The told, observed, assumed marking is not in the original version of this activity and it is the part most worth keeping. Do not cut it for time.

Watch for step 4 answers that are the participant’s own goal with the word “shared” added. Ask what the other party gets. If the answer is a benefit to the community rather than to them, push once more.
Virtual: this transfers directly.

blocks.text: Activity: Build Momentum Without Control
Group Size: Individual work first, then pairs.
Materials: Paper or worksheet and a pen for each participant.
Purpose: Create forward motion on a stalled effort by choosing the smallest visible next step rather than the most important one.
Setup: Individual work first, then pairs. Works with a real situation or with the workshop scenario on page 41.
The activity (15 minutes)

Step 1 (2 minutes). Name one effort you care about that is currently stalled. Write one sentence describing what stalled looks like here: no meeting scheduled, no owner, nobody saying no but nothing moving.

Step 2 (3 minutes). List every reason it is stuck. Then label each one: capacity, clarity, or commitment. Most stalls get described as capacity problems. Check whether yours is really clarity or commitment wearing a capacity costume.

Step 3 (4 minutes). Design the smallest visible win. What is one thing that could happen in the next ten days, done by someone other than you, that other people would notice? It has to be small enough that nobody needs permission.
Step 4 (3 minutes). Decide where the win becomes visible. Who hears about it, in what forum, and who says it out loud? Momentum is a story people can see, not a task quietly completed.

Step 5 (3 to 5 minutes). Pair up and read your smallest visible win to your partner. The partner’s only job is to say whether they believe it can happen in ten days, and if not, what would have to shrink.
Debrief (3 to 5 minutes)

items: What did you first think the barrier was, and what did it turn out to be?
How small did the win have to get before it felt certain?
What is the ten-day step you are leaving here with, and who will notice it?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The step 2 relabeling is the finding. A room that arrived certain everything was a capacity problem usually leaves having relabeled half of it, and clarity and commitment are things you can act on without a budget.
Facilitator notes

items: The common failure is a next step that is really the whole project. Push for smaller. If a step needs a budget approval, a new hire, or a standing meeting, it is too big. A good answer sounds almost too easy.
Step 3 says done by someone other than you. Participants will quietly ignore that. Say it twice.
Virtual: this transfers directly, with breakouts of two for step 5.

blocks.text: Activity: Aligning Competing Priorities
Group Size: Groups of three to four.
Materials: Easel paper or a worksheet per group, markers.
Purpose: Practice working with stakeholders whose priorities genuinely conflict. Move past “we all want what is best for the community” to an agreement that names its tradeoffs.

Setup: Each group works either the workshop scenario on page 41 or a real situation offered by one member. Say this: “The hard cases are not misunderstandings. They are where two people both understand perfectly and want different things.”
The activity (20 minutes)

Step 1 (3 minutes). Name the two or three parties whose priorities are in real conflict. Write each party’s priority in their own words, not yours. If you can only write it as a criticism, you do not have it yet.
Step 2 (4 minutes). For each party, answer: what do they lose if your preferred path wins? Be specific. Cost, credit, control, staff time, relationships, risk of being blamed.

Step 3 (5 minutes). Find the constraint that is actually shared. Look for what every party is protecting against. It is often the same thing: looking bad publicly, doing more with the same staff, owning a failure.
Step 4 (5 minutes). Draft a proposal that says the tradeoff out loud instead of hiding it. Use the frame: here is what each of us gives up, here is what each of us gets, here is what we do first.
Step 5 (3 to 5 minutes). One group member reads the proposal aloud as if the least enthusiastic stakeholder were sitting there. The group notes exactly where it would draw pushback.
Debrief (4 to 5 minutes)

items: What changed once the loss was named out loud?
Where did you find a shared constraint, and was it the one you expected?
What is the difference between a compromise and an alignment, and which one did you build?
Which stakeholder would still say no, and what is your next move with them?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

Groups that skipped step 2 produce proposals everyone agrees with and no real stakeholder would sign. Groups that did it honestly produce proposals that are uncomfortable to read aloud. The second kind is what alignment sounds like.
Facilitator notes

items: Groups skip step 2 or answer it abstractly. Slow them down there. If nobody has named a concrete loss, the exercise has not happened yet and the rest will be pleasant and useless.
Step 1’s test, that you cannot write it as a criticism, is the most useful instruction here. Enforce it.
Virtual: breakouts of three with a shared document per group. Add five minutes.

blocks.text: Activity: No One’s in Charge Simulation

title: All six. This is the integrative activity.

blocks.text: Group Size: 6 to 32 participants, working in tables of 6 to 8.
Materials: One role card per participant printed and handed out privately, one situation brief per table, a timer visible to the whole room, an easel pad per table, and one decision sheet per table.
The decision sheet: a single page with four fields. What we decided. Who does what. By when. Who signed on.

Purpose: Put participants into a situation with a real deadline, no designated leader, incomplete information and conflicting incentives, so that influence behaviors show up under pressure instead of in theory.
The situation, shared with everyone

A county has received one-time funding to stand up a coordinated disaster preparedness effort for a flood-prone corridor of about 40,000 residents. Ten organizations have been invited to the table. The funder will accept exactly one plan, needs it in an hour, and will not mediate. Nobody has convened the group formally. Nobody has authority over anyone else.
Role cards, on page 27

Each participant receives one card with a public goal and a private constraint. Cards are not read aloud. Use as many as you need for your group size, and add an observer at each table if numbers allow.
Round structure (75 minutes of play, 30 of marking)

Round 1, unstructured (15 minutes). Groups get the situation and their role cards, and no instructions on how to proceed. Facilitators do not intervene, even when a group flounders. The floundering is the content.
Mark the moment (5 minutes). Each group writes two things on the easel pad: where are we right now, and how did we get here? Observers stay silent.

Round 2, process first (20 minutes). Introduce one constraint: before you go any further, your group must agree on how you will decide, before deciding anything. Five minutes to design the process, fifteen to use it.
Mark the moment (10 minutes). Same two questions on the easel pad. Then observers report what they saw, two minutes per table, no discussion or rebuttal.

Round 3, deadline (20 minutes). Groups must produce a completed decision sheet. With three minutes left, a facilitator visits each table in role as the funder and asks two questions: who is accountable for this, and which of you would still be at this table in a year?
Cross-table read (5 minutes). Post the decision sheets side by side. Give the room five minutes to look at all of them before the debrief.
Debrief (30 minutes)

items: What happened in Round 1? Who ended up leading, and how did that actually get decided?
What changed the moment you had to design the process before the decision?
Observers: who moved this group, and what specifically did they do?
Whose private constraint never came out? What did that cost the group?
Who went quiet, and did anyone go get them?
Look at the plans across tables. What did the strongest one have that the others did not?
What is the closest real version of this in your own work right now?

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: Resist rescuing groups in Round 1. The discomfort in the first ten minutes is the most valuable part of the lab, and facilitators tend to cut it short out of kindness.
If a group appoints a leader in the first two minutes, let it stand and make it a debrief question: how did that person get chosen, and who was not asked?
Watch for the participant who solves it by being the loudest. Name the pattern in the debrief without naming the person.
The most common finding is that groups spend Round 1 negotiating content and none of it on process. That is the central lesson of the lab. Do not give it away in advance.
Scaling down: with one table of six, cut to six roles and take five minutes off each round. Scaling up: run more tables on the same roles and compare plans in the debrief.
If you ran the Stakeholder Mapping Wall on page 19 earlier, keep it visible and ask in the debrief what participants would have done differently with it in front of them.
Virtual: see page 47. This is the hardest activity in the document to move online and it can be done.

blocks.text: Handout: Simulation Role Cards
Print, cut, and hand out privately. One per participant. Each card carries a public goal and a private constraint, and the private half is never read aloud.
Red Cross chapter. Strongest logistics capacity in the room, weakest local trust in this corridor. Privately, your metrics require you to be named as lead on any preparedness activity.
County emergency management. Formal legal authority, no discretionary staff time. Privately, you cannot be seen taking direction from a nonprofit.
Mutual aid group. Deep trust in the corridor, no formal structure. Privately, your members will walk if the money routes through government.
Faith network. Buildings and volunteers. Privately, your board will not approve participation unless your congregations are named in the plan.
School district. Reach into every household with a child. Privately, you cannot commit any staff time during the school day.
Community clinic. Trusted by residents who do not speak English. Privately, you are three months from a funding cliff and need this to cover a salaried position.
Housing nonprofit. You know exactly which residents are most at risk. Privately, you will not share your client list under any circumstance.
Business association. You can move money and press coverage fast. Privately, you need a visible ribbon-cutting within 90 days.
Neighborhood council. You can bless or block this plan in the eyes of residents. Privately, a previous coordinated effort burned you and you start skeptical.
Observer, one per table. You say nothing for the whole simulation. Track who talks, who gets interrupted, who moves the group, and who is never asked.
FACILITATOR PREP
Cards printed and cut: ______ Tables: ______ Observers assigned: ______
Lived Experience 1: Convening for Alignment

title: 2. Designing the decision process, and 3. Building legitimacy.

blocks.text: Group Size: Five in role, plus observers.
Materials: The scenario on page 41, role constraints cut and handed out privately.
Purpose: Create alignment across stakeholders who do not report to you, by shaping the conditions for it rather than by directing the group.
The four phases
Phase 1 (5 minutes). Identify the meeting or initiative. Clarify the desired outcome and who needs to be aligned, including informal influencers.
Phase 2 (5 minutes). Prepare. Define the shared purpose. Anticipate each stakeholder’s priorities and constraints.
Phase 3 (10 to 15 minutes). In the meeting: ask questions that surface perspectives, highlight shared goals, make tradeoffs visible.
Phase 4 (5 minutes). Summarize alignment and clarify next steps. What was agreed, and who owns what.
Running this in the room

Use the scenario on page 41. Assign roles first: chapter ED, clinic director, neighborhood council chair, congregation lead, county emergency management staffer. Give each their private constraint. Anyone not in role observes and reports in the debrief.

items: Phases 1 and 2 (10 minutes): the ED prepares while the others read their roles and decide privately what they will and will not offer.
Phase 3 (15 minutes): run the meeting live. The ED convenes. The rest play their constraints honestly but do not volunteer them unasked.
Phase 4 (5 minutes): the ED summarizes alignment and next steps out loud, then observers report.

blocks.text: As field work instead. Assign the four phases against a real upcoming meeting and debrief next session. Participants bring the meeting outcome, not a summary of it.
Debrief

items: How did your approach compare to directing or pushing?
Which constraint never came out, and what would have surfaced it?

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The ED role is the hard one and should not go to a volunteer every time. Assign it to someone who will find it uncomfortable.
Observers report facts, not advice, or the debrief becomes coaching.

blocks.text: Lived Experience 2: Moving a Decision Without Authority

title: 2. Designing the decision process, and 6. Telling commitment from compliance.

blocks.text: Group Size: Five in role, plus observers.
Materials: The workshop scenario on page 41.
Purpose: Move a group from discussion to decision when nobody has clear authority. The work is facilitating clarity, surfacing tradeoffs, and guiding toward action.
The four phases
Phase 1 (5 minutes). Define the decision. What needs to be decided, and what happens if no decision is made?
Phase 2 (5 minutes). Identify the key stakeholders and what alignment would actually require from each.
Phase 3 (10 to 15 minutes). During the discussion: surface risks, constraints and tradeoffs. Offer a recommendation. Test alignment by asking “Is this workable?” rather than “Does everyone agree?”
Phase 4 (5 minutes). Confirm the decision and next steps, with clear ownership and a date.
Running this in the room

Use the workshop scenario on page 41, picking up at the point where the group has met twice and still has not decided whether the alarm effort runs through the existing food distribution or as a standalone event. Same roles as Lived Experience 1.

items: Phases 1 and 2 (10 minutes): the ED defines the decision and what alignment would require. Others read their constraints.
Phase 3 (15 minutes): run the discussion live, to a decision. The ED must offer a recommendation, not just facilitate.
Phase 4 (5 minutes): confirm the decision, the owner and the date, out loud, in front of everyone.

blocks.text: As field work instead. Apply the four phases to a live decision that is currently stalled, and bring back what moved or blocked it.
Debrief

items: What moved the group toward a decision, or prevented it?
How did your actions influence clarity and commitment?
Did anyone in the room comply rather than commit, and how would you know?
What will you do to create faster alignment in future decisions?

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The requirement that the ED offer a recommendation is the whole exercise. Facilitating without recommending is comfortable and it is how decisions stall.
If the group reaches a decision in eight minutes, it is because nobody played their constraint. Say so and run it again with one minute of private re-reading.

blocks.text: Lived Experience 3: Rebuilding Accountability Through Influence

title: 4. Mobilizing action without control, and 6. Telling commitment from compliance.

blocks.text: Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: The workshop scenario on page 41.
Purpose: Create accountability without authority. Instead of enforcing an expectation, strengthen alignment, clarify what was actually agreed, and reinforce ownership through the relationship.
The four phases
Phase 1 (5 minutes). Identify a partner or stakeholder who is not following through.
Phase 2 (5 to 10 minutes). Conduct a one to one conversation. Ask “What is getting in the way?” and then listen for barriers and competing priorities rather than for excuses.
Phase 3 (5 to 10 minutes). Re-align. Reconnect to shared goals. Co-create clear next steps and expectations rather than restating the old ones.
Phase 4 (5 minutes). Increase visibility. Reinforce the commitment in a group setting or a follow-up that other people see.
Running this in the room

Use the workshop scenario on page 41. The congregation lead agreed to host, then stopped answering emails three weeks ago. Run this in pairs: one Executive Director, one congregation lead. Then switch roles and run it again with the other person’s real situation if time allows.

items: Phase 1 (3 minutes): the ED prepares. The congregation lead reads their private reason for going quiet and does not reveal it unless asked well.
Phases 2 and 3 (12 minutes): run the one to one live.
Phase 4 (5 minutes): the ED states how they would make the recommitment visible without embarrassing the partner.

blocks.text: As field work instead. Hold the real one to one between sessions and bring back what the actual barrier turned out to be.
Debrief

items: What changed in the partner’s level of engagement?
How did relationship-based influence compare to escalation or pressure?
What question finally got the real barrier out?
What will you do to maintain accountability moving forward?

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The private reason exists so that the ED has to earn it. If the person playing the congregation lead offers it in the first minute, the exercise is over. Brief them on that before you start.
Phase 4 trips people. Visibility that embarrasses a partner destroys the relationship you just repaired. Make participants say the actual words they would use.

title: Everyday Life Examples
duration: 8 to 12 minutes for one or two examples

blocks.text: Example 1: Parenting without authority
You are trying to get a child or teenager to follow through on homework, chores or managing their time, and you know that simply telling them what to do produces resistance.

What the skill looks like in action. You ask questions to understand their perspective, connect expectations to shared goals such as independence and trust, and involve them in making the plan. Accountability comes by agreement rather than command.
What changes. The child takes ownership rather than complying. Follow-through improves and the relationship gets stronger rather than more strained.
Example 2: Influencing a group of friends
You are coordinating friends to plan a trip or an event. Different preferences, different schedules, nobody in charge.

What the skill looks like in action. You clarify the goal, surface everyone’s needs and constraints, and help the group see where interests overlap. You suggest a path, test whether it is workable, and adjust rather than control.
What changes. The group moves from scattered opinions to a clear plan. People feel heard and are more willing to commit, which is what makes the plan actually happen.
Example 3: Community and civic involvement
You are on a neighborhood association, volunteer group or school committee working a community issue. Nobody has authority over anyone else.

What the skill looks like in action. You build relationships across the group, identify informal influencers, and connect people around a shared purpose. You facilitate, surface tradeoffs, and help the group move from discussion to action.
What changes. Participation becomes more active, decisions gain broader support, and the group acts rather than staying stuck in discussion.
How to use these in a session
Read one aloud, or put it on a slide and give the room 60 seconds. Then run these three prompts in order, in pairs or as a full group.

items: Where have you done this, outside of work?
What made it work there that you do not do at work?
What would it cost you to bring that behavior into your role on Monday?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

The point is not the example. The point is the third question, and it needs a pause after it. People answer the first two easily and go quiet on the third, because the honest answer is usually that it would cost them very little and they have not done it anyway.
Group Size: 6 to 12 seated in a circle. Above 12, split into two circles with a facilitator each.
Materials: None.
Purpose: Give a group time to think out loud about influence rather than practice it, which is what most rooms are short of.
How to run this discussion

items: Pick three questions, not six. Three covered well beats six covered thinly.
Set two ground rules out loud at the start: answer from your own experience rather than in general terms, and no one speaks twice until everyone has spoken once.
After each answer, ask one follow-up before moving on: “What makes you say that?” or “When did that last happen?”
The line under each question is facilitator context on what the question is reaching for. Do not read it aloud.
Silence after a question is working. Count to ten before you fill it.

blocks.text: The six questions
1. When you cannot direct an outcome, what sources of influence do you still have, and how intentionally do you use them?
Reaching for: trust, credibility, relationships, expertise and shared mission as levers.
2. How do you decide when alignment is good enough to move forward, even if full consensus is not achievable?
Reaching for: the balance between collaboration, timeliness and momentum.
3. What signals do you look for to determine whether people are genuinely committed, or simply compliant, to a shared decision?
Reaching for: buy-in, engagement, and the limits of positional authority.
4. How does your behavior change when you are one voice among many instead of the final decision maker, and what impact does that have on others’ willingness to act?
Reaching for: leadership presence, humility and relational dynamics.
5. Whose perspectives or voices tend to carry less formal power in our work, and how do our decisions change when those voices are intentionally included?
Reaching for: the link between equity, inclusion and effective influence.
6. What would it look like to measure your effectiveness not by decisions made, but by actions others chose to take?
Reaching for: a reframing of what success is.
Facilitator notes

items: Question 3 is the one to pick if you can only pick one. It is the idea this whole skill turns on and most rooms have never been asked it directly.
Question 6 works best as a closer rather than an opener.
Virtual: see page 47. Cut to three questions and use a round-robin order so nobody has to compete for the gap.

blocks.text: Session Formats

Six pre-built agendas follow. Each one is assembled from the activities in this document with time allocations, and each one is a starting point rather than a script. Pick by what the group needs rather than by what fits the calendar.
One hour, Foundations. For a group meeting the skill for the first time. Builds the distinction between influence and authority and gets people to notice where they already do this. Page 35.
One hour, Everyday Application. For a group that has met the concept and needs to use it. Lighter on theory, heavier on a real situation each person brings. Page 36.
Two hours, Facilitating Internal Conversations. For people who convene groups that do not report to them. The emphasis is on the conversation itself. Page 37.
Two hours, Moving Decisions Forward. For a group with stalled decisions. The emphasis is on process design and on naming tradeoffs. Page 38.
Four hours, Influence Simulation Lab. The deep version. Built around the simulation, and the only format where influence behavior shows up under real pressure. Page 39.
Four hours, Real-World Application Lab. The deep version for a group that would rather work their own situations than a scenario. Peer coaching throughout. Page 40.
Choosing between the two four-hour labs

Run the Simulation Lab when the group does not know each other well, or when you want the lesson to land through experience rather than through discussion. Run the Real-World Lab when people arrive with live problems they are willing to put on the table. The Simulation Lab teaches more. The Real-World Lab changes more next week.
A note on pre-work
Pre-work is optional in every case and every session works without it. Assign it when you have a group that will do it, and design the opening so that people who did not do it are not visibly behind.

What signals tell you people are committed rather than just compliant?

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: This is the tightest hour in the document. If the This or That debrief runs long, cut the Everyday Life Examples rather than the closing.
The 15 minutes for Lived Experience 1 is the shortened version. Phase 3 gets 8 minutes, not 15.

Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (10 minutes)

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: This is the one format where pre-work is not optional. Without a real situation, a participant has nothing to work on for four hours.
Peer coaching needs a rule or it becomes advice-giving. The rule: ask three questions before offering one suggestion.

blocks.text: Handout: The Riverside Corridor
Background

One copy per participant for any Lived Experience run in the room. Role constraints printed separately. Inside your region sits the Riverside corridor: roughly 12,000 residents across four neighborhoods, with the region’s highest rate of home fires and its lowest rate of smoke alarm requests. Two years ago the chapter ran an installation event there. Turnout was 11 homes against a target of 300. People remember it.
What is true today

items: A community clinic in the corridor is the most trusted institution among residents. It has never been asked to partner on preparedness.
The neighborhood council chair told your Disaster Cycle Services lead, informally, that residents do not open the door for people in vests.
Two congregations run a joint food distribution every other Saturday, reaching 400 households.
Regional leadership has asked for a corridor plan by quarter end and offered no new staff. Your most experienced volunteer there retired last year and was never replaced.
The county emergency management office holds a preparedness grant that requires a named community partner. Deadline is six weeks out.
You have no authority over the clinic, the council, the congregations, the county, or your own regional timeline.

blocks.text: Role constraints, handed out privately
Chapter Executive Director. A quarter-end deadline, no new staff, and a two-year-old failure nobody has forgotten.
Clinic director. Your staff is at capacity. You will join only if the chapter supplies volunteers, and you will not say so unless asked directly.
Neighborhood council chair. Residents need to see the council leading this, not the Red Cross. You back a plan that puts your name first and quietly stall one that does not.
Congregation lead. You worry preparedness talk will crowd out the food line. Your board moves slowly. You will say yes in the room rather than say no.
County emergency management staffer. You need a named partner within six weeks or the grant lapses, and you cannot name one without recent local presence.
Which activity uses which part

items: Also used by Aligning Competing Priorities (page 24), Build Momentum (page 23) and the Stakeholder Mapping Wall (page 19).

blocks.text: Lived Experience 1, page 28. Convening these parties for the first time.
Lived Experience 2, page 29. The group has met twice and cannot decide between the food distribution or a standalone event. You need a decision today.
Lived Experience 3, page 30. The congregation lead agreed to host, then went quiet three weeks ago. A one to one today.
Handout: Job Aid
Leading through influence, on one page. Print it, put it in front of people, and let them keep it.
Before you engage
Name the decision. What specifically has to be decided, by when, and what happens if nothing is decided?
Map the room. Who is affected, who do they listen to, and who holds informal or moral influence rather than a title?
Name the loss. For each person you need, what do they give up if you get your way? Cost, credit, control, time, risk.
Pick the sequence. Who do you talk to first, second, and only in the room? Alignment gets built before the meeting, not during it.
In the conversation
Ask before you advocate. “What matters most to you in this?” and “What concerns do you have?”
Make the tradeoff visible instead of arguing around it.
Offer a recommendation, then test it. “Is this workable?” gets you further than “Does everyone agree?”
Speak last where you can. Your view lands differently once everyone else has spoken.
To close
Say the decision out loud, including the part that was not decided.
Name owners and dates. No owner means no decision.
Give the credit away, publicly and specifically.
Warning signs you are reaching for authority you do not have

items: You are escalating before you have asked what is getting in the way.
You are repeating your case louder instead of asking a question.
Everyone agreed in the room and nothing happened afterward.
You can describe what you need but not what they need.

blocks.text: How to measure yourself
Not whether the decision went your way. Whether people acted, whether they followed through without being chased, and whether they would come back to the table next time.
Further Learning
Six places to go next, with a line on what each is for. The first book is the canonical text on this skill and is worth reading even if you read nothing else here.
Books

Influence Without Authority, Allan R. Cohen and David L. Bradford. The founding text of this field. Its core idea is exchange: work out what the other person values, and what you have that they want. That idea is not taught anywhere in this document and it is the best next thing to learn.
How to Lead When You Are Not in Charge, Clay Scroggins. Real leadership is about influence, attitude and taking ownership rather than formal power. The most readable of the six.
Lead With Influence, Matt Norman. A process-oriented take, useful if you prefer a sequence to a set of principles.

You Are It: Crisis, Change, and How to Lead When It Matters Most, Marcus, Dorn, McNulty and Henderson. Written for the moments when the pressure is real and the authority is unclear. The closest of the six to disaster work.

Building Communities from the Inside Out, John McKnight and John Kretzmann. The asset-based community development text. Belongs to Asset Mapping more than to this skill, and it is the reason the phrase keeps appearing here.
How to Win Friends and Influence People, Dale Carnegie. Old, still useful on the interpersonal half, and worth reading with a critical eye rather than as instruction.
Shorter
Harvard Business School Online, on influence without authority. The shortest way in. Fifteen minutes and it covers the ground the pre-work assumes.
Wharton, Influencing Without Authority: A Four-Part Formula. Four tools, briskly explained. Pairs well with the job aid on page 42.
What It Takes to Build Influence at Work, podcast. For a commute. Techniques for understanding colleagues and earning their respect.
Inside the Red Cross
Three skills in this set draw on the same ground and are worth doing near this one: Building Trust with Others, Stakeholder Mapping, and Aligning Our Priorities with Partners.

Optional, and worth sending, because the strongest moment in most deliveries is when a participant applies the scoring method to a real decision they arrived with rather than to a scenario. Send it four days ahead and do not chase it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Look at where your time actually goes (10 minutes)
Not where it should go. Where it went last month. Write down:

items: Your current initiatives, programs, or key areas of work. Six to ten of them.
Roughly what share of your time each one took last month. Percentages are fine and they should add up to more than a hundred, which is itself the finding.
Which of them has expanded, shifted, or become unclear in scope without anyone deciding that it should.

blocks.text: 2. Answer four questions honestly (10 minutes)

items: Which efforts feel most aligned with your goals and the mission?
Which feel misaligned, unclear, or difficult to sustain?
Where are you overextended, and where are you under-using something you have?
What could be paused, redesigned, or concluded, if it were allowed?

blocks.text: 3. Bring one real example (10 minutes)
The session uses this directly. Choose a real decision, recent or upcoming, involving one of these:

items: Competing priorities or a resource constraint.
A decision about continuing, adapting, or discontinuing work.
A situation where alignment across stakeholders was hard.

blocks.text: Then write four or five sentences on it: what made it complex, what options were considered, how the decision was actually made, and what you would want to do differently with a more structured approach.
If you have time: two things worth reading

items: Anything short on the Eisenhower matrix, urgent against important. Ten minutes, and it is enough to have the vocabulary.
One page on weighted criteria scoring. The mechanics are simple; the discipline is choosing the criteria before you look at the options.

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. Every activity in the document supplies its own material for exactly that reason, and the first icebreaker builds a priority list in the room in four minutes.
Part 1 is the piece that does the work. If you can only ask for one thing, ask for the time percentages, and be ready for the fact that many people have never written them down.
Group Size: Small groups of three to five.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard, markers. Optional: the fallback list below, printed.
Purpose: Introduce tradeoffs, constraints, and the need for criteria, in twelve minutes and without teaching anything.
Step 1: set up (2 minutes)
Say to participants: “Think about all the things your team, organization, or group is currently trying to accomplish.”
Break participants into small groups of three to five people.
Step 2: create the list (3 to 4 minutes)
Instruct each group: “Create a list of eight to ten current or typical priorities, projects, or initiatives you are working on or could be working on.”
Each group writes their list on paper or flip chart.
If a group cannot get to eight, give them the fallback list and have them choose from it. Do not let a group stall here.
Fallback list

Disaster Action Team coverage. Volunteer recruitment. Preparedness outreach. Priority community engagement. Partner relationship-building. Staff training. Fundraising support. Reporting and administrative requirements. Community events. Internal meetings and planning.
Step 3: apply the constraint (3 minutes)
Say: “You now have a constraint. You only have capacity to meaningfully advance three of these this quarter.”
Groups must choose three, and they must agree as a group. No abstentions and no ties.
Step 4: identify criteria (3 to 4 minutes)
Ask groups: “How did you decide? What criteria did you use?” Capture responses on the board. Impact, urgency, feasibility, alignment, and who would be upset are the usual five.
Debrief

items: What criteria came up most often?
Where did your group struggle to agree, and was that about the option or about the criterion?
What tradeoffs did you have to make?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

items: Scarcity creates clarity. Nothing about the list changed; the constraint changed.
Groups use criteria even when they have not named them. Naming them is the skill.
Different people define importance differently, and that is not a failure of the group, it is the reason a shared criterion is worth the argument.
Choosing something means delaying, reducing, or not choosing something else. Say that plainly.

blocks.text: Close with this: “The purpose is not to find the right three. It is to notice how quickly this became difficult when several worthwhile things competed for limited capacity.”
Facilitator notes

items: The name is the point. Three, not one. Three is enough to feel like a real portfolio and few enough to hurt.
Watch for a group that picks three and finishes early. Ask them what they told the people whose work did not make it. That is where the activity actually is.
This is the best opener for a room that is skeptical about the topic, because it is over before anyone can decide it is theoretical.

blocks.text: Group Size: Small groups of three to five.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard, markers.
Purpose: Make continuation, pause and stop decisions under reduced capacity. This is the stewardship opener, and it is the one that makes people uncomfortable.
Step 1: set up (2 minutes)
Say: “Think about your current workload, or a typical set of responsibilities.”
Break into groups of three to five.
Step 2: create the work list (3 minutes)
Instruct groups: “List six to eight ongoing responsibilities, projects, or commitments you are managing.”
Step 3: introduce the constraint (2 minutes)
Say: “Your capacity has suddenly been reduced by thirty percent. You cannot do everything.”
Step 4: make decisions (5 minutes)
Groups sort every item into continue, pause or delay, or stop. Every item gets a category. They must agree as a group.
Step 5: share out (3 minutes)
Ask one or two groups to share what they chose to stop, and why. Only the stops. The continuations are not interesting and they take all the time.
Debrief

items: How did you determine what to stop rather than continue?
What made certain decisions harder, and was it the work or the person attached to it?
Did you prioritize short-term needs or long-term impact? Which one lost?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

items: Stewardship requires deciding what to end, not only what to grow.
Capacity constraints are constant, not exceptional. Most groups treat this scenario as hypothetical and are already living in it.
Effective prioritization aligns work with what is sustainable, and sometimes that requires difficult choices about work that is genuinely good.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: Groups will try to negotiate the constraint. Do not let them. That negotiation is exactly what organizations do instead of prioritizing.
Watch for the group that puts nothing in stop. Ask them where the thirty percent went.

blocks.text: Group Size: Groups of three to five.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard, markers, paper for each group.
Purpose: Allocate resources across competing priorities and then adjust when the constraint changes. The second constraint is the whole activity.
Step 1: form groups (1 minute)
Divide participants into groups of three to five.
Step 2: create categories (4 minutes)
Instruct groups: “List five to seven major areas where time or resources are spent.” Staffing, operations, outreach, training, planning, partnerships are the usual ones.
Step 3: allocate the budget (5 minutes)
Say: “You have a total budget of one hundred points. Distribute those points across your categories.”
Points, not dollars. Points make people argue about proportion, and dollars make them argue about accuracy.
Step 4: introduce the constraint (3 minutes)
Say: “Your budget is now cut by twenty percent.” Groups must reduce their allocations to eighty total points.
Step 5: adjust and decide (4 minutes)
Groups revise, and they must be able to say two things: what got reduced, and what got protected.
Step 6: share out (3 minutes)
Ask each group for one sentence: what did you protect, and what did that cost?
Debrief

items: What did you protect, and why?
What was easiest to cut? What was hardest, and was the hard one also the least valuable?
How did your priorities shift when the constraint changed?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

items: Prioritization is about aligning resources to strategy. The first allocation shows what you say you value; the revision shows what you actually value.
Constraints clarify what matters most. Groups almost always cut across the board first and then have to go back and make a real choice.
Stewardship requires ongoing adjustment. A budget is a decision that has to be remade, not a decision that was made once.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The across-the-board cut is the teachable moment. When a group does it, say: you have just reduced every activity by twenty percent, which means everything now runs slightly worse and nothing was decided. Then let them redo it.
This is the best of the five for a group that manages actual budgets, and the one to skip for a group that does not.

blocks.text: Group Size: Groups of four to five.
Materials: Flip chart or whiteboard, markers, paper for each group.
Purpose: Tradeoffs, stakeholder pressure, and a fixed budget, in a setting nobody can hide behind their professional expertise in. It gets further faster than any work scenario.
Step 1: form groups (1 minute)
Divide participants into groups of four to five.
Step 2: read the scenario aloud (2 minutes)
Read this once, at the start, and do not repeat it later:

“You are planning a wedding. The budget is twenty-five thousand dollars. The guest list caps at one hundred people. One partner wants a simple event and the other wants a large, elegant celebration. One family wants to invite many relatives; the other cares most about the venue and how it looks. A preferred vendor is very expensive. The wedding is in three months. You must decide how to allocate the budget and what to give up.”
Step 3: generate categories (4 minutes)
Instruct groups: “Create a list of six to eight wedding elements you need to budget for.” Venue, food, guest list, music, photography, decorations, attire, transportation.
Step 4: prioritize and allocate (6 minutes)
Groups must do three things: choose their top three or four priorities, decide where to spend more and where to spend less, and identify what they will cut or scale back.
Step 5: the twist (2 minutes)
Say one of the following, and pick before the session rather than in the moment:

items: “Your budget has been reduced by five thousand dollars.”
“Your guest list just increased by twenty-five people.”

blocks.text: Groups adjust. They have two minutes, which is deliberately not enough.
Step 6: share out (4 minutes)
One or two groups explain their top priorities and their biggest tradeoff.
Debrief

items: What were your top priorities, and why?
What tradeoffs did you make, and what was hardest to give up?
How did you handle the competing preferences between the two families?
How did your decisions change after the constraint shifted?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

items: You cannot satisfy every stakeholder. Tradeoffs are not a failure of the plan, they are the plan.
Prioritization balances impact, feasibility and expectations, and expectations are the one that gets left out of the framework and then decides everything.
Stewardship includes managing relationships, not only resources. The group that optimized the budget perfectly and upset both families did not do well.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The scenario is read once. Do not read it a second time before the group task.
Expect one group to solve it by eloping. Take it seriously and ask what the organizational equivalent would be. The answer is usually a very good one about scope.
Some rooms find weddings a poor fit. A neutral alternative with the same structure: planning a community event with a fixed budget and two partner organizations who each want something different.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
If the wedding framing does not fit this room, your substitute scenario: ___
Group Size: Groups of three to five.
Materials: The five requests below, printed one set per group, or on a slide.
Purpose: Separate stakeholder volume from actual priority. This is the stewardship opener and it sets up the honest no.
Step 1: set up (2 minutes)
Say: “You are going to receive five requests. All five are reasonable. All five come from people you need. You have capacity for one this month and one more next quarter.”
Break into groups of three to five.
Step 2: the requests (2 minutes)
Hand out or display all five at once.

items: A local elected official requests a visible preparedness event in their district.
Disaster leadership requests more support for Disaster Action Team coverage.
A priority community coalition requests deeper engagement, having asked twice before.
Volunteer leaders request more training and support.
A partner organization asks the Red Cross to join a new community initiative.

blocks.text: Step 3: decide (6 minutes)
Groups answer four questions and write the answers down:

items: Which request receives immediate attention?
Which one is delayed, and until when? Not delayed indefinitely. Name the quarter.
What criteria guided the decision?
How would the decision be communicated to the people who did not get a yes?

blocks.text: Step 4: share out (3 minutes)
Take only the fourth answer from two or three groups. How would you say it? Push for the actual words.
Debrief (2 minutes)

items: Which request was hardest to say no to, and was that about impact or about the person?
What did the elected official get from you that the coalition did not?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis

items: The loudest request is not always the highest priority. Volume, visibility and proximity all distort a decision, and none of them is a criterion.
Stakeholder pressure fills the space where criteria are unclear.
Trust depends on transparency and follow-through, not on saying yes.
A clear not now is more trustworthy than an unrealistic yes. Most participants know this and almost none of them do it.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The third request, the coalition that has asked twice before, is the one to draw out. Groups routinely delay it for the third time without noticing that they are the pattern the community is describing.
Fifteen minutes is right. Do not extend into a full scenario; the Grant Is Ending simulation is where that belongs.

blocks.text: Group Size: Groups of four to six. Three groups is ideal, so the share-out has range without taking twenty minutes.
Materials: The criteria scoring worksheet (page 46), one per group. The stakeholder cards (page 24), one set per group. The communication planner (page 52). Flip chart and markers.
Purpose: Make a real allocation decision among four genuinely good options, using criteria the group chooses and weights, and then defend it to people who wanted something else.
The scenario (3 minutes, read aloud)

“A Red Cross chapter has capacity to make one major strategic investment this year. Several priorities are competing for the same limited resources. Available to commit: one staff position, seventy-five thousand dollars in flexible funding, limited volunteer recruitment capacity, limited leadership time, and existing commitments that are already underway and are not going away.”
The four options

Option A: expand Disaster Action Team capacity. DAT coverage is inconsistent across several counties. Disaster leadership is concerned that response times will suffer if volunteer coverage does not improve.

Option B: deepen investment in a designated priority community. The community has strong need, growing partner trust, and an opening for deeper resilience work. It supports long-term relationship-building and requires sustained staff attention.
