Option C: invest in volunteer recruitment and retention. Volunteer numbers have declined. Several programs are struggling to maintain reliable coverage. Volunteer Services believes this must be addressed before any further expansion.

Option D: expand preparedness programming. Several communities have requested workshops, smoke alarm events, and disaster education. This increases visibility and reach and may spread staff and volunteers thin.
The intentional challenge

Every option has value. No option is clearly wrong. Groups must navigate: chapter-wide need against priority community investment, immediate response capacity against long-term resilience, visibility against sustainability, new work against existing commitments, and stakeholder pressure against transparent criteria.
Stakeholder cards (2 minutes to distribute)
Deal one card to each member of each group. Each person reads their card silently and does not show it to anyone. They argue from it for the first ten minutes of the group task.
If a group has fewer than six people, deal the Executive Director, the Disaster Program Manager, and the community resilience lead first. Those three carry the sharpest disagreement.
The group task (25 minutes)

items: Diagnose the situation. Five minutes. What is actually being decided here, and what is not on the table? Groups that skip this step spend the rest of the activity arguing about different questions.
Select four to six decision criteria and weight them. Five minutes. Use the scoring worksheet. The weighting argument is the real work of this activity and it should take most of these five minutes.
Score each option against the criteria. Eight minutes. Follow the method on the worksheet, including the check at the end.
Name the tradeoffs. Three minutes. What does the recommendation cost, specifically and in named terms?
Recommend one primary investment, and one secondary if capacity allows. Two minutes.
Write the communication statement. Two minutes. Four sentences using the planner on page 52. What was decided, why, what is delayed, and what happens next.

blocks.text: Share out (7 minutes)
Each group reads only two things: their weighted criteria, and their communication statement. Not their reasoning and not their scores. Two minutes each.
Then ask the room one question: which group would you find most credible if you were the person whose option was not chosen?
Facilitator debrief (8 minutes)

items: Which criteria influenced your decision most?
Where did your group disagree, and was it about the criteria or about the scores?
Did urgency and importance point to the same option?
What did your group protect? What did you delay or reduce?
How did capacity influence the decision, and did you consider it before or after choosing?
How would you explain this to a stakeholder who disagreed?

blocks.text: Final facilitator reinforcement

items: Strategic prioritization often means choosing between multiple good options, not between a right one and a wrong one.
The strongest decision is not always the most popular or the easiest.
Transparent criteria let leaders explain decisions with integrity, including to people who lost.
Prioritization is not complete until the tradeoffs are named out loud.
Capacity must be considered before commitments are made, not discovered afterward.
Trust is built by explaining what was decided, why, and what happens next.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The most common failure is groups scoring before weighting. Weighting after you have seen the options is how a group produces a number that agrees with what they already wanted.
Groups that finish early have skipped the diagnose step. Send them back to it.
Option C, volunteer recruitment, is the one that usually wins on criteria and usually loses in the room, because it is the least visible. Name that if nobody does.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
How many groups, and how you will divide them: _________________________
A local version of this decision your chapter actually faced: __________
Stakeholder Cards: The Resource Allocation Challenge
Six cards. Print, cut along the divisions, and deal one per person. Each person argues from their card for the first ten minutes of the group task, then drops the role and decides as themselves.
Each card gives a position, what is underneath it, and one thing the person will not say out loud. The third line is what makes these worth using.
Card 1: Executive Director
Position. Wants chapter-wide impact and equitable coverage across all counties.
Underneath. Is accountable to a board that reads a map. A concentration of effort in one community is hard to defend at a board meeting even when it is the right call.
Will not say. That the equity argument and the coverage argument point in different directions, and that they have been using them interchangeably.
Card 2: Disaster Program Manager
Position. Wants stronger DAT response capacity. Coverage gaps are real and measurable.

Underneath. Has been carrying overnight calls personally for four months and knows this is not sustainable, and also knows that saying so sounds like a personal complaint rather than an operational risk.
Will not say. That two of the counties have had no functioning DAT for over a year and it has not come up because nothing has happened there yet.
Card 3: Community resilience lead
Position. Wants deeper investment in the priority community. Trust is finally there and the window is now.
Underneath. Has personally promised people things that require this investment to be real. The relationships run through them and nobody else has them.
Will not say. That if this does not get funded, they will keep doing it anyway, on top of everything else, until they leave.
Card 4: Volunteer Services lead
Position. Wants recruitment and retention prioritized before anything expands.
Underneath. Every other option on the table quietly assumes volunteers who do not currently exist. This is the constraint underneath all four options and it is being treated as one option among four.
Will not say. That the retention problem is partly caused by how the last two expansions were staffed, which would mean naming colleagues.
Card 5: Community partner representative
Position. Wants continued local engagement and follow-through on what was already started.
Underneath. Has watched three organizations arrive, run something for two years, and leave. Is evaluating whether the Red Cross is the fourth.
Will not say. That they will publicly support whatever is decided and privately stop investing their own people if the answer is another pilot.
Card 6: Board member
Position. Wants visible outcomes and measurable progress within the year.
Underneath. Is the one asked by donors what the chapter accomplished, and has nothing to say about relationship-building that survives that conversation.
Will not say. That they would support the slower option if someone gave them the language for it, and nobody ever has.
How to use the cards

items: Ten minutes in role, then drop it. Groups that stay in role all the way through produce a stalemate rather than a decision.
Tell people they may reveal the third line if they choose to, and that most stakeholders in real life do not.
In the debrief, ask what changed when someone said the quiet part. It is usually the whole decision.

blocks.text: Group Size: Groups of four to six.
Materials: The stewardship assessment worksheet (page 50), one per group. The stakeholder cards (page 28). The communication planner (page 52). Flip chart.
Purpose: The stewardship simulation. A program that worked, a funding cliff, and five real options. This is the hardest activity in the skill and it should be run last.
The scenario (3 minutes, read aloud)

“Three years ago a chapter launched a Community Resilience Initiative in a priority community. It built strong relationships, supported preparedness activities, connected residents to partners, and increased trust. Conditions have now changed.”
What is going well

items: Community trust is strong.
Partners value Red Cross participation.
Residents recognize the initiative by name.
Preparedness knowledge has measurably increased.
Several local leaders are now actively engaged.

blocks.text: What has changed

items: Grant funding ends in six months.
Staff capacity has decreased.
Volunteer participation is inconsistent.
New chapter-wide response needs are increasing.
Community partners want the work to continue unchanged.
Leadership is concerned about sustainability.
Other communities in the chapter also have significant needs.

blocks.text: The intentional challenge

There is no easy answer. The initiative has real value and it cannot continue unchanged without resources that do not exist. Groups must navigate community trust, program impact, funding constraints, staff and volunteer capacity, chapter-wide obligations, and the emotional difficulty of changing work that people care about.
The group task (28 minutes)

items: Assess the initiative against the six stewardship criteria: impact, alignment, capacity, community value, sustainability, and relationship implications. Ten minutes, using the worksheet. Score each one and write one line of evidence, not one line of opinion.
Decide: continue, adapt, scale, pause, or conclude. Five minutes. One choice, and the group must agree.
Identify what resources are needed to make that decision real. Four minutes.
Identify which relationships must be protected regardless of the decision, and name the person, not the organization. Three minutes.
Develop the transition or stewardship plan. Four minutes. What moves, to whom, by when, and what does the Red Cross keep.
Prepare the communication message. Two minutes, using the planner. Who hears it first is part of the answer.

blocks.text: Share out (6 minutes)

Each group states their decision in one word, then reads their communication message. Do not let them explain the reasoning first. The message either stands on its own or it does not, and that is the finding.
Facilitator debrief (8 minutes)

items: What decision did your group make, and what evidence supported it?
What made the decision difficult, and was it the evidence or the relationships?
How did you weigh community trust against capacity?
Who did you decide should hear this first, and why?
What would happen if the initiative continued unchanged?
What would happen if it ended abruptly?

blocks.text: Final facilitator reinforcement

items: Good stewardship is not preserving every initiative forever.
Stewardship means aligning resources, relationships and impact as conditions change.
Ending, pausing or adapting work does not mean the work failed. Saying so out loud is part of the job.
Transition planning is part of responsible leadership, not an admission of one.
Trust is maintained through honesty, clarity and follow-through, and it is lost through a continuation nobody can staff.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: Most groups choose adapt. That is usually right and it is also the answer that lets people avoid the hard conversation, so push: what specifically is different, and who is doing less?
Groups that choose conclude often do the best work, because they are forced to take the relationships seriously. Do not let the room treat conclude as the harsh answer.
The six criteria are scored in ten minutes, which is tight. That is deliberate. Groups that spend twenty minutes on assessment never get to the plan, and the plan is where the skill is.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
A real transition your chapter or region has faced, for the debrief: ____
What you will say if a participant says this is exactly our situation: __
Stakeholder Cards: The Grant Is Ending
Six cards. Print, cut, and deal one per person. Same rule as the other deck: ten minutes in role, then drop it and decide as yourself.
Card 1: Community partner
Position. Wants the initiative to continue unchanged.
Underneath. Has rearranged their own organization around this work. Continuation is not a preference, it is a staffing plan they already made.
Will not say. That they could carry part of it themselves with six months of support, and they have not offered because nobody asked and offering feels like volunteering for more work.
Card 2: Executive Director
Position. Needs to balance the whole chapter, not one community.
Underneath. Knows this is the best work the chapter has done in years and cannot fund it out of a budget that is already committed.
Will not say. That the reason there is no plan for after the grant is that nobody wrote one at the start, including them.
Card 3: Disaster Program Manager
Position. Wants more capacity for response readiness, which means wants this to end.
Underneath. Is not opposed to the initiative and is opposed to being the only part of the chapter that absorbs every new demand.
Will not say. That the relationships this initiative built are the reason the last two responses in that community went as well as they did.
Card 4: Community resilience lead
Position. Believes the initiative should adapt, not end.
Underneath. Adapt is the answer they can defend. Continue is the answer they want. They have not worked out what adapt would actually mean.
Will not say. That most of the initiative currently runs through their own calendar and that nobody else could pick it up in six months.
Card 5: Volunteer leader
Position. Says the current workload is not sustainable.
Underneath. Three of the most reliable volunteers have quietly reduced their hours and have not told anyone why.
Will not say. That volunteers would carry more of this if they were asked to lead something rather than staff something.
Card 6: Resident representative
Position. Fears losing support and losing trust.
Underneath. Has personally vouched for the Red Cross to neighbors who were skeptical. If this ends badly, the cost is theirs and it is local and it lasts.
Will not say. That what they actually need is to know the answer early enough to tell people themselves, rather than the answer being a particular one.
How to use the cards

items: Card 6 is the one to make sure gets dealt. If a group is small, deal cards 1, 4 and 6.
The pattern across all six cards is that the honest information is available and nobody is asking for it. Name that in the debrief.
Ask the room which of the six they are, in their real job. It is a quiet question and it lands.

blocks.text: Group Size: Groups of four to six.
Materials: Flip chart and markers. The communication planner is useful and optional.
Purpose: What to do when a community names a priority the Red Cross cannot lead on. This is the shortest core experience and it prevents more damage than the other two combined.
The scenario (2 minutes, read aloud)

“A community coalition has identified affordable housing as its top priority. Residents describe rising rent, overcrowded housing, fear of displacement, limited transportation, and increased vulnerability during disasters. Red Cross programs and resources are focused on disaster preparedness, home fire safety, disaster response, community resilience, and partner coordination.”
The tension

Community priorities and Red Cross priorities will not always be identical. A community may name housing, transportation, food access, or employment as its highest priority. Being community-centered does not mean the Red Cross must solve every issue a community names. It means listening deeply enough to understand the context and then being honest about where mission, programs, relationships and strengths can genuinely contribute.
The group task (18 minutes)

items: Identify what the community is actually naming as the priority. Three minutes. Housing is the headline; underneath it there are four or five distinct things and only some of them are housing.

Identify where genuine mission alignment exists. Five minutes. Look at the residents’ own words. Increased vulnerability during disasters is a direct overlap. Overcrowding is a fire safety overlap. Displacement is a preparedness and continuity overlap.
Identify what the Red Cross should not promise. Four minutes. Write the actual sentence you would not say.
Identify partner connections or referral pathways. Three minutes. Who is already working on this, and what would a real introduction cost us?
Develop a response that honors the community priority and stays mission-aligned. Three minutes. Four sentences maximum.

blocks.text: Share out (4 minutes)
Each group reads only the sentence they would not say, and then their response. The list of things nobody should promise is the most useful artifact this activity produces.
Facilitator debrief (6 minutes)

items: How did your group honor the community’s stated priority while being honest about limits?
Where did alignment genuinely exist, and where were you reaching?
What would be inappropriate for the Red Cross to promise here?
How does an organization stay a trusted partner without becoming responsible for everything?
What role can partnership and referral play, and what makes a referral worth more than a phone number?

blocks.text: Final facilitator reinforcement

Community priorities should not be dismissed because they do not fit our programs. Mission alignment requires humility and clarity. Trust grows when organizations are honest about what they can do, what they cannot, and who else should be involved. Stewardship includes protecting the organization from overcommitment while still honoring community wisdom.
Facilitator notes

items: The failure mode to watch for is a group that finds alignment everywhere. If every resident concern maps neatly onto a Red Cross program, the group is not being honest, they are being accommodating. Push on one.
The opposite failure is a group that concludes there is nothing here. There is: three of the five resident concerns have direct disaster relevance.
This activity pairs well with the Grant Is Ending, and it should come first. It is about what we take on; the other is about what we put down.

blocks.text: Scenario Bank

Six leadership situations where prioritization and stewardship collide. These are premises, not full activities, and they are deliberately short so that a facilitator can run any of them in fifteen minutes using the protocol below.
The shared protocol
Any of the six can be run this way, in fifteen minutes, in groups of three to five.

items: Read the scenario aloud. One minute.
Individually: what is the actual decision here, in one sentence? Two minutes. Compare in the group; they will not match.
Name three criteria that should govern the decision. Four minutes.
Make a recommendation and name what it costs. Five minutes.
One sentence you would say to the person who is most affected. Three minutes.

blocks.text: Alternative uses: written reflection, a pair conversation, or a practice assessment against the proficiency thresholds in Appendix C.
Scenario 1: Depth against breadth

A leader must decide whether to concentrate limited staff time and resources in a single priority community with significant need and opportunity, or to maintain a broader level of support across multiple communities in the chapter footprint.
The weighing: concentrated impact against broad reach, equity across communities, and sustainability of engagement over time.
Scenario 2: Competing needs, one shared resource
Two communities need support at the same time and only one regional staff member is available.

The leader must determine how to prioritize the immediate response, how to support the community that cannot be served first, and how to communicate the decision in a way that maintains trust with both.
Scenario 3: Internal misalignment on priorities
Internal teams hold genuinely different views on where effort should go: volunteer growth, response readiness, fundraising and sustainability, or long-term relationship-building.
The leader must guide alignment across these perspectives and establish shared priorities despite the disagreement, without simply choosing the loudest team.
Scenario 4: Community need against organizational scope
A community identifies a significant issue, such as housing instability, disaster risk, or long-term recovery needs, and expects organizational support.
The leader must determine what role the organization can realistically and responsibly play, how to align community expectations with capacity and expertise, and how to engage without overextending.
Scenario 5: Transitioning or concluding work
A long-standing initiative has established relationships and history and is valued by stakeholders, and it no longer aligns with current strategy or available capacity.
The leader must guide a transition, adaptation or closure decision that balances strategic alignment with relational responsibility.
Scenario 6: Low trust and decision-making
Trust is low between teams, departments or partners, and this is directly limiting the ability to make and implement prioritization decisions.
The leader must consider how trust influences alignment, whether to prioritize relationship-building before making major decisions, and how to move forward while rebuilding credibility.
How these map to the four components
Analyze the situation. Identify competing priorities, constraints, stakeholder dynamics, and the pressures shaping the decision. Scenarios 1, 3 and 6 lead with this.
Apply the skill. Facilitate the decision, guide the tradeoffs, and structure alignment across perspectives. Scenarios 2 and 3.
Evaluate. Assess decision quality, feasibility, alignment, and relational impact. Scenarios 4 and 5.
Adapt. Adjust priorities, refine approaches, and strengthen stewardship over time. Scenario 5 most directly.
Facilitator notes

items: Scenario 6 is the one people skip and the one that explains the other five. A group that cannot make decisions usually has a trust problem wearing a process costume.
Scenario 5 names an Executive Director specifically. In practice this decision often sits with someone who does not have the authority to make it, which is worth surfacing.
Use two scenarios, not six. Six is a bank to choose from, not an agenda.

blocks.text: Group Size: 6 to 20. Above twenty, put every question to pairs first.
Materials: None. Do not use slides. A flip chart only in stage 4.
Purpose: Get a group to examine how they actually make prioritization decisions, rather than how they would describe making them. Nothing here is taught.
How to use this guide

There are more questions here than an hour holds. That is deliberate. Choose one core question per block and hold the rest in reserve. A session that gets through eight questions well is far better than one that gets through thirty.
The facilitator synthesis lines are the difference between a question bank and a session. Use them at the end of each block, in your own words, and keep them short.
Session flow

items: 0 to 8 minutes: Opening. What prioritization means to this room.
8 to 25 minutes: How decisions actually get made now.
25 to 42 minutes: Tradeoffs, constraints and alignment.
42 to 54 minutes: Stewardship and sustainability.
54 to 60 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: Stage 1: Opening, 0 to 8 minutes
Open with: “This is not a training. You will not hear me talk for long. We are going to think about how decisions actually get made, which is usually different from how we describe them.”

items: Core question: when you hear the word prioritization, what does it mean to you?
Then: can you share an example of a time you had to make a difficult tradeoff between competing priorities?

blocks.text: Hold in reserve: how do you currently decide what comes first in your role?
Synthesis. Notice how many of these definitions are about importance and how few are about capacity. That gap is what the hour is about.
Stage 2: How decisions actually get made, 8 to 25 minutes
Two blocks, about eight minutes each.
Block A: the role of prioritization

items: Core question: what happens when priorities are unclear or constantly shifting?
Reserve: why is prioritization critical in leadership and operations? How does it influence outcomes, alignment and use of resources? What are the risks of trying to do too many things at once?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Constantly changing priorities have a cost that never appears in a budget: everything restarts, and organizations overestimate what can be done in a month and underestimate what can be done in a year.
Block B: current approaches

items: Core question: what criteria, formal or informal, do you use when you make prioritization decisions?
Reserve: how do you determine what is most important? How are decisions typically communicated? To what extent are decisions made individually rather than collaboratively?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Every one of you used criteria. Almost none of them were written down or agreed with anyone else. That is not a personal failing, it is the normal state, and it is what makes decisions feel arbitrary to the people they land on.
Stage 3: Tradeoffs, constraints and alignment, 25 to 42 minutes
Block C: tradeoffs and constraints

items: Core question: how do you decide what to continue, pause, or stop?
Reserve: how do you approach situations where time, funding or capacity are limited? What types of tradeoffs come up most often? What makes it difficult to let go of existing work?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Nearly all the difficulty in that last question was relational rather than analytical. We usually know what should stop. What we do not know is how to tell the person attached to it.
Block D: alignment and stakeholders

items: Core question: where do you see misalignment between stated priorities and where resources actually go?
Reserve: how do you ensure different perspectives are considered? How do competing expectations influence decisions? What role does transparency play in building trust around decisions?

blocks.text: Synthesis. People can disagree with a decision and still trust the process. What damages trust is not disappointment, it is inconsistency, opacity, and decisions that feel arbitrary.
Stage 4: Stewardship and sustainability, 42 to 54 minutes
This is the block to use a flip chart for, because the answers are worth keeping.

items: Core question: how do you determine whether a program or initiative should continue, adapt, or conclude?
Then: what signals tell you something is no longer effective or aligned?
Reserve: what does good stewardship of resources look like in your role? How do you balance short-term needs against long-term sustainability?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Launching something is exciting. Sustaining something is leadership. Notice that most of the signals you just named are ones you have already seen somewhere and have not acted on yet.
Stage 5: Close, 54 to 60 minutes

items: What is one insight or takeaway from this discussion?
What is one small change you could make to improve how you prioritize or make decisions?

blocks.text: Take the second answer around the whole room, one sentence each, no elaboration. Then close: “Prioritization is not about doing less. It is about making intentional choices, and about being able to say why.”
Questions held in reserve for a room that goes fast

items: What are the biggest challenges you face in setting priorities? In making tradeoffs? In aligning resources with decisions?
Where do prioritization processes break down or become unclear?
What would a strong prioritization process look like in your team?
How could decisions become more transparent and consistent?
What tools, structures or practices would improve your ability to decide?
How might you strengthen how work is sustained, adapted, or concluded over time?

blocks.text: Troubleshooting
If no one responds. Give thirty seconds of silence out loud, then send the question to pairs before opening it back up.
If answers stay abstract. Ask for the specific decision, the specific week, the specific person who was disappointed. Concrete beats principled every time.
If one voice dominates. Change the format rather than confronting the person. Move to pairs. Then take answers from the other side of the room first.
If the group blames leadership above them. Legitimate and also a dead end. Ask: what is the largest decision you do control, and how did you make it?
If the group wants tools immediately. Say the tools are in the document and are twenty minutes to learn. Then ask what would still be hard once they had them. That answer is the session.
Facilitator notes

items: The hardest discipline is not answering. You will know the answer to most of what gets asked.
If you have fifty minutes rather than sixty, cut stage 3 block D. Do not compress all five stages.
Do not capture on a flip chart before stage 4. Visible capture turns a dialogue into a brainstorm.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Your own difficult tradeoff, ready but held back: _______________________
The five core questions you will definitely ask: ________________________
Session Formats
Five written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document, so the pages are the plan.
20 minutes. One icebreaker and one framework. For a staff meeting or the front of something else.
1 hour. Constraints, the two sorting frameworks, and a real application to the participant’s own list.
2 hours, prioritization. Criteria, scoring, and the resource allocation simulation. The workhorse session.
2 hours, stewardship. Continue, adapt, scale, pause, conclude, and the Grant Is Ending simulation.
4 hours. Both halves, with the Socratic hour at the front.
Choosing between them

items: The two two-hour sessions are genuinely different sessions, not two versions of one. Run them a month apart with the same group and they build on each other.
If someone asks for a session and gives no constraint, run the two-hour prioritization session.
The stewardship session needs a room with real programs they are responsible for. It does not work with people who are early in a role.
The four-hour is long and it holds, because the second half is emotionally different from the first rather than more of it.

blocks.text: What every format shares

items: A constraint imposed early. Every activity in this document works because something is taken away.
Criteria made visible before options are compared. This is the single discipline the whole skill teaches.
A named tradeoff at the end. What was delayed, reduced, or not pursued, said out loud.

blocks.text: A note on the two workshops
Purpose: Establish one idea: prioritization is about capacity, not importance. Do not try to teach a framework in twenty minutes.
Materials: Flip chart, markers.
Agenda

items: 3 minutes: Framing.
12 minutes: You Can Only Pick Three.
5 minutes: Debrief and one commitment.

blocks.text: Framing (3 minutes)

Say this: “Prioritization is not about deciding what matters. Many things matter. It is about deciding where limited staff time, volunteer capacity, funding and attention can create the most impact. Avoiding that decision does not remove the tradeoff. It just makes it invisible, and it lets it get made by whoever asked most recently.”
One question to the room, two or three answers: “What is currently on your list that is really an aspiration rather than a priority?”
You Can Only Pick Three (12 minutes)
Page 13. Run it exactly as written, including the criteria step, which is the part that makes it teach something.
Debrief and commitment (5 minutes)

items: What criteria came up most often across the groups?
What did you have to give up, and who would need to hear about it?

blocks.text: Close by asking everyone to name one thing on their own list that could be delayed this quarter. Take five out loud.
Facilitator notes

items: Twenty minutes buys one felt experience. The felt experience is the moment a group has to cut something good.
Do not introduce must, should, may here. Naming a framework in the last two minutes guarantees it is not remembered.

blocks.text: Purpose: Two sorting frameworks, applied to the participant’s own work rather than to a scenario. People leave with a sorted list of their own.
Materials: The must, should, may and urgent against important handout (page 48), one per participant. Flip chart.
Agenda

items: 5 minutes: Framing.
15 minutes: You Can Only Pick Three.
15 minutes: The two frameworks, taught.
15 minutes: Apply to your own list.
10 minutes: Debrief and commitment.

blocks.text: Framing (5 minutes)
The capacity line, as in the twenty-minute session. Add one thing: “Capacity is a resource, not an obstacle. We would not commit money we did not have. We commit time we do not have every week.”
You Can Only Pick Three (15 minutes)
Page 13. Full version with the criteria step and the debrief.
The two frameworks (15 minutes)
Page 9. Must, should, may in seven minutes, including the pitfall. Urgent against important in eight, including the fourth box, which is the one nobody talks about.
Use the room’s own criteria from the icebreaker as the bridge: “You named impact and urgency. These two frameworks are what happens when you take each of those seriously on its own.”
Apply to your own list (15 minutes)

items: Individually, five minutes: list eight to twelve things you are currently responsible for.
Individually, five minutes: sort them must, should, may. Then count the musts.
In pairs, five minutes: each person defends two of their musts to their partner, who plays skeptic. Most musts do not survive.

blocks.text: Debrief and commitment (10 minutes)

items: How many of your musts survived the challenge?
What is sitting in your important-but-not-urgent box that has been there for months?
Name one thing you will move from must to should this week, and who you have to tell.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The pair challenge is the best fifteen minutes in this session. Protect it, and be explicit that the partner’s job is to be difficult.
A common answer to the second debrief question is relationship-building. That is worth naming: the work this whole skill set exists to support lives permanently in the box that always loses.

title: Two-Hour Workshop: Aligning Limited Resources with the Highest-Impact Work

blocks.text: Purpose: Foundations of strategic prioritization. Through discussion, tools and a facilitated allocation exercise, participants work out how leaders decide when several things are important, resources are limited, and stakeholders want different outcomes.
Materials: Criteria scoring worksheets, stakeholder cards, communication planners, reflection sheets, flip charts and markers, projector optional.
Agenda

items: 10 minutes: Welcome and framing.
15 minutes: Icebreaker, You Can Only Pick Three.
30 minutes: Prioritization tools and decision criteria.
45 minutes: The Chapter Resource Allocation Challenge.
20 minutes: Reflection and close.

blocks.text: Ten plus fifteen plus thirty plus forty-five plus twenty is one hundred and twenty minutes.
Welcome and framing (10 minutes)
Introductions, objectives, discussion norms. Then the framing messages, which the facilitator states directly:

items: Not every important need can be addressed at the same time.
Prioritization is not doing less for its own sake. It is focusing limited resources where they create the most impact.
Avoiding prioritization does not eliminate tradeoffs. It makes them invisible.
Capacity is a resource, not an obstacle.
Strategic prioritization requires weighing impact, urgency, feasibility, equity, capacity, sustainability and mission alignment.
Transparent criteria help people understand decisions even when they disagree with the outcome.

blocks.text: Define the six terms from page 9: strategic prioritization, capacity, tradeoffs, opportunity cost, decision criteria, resource allocation. Two minutes, and do not skip this, because the group task later leans on all six.
Icebreaker: You Can Only Pick Three (15 minutes)
Page 13.
Prioritization tools and decision criteria (30 minutes)
Page 9. Three topics, ten minutes each.

items: Must, should, may, with the pitfall and the three discussion questions.
Urgent against important, with all four boxes and the facilitator talking point.
Criteria-based prioritization and the scoring method on page 46. Teach the method here, in the room, on a small shared example, before anyone uses it in the simulation.

blocks.text: The Chapter Resource Allocation Challenge (45 minutes)
Page 22. Scenario, stakeholder cards, group task, share-out and debrief.
Reflection and close (20 minutes)
Participants reflect individually, five minutes, using the reflection sheet on page 54:

items: One assumption that was challenged today.
One criterion you should use more consistently.
One current priority that may need to be reassessed.
One way urgency is crowding out importance in your work.
One action you can take to make prioritization more transparent.

blocks.text: Then in pairs, five minutes, and whole group, ten minutes, on the closing question: “What would change if your team approached prioritization as a structured process rather than as a reaction to competing demands?”
Facilitator notes

items: The scoring method must be taught before the simulation, not during it. Ten minutes of teaching saves twenty minutes of confusion.
The twenty-minute close looks generous and is not. Groups come out of the simulation with a great deal to say.

blocks.text: Purpose: Sustaining impact through alignment, adaptation and trust. Participants work out how leaders decide whether work should continue, adapt, scale, pause or conclude when conditions change.
Materials: Stewardship assessment worksheets, the second stakeholder card deck, communication planners, reflection sheets, flip charts.
Agenda

items: 5 minutes: Welcome and framing.
15 minutes: Icebreaker, The Loudest Request.
30 minutes: Stewardship, alignment and transition decisions.
25 minutes: Community Priority and Mission Alignment.
35 minutes: The Grant Is Ending.
10 minutes: Reflection and close.

blocks.text: Five plus fifteen plus thirty plus twenty-five plus thirty-five plus ten is one hundred and twenty minutes.
Welcome and framing (5 minutes)
If this group did the prioritization session, connect the two: “Prioritization determines where resources go. Stewardship determines how they are managed over time.” Then:

items: Good stewardship is not maintaining every activity forever.
Programs and partnerships must be revisited as conditions change.
Responsible leaders sometimes adapt, scale back, pause or conclude work while preserving trust.
Stewardship includes people, funding, partnerships, community trust, volunteer capacity and organizational credibility.

blocks.text: Icebreaker: The Loudest Request (15 minutes)
Page 20.
Stewardship, alignment and transition decisions (30 minutes)
Three topics, ten minutes each.

items: The stewardship mindset. Stewardship means caring for resources, programs, partnerships and trust so that impact is sustained. It asks: is this still aligned, still effective, still sustainable, are we using resources responsibly, are we maintaining trust through our decisions. Talking point: stewardship is not ownership. Leaders are not responsible for protecting every activity forever; they are responsible for protecting mission impact, community trust and responsible use of resources.
Continue, adapt, scale, pause, conclude, from page 9, with examples for all five and the four key discussion questions.

Community priorities and mission alignment. Community priorities and Red Cross priorities will not always be identical. Being community-centered does not mean solving every issue a community names; it means listening deeply, understanding the context, and identifying where mission and resources can contribute meaningfully without overpromising.

blocks.text: Community Priority and Mission Alignment (25 minutes)
Page 30. Run at 25 minutes by shortening the group task to fifteen and the debrief to five.
The Grant Is Ending (35 minutes)
Page 26. Run at 35 minutes by giving the assessment eight minutes rather than ten and the share-out four rather than six. If you have the full 45, take it from the framing.
Reflection and close (10 minutes)
Individually, four minutes, using the reflection sheet:

items: One stewardship decision you may need to revisit.
One relationship you would need to protect during a difficult transition.
One signal that a program may need to adapt.
One way you can communicate tradeoffs more transparently.
One action you will take within the next month.

blocks.text: Then whole group, six minutes, on the closing question: “What would change if your team treated stewardship as an ongoing responsibility rather than something that only happens when a program is in trouble?”
Facilitator notes

items: This session is emotionally heavier than the prioritization one. Expect someone to bring a real program they are about to lose. Make room for it in the debrief rather than after.
The two simulations back to back is a lot. If the room is flagging, cut Community Priority and Mission Alignment and give the time to the Grant Is Ending at its full 45.

blocks.text: Purpose: Both halves of the skill in one day: how decisions get made now, how to make them with visible criteria, and what to do with work that is already running.
Materials: Everything. Both card decks, scoring worksheets, stewardship assessments, communication planners, reflection sheets, flip charts for four groups.
Agenda

items: 60 minutes: Socratic discussion.
15 minutes: Break.
30 minutes: The four decision tools.
45 minutes: The Chapter Resource Allocation Challenge.
15 minutes: Break.
15 minutes: Icebreaker, The Loudest Request.
45 minutes: The Grant Is Ending.
45 minutes: Application to real work, and close.

blocks.text: Hour 1: Socratic discussion
Page 34. Full sixty minutes, five stages, no slides. It goes first because it surfaces how the room actually decides, and everything after it is a response to what they said.
Hour 2: tools and the allocation simulation
Page 9 for thirty minutes, teaching all four tools including the scoring method. Then page 22 for the full forty-five.

The bridge line, after the Socratic hour: “You told me this morning that you use criteria and that they are almost never written down. The next thirty minutes is what happens when you write them down.”
Hour 3: stewardship
The Loudest Request for fifteen minutes, page 20, then the Grant Is Ending at its full forty-five, page 26.
Hour 4: application and close (45 minutes)
This is the hour the two-hour sessions do not have, and it is the one that makes the day worth four hours.

items: Individually, ten minutes: take the real example you brought, or one from your current work, and run the scoring method on it. Real criteria, real weights, real options.
In trios, fifteen minutes: five minutes each. Present your scoring to two colleagues, whose only job is to challenge the weights. Not the scores. The weights.
Individually, ten minutes: write the communication statement for your real decision, using the planner on page 52.
Whole group, ten minutes: take one sentence from each person. The sentence is what they will stop, delay, or reduce, and when.

blocks.text: If you only have three hours
Cut the Socratic hour and open with the four tools. The day loses its best hour and keeps both simulations, which is the right trade if the room is new to the material.
Facilitator notes

items: Two breaks, not one, and put them where they are marked. The middle of this day is dense.
The fourth hour only works if people brought a real decision. Chase the pre-work for this format specifically.
Consider co-facilitating. The Socratic hour and the simulations want different facilitator temperaments.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Who is co-facilitating, and which sections: ____________________________
What happens after this session, and who owns it: ______________________
Handout: The Criteria Scoring Worksheet
A method for comparing several genuinely good options against criteria a group has agreed. Ten minutes to teach, fifteen to run. Use it in the resource allocation simulation and on real decisions.
Before you start
This produces a recommendation, not an answer. The arithmetic is a way of making a disagreement visible, and the most valuable part of the whole method is step 2, before anyone looks at an option.
Step 1: choose four to six criteria
From the twelve on page 9, or your own. Four to six. Fewer than four and the comparison is crude; more than six and the weighting stops meaning anything.
Step 2: weight them, and do this before you look at the options
Distribute ten points across your chosen criteria. All ten must be spent, and no criterion can receive zero, because a criterion worth zero is not a criterion, it is a criterion you have discarded.

This is the step that does the work. A group that agrees the criteria and then argues for ten minutes about the weights has already done most of the thinking, and the argument is the point rather than an obstacle to it.
Step 3: score each option, 1 to 3
Three points, not five, because five invites a precision the evidence does not support.
1, weak. This option does little or nothing for this criterion, or works against it.
2, partial. This option helps somewhat, or helps in some places and not others.
3, strong. This option clearly and directly advances this criterion.
Score honestly rather than strategically. If a group cannot agree on a score, record the disagreement rather than averaging it; that disagreement is usually about a fact somebody should go and check.
Step 4: multiply and total
For each option, multiply the score by the weight for every criterion and add them up. Highest total is the leading option.
Option A total: ______ Option B total: ______ Option C total: ______ Option D total: ______
Step 5: the check, which is not optional
Look at the ranking. Ask the group one question: does this feel wrong?

If it does, the criteria or the weights are wrong, not the arithmetic. Go back and fix them once, and rerun. Once. A group that revises three times is no longer scoring, it is reverse-engineering the answer it wanted, and it would have been more honest to skip the exercise.

If it still feels wrong after one revision, the honest conclusion is that a criterion that matters has not been named. Find it. It is usually something relational or political that nobody wanted to write down.
Step 6: record what you are giving up
The recommendation is not finished until this is written.
What this delays, reduces, or does not fund: __________________________
Who is most affected, and what they will notice: ______________________
What would have to change for us to revisit this, and when we will: ____
A worked fragment

Four criteria, weighted 4 for community impact, 3 for staff capacity, 2 for equity, 1 for visibility. An option that scores 3 on impact, 1 on capacity, 3 on equity and 3 on visibility totals 12 plus 3 plus 6 plus 3, which is 24. An option scoring 2, 3, 2 and 1 totals 8 plus 9 plus 4 plus 1, which is 22. Close enough that the decision is not settled by the number, which is exactly the situation the method is for: it tells you the two options are near-equivalent and the real choice is about something else.
Common failure modes

items: Weighting after seeing the options. Produces a number that agrees with what the group already wanted.
Using a five-point scale. Every option ends up scoring 3 or 4 and nothing separates.
Treating the total as the decision. It is an input. A leader who says the scoring favored B and we are choosing A because of the following is being more transparent than one who never scored at all.
Skipping step 6. Then the tradeoff was never named and the delayed work is still quietly expected.

blocks.text: Handout: Must, Should, May and Urgent against Important
Two sorting frameworks on one page. Print one per participant for the one-hour and two-hour sessions.
Must, should, may
List what you are responsible for, then place each item in one of the three. Every item gets a category.
Must. Mission-critical, required, time-sensitive, or creates significant risk if not done.
Should. Important, advances goals, and can be adjusted, sequenced or delayed if capacity is constrained.
May. Valuable if resources allow, and postponable without major consequence.
The check
Count your musts. If more than about a third of your list is in must, take the two you are least sure of and defend them to someone else against the definition. Most do not survive.
Urgent against important
Place the same items into these four. This is a diagnostic rather than a decision tool: it tells you what your week is actually made of.
Important and urgent. Immediate action, significant consequences.
Important, not urgent. Long-term value, no immediate pressure. This is where relationship-building, volunteer development and resilience work live, and it is the box that loses every argument.
Urgent, not important. Feels immediate, does not advance strategy. Last-minute requests, visibility-driven asks, administrative work that could be delegated.
Neither. Low value. Meetings without a purpose, reports nobody reads, commitments that outlived their reason.
The two questions
For anything you are unsure about: what happens if this does not happen today, and what happens if this does not happen six months from now? The gap between those two answers places the item.
One thing to do this week
One item moving from must to should: __________________________________
Handout: The Stewardship Assessment
Six criteria for deciding what happens to work that is already running. Use it in the Grant Is Ending simulation and on real programs. One sheet per program.
How long it has been running: ______ Who from the Red Cross touches it monthly: ______
Score each criterion 1 to 3, and write one line of evidence
Evidence, not opinion. If you cannot write the evidence line, the score is a guess and should be marked as one.
1. Impact. Is the work producing the outcomes it was meant to produce? Score ____
2. Alignment. Does it still fit the mission, the strategy, and what the community currently names as a priority? Score ____
3. Capacity. Can it be staffed and resourced at quality for the next twelve months, honestly? Score ____
4. Community value. Do the people it serves value it, and would they notice if it stopped? Score ____
5. Sustainability. Could it survive a funding change, a leadership change, or the departure of the person who holds it? Score ____
6. Relationship implications. What happens to trust and to specific relationships under each option? Score ____
Reading the scores
The total matters less than the shape. Look at which criteria are low.

items: High impact and community value, low capacity and sustainability: this is the adapt case, and adapt means somebody else carries part of it.
High capacity, low impact and alignment: this is the conclude case, and it is the hardest to say because nothing is going wrong.
High everything: scale, if there is genuinely somewhere to scale to and someone to run it.
Low capacity, everything else strong, and the constraint is temporary: pause, with a date.
Low relationship implications score is a stop sign on every option. Deal with that first.

blocks.text: The decision
Circle one: continue / adapt / scale / pause / conclude
What the Red Cross keeps, and until when: _____________________________
Who takes on what, and have they been asked: _________________________
Which relationships must be protected regardless, named by person: ____
Handout: The Communication Planner
Four sentences. Every prioritization and stewardship activity in this document ends with one of these, because a decision that has not been communicated has not been made.
Who hears it, and in what order
Order matters more than wording. The person most affected should not hear it third, and they should not hear it from someone else.
Who will hear it from someone other than us, and what will they hear: __
The four sentences
1. What was decided. One sentence, in plain terms, with no preamble. Leading with context reads as softening and people stop trusting the rest.
2. Why, in terms of the criteria. Not because of budget. Name the actual criteria that governed it. This is the sentence that makes disagreement survivable.
3. What this delays, reduces, or does not fund. Say the cost out loud. A decision presented as costless is not believed, and it leaves the delayed work quietly still expected.
4. What happens next, and when. A date. Not soon, not in the coming months. A date, even if the date is when you will next have information.
The test
Read the four sentences to someone who was not in the decision. Then ask them two questions: what was decided, and why. If they cannot answer both, rewrite sentence 2.
What not to do

items: Do not lead with appreciation. It reads as the thing that comes before bad news, and it makes the appreciation worthless.
Do not present a decision as still open when it is not. Consultation after the fact costs more trust than no consultation.
Do not say we hope to revisit this without a date. That is a no in a costume, and everybody knows it.
Do not explain the internal process. People need the criteria, not the meeting history.

blocks.text: A worked example

“We are putting this year’s flexible funding and the open position into volunteer recruitment and retention. We weighted staff and volunteer capacity most heavily, because every other option we considered depends on volunteers we do not currently have. That means the deeper investment in the priority community does not get the additional staff time this year, and the preparedness expansion is on hold. I will come back to both of you in January with what capacity looks like then, and I would rather talk through what this means for your work before that.”
Handout: Reflection Sheet
Used at the close of any session of an hour or more. One page, and participants take it with them.
After a prioritization session
One assumption that was challenged today: ____________________________
One criterion I should use more consistently: _________________________
One current priority that needs reassessing: __________________________
One way urgency is crowding out importance in my work: ________________
One action to make my prioritization more transparent: ________________
After a stewardship session
One stewardship decision I need to revisit: ___________________________
One relationship I would need to protect in a transition: _____________
One signal that a program of mine may need to adapt: __________________
One way I can communicate tradeoffs more transparently: _______________
One action I will take in the next month: _____________________________
The commitment
The thing I will stop, delay, or reduce: ______________________________
What I will say to them, in one sentence: _____________________________
The closing questions
What would change if your team approached prioritization as a structured process rather than as a reaction to competing demands?
What would change if your team treated stewardship as an ongoing responsibility rather than something that only happens when a program is in trouble?
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. Each entry says what it is for.
Start here

Kahane, A. (2021). Facilitating Breakthrough: How to Remove Obstacles, Bridge Differences, and Move Forward Together. Berrett-Koehler. On making decisions with people who do not agree and cannot be compelled. The most directly useful book on this list for anyone facilitating a prioritization conversation across organizations.

Kaner, S. (2014). Facilitator’s Guide to Participatory Decision-Making, 3rd edition. Jossey-Bass. The groan zone, and why groups that converge quickly converge badly. Chapter on gradients of agreement is directly usable in the resource allocation simulation.
On prioritization and decision quality

Kahneman, D., Lovallo, D. and Sibony, O. (2019). A Structured Approach to Strategic Decisions. MIT Sloan Management Review. Why criteria set in advance beat judgment applied afterward, with the evidence. Short.
Rumelt, R. (2011). Good Strategy, Bad Strategy. Crown Business. The chapter on why organizations produce lists of priorities instead of strategies is the one to read. Blunt and correct.

Covey, S. (1989). The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People. The origin of the urgent-important matrix in popular use, and the source of the phrase important but not urgent. Read the one chapter, not the book.
On stewardship, sustainability and endings

Grantmakers for Effective Organizations, resources on exit and transition. Practical material on what happens when funding ends, written from the funder side, which is the side most Red Cross staff have to anticipate. https://www.geofunders.org/
Community Tool Box, University of Kansas, chapters on sustaining the work. Free, practical, and specific about the mechanics of transferring or concluding a community initiative. https://ctb.ku.edu/

Mobilizing for Action through Planning and Partnerships (MAPP), NACCHO. A community health planning framework whose prioritization phase is the closest public-health analogue to this skill. https://www.naccho.org/
On equity in decision-making

Interaction Institute for Social Change, materials on facilitative leadership. On whose voice shapes a decision and at what stage, which is the part of prioritization most likely to be skipped. https://interactioninstitute.org/
PolicyLink, resources on equitable resource allocation. Useful when equity is one of the weighted criteria and the group cannot agree what it means operationally. https://www.policylink.org/
Red Cross learning

Percipio has a set of courses on setting and managing priorities, connecting goals to key priorities, and prioritizing stakeholders. They require a Red Cross sign-in. Search Percipio for setting and managing priorities.
If you read one thing
The Kahneman, Lovallo and Sibony article. Twenty minutes, and it is the evidence behind why step 2 of the scoring worksheet comes before you look at the options.

Optional and worth sending, because four activities in the session work better when the participant arrives with a map already in hand. Send it four days ahead and do not chase it. The session works identically for people who did none of it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Read one thing (5 minutes)
A one-page overview of the Social Ecological Model, from the Centers for Disease Control.
https://www.cdc.gov/violence-prevention/about/

It is short, free, and introduces the nested-levels idea in plain public health language before anyone hears the term. One thing to know going in: the CDC version has four levels and the version used in this session has five, adding organizational. The extra level is where most Red Cross partnership work lives.
2. Watch one thing (5 minutes)
In a World of Systems, a short animated film based on Donella Meadows’ work, illustrated by David Macaulay.
https://donellameadows.org/systems-thinking-resources/
It makes systems thinking concrete and visual, using plumbing, traffic and fisheries, with no jargon at all. It is a gentler on-ramp than the model itself.
3. Map one program (10 minutes)

This is the piece that does the work, and it is the same exercise the session opens with. Take one program you already run. Just one. Then for each of the five levels, write down what is actually happening there today and mark whether your presence is strong, present, or a gap.

items: Individual: direct services, skills or support reaching one person at a time.
Interpersonal: relationships, trust and social connection the program builds or relies on.
Organizational: partner organizations, institutions or agencies involved.
Community: neighborhood-level or shared-identity presence and coordination.
Systems: policy, funding structures, or institutional advocacy the program touches.

blocks.text: You are not trying to fix anything. You are trying to see clearly. Most maps come out lopsided, heavy at one or two levels and empty at the others. That is not a failure. It is an accurate starting point, which is more than most of us have.
Bring the map. If you would rather use the printed form, it is the Program Mapping Template on page 44. If you only have five minutes, do this part and skip the reading and the video.
Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. Every session that uses the map allocates in-session time to produce one, so nobody is stranded; what you lose is the depth of the map rather than the activity. Chase the pre-work specifically for the four-hour session, whose last hour works on the participant’s own real program.
Group Size: 8 to 25, with a sweet spot of 12 to 18.
Materials: Open floor space. That is genuinely it, and it is genuinely required. This cannot be run around a conference table.

Purpose: Put the felt sense of an interconnected system in the room before anybody hears the word system. It is the only activity here that works on the body rather than the intellect, and it is the strongest thing in this skill.
Set up (4 minutes)

Explain the shape first. An equilateral triangle is one where all three sides are the same length, so the three people stand an equal distance apart. Draw it on a flip chart if the room looks unsure. It matters, because a participant who is aiming for any old triangle will stand still.

Then model it once. Pick two people yourself, say their names out loud, and walk the room through what you are doing: “I am staying the same distance from each of them. When she moves, I move. When he moves, I move.” Ten seconds of demonstration saves two minutes of confusion.

Then say this: “Form a circle. Silently pick two other people. Do not tell them, and do not tell anyone else. They will not know you picked them, and they do not have to pick you. Some of you will be picked by five people and some by nobody. On go, try to keep an equilateral triangle with your two, moving as they move.”
The not-telling is not a game rule for its own sake. It is the point of the activity: you are being moved by people who have no idea they are moving you, and you are moving people you did not choose.
Round 1: the cascade (5 minutes)

items: Run it for 60 to 90 seconds. The room will move continuously and will not settle. Let that happen.
Stop, and check that everyone understood. Ask whether anyone thinks they were picked by nobody. Nobody knows, which is the answer.

blocks.text: Round 2: the tap (5 minutes)

items: Same activity, and everyone picks two new people. Not the two from round 1. This matters: the connections reshuffle, so nobody can rely on what they learned about the room in the first round, and the cascade travels a different route.
New rule: if you are tapped on the shoulder, take a knee. If anyone in your triangle kneels, you kneel too.

Offer an accessibility alternative before you start, and name it specifically: stop moving and raise a hand works in place of kneeling. Offer it for round 1 as well if anyone needs to sit out the movement, and give them the observer job instead: watch the room and count how long it takes for the kneel to reach the far side.
Tap one person. Watch the cascade. It usually takes under fifteen seconds to reach everyone.

blocks.text: Debrief (8 minutes)
Two beats, in this order. The second one is the point and facilitators routinely stop after the first.
First, the cascade. Ask: “How many people did I touch?” Then: could you tell who you were moving? Who moved because of you? Reveal: when you moved, you moved everyone.

Second, the stasis trap. Ask: “What were you trying to do in there?” Most will say find equilibrium, or stop moving. Reveal: stasis was never the goal. The system was always going to keep adjusting. Your job is not to stabilize it. It is to stay skillful at responding to movement.
The bridge line

Say this to move from the icebreaker into content: “That is what we mean by designing across levels. When you design at one level, you are moving everyone in the system, whether you can see it or not.”
Debrief, the third question

If you have the time, ask one more: “Which of the people you were tracking is the SEM level you are not tracking right now? Where might you be moving a level you cannot see?” It will not land until later in the session, and that is fine.
Callbacks

items: “Remember when we were trying to stop moving?”
“Each SEM level is a person you chose in the triangle.”
“Which person in the circle are you tapping with this intervention?”

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: Do not skip the modeling. Facilitators who describe the triangle without showing it lose ninety seconds to questions and get a round where half the room is standing still.
Run this first when you use it. It sets the embodied foundation that Levels Quick-Sort and Your Strongest Level both build on, and it does not work as well after a sitting-down activity.
The room will be loud and slightly chaotic. That is correct. Do not tidy it.
Below about eight people the cascade is too fast to see. Above twenty-five it is hard to keep the circle. If your room is outside that range, use Levels Quick-Sort as your opener instead.
This does not work virtually. Appendix B says what to do instead.

blocks.text: Group Size: Any up to about thirty. Above that, have people hold up fingers one to five instead of calling out.
Materials: The sorting set on page 16, printed or on a slide. Chart paper with the five levels as columns, which is what makes the callbacks work.
Purpose: Give the room the vocabulary in ten minutes, and let them discover on their own that the interesting interventions do not sort cleanly.
Set up (1 minute)

Post the five levels as columns on chart paper. Say this: “I am going to read ten real interventions, one at a time. After each one, call out which of the five levels it operates at. Do not think too hard.”
The activity (6 minutes)

items: Read each item aloud. Wait for the room to call out a level.
When the room disagrees, do not resolve it. Write the item under both levels on the chart paper and move on. This is the whole design.
Move quickly. About thirty seconds per item.
After all ten: “Which were hard to place? Why?”

blocks.text: Debrief (3 minutes)

items: What was easy? What was hard? Which ones split the room, and why?

blocks.text: Reveal: the hard ones are where layered work lives. Single-level thinking misses them entirely, and a program that operates at two levels at once is not a filing problem, it is the thing we are trying to build.
Callbacks

items: “Remember the volunteer training one? It was individual and community at the same time.”
Pull the chart paper back out before any cross-level design work.
“When you map your own program, look for the hard ones.”

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: Four of the ten items are deliberately ambiguous. Do not improvise replacements without keeping that ratio, because ten unambiguous items produce a fast, pleasant activity that teaches nothing.
If the room settles too quickly on an ambiguous one, ask the dissenting answer out loud: “Who said interpersonal? Say more.”
Leave the chart paper up all session.

blocks.text: Handout: The Sorting Set
Ten interventions for Levels Quick-Sort. Read them aloud in this order. Four are deliberately ambiguous and those are the ones the activity is for.
The ten, in order
1. Installing a smoke alarm in a family’s home.
2. Training a resident to serve as their neighborhood’s preparedness coordinator.
3. Advocating for a local ordinance requiring fire-resistant roofing on rebuilds.
4. A monthly potluck for residents of a mobile home park, with a loose preparedness agenda.
5. Signing an agreement with the county housing authority to share vulnerability data.
6. Running a volunteer training course.
7. Funding a small nonprofit to add a part-time resilience position for two years.
8. A social media campaign about what goes in a seventy-two hour kit.
9. Pairing a new volunteer with a long-time resident to canvass a block together.
10. Convening the four organizations already working on senior isolation, so they meet each other for the first time.
Facilitator answer key
Do not hand this out. There are no wrong answers in the activity; there are answers that are more interesting than others.
1. Smoke alarm install. Individual, cleanly. Useful as the first one because everybody gets it right and the room warms up.

2. Training a neighborhood coordinator. Ambiguous. Individual, because one person gains a skill. Community, because a role now exists in that neighborhood that did not exist before, and it outlasts the person if the neighborhood keeps filling it. If nobody says community, ask what happens when that person moves away.
3. Fire-resistant roofing ordinance. Systems, cleanly. Worth pointing out that it reaches everybody in the jurisdiction, including people who will never meet the Red Cross.

4. Monthly potluck. Ambiguous, and the best one in the set. Interpersonal, because it builds trust between specific neighbors. Community, because it creates a standing structure. Almost nobody says individual, and yet it is the intervention most likely to produce the outcome in the wildfire story on page 5.

5. Data-sharing agreement with the housing authority. Organizational. Some rooms argue systems, which is a good argument: if it changes how the county targets its own resources, it has become systems. Let that run for thirty seconds.

6. Volunteer training course. Ambiguous, and the classic one. Individual, because volunteers gain skills. Community, because a trained volunteer corps is community capacity, not a set of individuals. This is the item to callback to all day.
7. Funding a resilience position at a small nonprofit. Organizational, cleanly. It is also the only item in the set that directly addresses the organizational casualty trap.

8. Social media campaign about kit contents. Individual. Rooms often want to say community because it reaches many people. Reach is not a level. Say that out loud; it is one of the two or three most useful corrections in the whole session.

9. Pairing a new volunteer with a long-time resident. Interpersonal, and it is the only clean interpersonal item in the set, which is itself worth noticing. Most rooms have no ready vocabulary for this one.

10. Convening four organizations that have never met. Ambiguous. Organizational, because it is organizations in a room. Community, because coordination is a community-level property. Some rooms say systems, which is defensible if the convening changes how funding flows. Save this for last; it is the hardest and it sets up the whole design work that follows.
If you want a shorter version
Use items 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Five minutes, and it keeps three of the four ambiguous ones.
Writing your own

If you replace items with local ones, keep the ratio: six that sort cleanly and four that genuinely do not. An item is properly ambiguous when two different levels each have a real argument, not when the item is vague.

title: Your Strongest Level
duration: 10 minutes, or 15 with a full share-around in a room over...

blocks.text: Group Size: Any. See the note on scale below.
Materials: Index cards or sticky notes, one per person. The five levels visible on chart paper or a slide.
Purpose: Personal diagnosis, and a physical artifact that gets referenced three more times during the day.
The activity (5 minutes)

items: Say: “Which level is your strongest? Where do most of your hours actually go?” Pause 60 to 90 seconds. Do not fill the silence.
Say: “Which level do you most consistently neglect?” Pause again.
“Write both on your card, with your name on it.”
Say this before anyone writes: “You will not have to share this unless you want to.”

blocks.text: Sharing out (2 to 5 minutes)
Two options, and pick before you deliver rather than in the moment.

Quick share-around. Each person reads their two words, no discussion. Good for rooms under fifteen and for groups that already know each other. At twenty-five people this is six minutes on its own, so budget fifteen for the activity.

Volunteers only. Invite two or three people to name their neglected level out loud, then move on. Use this when the room is senior, mixed-rank, or new to each other. It honors the promise you just made.
Debrief (3 minutes)

items: Patterns? Did most of us name the same neglected level? It is usually systems.
Why? What are the structural reasons? What are the personal ones?

blocks.text: Reveal: your neglected level is your growth edge. Keep your card.
The last two words matter. Say them out loud, because every callback for the rest of the session depends on people still having the card.
Callbacks

items: “Pull out your card. Did your map confirm what you wrote?”
“Who in the room named your neglected level as their strongest?” This is the sentence that starts partnerships inside a chapter.
“Your commitment should connect to the level you wrote down.”

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: Systems is the near-universal neglected answer. Have a response ready that is not reassurance: systems work is slow, unglamorous, and usually somebody else’s job description, which is exactly why it is nobody’s.
Watch for the person who names the same level as both strongest and neglected. That is usually true and worth a private word at the break.
If you are running the volunteers-only version, do not then ask people to hold their cards up. That is the same thing wearing a hat.

blocks.text: Group Size: 8 to 20, with a sweet spot of 12 to 16. Pairs or trios.
Materials: The challenge cards on page 20, printed and cut, one per pair. Chart paper with the five levels as columns.
Purpose: Show the room that layered work is already happening in their community and nobody planned it. This is the asset-based opener and it changes the tone of everything after it.
The activity (8 minutes)

items: Each pair or trio draws one challenge card.

Three minutes to name three different actors in their own community who would already be doing something about that challenge. A person, a group, an agency, a school, a faith community, a neighbor, a coalition.
Each pair shares their three. As they do, you tag each actor with a level on the chart paper. Light touch, no quiz, and do not correct anybody.

blocks.text: Debrief (5 minutes)
First. Ask: “What do you notice?” Almost every level has actors on it. Reveal: layered work is already happening in their community, and they did not have to plan it.
Then the deeper move. Ask: “Are your three actors coordinated? Do they know each other?” The answer is almost always no. Reveal: the layers exist. The coordination does not. That gap is the job.
Do not skip the second beat. The first one on its own is a nice observation; the second one is the skill.
Callbacks

items: “Remember the wildfire card? The housing one? The mental health one?”
“Your three actors were already there. Which one will you reach out to this week?”
“Your strongest discovery might be the layer that is already running and you did not know it.”

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The cards are a prompt and nothing more. Any list of real community challenges works, and a locally written set works better than the one on page 20.
When a pair names three actors all at the same level, that is a finding rather than a mistake. Say so, and ask who else is working on this that they have not thought of.
This pairs naturally with Find Your Layer Partners later in the session. The actor a pair names here is often the person they call.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Which challenges are live in the communities this room works in?
Handout: Challenge Cards
Twelve cards. Print, cut along the divisions, and deal one per pair. Used in The Map You Already Have and in the MOBILIZE Challenge on page 29.
Each card is one line. That is deliberate: a longer card gets read instead of discussed, and the point is what the room already knows about the challenge rather than what the card tells them.
The twelve

items: SOCIAL ISOLATION. Older adults in this community are increasingly cut off from the people around them.
WILDFIRE RISK. Neighborhoods on the edge of open land face a fire season that keeps getting longer.
HOUSING INSTABILITY. Rising rents and overcrowding are pushing families out, and pushing others into unsafe housing.
CLIMATE DISPLACEMENT. People are arriving in this community because they can no longer live where they were.
LACK OF COORDINATION. Several organizations are serving the same families and none of them know it.
MENTAL HEALTH AFTER DISASTER. The event ended a year ago. The effects on people did not.
HOME FIRE DEATHS. This community loses people to home fires at a rate above the state average.
LANGUAGE ACCESS. Emergency information does not reach a significant part of this community in a language they use.
VOLUNTEER DECLINE. The people who have carried this work for twenty years are aging out and nobody is replacing them.
TRANSPORTATION. In an evacuation, a meaningful number of households have no way to leave.
DISTRUST. Previous organizations made promises here that were not kept, and people remember.
ORGANIZATIONAL EXHAUSTION. The local partners who show up for everything are running on empty.

blocks.text: How to use them

items: One card per pair. Do not let a pair swap for one they like better; the uncomfortable card produces the better conversation.
The last two, distrust and organizational exhaustion, are harder than the others and are worth saving for a room that has already warmed up.
Write local ones. A challenge card naming an actual neighborhood is worth three of these.

blocks.text: Group Size: Individual work, in a room. Pairs at the end.
Materials: The Program Mapping Template on page 44, one per person, printed. A pen.
Purpose: The foundational practice. Everything else in this skill assumes a map exists, and this is where it comes from.
Step 1: choose a program (2 minutes)
One program the participant actually runs or is responsible for. Not the best one and not the newest one. Ideally one they have a nagging feeling about.
If they did the pre-work they already have a map; this is the round where it gets sharper.
Step 2: fill the five levels (8 minutes)
For each level, list every activity, partner and output currently happening there. Concrete nouns only. Not “community engagement” but “the neighborhood association meets in our space on Thursdays.”

The hardest level for most people is interpersonal, because it is the one that has never had a line in a work plan. The prompt that unlocks it: which relationships does this program depend on, and whose are they?
Step 3: mark presence (5 minutes)
For each level, circle strong, present, or gap. Be honest about the difference between strong and present. Present means something exists. Strong means it would survive a bad quarter.
Step 4: name the first move (5 minutes)
Circle the biggest gap. Then write one small, concrete action that would begin to close it: a single conversation, a partnership inquiry, a meeting to attend. Put a date on it.
One action, not a plan. A first step and a date, not a plan to plan.
Debrief
What. How lopsided did your map turn out?
So what. Most maps are heavy at one or two levels and empty at the rest. That is not failure, it is an accurate starting point.
Now what. What is the one move from step 4 you will actually try this month, and who has to know?
Facilitator notes

items: The step 2 prompt about whose relationships they are is the sharpest question in this practice. Ask it out loud to the whole room at the four-minute mark.
