Watch for maps that are strong at every level. Ask what would happen at each one if the program lost its funding tomorrow, and let the map be redrawn.
Collect nothing. The map goes with the participant and gets used in three later activities.

blocks.text: Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: The ripple diagram on page 46, one per person.
Purpose: Trace what happens at the other four levels when you make a move at one. This is the practice that turns the framework from a filing system into a forecasting tool.
Step 1: pick a real decision (2 minutes)
In pairs, each person names one real move they are considering or have recently made. It must be specific and it must be theirs. Cutting a program counts. Adding a partner counts.
Step 2: trace forward, alone (8 minutes)
Working individually and in silence, answer one question on the ripple diagram: if I make this move at this level, what happens next at each of the other four?

Push past the first answer at each level. The first answer is usually nothing happens, and that is almost never true. If a program grows at the individual level, somebody’s relationships carry the extra load, some organization absorbs the referrals, and a community gets a slightly different reputation for what the Red Cross is.
Step 3: the partner’s job (5 minutes)
Swap diagrams. Your partner’s only job is to name one ripple you did not write down. Not to improve your plan. One missing consequence, at one level.
Debrief
What. Which level was hardest to fill in?
So what. Blind spots cluster by role. Most people consistently miss the same one or two levels, and it is usually the ones they do not personally work at.
Now what. What is the ripple you had not seen, and does it change the move?
Facilitator notes

items: This is the practice most likely to change somebody’s actual decision, and it is the one most likely to be cut for time. Protect it.
Ripples are not all bad. Ask for at least one that is an opportunity rather than a cost.
Pairs sometimes turn step 3 into consulting. Interrupt: one ripple, not advice.

title: Find Your Layer Partners (field assignment)
duration: 15 minutes in the room to prepare, then one real...

blocks.text: Group Size: Individual, then pairs.
Materials: The completed program map. Nothing else.
Purpose: Fill a gap by finding somebody who is already strong there, rather than building the capacity from scratch. This is the cheapest move in the whole skill.

This is a field assignment. The preparation happens in the room and the practice itself happens afterward, with a real person, on the phone or in their office. Sessions that schedule the conversation itself as an in-session activity are scheduling something that cannot happen.
In the room: prepare (15 minutes)

items: Five minutes. Look at your map and name the level where you are weakest. Then name one organization or person who is already strong at that level in your community. If nobody comes to mind, that is the finding, and the first call is to somebody who would know.

Five minutes. Write the opening, in the words you would actually use. Something close to: here is what we do well, here is where we are thin, and I am wondering whether our work might reinforce yours.
Five minutes. In pairs, say it out loud to each other. Your partner says one thing: whether it sounded like an ask or like an offer. Most first drafts sound like an ask.

blocks.text: In the field: the conversation
The goal is not a formal partnership and it is not a memorandum of understanding. It is one honest conversation that opens the possibility of one. Three things to find out:

items: What are they already doing at the level where you are thin?
What would make working with the Red Cross worth their time, in their terms rather than yours?
What would they need from you that you have not thought to offer?

blocks.text: Debrief, at the next session or by email
What. Who did you name as your one real contact at your weak level?
So what. The people already doing this work are usually closer than they feel. Most participants name someone they have met.
Now what. What is the honest conversation you will have with them, and by when?
Facilitator notes

items: The pair rehearsal in step 3 is what makes this work. Without it people leave with an intention and no sentence.
The most common weak level is systems, and the most common answer to who is already strong there is nobody I know. Push: who in your community sits on a committee you have never attended?
If you are running a multi-session series, collect the names and ask about them next time. That single follow-up roughly doubles the completion rate.

blocks.text: Group Size: Individual, then pairs.
Materials: The sustainability audit on page 47, one per person.

Purpose: Look at what the chapter is spending from its partners rather than what it is spending from its own budget. This is the only activity in the skill that addresses the organizational casualty directly.
Framing (2 minutes)

Say this: “After a major disaster, the small nonprofits and faith communities that showed up completely sometimes do not survive it. Not because they failed, but because they succeeded so thoroughly that they spent everything they had, and the money to replenish them came slowly or never. The community ended up less resilient after the response than before it. This activity is about whether you are doing a slow-motion version of that to somebody right now.”
Step 1: name one partner (3 minutes)
One organization you regularly ask things of. Pick the one you ask most, not the one you have the best relationship with, although they are often the same.
Step 2: what are you asking them to spend (5 minutes)

Time, money, trust, staff capacity, standing in their own community. Be specific and count in units they would recognize: hours of a person who has other work, a room they cannot rent out that day, credibility they lend you when they say we vouch for these people.
Step 3: what is your plan for their recovery (5 minutes)
The actual plan, not the intention. This is the step where most people stop writing.
Step 4: the multiplier (5 minutes)
If you asked this three times as often, would they survive it? If not, what is the alternative ask that gets you most of what you need and protects them? Write that sentence out.
Debrief
What. Did you actually have an answer to step 3, or did you find out you did not?
So what. Most leaders have a clear ask and a fuzzy or nonexistent sustainability plan. That asymmetry is the trap, and it is not a character flaw. Nobody has ever been asked for the second half.
Now what. What is one thing you will change about the next ask you make of that partner?
Facilitator notes

items: The silence at step 3 is the activity. Do not rescue it and do not fill it with examples.
Some participants will name a partner who has already stopped answering their calls. That is a live wound and it is also the best case study in the room. Ask before you use it.
This pairs well immediately after the MOBILIZE Challenge, where groups have just spent resilience resources freely on paper.

blocks.text: Group Size: Pairs.
Materials: The program audit worksheet on page 48. Two completed program maps, one per program.
Purpose: Test whether two programs actually reinforce each other or just run in parallel because they happen to share a topic.

Prerequisite, and it is a real one: this practice needs two programs mapped, not one. If your session only ran Map Your Program Across Levels once, spend the first five minutes here mapping the second program roughly rather than fully. A rough second map works. No second map does not.
Step 1: end results (8 minutes)
For each program, separate what is officially claimed from what actually happens, or could happen, that nobody has written down.

items: Program A, stated outcomes, the explicit ones that appear in a document.
Program A, actual outcomes, the implicit ones that happen anyway.
Program B, stated.
Program B, actual.

blocks.text: The implicit column is where the connections are. A smoke alarm program’s stated outcome is alarms installed. Its actual outcome includes several hundred conversations in living rooms with people nobody else visits.
Step 2: parallel or intersecting (8 minutes)

items: Where do these two programs run parallel, never actually touching?
Where might they intersect, and why? Check each level for a possible connection point: individual, interpersonal, organizational, community, systems.

blocks.text: Step 3: what would need to change (5 minutes)
What would have to be true, structurally, relationally, operationally, for these two to actively amplify each other, or to serve a shared goal that neither one currently states?
Step 4: three sentences, and a check (4 minutes)
Write the answer to step 2 in exactly three sentences: reinforce or parallel, and why. Then read it to one colleague and ask whether it matches what they see.
The three-sentence limit is not decoration. An audit that cannot be said in three sentences has not reached a conclusion.
Debrief
What. Reinforcing or parallel? Take a show of hands. Parallel usually wins.
So what. Two programs sharing a topic is not the same as two programs reinforcing each other. Most chapters have several pairs like this and have never looked.
Now what. What is the single cheapest change that would connect them?
Facilitator notes

items: Suggest a pair the participant does not think has any intersection. Those produce better findings than the obvious pairs, which people have already thought about.
The colleague check works better as a real assignment than as an in-room step. If your session ends here, assign it.

blocks.text: Group Size: 3 to 5 per table, 2 to 6 tables.
Materials: Large paper for each table, markers, and the five-level grid drawn in advance. See the note below on drawing it.
Purpose: Design an intervention that works at all five levels, on a real community problem, in a group. This is the centerpiece of the two-hour and four-hour sessions.
Drawing the grid

Before the session, draw a five-row grid on each sheet of large paper: one row per level, top to bottom, individual through systems, with two columns headed activities and partners. Do this yourself. Groups that draw their own grid spend eight minutes drawing and produce five different geometries you cannot compare in the share-back.
Phase 1: choose and frame (10 minutes)
Each table takes one problem. Offer these three, or use a live local one:

items: Chronic flooding in low-income neighborhoods.
Housing instability for seniors.
Social isolation among older adults after a disaster.

blocks.text: Ten minutes to agree what the problem actually is, in one sentence, before designing anything. Tables that skip this design four different problems at once and find out in the share-back.
Phase 2: design across all five (25 minutes)
Fill every row. Specific activities and identified partners at each level, with real names where possible. The rule is that no row may be left blank, and no row may say raise awareness.
Circulate. Observers, meaning you, are encouraged to ask one question at each table: what happens to the people at the level you did not address?
Phase 3: reinforce and undermine (10 minutes)
Still at the table, three questions:

items: Which of your levels reinforce each other? Draw the arrows on the paper.
Which might undermine each other? This one is rarely asked anywhere and it produces the best material of the hour.
Which level would you actually start with first, and why that one?

blocks.text: Phase 4: share back (10 minutes)

Ninety seconds per table, strictly timed. Each table says three things only: the problem in one sentence, the level they would start with, and the one place their design might undermine itself. Not the whole design.
With six tables that is nine minutes. Keep the timer visible.
Debrief (5 minutes)

items: Which level was hardest to fill in, and was it the same one for everybody?
What did you design at the interpersonal level, and would it have appeared in a work plan?
What did the undermining question surface?

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The interpersonal row is where every table stalls. Have one example ready: a program that pairs people rather than serving them.
Do not let a table design five separate programs. The test is whether one thing is happening at five levels or five things are happening at one level each.
Ninety-second share-backs feel brutal and are correct. Five-minute share-backs eat twenty-five minutes and the room stops listening after the second table.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
A local problem to offer as a fourth option: ____________________________
Your example of an interpersonal-level activity: _________________________
Group Size: 3 to 6 per group, 3 to 5 groups.

Materials: The MOBILIZE deck if you have it, or the challenge cards on page 20 and the resilience cards on page 31, printed and cut. One challenge card and five resilience cards per group, dealt at random.
Purpose: A constraint game. Groups get a problem and five assets they did not choose, and have to build a response that uses all five across all five levels. The constraint is what makes it work.
Which cards to use
There is a full MOBILIZE deck, fifty-two cards of challenges and resilience with artwork, and it is the better set. It has not been printed yet and exists as a PDF.

items: If you have the printed deck, use it.
If you do not, print the twelve challenge cards on page 20 and the twenty resilience cards on page 31. They are written to run the same activity and they work.
If you are going to run this more than once or twice, get the real deck printed. Ask Nate Millard for the PDF.

blocks.text: Set up (5 minutes)
Deal each group one challenge card and five resilience cards, face up, at random. Do not let groups trade.

Say this: “You have a challenge and five things this community already has. Design a response to the challenge that puts all five of these to work, across all five levels. Every resilience card has to be assigned to at least one level. You did not choose your hand, and that is the point: this is closer to how a real community looks than a wish list would be.”
Design (25 minutes)

items: Ten minutes: place the five resilience cards on the five levels. Some will obviously fit one level. At least one will be awkward, and the awkward one is the interesting one.
Fifteen minutes: design the actual response. What happens, who does it, and how do the five cards connect to each other rather than sitting in five separate boxes.

blocks.text: One rule to state up front: a resilience card may be used at more than one level, and a level may hold more than one card. What is not allowed is a level with nothing on it.
Share back (10 minutes)
Two minutes per group. Each group names their challenge, their hardest card to place, and the connection they are proudest of.
Debrief (5 minutes)

items: Which card was hardest to place, and what did you do with it?
Did anybody design something they could actually do on Monday? What made the difference?
What did you notice about a design built from what already exists, rather than from what you would ask for?

blocks.text: Why the random deal matters

Multi-disciplinary groups naturally bring different level expertise. An Executive Director used to systems work and a program manager focused on individual services will see completely different opportunities in the same hand, and the conversation that produces is the learning. A group that chose its own cards would choose the comfortable ones.
Facilitator notes

items: Deal from a shuffled deck in front of the room. Visible randomness stops the negotiation before it starts.
The awkward card is the whole activity. When a group asks whether they can swap it, say no and ask what it would take to use it.
This runs hot and loud. Give a two-minute warning before the design phase ends or nobody will be ready.
Follow it with the Sustainability Audit when you have the time. Groups have just spent five community assets freely on paper, and the audit asks what that costs in real life.

blocks.text: Handout: Resilience Cards
Twenty cards. Print, cut, shuffle, and deal five per group for the MOBILIZE Challenge. Each one is something a community might already have.
They are deliberately uneven. Some are obviously useful and some are awkward, and a hand of five that contains at least one awkward card is a better hand.
People

items: A retired nurse who has lived on the same block for thirty years and knows every household.
A high school senior who runs the most-followed local account on social media.
A former city council member who is bored and wants something to do.
A pastor whose congregation has shrunk but whose building has not.
A landlord who owns nine buildings and answers the phone.

blocks.text: Places

items: A church with a commercial kitchen and a parking lot.
A library branch open six days a week with a meeting room nobody books.
A laundromat where the same forty families come every week.
A mobile home park with one entrance and a residents’ association.
An elementary school with a service-learning requirement and no projects.

blocks.text: Organizations

items: A food bank with a delivery route that reaches homebound residents weekly.
A volunteer fire department that is respected and understaffed.
A community health clinic with a promotora program already funded.
A neighborhood association that meets monthly and is mostly complaints.
A regional foundation with money and no local relationships.

blocks.text: Structures and standing

items: A county emergency management plan that is being rewritten this year.
A text alert list with eleven hundred subscribers, run by one person.
A standing seat at a coalition table that nobody from the Red Cross has used in two years.
Twenty years of goodwill from a disaster response people still talk about.
A grant ending in nine months that has to be spent on something.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The awkward ones are the last card in each group and the last card overall. A hand containing the bored former council member, the complaints-only neighborhood association, or the expiring grant is a good hand.
Write local ones. A resilience card naming a real organization in the room’s territory is worth five of these, and writing them is a good exercise for a facilitator preparing to deliver.
If you are short of print time, the twenty above work read aloud: deal by reading five to each group and having them write them down.

blocks.text: Group Size: 4 to 6 per group.
Materials: Large paper and markers per group. The five-level grid drawn in advance, same as the Design Studio.

Purpose: Design a five-level campaign for something completely fictional. Fiction removes the defensiveness, and groups design far more freely when nothing they say can be taken as criticism of a program somebody in the room runs.
Why fiction

When a group designs a layered intervention for a real Red Cross program, half the energy goes into protecting what already exists. Somebody at the table owns the individual-level work and hears every gap as a performance review. With an invented product nobody owns anything, the group designs aggressively, and the transfer back to real work happens in the debrief where it is safe.
The brief (5 minutes)
Read this aloud:

“You work for a company that has invented a food. It is genuinely good for people: it is cheap, it keeps for a year without refrigeration, it tastes fine, and eating it three times a week measurably improves health. Nobody has heard of it. Your job is to make it normal in one American city within two years. Not to sell the most units. To make it something people in that city eat without thinking about it.”
Then: “You have to work at all five levels. Fill every row.”
Design (20 minutes)
Groups fill the five-level grid. Individual, interpersonal, organizational, community, systems. Specific tactics, not categories.

Groups get there fast, and they get there without help, which is the finding. They will invent school procurement contracts, they will get it into church potlucks, they will find the person on each block who tells everyone what to buy, they will lobby for it to be reimbursable. Almost nobody proposes only advertising.
Share back (10 minutes)
Two minutes per group. Best idea at each level, in one line each.
Debrief (10 minutes)
This is where the whole activity pays, and it needs the full ten minutes.

items: You just designed across five levels in twenty minutes, without a framework and without arguing. Why was that easy?
Which level did you go to first? Almost nobody starts at individual. Why do our real programs?
What did you propose here that you would not propose for one of our programs? What is stopping you?
Name the real program of yours that would most benefit from being designed the way you just designed a snack food.

blocks.text: The answer to the third question is usually about permission, about who owns the program, or about not wanting to imply that current work is inadequate. Let that be said out loud. It is the most useful thing the room will say all day.
Facilitator notes

items: Keep the brief exactly this bland. A dramatic product invites jokes; a boring one invites design.
Do not let a group turn it into a marketing pitch with a logo. If it starts happening, ask what happens at the systems level and it self-corrects.

Use this instead of the Design Studio when the room is defensive, when several people in it own the programs under discussion, or when a previous session on this skill went badly. Use the Design Studio when the room is ready to work on something real.
It also works as a first-hour opener for a four-hour day with a skeptical group, with the Design Studio in the afternoon on a real problem.

blocks.text: Group Size: 6 to 20. Above twenty, put every question to pairs first.
Materials: The five levels visible on chart paper. Nothing else. Do not use slides.
Purpose: Get a group to examine how their programs actually relate to each other, rather than how they would describe them. Nothing here is taught.
How to use this guide

There are more questions here than an hour holds. Choose one core question per stage and keep the rest in reserve. A session that gets through six questions well is much better than one that gets through fifteen.
The synthesis lines are what turn a question bank into a session. Use them at the end of each stage, in your own words, and keep them short.
Session flow

items: 0 to 8 minutes: Opening. Where your work naturally lives.
8 to 25 minutes: What happens when a level is missing.
25 to 42 minutes: Reinforcing or parallel.
42 to 54 minutes: What it would take to design this way by default.
54 to 60 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: Stage 1: Opening, 0 to 8 minutes

Open with this: “This is not a training. You will not hear me talk for long. We are going to think about how your programs actually relate to each other, which is usually different from how we describe them.”

items: Core question: which level does your work most naturally focus on? Which does it most neglect?

blocks.text: If the room has done Your Strongest Level, they have the answer on a card and this takes two minutes. If not, give them sixty seconds of silence first.
Reserve: where do most of your hours actually go, as opposed to where you would say your priorities are?
Synthesis. Notice how many of us named the same neglected level. That is not a coincidence of personality. It is structural, and we will come back to why.
Stage 2: What happens when a level is missing, 8 to 25 minutes
Two blocks, about eight minutes each.
Block A: the failure you have seen

items: Core question: when have you seen a program succeed at one level and fail because another level was not aligned?
Reserve: what happened to the people at the level nobody addressed? What did it cost, and who paid it?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Every one of those stories is a design problem rather than an execution problem. The program worked. The design was one level short.
Block B: the wrong-level solution

items: Core question: where are you treating a community-level problem with an individual-level solution?
Reserve: what would it cost to address it at the right level? What makes the individual-level version so much easier to fund?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Individual-level work is easier to count, easier to fund and easier to report. That is why it wins, and why it is usually not sufficient on its own.
Stage 3: Reinforcing or parallel, 25 to 42 minutes
Block C: your own portfolio

items: Core question: are your programs reinforcing each other across levels, or just running in parallel on the same topic?
Reserve: name two of your programs. What would have to be true for them to amplify each other? Whose job would that be?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Sharing a topic is not the same as reinforcing. Most of us have at least one pair like that and have never had a reason to look.
Block D: what is already there

items: Core question: who in your community is already working at the layers you are not reaching?
Reserve: do they know each other? Do they know you? What would it take to be in the same room?

blocks.text: Synthesis. The layers usually exist in a community already. What is missing is not capacity, it is coordination, and coordination is cheaper than capacity.
Stage 4: Designing this way by default, 42 to 54 minutes
This is the stage to capture on a flip chart, because the answers are worth keeping.

items: Core question: what would have to change in how your chapter plans, operationally, culturally, relationally, for a layered strategy to become the default rather than the exception?
Then: what would it mean to design backward from systems change rather than forward from individual service delivery?
Reserve: what would you have to stop doing? Who would have to agree? What would your board need to hear?

blocks.text: Synthesis. Almost everything the room just named is a structure rather than a skill: a meeting that does not exist, a template that does not ask the question, a plan with no row for relationships. Those are all changeable and none of them require anybody to be better at their job.
Stage 5: Close, 54 to 60 minutes

items: What is one idea you are taking with you?
What is one thing you will try differently at a level you usually neglect?

blocks.text: Take the second answer around the whole room, one sentence each, no elaboration. Then close: “The framework is not something you apply to your work from the outside. It is a different way of seeing the work you are already doing.”
Questions held in reserve for a room that moves fast

items: What is your organization good at that has nothing to do with what you are funded for?
Which of your programs would still exist in some form if the Red Cross left tomorrow?
When you ask a partner organization to mobilize, what are you asking them to spend, and what is your plan for their sustainability?
What is the most important thing you do that produces nothing measurable?
Which level does your board understand best? Which does it understand least?

blocks.text: Troubleshooting
If no one responds. Give thirty seconds of silence out loud, then send the question to pairs before opening it back up.
If answers stay abstract. Ask for the specific program, the specific neighborhood, the specific person who was affected. Concrete beats principled every time.
If one voice dominates. Change the format rather than confronting the person. Move to pairs, then take answers from the other side of the room first.
If the room says this is above my pay grade. Often true and always a dead end. Ask what the largest decision they do control is, and which level they made it at.
If the room wants the framework explained. Give them the five level names in one minute and go back to the question. A room that gets a lecture in a Socratic hour stops offering anything.
Facilitator notes

items: The hardest discipline is not answering. You will know the answer to most of what gets asked.
If you have fifty minutes rather than sixty, cut stage 3 block D. Do not compress all five stages.
Do not capture on a flip chart before stage 4. Visible capture turns a dialogue into a brainstorm.
The coffee chat tells viewers a discussion guide exists in the manual. This page is it. If you are sending the recording to a chapter, send this page with it.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Your own program that failed because a level was missing: _______________
The four core questions you will definitely ask: ________________________
Session Formats
Five written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document, so the pages are the plan.
20 minutes. The five levels and one sorting exercise. For a staff meeting or the front of something else.
1 hour, seeing the five levels. Vocabulary plus a map of the participant’s own program. The default one-hour session.
1 hour, finding the partner you are missing. Starts from what is already in the community and ends with a name and a date.
2 hours. Layered Impact. Concept, real program mapping, and small-group design work.
4 hours. The full practice day. Both core experiences, the audit, and commitments.
Choosing between them

items: The two one-hour sessions are different sessions, not two versions of one. Run them a month apart with the same group and they build.
If someone asks for a session and gives no constraint, run the two-hour.
The four-hour needs a room with real programs they are responsible for, and it needs the pre-work. Chase it for this format specifically.
The twenty-minute version teaches vocabulary and nothing else. That is a legitimate goal and it is worth being honest that it is the goal.

blocks.text: What every format shares

items: The five levels named early, with the interpersonal one explained rather than listed.
Something of the participant’s own on the table. A real program, not a case study.
A named first move at the end: one action, one level, one date.

blocks.text: A note on materials

Three things need printing before any session over an hour: the program mapping template, the sorting set, and whichever card decks the session uses. The mapping template is the one that cannot be improvised.
Purpose: Give a group the five levels and one moment of noticing that the interesting interventions do not sort cleanly. Do not attempt more.
Materials: The sorting set on page 16. Chart paper with five columns.
Agenda

items: 4 minutes: The five levels.
10 minutes: Levels Quick-Sort.
6 minutes: The one question, and close.

blocks.text: The five levels (4 minutes)

Say this: “Resilience does not live in one place. It lives in five, at the same time. In the individual who knows what to do. In the relationship between two neighbors who trust each other enough to check in. In the organization still open after the disaster. In the community with a shared will to rebuild. And in the systems that make all of that possible.”
Then: “Most of what we build touches exactly one of those five.”
Levels Quick-Sort (10 minutes)
Page 15. Run it as written, including writing the split items under two columns. The splitting is the content.
The one question and close (6 minutes)
Ask: “Take one program you run. Which of these five levels is it strongest at, and which is empty?”
Sixty seconds of thinking, then take four or five answers. Close with: “That gap is not a failure. It is an accurate starting point, which is more than most of us have.”
Facilitator notes

items: Twenty minutes buys vocabulary and one moment of noticing. Do not add the mapping template; a map started and not finished is worse than no map.
If the room is standing and there is floor space, The Triangle is a better twenty minutes than this. It teaches less and lands harder.

title: One-Hour Workshop: Seeing the Five Levels

blocks.text: Purpose: Vocabulary, then a real map of a real program, then one first move. Everyone leaves with something on paper about their own work.
Materials: Sorting set, program mapping templates one per person, index cards, chart paper.
Agenda

items: 10 minutes: Levels Quick-Sort.
10 minutes: The five levels, with the home fire example.
20 minutes: Map Your Program Across Levels.
10 minutes: Your Strongest Level.
10 minutes: Close and commitment.

blocks.text: Ten plus ten plus twenty plus ten plus ten is sixty minutes.
Levels Quick-Sort (10 minutes)
Page 15. Opening the session with the sort rather than a definition means the vocabulary arrives after the room has already used it.
The five levels (10 minutes)

Page 10. Five glosses in three minutes, then the home fire campaign walked all the way through in seven. Do not skip the interpersonal layer; it is the one nobody has language for and the one the sort just exposed.
Map Your Program Across Levels (20 minutes)
Page 21. Four steps, ending with one action and a date.
Your Strongest Level (10 minutes)
Page 18. Run it after the map rather than before, in this format. The map has just told people the answer and the card becomes a commitment rather than a guess.
Close and commitment (10 minutes)

items: How lopsided was your map? Show of hands: who had a level completely empty?
Read your first move to the person next to you, with the date.
Round the room: one sentence each, the level you are going to work on.

blocks.text: Facilitator notes

items: The twenty minutes for mapping is tight and it should be. People who have not finished have still found their gap, which is the point.
If the room did the pre-work, cut mapping to fifteen and give the extra five to the close.

title: One-Hour Workshop: Finding the Partner You Are Missing

blocks.text: Purpose: Start from what already exists in the community rather than from the framework. Everyone leaves with a name and a date. Use this as the second session with a group that has already met the five levels.
Materials: Challenge cards, chart paper with five columns, program maps if the group has them.
Agenda

items: 15 minutes: The Map You Already Have.
10 minutes: The five levels, briefly, named onto what just happened.
15 minutes: Find Your Layer Partners, the in-room preparation.
10 minutes: Ripple Tracing, shortened.
10 minutes: Close and commitment.

blocks.text: Fifteen plus ten plus fifteen plus ten plus ten is sixty minutes.
The Map You Already Have (15 minutes)
Page 19. Opening here means the room supplies the content and you supply the labels, which is the right order for a group that is skeptical about frameworks.
The five levels (10 minutes)

Page 10, but delivered as naming rather than teaching: point at the chart paper the room just filled and give each column its name and its one-line definition. Then the sentence that matters: the layers exist here already, and the coordination does not.
Find Your Layer Partners (15 minutes)
Page 23, the in-room preparation only. Weakest level, one name, the opening sentence written out, and the pair rehearsal. The conversation itself happens in the next two weeks.
Ripple Tracing, shortened (10 minutes)

Page 22. Run steps 1 and 2 only, at two and six minutes, with two minutes of pair share. Applied to the partnership they just named: if this partnership happens, what changes at the other four levels?
Close and commitment (10 minutes)
What. Who did you name as your one real contact at your weakest level?
So what. The people already doing this work are usually closer than they feel. Most of you named somebody you have already met.
Now what. What is the honest conversation you will have with them, and by when? Say the date out loud.
Facilitator notes

items: This session lives or dies on the pair rehearsal. Protect the five minutes.
Collect the names and dates if you will see this group again. Ask about them next time, by name.

blocks.text: Purpose: From the concept, through a real program map, into small-group design work. Participants leave with one concrete gap identified in a current program and one action they will take within thirty days.
Group Size: 3 to 5 per table, 2 to 6 tables.
Materials: Program mapping templates, one per person, printed. Sorting set. Index cards. Large paper with the five-level grid drawn, one per table. Markers.
Agenda

items: 15 minutes: Welcome and Your Strongest Level.
20 minutes: The five levels, with Red Cross examples.
20 minutes: Map Your Program Across Levels.
60 minutes: The Layered Design Studio.
5 minutes: Close.

blocks.text: Fifteen plus twenty plus twenty plus sixty plus five is one hundred and twenty minutes.
Welcome and Your Strongest Level (15 minutes)
Page 18. Five minutes of framing, ten for the activity. Keep the cards; they come back at the close.
The five levels (20 minutes)
Page 10. Ten minutes on the five glosses with an example each, then the home fire campaign walked all the way through, which is the twenty minutes of Red Cross content this agenda item calls for.
If the room already knows the model, run Levels Quick-Sort here instead and give the ten saved minutes to the Studio.
Map Your Program Across Levels (20 minutes)
Page 21. Individual work, using the pre-work map or starting fresh.
The Layered Design Studio (60 minutes)
Page 27. Four phases, ending with ninety-second share-backs.
Close (5 minutes)

Pull out the card from the first fifteen minutes. Ask: “What is the one level you will invest in differently starting this month, and did your map agree with what you wrote at the beginning?” Take four or five answers.
Facilitator notes

items: The Studio needs its full hour. If you are running behind at the ninety-minute mark, cut the mapping debrief rather than the Studio share-back.
Draw the grids on the large paper before the room arrives. Doing it live costs eight minutes you do not have.

blocks.text: Purpose: The full day. From the felt sense of a system, through vocabulary and mapping, into two pieces of design work and a real audit, ending with commitments at three different levels.
Group Size: 3 to 5 per table, 2 to 6 tables.

Materials: Everything. Mapping templates, audit worksheets, sustainability audits, ripple diagrams, both card decks, index cards, large paper with grids drawn, markers, open floor space for the first twenty minutes.
Prerequisite: Send the pre-work and chase it. The last hour works on the participant’s own real program and it is much thinner without a map.
Agenda

items: 20 minutes: The Triangle.
20 minutes: The five levels, with Red Cross examples and the gaps we commonly miss.
20 minutes: Map Your Program Across Levels.
10 minutes: Your Strongest Level.
15 minutes: Break.
60 minutes: The Layered Design Studio.
15 minutes: Ripple Tracing.
15 minutes: Break.
45 minutes: The MOBILIZE Challenge.
20 minutes: The Sustainability Audit.
15 minutes: Commitments and close.

blocks.text: Twenty plus twenty plus twenty plus ten plus fifteen plus sixty plus fifteen plus fifteen plus forty-five plus twenty plus fifteen is two hundred and fifty-five minutes. That is fifteen over. See the next section.
Making it fit
Pick one, before the day rather than during it.

items: Drop Ripple Tracing. Fifteen minutes, and it is the most self-contained thing on the agenda. This is the default cut.
Or shorten the Design Studio to 45 minutes by cutting phase 3, the reinforce-and-undermine questions. This costs more than it saves and is the second choice.
Or take ten off the second break and five off the close, which is the worst option and is what happens if you do not decide in advance.

blocks.text: An agenda that runs over is not a scheduling detail. It is the reason facilitators cut the debriefs, and the debriefs are where this skill is learned.
Hour 1: feel it, name it, map it
The Triangle on page 13, then the five levels on page 10, then the mapping practice on page 21, then Your Strongest Level on page 18.

The order matters. The Triangle produces the felt sense, the five levels give it names, the map applies it to something real, and the card records the diagnosis. Reversing any two of those weakens the day.
Hour 2: design something
The Layered Design Studio on page 27, full sixty minutes, on a real community problem. Then Ripple Tracing on page 22 if you kept it.
Hour 3: design under constraint
The MOBILIZE Challenge on page 29. Groups get a challenge and five assets they did not choose. This hour is louder and less controlled than hour 2 and it should be; it is the one people remember.
Hour 4: what it costs

The Sustainability Audit on page 24, which asks what the chapter is spending from its partners. Running it right after the MOBILIZE Challenge is deliberate: groups have just spent five community assets freely on paper.
Commitments and close (15 minutes)
Each participant writes one sentence in this form and reads it out: “In the next ninety days, I will design ______ at the ______ level, for ______.”

Then three commitments, one each: one systems-level action, one organizational-level action, one individual-level action. Collect them. Follow up at ninety days, and say at the time that you are going to.
If you swap the Design Studio for the Superfood Launch
Do it when the room is defensive or when several people present own the programs that would come up. Page 32. Same sixty minutes, and the transfer back to real work happens in its debrief.
Facilitator notes

items: Two breaks, and put them where they are marked. The middle of this day is dense.
Consider co-facilitating. The Triangle and the MOBILIZE Challenge want a facilitator who is comfortable with noise; the Sustainability Audit wants one comfortable with silence.
No presentation on this agenda is longer than twenty minutes. That is deliberate. If you find yourself building slides, you are rebuilding a different day.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Which cut you are making to reach 240 minutes: ________________________
Who is co-facilitating, and which segments: ____________________________
The ninety-day follow-up: who owns it and when: ________________________
Handout: Program Mapping Template

Use this to map one current program across the five levels. For each level, note what is actually happening there today, then mark how strong that presence is. The goal is not to fill every box. It is to see the shape of the program honestly.
Print one per person. This is the handout that cannot be improvised, and four activities in this document depend on it.
Individual

The gap
