One small, concrete action to begin closing it. A conversation, a partnership inquiry, a meeting to attend:
Handout: The Ripple Diagram
Used in Ripple Tracing. One per person. The question is always the same: if I make this move at one level, what happens next at each of the other four?
The level it happens at, circle one:
Individual Interpersonal Organizational Community Systems
What happens next at each of the other four
Write in every box except the one you circled. If your first answer is nothing happens, that is almost never true. Write the second answer.
The two follow-ups
Which of these is an opportunity rather than a cost? _____________________
The ripple my partner named that I had not written down:
Does it change the move? Yes / No / Not sure yet
How to print it
A five-box column works fine. If you have design time, lay it out as one center box with four arrows radiating outward, which makes the tracing visually obvious. The content is the same either way.
Handout: The Sustainability Audit
Four questions about one partner. Used in the Sustainability Audit practice and worth running once a year on the partners a chapter leans on most.
1. What am I asking them to spend?
Time, money, trust, staff capacity, standing in their own community. Count in units they would recognize.
2. How often am I asking?
Times in the last twelve months: ______ Times they said yes: ______
Times they said no, or did not answer: ______
3. What is my actual plan for their recovery or sustainability after this ask?
The plan, not the intention. If there is not one, write none, which is a real answer and the most useful one on this page.
4. The multiplier
If I asked this three times as often, would they survive it? Yes / No / I do not know
If not, what is the alternative ask that gets me most of what I need and protects them?
One thing I will change about the next ask
Handout: Program Audit Worksheet

Use this to test whether two of your chapter’s programs are actually reinforcing each other, or just running in parallel because they happen to share a topic. Map each program separately with the Program Mapping Template first, then bring both maps here.
Be honest. This works best as a real audit rather than a defense of what you already run. It is worth trying with two programs you do not think have any intersection at all.
Step 1: end results
What does each program actually produce? Separate what is officially claimed from what actually happens, or could happen, that nobody has written down.
Step 2: parallel or intersecting
Where do these two programs run parallel, never actually touching?
Where might they intersect, and why? Check each level for a possible connection point.
Step 3: what would need to change
What would need to change for these two to actively amplify each other, or to serve a shared goal that neither one states explicitly?
Your answer, in three sentences
Reinforcing or parallel, and why. Exactly three sentences.
Check it against someone else
Read your three sentences to one colleague and ask whether it matches what they see.
Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. Each entry says what it is for.
Start here

Meadows, D. (2008). Thinking in Systems: A Primer. Chelsea Green. The foundational text, written accessibly without losing rigor. If systems thinking is new, start here and read the first four chapters.

In a World of Systems. Short animated film based on Meadows’ work, illustrated by David Macaulay. Ten minutes, no jargon, and it makes the ideas visual using plumbing and traffic. https://donellameadows.org/systems-thinking-resources/
On the model itself

The Social-Ecological Model. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The clearest short introduction, and free. Note that the CDC version has four levels: individual, relationship, community, societal. The Red Cross version adds organizational, which is where most partnership work lives. https://www.cdc.gov/violence-prevention/about/
Bronfenbrenner, U. (1979). The Ecology of Human Development. Harvard University Press. The original. Worth knowing it exists.
On coordinating across organizations

Kania, J. and Kramer, M. (2011). Collective Impact. Stanford Social Innovation Review. The article that named and defined collective impact. Short, practical, and directly applicable to building at the organizational and systems levels. https://ssir.org/articles/entry/collective_impact
Kretzmann, J. and McKnight, J. (1993). Building Communities from the Inside Out. ACTA Publications. Asset-based community development. The Map You Already Have is this, in miniature.
On what goes wrong
Corbett, S. and Fikkert, B. (2009). When Helping Hurts. Moody Publishers. What happens when individual-level solutions are applied to systems-level problems.

Pfefferbaum, B., Van Horn, R. and Pfefferbaum, R. (2017). A Conceptual Framework to Enhance Community Resilience Using CART. American Journal of Community Psychology. The Communities Advancing Resilience Toolkit. Research-based, and specifically about resilience as a community-level rather than individual-level property.
Red Cross learning, and where to start
The microlearning for this skill is nine cards, about five minutes on a phone. https://app.7taps.com/6MvEGcdg2nSn
If you read or watch one thing, make it the Meadows film. Ten minutes, and it does more for the underlying habit of mind than any of the books.

Optional. The session does not depend on it, because Name the Program (page 18) produces a working program in the room. Pre-work makes the session sharper because participants arrive with a real case rather than a remembered one. Send it three days ahead and do not chase it.
This page is written to the participant and can be sent as is.
1. Pick a program (5 minutes)
Choose one real program, coalition or partnership you are currently leading or supporting. Pick one you would be uncomfortable stepping away from, not the one that would be easiest to hand over.
Write down what it is, how long it has been running, and who from the Red Cross touches it in a normal month.
2. Answer three questions honestly (10 minutes)

items: Who makes most of the decisions? Not who is consulted. Who decides.
If your organization stepped away tomorrow, what would continue and what would stop immediately? Write both lists.
What signs would show you that the community truly owns this work?

blocks.text: 3. Bring three things (5 minutes)
Write these down and bring them. The session uses all three.

items: One example of strong community ownership you have seen, anywhere.
One example where an organization, ours or anyone’s, held too much control.
One question you hope to explore.

blocks.text: If you have time: two frameworks worth twenty minutes

items: The IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation: inform, consult, involve, collaborate, empower. One page. https://iap2.org/resources/
Kretzmann, J. P. and McKnight, J. L. (1993). Building Communities from the Inside Out. The founding text of asset-based community development. The introduction alone is enough.

blocks.text: One question afterward: where does your program currently sit on that spectrum, and where do you tell people it sits?
Facilitator note

Assume roughly half the room will not have done this. That is what Name the Program is for. The two-list question in part 2 is the one that does the work, and it is worth saying in the invitation that the “what would stop” list is expected to be longer. Without that, people write a short honest list and then feel bad about it.
Group Size: 4 to 20 participants, working in groups of 3 to 5
Materials: Flip chart paper or a whiteboard, markers, sticky notes optional. One marker per group, and this matters.
Purpose: Let the room watch centralized control happen to itself, in seven minutes, before anyone has defined the term.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Think about a coalition, program or community initiative you have been part of. In many partnerships one organization unintentionally becomes the center of everything: meetings, communication, decisions, momentum.”
“This activity explores what ownership actually looks like in practice, and how leadership dynamics show up even in small moments.”
The Activity

items: Divide participants into groups of three to five.
Give each group one piece of flip chart paper and hand one marker to one participant. Say nothing else about the marker.
Ask groups to create a quick visual map answering: what makes a community initiative feel community-owned instead of organization-owned?
Allow five to seven minutes.
When time is up, ask each group to circle one behavior on their sheet that supports shared ownership, and one that creates dependency or centralized control.

blocks.text: What the facilitator watches for while they work
Do not intervene. Just note it.

items: Who controls the marker, and does it move?
Who speaks most?
Does leadership shift naturally, or does the person with the marker stay in charge?
Does anyone invite a quieter voice in?
Does anyone ask for the marker, and how do they ask?

blocks.text: Sharing out

Each group shares one sign of community ownership, one sign of organizational over-control, and whether the marker stayed with one person or became shared. Record the themes where everyone can see them.
Debrief: WHAT happened

items: What happened with the marker in your group?
Who naturally took leadership?
How were decisions made?
Did anyone deliberately create space for someone else?
What behaviors increased or reduced participation?

blocks.text: Debrief: SO WHAT does it reveal

items: How do organizations unintentionally centralize power?
What does ownership actually look like behaviorally, rather than as a value?
How can facilitation strengthen or weaken community leadership?
What parallels exist between this and real coalition work?

blocks.text: Debrief: NOW WHAT will you try

items: What is one thing you can do to share ownership more intentionally?
How can you shift from being the driver to being a partner?
What practices help communities lead rather than simply participate?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The marker is the whole activity and almost nobody notices it is deliberate until the debrief. Handing it to one person without comment reproduces, in ninety seconds, exactly what a chapter does over three years. When you reveal it, do so lightly; a group that feels tricked stops volunteering.
In perhaps one group in four the marker moves on its own. Ask that group what made it move, and use their answer rather than yours.
Connects to

Adaptive leadership, asset-based community development, facilitative leadership, shared decision-making, coalition building, and the IAP2 spectrum. Pairs well with Asset Mapping, Inclusive Facilitation, and Stakeholder Mapping.
Group Size: Any
Materials: Sticky notes or index cards, pens, wall space or a shared digital board.
Purpose: Separate participation from ownership using the only test that matters, which is what survives our absence.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Many programs are successful while an organization is actively involved. Sustainability is tested when that organization steps back. This activity explores the difference between participation and real ownership.”
The Activity

items: Ask participants to think of a real program, coalition or initiative they know.
Two minutes, individually: if your organization disappeared tomorrow, what would continue and what would stop?
Each person writes one thing that would survive and one thing that would likely collapse, one per note.
In pairs or threes, discuss the patterns.
As a full group, create two columns: Signs of Sustainability and Signs of Dependency. Participants post their notes into each.

blocks.text: Sharing out
Ask each group for one example of sustainable community ownership and one of organizational dependency. Cluster the themes visually as they come.
Debrief: WHAT happened

items: What tended to survive without the organization?
What depended heavily on organizational leadership?
What patterns emerged across the room?
What surprised you?

blocks.text: Debrief: SO WHAT does it reveal

items: What is the difference between support and control?
How do organizations unintentionally become bottlenecks?
Why is sustainability tied to community leadership rather than to funding?
What does readiness for ownership transfer actually require?

blocks.text: Debrief: NOW WHAT will you try

items: What is one dependency you could reduce?
How can you build more local leadership into your work?
What would help communities operate more independently?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

The dependency column always fills faster and gets longer. Say so out loud when it happens, without softening it. The room needs to see that this is normal across every chapter in the group rather than a private failing, or people stop being honest for the rest of the session.
Relationships are the most common item in the dependency column. That is worth pausing on: relationships held by one person are the single most fragile asset a chapter owns.
Connects to
Sustainability planning, systems thinking, community resilience, adaptive leadership, collective impact, capacity building.
Group Size: Any
Materials: Two signs, one labelled PARTICIPATION and one labelled OWNERSHIP, posted on opposite walls. The scenarios below.
Purpose: Establish that the room disagrees about where the line is, which is more useful than establishing where it is.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Organizations often say communities are engaged, but engagement can mean very different things. I am going to read some situations. Move to the side of the room you think it belongs on. If you are torn, stand in the middle and be ready to say why.”
The scenarios
Read in this order. The first two are easy on purpose.

items: 1. Community members attend meetings planned entirely by an organization.
2. A coalition rotates leadership among community partners.
3. Residents lead outreach while the organization provides logistical support.
4. An organization sets goals and asks the community for feedback afterward.
5. Community members sit on an advisory board that the organization convenes and chairs.
6. A partner runs the program using their own methods, which are not the ones we would have chosen.
7. Community members are paid by the organization to deliver the program.
8. The community continues the work after our funding ends, at a smaller scale.

blocks.text: The Activity

items: After each scenario, ask two or three people to say why they chose their side.
When opinions differ, let the disagreement run for a moment before moving on. That is the activity.
After all eight, ask the room to name the characteristics that distinguish ownership from participation. Capture them.

blocks.text: Debrief: WHAT happened

items: Which scenarios created the most disagreement?
What signals made something feel community-led?
What language or behaviors indicated control?

blocks.text: Debrief: SO WHAT does it reveal

items: Why does shared decision-making matter more than shared activity?
How do organizations mistake engagement for ownership?
What actually shifts a program from consultation to empowerment?

blocks.text: Debrief: NOW WHAT will you try

items: How can you create more authentic shared leadership?
What changes would move your work closer to community ownership?
Where might a community need more authority, rather than more invitation?

blocks.text: Facilitator note

Scenarios 5, 6 and 7 are the hard ones and they are where the fifteen minutes are actually spent. Number 6 is the crux of the whole skill: if the only acceptable version of the work is our version, we are still holding control. Number 7 splits every room, and both sides are right, which is worth saying.
If nobody stands in the middle, prompt for it. The middle is where the honest answers are.
Accessibility
This activity assumes people can cross a room. Offer a seated alternative from the start rather than when asked: two raised hands, one for each side, or colored cards on the table.
Connects to
The IAP2 spectrum, shared leadership, community engagement, facilitation, participatory decision-making.
Materials: Ownership Map handout (page 41) for each participant, board and markers, the maturity model (page 9) posted.
Purpose: Produce the real program the rest of the session works on, in the room, without depending on anyone having done pre-work.
Why this comes first

Both core experiences act on a real program, and the practice lab is explicitly built on a program from the participant’s own context. If you rely on pre-work to supply it, part of the room spends an hour on a hypothetical. Fifteen minutes here removes that, and the placements the room produces out loud are more honest than the ones people write alone.
Choose how the room does it
Pick one before the session.

Option A, everyone brings their own. Each participant names a program they are responsible for and works it all session. Best when most people did the pre-work and for mixed groups. Most personally useful, least shared discussion.

Option B, one volunteered program. One participant offers a real program and the room works it. Best for a single chapter team, sharpest conversation, and it asks a lot of the volunteer. Ask privately beforehand.
Option C, one supplied program. You provide one and everyone works it together. Safest with a new group. Use one of the scenario cards from page 26 so the session builds toward the card activity.
Setup (say this to participants)

“Before we talk about transferring ownership we need something to transfer. In the next fifteen minutes you are going to put one real program on paper, including the parts that are uncomfortable. This stays in front of you all session.”
The Activity
Step 1 (3 min): Name it

items: What is the program, how long has it run, and who is it for?
Who from the Red Cross touches it in a normal month, and doing what?

blocks.text: Step 2 (5 min): Who decides
On the Ownership Map, for each of these, write a name. Not an organization, a person.

items: Who decides what the program does next?
Who sets the agenda when the group meets?
Who holds the relationships with partners?
Who would a new partner call first?
Who would notice within a week if it stopped?

blocks.text: Step 3 (4 min): Place it

items: Using the maturity model on the wall, place this program at a level from one to five.
Write the evidence next to it. Not the aspiration, the evidence.
Then ask a neighbour to challenge your placement. Most drop a level, and the drop is the point.

blocks.text: Step 4 (3 min): Read it back to the room
Take three or four, not everyone.

items: What level did you put it at, and did it survive the challenge?
How many of your five names were Red Cross names?
What would stop within a month if you stepped away?

blocks.text: Closing

Tie back to the skill: most rooms find four or five Red Cross names on a sheet meant to describe a community program, and most placements drop a level under challenge. Both are normal. The rest of the session is about which single name could change.
Facilitator note

The challenge in step 3 has to be done by a neighbour rather than by you. People will not challenge their own placement honestly and they will challenge somebody else’s with enthusiasm. If you do it, it lands as a correction rather than a discovery.
If somebody chooses a program that is already community-led, congratulate them and ask them to pick a harder one. A program with nothing wrong with it teaches nothing for the next two hours.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which option will you run, and why does it fit this group?
If Option B, who have you asked, and what did you agree is off limits?
Materials: One scenario card (page 26) and four to five character cards (page 23) per group, printed and cut. A slide or flip chart with the four group task questions. A timer.
Purpose: Design a real ownership transfer while having to reconcile the perspectives, priorities and constraints of the actual people who would have to agree to it.
What this is, and what it is not

This is deliberation with personas, not role play. Participants do not act as their characters. They hold the cards on the table in front of them and have to answer, for every part of their plan, how each of those people would respond to it. That is a harder and more useful discipline than performing a role, and it is the difference between a plan that sounds good in the room and one that would survive a real partner meeting.
Setup (say this to participants)
“Community mobilization is not just about launching programs. It is about making sure they are owned and sustained by the community. Today we are on what it actually takes to transfer ownership.”
Anchor question, take two or three quick responses only: “What makes ownership transfer hard in real life?”
Explain the activity (3 min)

items: Groups of four to six. Each group gets one scenario card and four to five character cards.
Say: “Your group will design a strategy to transition this program. The catch is that you have to work through the perspectives, priorities and constraints of the people at your table.”
Post the four group task questions where everyone can see them.

blocks.text: The four questions every group answers

items: Who should own this program long-term?
What does the Red Cross let go of?
What support, if any, remains?
What risks have to be addressed before transfer?

blocks.text: Group activity (17 min)
Move between groups and push. Four interventions, matched to what you see:
If they are too optimistic. “What could go wrong here in six months?”
If they are holding too much control. “Is this really community-owned, or still Red Cross-led with extra steps?”
If they are ignoring a character. “How would this person respond to this plan?” Pick the card they have not touched.
If they are rushing the transfer. “What signals tell you this partner is actually ready?”
The twist, dropped in at minute 15 to 18
Choose one and announce it to the whole room mid-activity, without warning.

items: “New constraint: Red Cross staffing or funding is reduced.”
“The Red Cross staff member who has been leading this work is transitioning out of their role in 60 days.”

blocks.text: The second one is stronger with experienced groups because it is the situation most of them will actually face.
Share-out (10 min)
Each group has 60 to 90 seconds and answers three things: who owns the program, one thing they had to let go of, and one risk they had to solve.
Do not let this become reporting. Push comparison as they go: “Did anyone make a different decision about ownership?” and “What made this hard to let go of?”
Debrief and synthesis (10 min)
Ask three or four at most. Depth beats coverage.

items: What made ownership difficult to transfer?
Where did you feel the tension between control and trust?
What signals showed a partner was, or was not, ready?
What did you realize the Red Cross needs to stop doing?

blocks.text: Key takeaways, said clearly at the close

items: Ownership transfer is not a handoff. It is a process.
It requires four things: clarity of roles, willingness to let go, investment in partner capacity, and trust built over time.
If the Red Cross is still doing everything, it is not ownership.

blocks.text: Optional extension, if you have five more minutes

Ask: “Using the maturity model on the wall, where does your final plan land, one to five?” Then: “What would it take to move it one level higher?” This is the strongest closing question in the skill and it needs the model posted (page 9).
Facilitator note

The characters are the mechanism. A group that reads the scenario and ignores the cards will produce a competent transition plan in eight minutes and learn very little. The moment the activity works is when somebody says “Carla is not going to believe this” or “Maria cannot take that on without funding,” and the plan has to change. If a group is moving fast, that is the signal to hand them the card they are ignoring.

Deal the cards deliberately rather than at random once you know your room. Pairing Maria (no capacity) with Marcus (wants sustainability, not dependency) produces the sharpest funding conversation. Pairing Tasha (fears abandonment) with Harold (fears change) produces the sharpest trust conversation.
Fifteen characters supports three groups without reusing a card. If you have more than three groups, reuse is fine; comparing how two groups handled the same character is worth something.
FACILITATOR PREP
Which scenario or scenarios will you use, and why do they fit this group?
Which twist will you drop in, and at what minute?
Character Cards

Fifteen cards. Print, cut along the divisions, and deal four to five per group alongside one scenario card. Each card gives a person with a real constraint, a real motivation, and a question they will actually ask.
The strength named on each card is the CliftonStrengths theme that drives how that person engages, and it is there to help the facilitator predict the objection rather than to be taught.

1. Maria Lopez, Nonprofit Executive Director. Community partner leader. Strength: Responsibility. Runs a small, trusted local nonprofit doing food access and family services. Dependable and stretched thin. Strong relationships with residents and partner agencies; a trusted voice locally. Worried about taking on more without funding or staffing. Works best with clarity, shared accountability and tangible resources. She will ask: “Who is responsible for what, and how is this funded?” She wants ownership to be realistic, not aspirational.

2. James Carter, City Council Member. Local government influencer. Strength: Strategic. Elected, with ties to economic development and infrastructure. Can unlock funding, visibility and policy support, and understands systems-level change. Needs alignment with city priorities and is hesitant without clear public value. Engage early with data, community benefit and alignment to existing plans. He is thinking: “How does this fit the bigger picture, and who owns it long-term?”

3. Tasha Williams, Grassroots Community Leader. Trusted community connector. Strength: Relator. Leads an informal neighborhood network and organizes local events. Not tied to any formal organization and highly respected. Deep trust and strong engagement. Skeptical of organizations handing things off without ongoing support or presence. Values consistency, transparency and shared decisions. She is asking: “Are you really staying involved, or are you just leaving this to us?” She supports ownership, but only if it feels like partnership rather than abandonment.

4. Dr. Alan Chen, Hospital Community Outreach Director. Institutional partner. Strength: Analytical. Leads community health initiatives for a regional hospital system. Access to data, funding streams and institutional credibility. Needs clear metrics and defined outcomes; hesitant to take on a program without evidence it works. Engage with data, an evaluation plan and success indicators. He is focused on: “What results are we measuring, and how do we know this works?”

5. Denise Robinson, Local Business Owner. Private sector partner. Strength: Achiever. Owns a small retail business, active in the Chamber of Commerce. Well connected in the business community and can mobilize resources and sponsorships. Limited time; prioritizes visible return. Works best with organized efforts that show quick wins. She is thinking: “What is the impact, and how quickly can we see it?”

6. Pastor Robert Jenkins, Faith-Based Leader. Community anchor. Strength: Belief. Leads a large church that regularly supports outreach and disaster response. A trusted voice who can mobilize volunteers quickly. Wants alignment with mission and values; cautious about long-term commitments without clarity. Works best with mutual respect, clear purpose and defined roles. He is asking: “Does this align with our mission, and what are we committing to long-term?”

7. Kayla Nguyen, Young Professional and Emerging Leader. Next-generation community builder. Strength: Ideation. Works in marketing, volunteers across several initiatives, eager to make an impact. Creative, a strong communicator, brings new perspectives. Limited experience with long-term ownership and may underestimate the complexity. Thrives paired with experienced leaders who ground ideas in execution. She is thinking: “We could do so much with this.” Excited about ownership, and needs structure to sustain it.

8. Harold Thompson, Long-Time Volunteer. Legacy contributor. Strength: Consistency. Has volunteered for years across multiple Red Cross efforts. Holds institutional knowledge, dependable, respected by other volunteers. Prefers familiar approaches and is hesitant about shifting ownership or changing roles. Engage by honoring the experience while explaining the why. He is thinking: “This has worked before, why change it?” He needs reassurance that transfer will not break what already works.

9. Latoya Brooks, School District Administrator. Youth and family systems partner. Strength: Discipline. Oversees student services and family engagement across the district. Access to families, strong systems, ability to scale. Limited flexibility; must align with school policy and priorities. Works best with defined processes, timelines and compliance considerations. She is asking: “How does this fit into our system, and who manages it day to day?”

10. Marcus Reed, Philanthropic Foundation Officer. Funding partner. Strength: Futuristic. Manages grantmaking for a regional foundation supporting community resilience. Can provide funding and strategic guidance, and values innovation. Wants to fund sustainable community-led efforts, not ongoing external dependency. Engage with impact goals, a sustainability plan and a transition strategy. He is thinking: “How does this continue after the funding ends?”

11. Rosa Martinez, Community Health Worker. Frontline practitioner. Strength: Empathy. Works directly with vulnerable populations, connecting them to services. Trusted by clients, understands real needs, strong on-the-ground insight. Overextended, with limited time and resources for new responsibilities. Works best when an effort reduces burden rather than adding to it. She is asking: “Will this actually help people, or just add more work?”

12. Tyler Benson, Emergency Management Director. Response system leader. Strength: Command. Leads local preparedness and response coordination. Strong in a crisis, understands systems and coordination. Focused on immediate response and less engaged in long-term community-led work. Engage by connecting ownership to preparedness and response outcomes. He is thinking: “How does this make us more prepared?”

13. Angela Price, Housing Authority Director. Stability and recovery partner. Strength: Responsibility. Oversees housing programs and partnerships for vulnerable populations. Access to critical resources and an understanding of housing systems. Navigates strict regulation with limited flexibility. Works best with partners who understand compliance and long-term planning. She is asking: “Who maintains this, and how does it stay compliant?”

14. Devin Scott, Local Media Representative. Storyteller and amplifier. Strength: Communication. A reporter or media figure focused on community issues. Can elevate visibility and shape public perception. Needs a clear, compelling story and is less engaged in operational detail. Engage with strong narrative and clear community impact. He is thinking: “What is the story here?”

15. Carla Simmons, Skeptical Resident. Community voice, hard to engage. Strength: Deliberative. A long-time resident who has watched programs come and go. Represents an authentic community perspective and asks hard questions. Distrustful of organizations and hesitant to believe in sustainability. Requires consistent engagement, transparency and follow-through. She is asking: “Why should we trust this will last?” Ownership has to be proven, not promised.
How the deck is built, for facilitators dealing it deliberately
Capacity versus commitment. Maria, Rosa, Angela. All three want to help and cannot absorb more without something being taken off them.
Power and influence. James, Tyler, Marcus. Each can unlock something, and each needs the plan to serve a different agenda.
Trust and credibility. Tasha, Carla, Harold. The three hardest conversations in the deck, and the three most important.
Innovation versus sustainability. Kayla, Denise, Marcus. Enthusiasm meeting the question of what happens in year three.
Systems and structure. Latoya, Angela, Alan. Nothing happens without process, compliance and evidence.
Mission and narrative. Robert, Devin. Why this matters, and who hears about it.
Scenario Cards
Eleven scenarios. Print, cut, and deal one per group alongside four to five character cards. Every scenario is built to force a genuine tradeoff rather than to have a right answer.
These also fill the case study slot in the two-hour and four-hour workshops. If you need one strong scenario for a whole room, use 11.

1. Community Preparedness Workshops. Education and preparedness. The Red Cross has led monthly preparedness workshops. Attendance is strong and staff capacity is limited. Tension: you have been asked to transition facilitation to a community partner within six months. Complication: no single partner has both the capacity and the experience to take it on fully. Decision point: transfer full ownership, co-own, or pause expansion? Success looks like: workshops continue consistently without the Red Cross leading every session.

2. Resilience Hub Activation. Community resilience infrastructure. A resilience hub offering cooling, warming, resources and information was launched with Red Cross support. Tension: the community expects the Red Cross to keep leading operations. Complication: local partners are willing but unclear on roles, funding and accountability. Decision point: who owns daily operations, and what does the Red Cross step back from? Success looks like: the hub operates under local leadership with the Red Cross supporting.

3. Shelter Support Services. Disaster response support. During recent disasters a partner helped provide feeding and basic services in shelters. Tension: there is interest in formalizing this as a community-led function. Complication: the partner lacks training and consistency across events. Decision point: formalize ownership now, or keep it Red Cross-led? Success looks like: the partner delivers reliably during disasters with minimal oversight.

4. Home Fire Campaign Follow-Up. Prevention and casework follow-up. Smoke alarm installations are completed but follow-up with families is inconsistent. Tension: a local nonprofit could take this on, and it is not in their current scope. Complication: no funding is tied to follow-up work. Decision point: transfer ownership, or redesign the program? Success looks like: families receive consistent follow-up without the Red Cross managing every case.

5. Volunteer Recruitment and Engagement. Capacity building. Volunteer recruitment is lagging in a key community. Tension: a partner organization offers to lead recruitment locally. Complication: they want flexibility that may not align with Red Cross standards. Decision point: how much control do you give up, and what standards are non-negotiable? Success looks like: a sustained volunteer pipeline that meets minimum operational standards.

6. Community Resource Navigation. Recovery and social services. The Red Cross has been connecting clients to housing, food and services after a disaster. Tension: a coalition wants to own this as an ongoing community service. Complication: there is no clear system for tracking outcomes or accountability. Decision point: transfer fully, or maintain partial oversight? Success looks like: partners coordinate services effectively without duplication or gaps.

7. Youth Preparedness Initiative. Youth engagement. Preparedness programming runs in schools through the Red Cross. Tension: the school district wants to embed it into their own system. Complication: this requires curriculum alignment and staff training. Decision point: hand off the curriculum, or maintain involvement? Success looks like: the program is integrated into the school system and sustained annually.

8. Disaster Recovery Casework Support. Long-term recovery. Local partners want to support casework functions during recovery. Tension: quality and consistency are critical. Complication: partners vary widely in experience and capacity. Decision point: how do you ensure quality, and what level of ownership is appropriate? Success looks like: partners contribute meaningfully without compromising service quality.

9. Community Event-Based Outreach. Engagement and awareness. The Red Cross has been attending community events to share resources. Tension: local organizations could represent this work, and messaging may vary. Complication: brand consistency and accuracy are real concerns. Decision point: transfer outreach responsibility, or keep it centralized? Success looks like: community-led outreach that is accurate, consistent and trusted.

10. Food Distribution Partnership. Basic needs and relief. The Red Cross supported emergency food distribution during a crisis. Tension: partners want to continue it as an ongoing program. Complication: supply chain and funding are both uncertain. Decision point: transition ownership, or sunset the program? Success looks like: the program continues only if it is sustainable and community-led.
11. Community Coalition Dependency
Community mobilization and coalition building. This one is longer than the others and is the strongest single scenario in the deck. Use it when you want the whole room on the same case.

Situation. A community coalition was formed to address local resilience needs such as housing stability, preparedness and resource coordination. It was initiated and heavily led by a Red Cross staff member, who organized meetings, set agendas and coordinated partners.
Tension. The coalition is active and engaged, and members have become reliant on the Red Cross to lead, organize and drive progress.

Complication. Meetings stall or lose focus without Red Cross facilitation. No shared leadership structure exists. Partners say they want it to continue but hesitate to step into leadership. The Red Cross staff member’s time is becoming limited.
Decision point. Do you step back and risk the coalition losing momentum? Do you continue leading and risk long-term dependency? How do you transition leadership without disengaging partners?

Success looks like. The coalition has shared or community-led leadership, functions without the Red Cross managing every detail, maintains engagement and forward movement, and has clear roles, ownership and accountability.
Facilitator notes for scenario 11

This scenario is designed to surface the control-versus-sustainability tension, the fear of letting something fail, the difference between convening and owning, and how leadership gets built inside a coalition rather than appointed.

The question to close on: “At what point did this stop being a community coalition and start being a Red Cross-led group?” Almost every group can name the moment, and almost none of them noticed it at the time.
Facilitator notes for scenarios 1 to 10

The capacity trap, scenarios 1, 3, 4 and 8. A willing partner without capacity is not a transfer plan. Watch for groups who solve these by finding enthusiasm. Ask what gets taken off that partner’s plate to make room.

The standards trap, scenarios 5, 8 and 9. These force the question of what is genuinely non-negotiable versus what is our preference. Groups usually start with a long non-negotiable list and shorten it under questioning, which is the learning.
The sunset option, scenarios 4 and 10. Both permit ending the program. Very few groups choose it and it is often the right answer. Name it as legitimate before they start.

The systems opportunity, scenarios 2, 6 and 7. Each has an obvious institutional home. The interesting question is what the institution needs before it can say yes, which is where the Latoya and Angela cards earn their place.
Materials: Ownership Map from Name the Program, Transition Plan handout (page 42), the maturity model posted, pens.
Purpose: Take the participant’s own program from an honest analysis to a transition plan they have already rehearsed saying out loud.
Setup (say this to participants)

“The scenario work was somebody else’s program, which makes it easy to be brave. Now we do yours. In the next hour you are going to map who actually holds this, design what shifts, and then practice the conversation, because a plan you cannot say out loud is not a plan.”
Part 1: Analyze (15 min)
On the Ownership Map, go past the five names from the opener.

items: List every recurring task this program requires in a month. Meetings, communications, scheduling, reporting, supplies, follow-up, the lot. Aim for ten.
Next to each, write who does it today. A person, not an organization.
Mark each one: could only we do this, could somebody else do this with support, or could somebody else do this now?
Then the hard one. For every task marked “only we can do this”, write why. Half of those reasons will turn out to be habit rather than capability.

blocks.text: Part 2: Design (20 min)
On the Transition Plan handout. The rule is one level, not five: design the move from where you are to one level deeper, not to level five.

items: Which single task moves first, and to whom by name?
What does that person need before they could hold it? Training, a relationship, access, money, permission, or cover from their own leadership?
What do we keep, and for how long? Name an end date for our involvement even if it is two years out.
What would you have to tolerate? Name one specific way it will be done differently and worse before it is done differently and better.
What does the first ninety days look like, with dates?

blocks.text: Part 3: Practice the conversation (15 min)
In pairs. This is the part that gets cut and it is the part that transfers.

items: Partner A has three minutes to make the ask out loud, as if to the person they named. Partner B plays that person, using their real constraints. If you have the character cards, deal one to Partner B that resembles them.
Partner B’s only job is to raise the objection that person would actually raise. Not to be difficult, to be accurate.
Two minutes of feedback: what landed, what sounded like a request for a favor, and what was missing.
Swap.

blocks.text: Part 4: Commit (10 min)

items: One shift you will make within thirty days, written as a sentence with a name and a date in it.
One thing you will stop doing to make room for it. A transfer that adds to your workload is not a transfer.
Who you will tell, so it is not private.

blocks.text: Take these out loud, one sentence each, round the room.
Debrief

items: What did you find under the tasks you had marked as only-we-can-do-this?
What did the conversation practice change about your plan?
What are you going to stop doing, and how does that feel?
What is the first thing that will happen on this, and when?

blocks.text: Facilitator guide

The ten-task list is the engine. Most participants have never written out everything a program actually requires in a month. Seeing it listed, with one name next to eight of the ten items, does more than any framing you could offer.

Push hard on “only we can do this”. The honest reasons are usually access, liability, or a specific credential. The dishonest ones are speed, quality preference, and the fact that we already know how. Ask which kind each one is.
One level, not five. Groups that design a full transfer produce something impressive and inert. Groups that design the next single shift come back next month having done it.

The tolerance question is where people go quiet. Naming in advance the specific way it will be done worse is what makes it survivable when it happens. Do not let anyone answer “nothing, I am fine with it.”

Protect part 3. When you are behind, the instinct is to cut the role play and keep the planning. Do the reverse. The plan is written down and can be finished later; the discomfort of making the ask out loud only happens in the room.
Facilitator note
If the group has just done the card activity they will be warmed up and slightly tired. Consider a break before this, and consider running part 3 standing up.

Somebody will say their program cannot be transferred because of a Red Cross requirement. Sometimes true. Ask which specific requirement and whether they have checked it recently; roughly half the time the requirement turns out to be a practice rather than a rule.
FACILITATOR PREP
Bring one program of your own that you held too long, and be able to say what it cost.
What you would not let go of, and why: ________________________________
Decide what happens to the commitments from part 4, and say so at the close.
Format: Facilitated dialogue. Participants build shared understanding through guided questioning rather than lecture.
Purpose: Get a room to say out loud that being indispensable is a problem, which is a thing people know and rarely admit.
Agenda at a glance

items: 0 to 10 minutes: When does a program belong to the community?
10 to 20 minutes: Exploring ownership
20 to 30 minutes: The ownership spectrum
30 to 40 minutes: The ownership trap
40 to 50 minutes: Letting go of leadership
50 to 55 minutes: Signs of ownership
55 to 60 minutes: Closing reflection

blocks.text: Opening (0 to 10 min)
Start with the central question and let people answer freely. Capture the answers where everyone can see them; you return to this at minute 55.
“When can we honestly say a community program belongs to the community?”

items: What makes something ours rather than theirs?
Can a community attend a program for years without actually owning it?
Who decides whether a program is successful?
Who makes the decisions?
Who would notice if the organization disappeared tomorrow?

blocks.text: Then introduce the tension: “Many organizations say they want community ownership. Why might they struggle to achieve it?” Probe: what are organizations afraid of losing? What happens when we become indispensable? Is dependency ever mistaken for success?
Facilitator synthesis. Most rooms answer the opening question with a feeling rather than a test. Push for the test. The useful ones are all about decisions and about what survives absence.
Section 1: Exploring ownership (10 to 20 min)

Present the scenario. A coalition has met monthly for five years. One organization schedules the meetings, creates the agendas, sends the communications, facilitates the discussions and tracks the action items. Everyone attends.
Ask: “Who owns this coalition?” Then let them argue.

items: Does attendance equal ownership?
If the lead organization stopped tomorrow, what would happen?
Is participation the same thing as leadership?
How would we know?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Transition on this line: “Perhaps ownership is not about who shows up. Maybe it is about who leads.” Do not offer it until the room has circled it themselves, which usually takes about six minutes.
Section 2: The ownership spectrum (20 to 30 min)
Draw the continuum: inform, consult, involve, collaborate, empower. Ask which level most community programs actually operate at.

items: Why do organizations stay at inform or consult?
What makes collaborate difficult?
What would empower actually look like here?

blocks.text: Then push harder:

items: Can you empower someone while still controlling the decisions?
Can communities own programs they did not help design?
Is it possible to transfer ownership without transferring power?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Allow disagreement here rather than resolving it. This is where the best learning in the hour happens, and a facilitator who supplies the answer converts a real argument into a definition.
Section 3: The ownership trap (30 to 40 min)
Ask participants to think of a project they are proud of. Then:

items: What would happen if you left tomorrow?
Who would continue the work?
What knowledge would disappear with you?
What relationships depend on you personally?

blocks.text: Pause. Then ask: “Could your success actually be creating dependency?” Expect discomfort and do not relieve it.

items: Why do organizations become the center?
Why do communities sometimes allow it?
Is being needed always a good thing?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. The line to land, once the room has felt it: sustainability and dependency look very similar in the beginning. This is the most important sentence in the hour.
Section 4: Letting go of leadership (40 to 50 min)
Ask: “What is harder, building a program or stepping back from one?”

items: Why is letting go difficult?
What fears come up when community members lead differently than we would?
Is ownership possible without accepting some loss of control?

blocks.text: Then the dilemma. A community member wants to facilitate the next meeting. You know they will not do it the way you would.

items: Should you let them?
What are the risks, and what are the benefits?
How much imperfection should we tolerate?
Is our goal quality control or community leadership? Are those always the same thing?

blocks.text: Facilitator synthesis. Nobody says no to the dilemma out loud, and plenty of people mean it. Ask what they would do if it were a meeting with a funder in the room, and watch the answer change.
Section 5: Signs of ownership (50 to 55 min)
Ask: “How would you know ownership is increasing?” Take answers before offering any. The room usually produces most of this list:

items: Community members create the agendas and facilitate.
Partners connect directly with each other.
Decisions happen without organizational approval.
Leadership rotates and new leaders emerge.
The work survives personnel changes.

blocks.text: Then: “Which measure matters more, what we do, or what continues without us?”
Closing reflection (55 to 60 min)
Return to the opening question and let people answer it again. The difference between the two answers is the session.

items: What are you currently holding that the community could lead?
What decision are you making that others could make?
What meeting could happen without you?
What relationship depends too heavily on you?
What would one small leadership shift look like this month?

blocks.text: Take the last answer from every person, one sentence each. Write them down and send them back afterward.
Closing thought, said as the last thing

“Community ownership is rarely one big transfer. It is usually a series of small leadership shifts. The goal is not for communities to need us forever. The goal is for communities to lead long after we are gone.”
Train-the-Trainer
Read this before your first delivery.
What this session is for

It is not an introduction to sustainability. It is the hour where competent, committed people notice that their own indispensability is the ceiling on the work. That recognition is uncomfortable and it is the entire point. If you teach content here, the core experiences afterward become planning exercises rather than repair.
Four guardrails

Do not relieve the discomfort in section 3. When you ask whether their success is creating dependency and the room goes quiet, wait. Facilitators consistently rescue this moment and it is the most valuable ten seconds in the hour.
Do not resolve section 2. The spectrum questions have no clean answers and the argument is the learning. Say “I do not know either” if you mean it.

Keep it off the community. Rooms drift toward explaining why a particular community was not ready. Redirect once: what did we do that made stepping back harder? That question holds for the rest of the hour.
Bring your own. Have a program you held too long, and be able to say what it cost. A room gives back roughly what the facilitator puts in.
Common failure modes

items: Section 2 runs long on definitions and sections 4 and 5 get compressed. Watch the clock at minute thirty.
One participant becomes the room’s example of good practice and everyone else stops being honest. Ask them what they are still holding.
The room agrees enthusiastically about ownership in the abstract. If nobody has named something of their own by minute thirty-five, ask the dependency question again, harder.

blocks.text: FACILITATOR PREP
Decide what happens to the closing commitments, and say so at the close.
Field Assignments
These are not room activities. They happen with a real program, which is the only place this skill is practiced. Assign one at the close of a session and open the next session with what people found.
Field Assignment 1: Give away one meeting
Pick one recurring meeting you currently run. Ask somebody else to facilitate the next one.

items: Ask a specific person, by name, at least a week ahead.
Offer to help them prepare if they want it. Do not offer twice.
Attend, and do not intervene. Sit somewhere other than where you normally sit.
Afterward, ask them what was harder than they expected.

blocks.text: Bring back. What you wanted to jump in and fix, and whether it mattered. This is the smallest possible version of the whole skill and it is the one that changes people.
Field Assignment 2: The introduction you have been holding
Find two partners who both work with you and do not work with each other, usually because everything routes through you.

items: Introduce them directly, and say why you think they should know each other.
Do not offer to convene the conversation, and do not ask to be on the call.
Wait three weeks.

blocks.text: Bring back. Whether anything happened, and how you felt about not knowing. Most chapters hold a network in one person’s head; this is what dismantling that looks like in practice.
Field Assignment 3: The month audit
For one program, write down every task it required of the Red Cross in the last month, and who did each one.

items: Mark each: only we could do it, somebody else could with support, or somebody else could now.
Count the hours in the third category.
Pick one and move it.

blocks.text: Bring back. The number of hours a month going into work somebody else could already be doing. In most chapters it is between four and twelve, and the number is more persuasive than any argument.
A note on all three

All three involve doing less rather than planning more, which is deliberate. This skill fails when it produces a transition plan and no behavior change, and the behavior is always some version of not doing the thing you would normally do.
Session Formats
Four written-out sessions. Everything in them is already in this document; nothing new has to be written to deliver any of them.
20 minutes. If We Left Tomorrow. One idea, delivered inside a meeting you were already having.
1 hour. Participation or Ownership. Establishes the distinction and places one real program on the maturity model.
2 hours. The Transfer Table. Adds the card activity and a real ownership design.
4 hours. From Holding to Handing Over. The full arc, ending with a transition plan and a rehearsed conversation.
How to choose

The distinction between participation and ownership can be taught in an hour. Actually designing a transfer cannot. If you have two hours, run the card activity, because working somebody else’s scenario is where people become willing to look at their own. If you have four, do both halves and protect the conversation rehearsal at the end; it is the part that produces behavior change.
20-minute version: If We Left Tomorrow

items: Run If We Left Tomorrow, page 14 (10 min)
Name the finding out loud: the dependency column is always longer, and relationships are usually top of it (3 min)
One round: name one thing on your dependency list you could move this month (5 min)
Close on the question: what are you holding that the community could lead? (2 min)

blocks.text: What they leave with: one named dependency and one intention.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Did your placement survive the challenge?
How many Red Cross names were on your sheet?

Notes on running it

items: This hour deliberately does not produce a transition plan. Say so at the close or the room will feel it stopped early.
The pairs challenge is the hour. Protect the full ten minutes; it is where the optimistic placements come down.

Purpose: Design a full ownership transfer for a supplied scenario, having to satisfy the real people who would have to agree to it.
Materials: Character and scenario cards printed and cut, the four group task questions posted, the maturity model posted, a timer, board and markers.

items: Welcome and framing (5 min)

items: What made ownership difficult to transfer in your scenario?

items: Who Owns the Marker before the card activity is deliberate. The room needs to have felt centralized control before it analyzes it.

title: Four-Hour Workshop: From Holding to Handing Over
duration: 4 hours, including two breaks totalling 25 minutes

blocks.text: Purpose: The complete arc: feel the problem, analyze somebody else’s case, then design and rehearse a transfer of your own.
Materials: All three handouts for every participant, both card decks printed and cut, the maturity model posted, the four group task questions posted, a timer.
Agenda

items: Welcome and framing (10 min)
Icebreaker: Who Owns the Marker, page 12 (15 min)
Icebreaker: Name the Program, page 18 (15 min)
The Ownership Maturity Model, worked against the programs now in the room, page 9 (15 min)
Core Experience: The Ownership Transfer Table, page 20 (45 min)
Break (15 min)
Icebreaker: If We Left Tomorrow, run as a bridge into your own work, page 14 (10 min)
Core Experience: Map, Design, Practice, page 29 (60 min)
Break (10 min)
Signs of ownership, and the stop, start, continue list (20 min)
Closing round: one shift, one thing you stop, one date, said out loud (15 min)

blocks.text: Stop, start, continue
Twenty minutes near the end, and it works better here than at the start because the room has evidence for it by now. Put the three columns up and build them with the room rather than reading them.
Stop. Being the automatic answer to every question. Assuming speed is the most important value. Making plans alone and asking for buy-in afterward. Measuring success only by what we delivered.

Start. Asking who else should lead this. Rotating responsibilities. Sharing decisions earlier. Naming power dynamics honestly. Building local leadership structures. Asking what will continue when we step away.
Continue. Supporting. Listening. Connecting people. Bringing resources where they are useful. Caring about quality and impact. Stepping back is not the same as caring less.
Notes on running it

items: The arc is feel it, analyze somebody else’s, then do your own. Write those three on the wall in the first ten minutes and point at them at each transition.
The morning is deliberately somebody else’s problem. People will not look honestly at their own program until they have been brave about a fictional one.
Protect the conversation rehearsal in the last part of Map, Design, Practice. It is the only place where anyone has to say the ask out loud, and it is what makes the plan real.
Keep the Ownership Maps in front of participants all day.

blocks.text: Closing debrief

items: Look at your placement from this morning. Would you still put it there?
What are you going to stop doing?
Who are you asking, and when?
What will you have to tolerate, and have you told anyone that you expect it?

blocks.text: What they leave with: an ownership map, a transition plan for one level of movement, a rehearsed conversation, and one shift with a name and a date on it.

Further Learning
Selected rather than exhaustive. The first three are what you hand someone who asks for more; the rest are for a facilitator or a chapter going deeper. Resource type is marked on each.
Start here

items: International Association for Public Participation. IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation. One page: inform, consult, involve, collaborate, empower. The single most useful tool in this skill for being honest about how much decision-making power a community actually holds. Reference. https://iap2.org/resources/

Kretzmann, J. P. and McKnight, J. L. (1993). Building Communities from the Inside Out: A Path Toward Finding and Mobilizing a Community’s Assets. Institute for Policy Research, Northwestern University. The founding text of asset-based community development, and the argument that communities already hold what sustains the work. Book.

Heifetz, R. A. and Linsky, M. (2017). Leadership on the Line: Staying Alive Through the Dangers of Change, revised edition. Harvard Business Review Press. The distinction between technical problems and adaptive challenges, and why the second kind cannot be solved by expertise. Transferring ownership is adaptive work, which is why it resists project management. Book.

blocks.text: On participation and power

items: Arnstein, S. R. (1969). A Ladder of Citizen Participation. Journal of the American Institute of Planners 35(4), 216 to 224. The blunter ancestor of the IAP2 spectrum, running from manipulation through tokenism to citizen control. Worth reading once for the rungs the modern version softens. Journal article. https://doi.org/10.1080/01944366908977225
Block, P. (2018). Community: The Structure of Belonging, 2nd edition. Berrett-Koehler. On belonging, invitation and the commitments that make a community rather than a service population. Book.

Mathie, A. and Cunningham, G. (2003). From clients to citizens: Asset-based community development as a strategy for community-driven development. Development in Practice 13(5), 474 to 486. The clearest short account of what changes when people stop being recipients. Journal article. https://doi.org/10.1080/0961452032000125857

blocks.text: On sustainability and local capacity

items: United States Agency for International Development (2022). Local Capacity Strengthening Policy. The most rigorous public statement of the idea that strengthening local systems, rather than delivering through them, is the point. Written for international development and it transfers directly. Policy document. https://www.usaid.gov/local-faith-and-transformative-partnerships/policy
Heifetz, R. A., Grashow, A. and Linsky, M. (2009). The Practice of Adaptive Leadership. Harvard Business Review Press. The applied companion, with the diagnostic tools. Book.

The best possible pre-work for this skill. Video. https://www.ted.com/talks/ernesto_sirolli_want_to_help_someone_shut_up_and_listen
